Context: what Orthodox theology is and w:
This curriculum teaches the faith of the Orthodox Church from the inside: what she believes, prays and has lived, and where each teaching comes from. This first stage asks the question every later stage depends on: **how does the Church know what she knows?**

**The word.** *Theología* (θεολογία) is Greek for "speaking about God" (*Theós*, God; *lógos*, word). In the Fathers it does not first mean an academic subject. It means knowing God and speaking truly of Him, above all of the Holy Trinity. The Greek curriculum shows how the word is built; here we use it as the Church uses it.

**The answer, in one sentence.** **God makes Himself known, and the Church keeps and hands on that knowledge as one living Tradition**, witnessed by the Scriptures, the councils, the Fathers, the services, the icons and the saints. None of these stands alone. Each is a voice of the same life.

| Witness | What it is | Where in this curriculum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Holy Scripture** | the written word of God, read in the Church | Stage 5 |
| **The ecumenical councils** | the bishops gathered, defining the faith | Stages 7 and 8 |
| **The Fathers** | the saints who taught the faith | Stage 9 |
| **The services** | the Church's prayer, full of doctrine | Stage 6 |
| **Icons and the saints** | the faith seen and lived | Stages 6 and 10 |
| **The canons** | the Church's rule of life | this stage |

**Why begin here.** A person can learn the doctrines one by one and still not know why the Church holds them. Orthodoxy does not answer "the Bible alone", nor "the Church's office alone", nor "my own reason". She answers that **the Holy Spirit keeps the whole Church in the truth**, and that truth is recognised by its agreement with what has always been believed. The lessons ahead take that answer apart and look at each piece.

**Three things to keep in mind:**

1. **Theology is tied to prayer and holiness.** The Fathers did not separate knowing God from loving Him. The next two lessons show why.
2. **The Church is one, in many local churches.** The faith is the same in Constantinople, Moscow, Belgrade, Bucharest, Antioch, Tbilisi, Alexandria and New York. The last lessons of this stage draw that map.
3. **Not everything is dogma.** The Church distinguishes what she has defined from what holy writers have held as opinion. Where Orthodox writers differ, these lessons say so and give each view fairly.

**The shape of the course.** Stages 2 to 4 follow the Creed: God and the Trinity, then Christ, then the Spirit, the Church and the life to come. Then come Scripture, worship, the councils, the Fathers, the spiritual life, and the Church across the world and today.
The theologian is one who prays: theolog:
The most quoted sentence on what a theologian is was written by a monk, about prayer.

**The saying.** In his chapters *On Prayer*, Evagrius of Pontus (about 345–399), a monk of the Egyptian desert, wrote, in paraphrase: **if you are a theologian, you will pray truly; and if you pray truly, you are a theologian.** (This is a paraphrase; the standard English translation is in copyright.) The chapters were preserved in the *Philokalia* under the name of St Nilus of Sinai, and the saying has been repeated by Orthodox teachers ever since.

**What it means.** Theology in this sense is not information about God. It is **knowledge of God that comes from meeting Him**, and the meeting happens in prayer. A person can know a great deal *about* God and not know Him, as one can know facts about a stranger. The theologian, for the Fathers, is the one who knows God as one knows a person: by being with Him.

**Three levels of the word.** The Fathers use "theology" in more than one way, and it helps to keep them apart.

| Sense | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Vision** | the direct knowledge of God in pure prayer, given to the saints. St John the Evangelist, St Gregory of Nazianzus and St Symeon the New Theologian are the three the Church calls **"the Theologian"** |
| **Doctrine** | right teaching about God, especially the Trinity, set out by the Fathers and councils |
| **Study** | the careful work of reading Scripture, the Fathers and the services, which serves the first two |

**The three belong together.** Study without prayer becomes clever talk. Prayer without right doctrine can wander into fantasy. Doctrine is the fence that guards the field where prayer grows.

**Scripture says the same.** Christ says: "And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent" (John 17:3, KJV). Knowing God here is not a thought in the head. It is eternal life.

**The Church's prayer is itself theology.** The great doctrines were first sung before they were defined, and they are still sung every Sunday. Lesson 15 of this stage returns to this.

**Why this matters for the whole course.** Every lesson ahead gives teaching that can be learnt like facts. The Orthodox claim is that it is meant to be prayed. **The test of a doctrine is not only whether it is logical, but whether it leads the person who holds it into communion with God.** The saints are the proof that it does.
Purity of heart: why Gregory says not ev:
If theology is knowledge of God, then something in the knower must change. St Gregory of Nazianzus says plainly what.

**Who.** St Gregory of Nazianzus (about 329–390), bishop and briefly Archbishop of Constantinople, preached five sermons in Constantinople in 380 that the Church calls the **Theological Orations**. For them he is called **St Gregory the Theologian**. His feast is on 25 January, and with St Basil the Great and St John Chrysostom he is honoured as one of the **Three Holy Hierarchs** on 30 January.

**The text** (First Theological Oration, Oration 27, section 3; tr. Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894):

> "Not to every one, my friends, does it belong to philosophize about God; not to every one; the Subject is not so cheap and low; and I will add, not before every audience, nor at all times, nor on all points; but on certain occasions, and before certain persons, and within certain limits."

He goes on: it is permitted "only to those who have been examined, and are passed masters in meditation, and who have been previously purified in soul and body, or at the very least are being purified."

**What he is saying.** Gregory is not barring ordinary believers from thinking about their faith. He is answering men who argued about the Trinity as a pastime, "after the races, or the theatre", as he puts it. **His point is that the knowledge of God is not available to a mind that is distracted and a heart that is impure.** "For the impure to touch the pure is, we may safely say, not safe, just as it is unsafe to fix weak eyes upon the sun's rays."

**The Gospel root.** "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God" (Matthew 5:8, KJV). Purity of heart is the condition of seeing.

**The three stages.** Orthodox spiritual writers describe the path to the knowledge of God in three stages, which Stage 10 will teach in full:

| Stage | Greek | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Purification** | *kátharsis* (κάθαρσις) | the passions are fought and the heart is cleansed through repentance, prayer and the commandments |
| **Illumination** | *phōtismós* (φωτισμός) | the mind (*nous*, νοῦς, the eye of the soul) is enlightened by grace |
| **Deification** | *théōsis* (θέωσις) | union with God by grace |

**The consequence for this course.** It means that **the saints, not the clever, are the Church's surest theologians.** A scholar can map the doctrines; a saint knows the One they describe. That is why later lessons give so much weight to the Fathers' holiness as well as their arguments. And it means that study of this kind is safest when it is joined to the life of the Church: prayer, fasting, confession and the Eucharist.
Revelation: how God makes himself known:
Theology begins not with human searching but with God's self-showing. The word for this is **revelation**.

**The Greek.** *Apokálypsis* (ἀποκάλυψις), "uncovering". God uncovers what we could not reach by ourselves: who He is, what He has done, what He wills for us.

**Why revelation is needed.** God is the Creator; we are creatures. **No created mind can climb up to the uncreated God by its own power.** We can know from creation that He exists and is powerful (Stage 2 shows how), but who He is, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and what His love has done, we know only because He has shown us.

**How God has revealed Himself.** The Church reads the history of revelation as one story:

| Moment | How God makes Himself known |
| --- | --- |
| **Creation** | the world itself speaks of its Maker |
| **The patriarchs and Moses** | God calls Abraham, speaks to Moses at the burning bush, gives the Law |
| **The prophets** | God speaks through Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the rest, preparing for the Messiah |
| **Jesus Christ** | God the Son becomes man. This is **the fullness of revelation**: "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (John 14:9, KJV) |
| **Pentecost** | the Holy Spirit descends on the apostles and makes the Church |

**Christ is the revelation, not just its messenger.** A prophet brings a word from God. Christ *is* the Word of God (John 1:1). The Orthodox teaching is that **in Christ revelation is complete**. Nothing new about God remains to be added after the apostles. What grows is the Church's understanding and expression of what was given once (Lesson 14).

**The Spirit keeps it alive.** Christ promised that the Spirit "will guide you into all truth" (John 16:13, KJV). This is why revelation does not become a dead deposit. The Holy Spirit, living in the Church, makes the same truth present and known in every generation.

**Revelation and experience.** Orthodox writers stress that revelation is not only a set of true statements. **It is God giving Himself to be known**, and the statements guard that gift. The prophets saw; the apostles touched and heard; the saints have known God in prayer. The Church's doctrine is the faithful description of that knowledge.

**Public and private revelation.** The Church distinguishes the revelation given once for all in Christ and handed down by the apostles from the visions and gifts given to individual saints. Saints' experiences confirm and illuminate the faith; they never add to it or change it. A vision that contradicted the faith would, by that fact, be judged false.

**The next lesson** asks how what was revealed has come down to us: by **Tradition**.
Holy Tradition: what is handed down:
In Orthodox teaching, Tradition is not one source of the faith beside others. It is the whole life of the Church in which every source lives.

**The word.** *Parádosis* (παράδοσις), "handing over" or "handing down". The Latin is *traditio*. It describes an act: something received and passed on, from Christ to the apostles, from the apostles to the Church, and on to each generation.

**Scripture uses the word itself.** St Paul writes: "Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle" (2 Thessalonians 2:15, KJV). There are two channels here, **by word** and **by letter**, and both are to be held.

**What Tradition contains.** It is easier to list than to define:

| Part | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Holy Scripture** | the Old and New Testaments, the heart of Tradition |
| **The Creed** | the Symbol of Faith of Nicaea and Constantinople |
| **The definitions of the councils** | Chalcedon on Christ, Nicaea II on icons |
| **The writings of the Fathers** | Athanasius, Basil, Chrysostom, Maximus and many more |
| **The services** | the Liturgy, the hymns of the feasts, the prayers of the Mysteries |
| **The canons** | the Church's rules of order and discipline |
| **Icons and the church building** | the faith in image and space |
| **The lives of the saints** | the faith lived out |

**Tradition is living, not antique.** Fr Georges Florovsky (1893–1979) and Vladimir Lossky (1903–1958), two of the most influential Orthodox theologians of the twentieth century, both stressed this. Lossky described Tradition as **the life of the Holy Spirit in the Church**: not the content handed on, but the Spirit who makes the content understood. On that view Tradition is not a museum; it is the Church remembering, in the Spirit, what she has always known.

**Tradition and traditions.** Orthodox teachers distinguish **holy Tradition** (with a capital, the faith itself) from the many **local customs** that grow up around it: a particular way of decorating eggs at Pascha, the cut of a priest's vestments, a regional melody. Customs can be loved and still change. Tradition cannot. Telling the two apart is a matter of discernment, and Orthodox writers do not always draw the line in the same place: some are quicker to treat inherited practice as part of the deposit, others quicker to treat it as custom.

**Tradition is not opposed to Scripture.** It is the setting in which Scripture was written, gathered and read. The next lesson shows how.

**The key sentence.** **The Orthodox Church does not hold "Scripture and Tradition" as two sources; she holds one Tradition, with Scripture at its heart.**
Scripture within Tradition:
The Bible is the highest written witness of the Church's faith. Orthodox teaching places it inside the Church's life, not above or outside it.

**The Church came first, in time.** The Church existed from Pentecost. The New Testament books were written within her over the following decades, by apostles and their companions, for churches that were already worshipping. They were gathered, read in the Liturgy and recognised as Scripture by the same Church. **The Scriptures are the Church's book.**

**The canon.** *Kanṓn* (κανών), "measuring rod", is the list of books the Church receives as Scripture. The Church came to recognise the New Testament canon over the first centuries; the earliest surviving list of exactly the twenty-seven books is in St Athanasius' Festal Letter of 367. The Orthodox Old Testament follows the **Septuagint**, the Greek translation used by the apostles, and includes books the Protestant Bible does not, such as Wisdom, Sirach and the books of Maccabees. Stage 5 teaches the canon in full.

**Scripture is inspired.** The Church teaches that the Scriptures are **inspired by God** (*theópneustos*, θεόπνευστος, "God-breathed", 2 Timothy 3:16). The human writers were not dictation machines: each wrote in his own language, style and setting. But the Holy Spirit spoke through them, so that what they wrote is the word of God.

**Why interpretation needs the Church.** The words of Scripture can be bent in many directions; St Vincent of Lérins makes exactly this point in the reading lesson of this stage. The same Spirit who inspired the Scriptures lives in the Church, and **the Scriptures are rightly understood within the faith from which they came**. That is why Orthodox Christians read the Bible with the Fathers, with the Creed, and above all in the services, where the Church sets each passage beside its feast and hymns.

**The Church as guardian.** St Paul calls the Church "the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth" (1 Timothy 3:15, KJV). The Church does not stand over Scripture as its judge. She stands under it as its servant and around it as its home.

**Where Scripture stands in worship.**

| Sign | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **The Gospel book on the altar** | it rests on the Holy Table, in the place of honour |
| **The Little Entrance** | it is carried in procession at the Divine Liturgy |
| **The readings** | the Epistle and Gospel are read at every Liturgy, by a lectionary through the year |
| **The Psalter** | all 150 psalms are read through every week in the monastic cycle |

**A short way to put it.** **Scripture is the summit of Tradition, and Tradition is the life in which Scripture is read.** To pit one against the other is, in Orthodox eyes, to cut a living body in two.
Faith and reason: theology and philosoph:
Orthodox theology uses reason, and the Fathers knew the philosophers well. But reason serves revelation; it does not judge it.

**The Fathers were educated men.** St Basil and St Gregory of Nazianzus studied in Athens, the university city of the Greek world. St Gregory of Nyssa and St Maximus the Confessor wrote with the full equipment of Greek philosophy. **They took words from the philosophers, such as *ousía* (essence) and *hypóstasis* (person), and filled them with new meaning to speak of the Trinity.** Stage 2 shows how.

**Philosophy as handmaid.** The Fathers used philosophy as a tool for clear thinking, to define terms, to answer objections and to show that the faith is not irrational. But they refused to let it decide what God could or could not be. Where Plato or Aristotle conflicted with revelation, as on the eternity of the world or the souls of men existing before birth, the Fathers held to revelation.

**The limits of reason.** Reason works on what it can grasp. **God's essence is beyond all grasping** (Stage 2 teaches this as *apophatic* theology). So reason can clear away errors and show what does not follow, but it cannot comprehend God. The Fathers liked to say that a God who could be fully understood would not be God.

**Faith is not the enemy of thought.** Orthodox faith (*pístis*, πίστις) is trust in God who reveals Himself, and this trust opens the mind rather than closing it. The Fathers argued with great care because they believed truth matters. But they argued from faith, not towards it.

**The danger the Fathers saw.** The great heresies of the early Church were often attempts to make the faith fit a philosophical system: Arius wanted a God who could not share His being; others wanted a Christ who was not truly human because matter seemed unworthy of God. **The councils defended the mystery against systems that made it tidier and smaller.**

| Reason can | Reason cannot |
| --- | --- |
| show that God exists, from creation | show that God is a Trinity |
| make terms precise | comprehend the divine essence |
| expose contradictions in false teaching | replace prayer, purification and grace |
| order and explain doctrine | create new doctrine |

**Different emphases among Orthodox writers.** Orthodox thinkers agree on the primacy of revelation but differ in how warmly they treat philosophy. Some, like Fr John Romanides (1927–2001), set the Fathers' experience of God sharply against speculative philosophy. Others, like Fr Dumitru Stăniloae (1903–1993) and Christos Yannaras (1935–2024), engage philosophy at length and see it as a partner in thought.

**Point across.** The **Philosophy** curriculum treats the same thinkers, Justin, Clement, Origen, the Cappadocians, Dionysius, Maximus and Palamas, as arguments to weigh. Here they are teachers of the Church.
The seven ecumenical councils as witness:
When the faith was challenged in ways that touched its heart, the Church gathered her bishops and spoke. The great gatherings received by the whole Church are the **ecumenical councils**.

**The words.** *Oikouménē* (οἰκουμένη) means "the inhabited world", the whole empire and beyond. An **ecumenical council** is a council of the whole Church. *Sýnodos* (σύνοδος), "a coming together", is the Greek word for council.

**The pattern goes back to the apostles.** In Acts 15 the apostles and elders met in Jerusalem about whether Gentile converts must keep the Law of Moses. Their letter begins: "For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us" (Acts 15:28, KJV). **That phrase is the model of every council: the Spirit and the bishops together.**

**The seven councils the Church receives as ecumenical:**

| Council | Year | What it taught |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nicaea I** | 325 | the Son is *homooúsios*, of one essence with the Father, against Arius; the first part of the Creed |
| **Constantinople I** | 381 | the full divinity of the Holy Spirit; the Creed completed |
| **Ephesus** | 431 | Christ is one person, and Mary is *Theotókos*, Mother of God, against Nestorius |
| **Chalcedon** | 451 | Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human |
| **Constantinople II** | 553 | the one person of Christ is God the Word; confirms Chalcedon in Cyril's terms |
| **Constantinople III** | 680–681 | Christ has two wills, divine and human, against Monothelitism |
| **Nicaea II** | 787 | the veneration of holy icons, against Iconoclasm |

**What a council does.** A council does not invent a doctrine. **It states what the Church has always believed, in words that shut out a particular error.** Nicaea did not discover that the Son is God; it chose the word *homoousios* because Arius' followers could agree to every looser phrase.

**Dogma and canons.** Councils issued two kinds of decision. A **definition** (*hóros*, ὅρος) of faith states doctrine and does not change. **Canons** regulate order and discipline, and the Church applies them with pastoral judgement (Lesson 17).

**More than seven?** All Orthodox receive the seven. Some Orthodox writers also hold that the **Council of Constantinople of 879–880**, under St Photios, and the **hesychast councils of 1341–1351**, which upheld St Gregory Palamas, have ecumenical authority, and they speak of an eighth and ninth council. Others hold that, whatever the authority of their teaching, which the Church does receive, no council since 787 has been formally recognised as ecumenical by the whole Church. Both views accept the doctrine those councils taught; they differ on the title.

**Stages 7 and 8** tell the history of each council. This lesson's point is simpler: **the councils are one of the chief ways the Church knows and says what she believes.**
Reception: how a council is known to be:
Not every large council of bishops was received by the Church. The history shows that a council's authority is confirmed by the Church's recognising its teaching as her own.

**The puzzle.** Several councils called themselves ecumenical, were summoned by emperors and attended by many bishops, and were later rejected. So what makes a council truly ecumenical?

**Councils the Church rejected:**

| Council | Year | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The "Robber Council" of Ephesus** | 449 | it upheld Eutyches' confused teaching on Christ by force; Pope Leo called it a *latrocinium*, a band of robbers; Chalcedon (451) overturned it |
| **Hieria** | 754 | over three hundred bishops condemned icons and called their council ecumenical; Nicaea II (787) rejected it |
| **Ferrara–Florence** | 1438–1439 | most of the Greek delegation signed a union with Rome; on their return clergy and people refused it. St Mark of Ephesus alone did not sign, and the Church honours him for it. A council in Constantinople in 1484 formally rejected the union |

**No single external test.** Numbers, imperial summons and representation of the great sees were all present at councils that failed. **No outward sign alone guarantees a council.**

**Reception.** Orthodox theologians call what happened next **reception**: the whole Church, bishops, clergy, monks and people, over time recognising a council's teaching as the apostolic faith, or refusing it. Nicaea I itself was fiercely disputed for over fifty years after 325 and was secured only at Constantinople in 381.

**How Orthodox writers explain it.** There are two emphases, both held within the Church:

1. **The council's own truth.** A true council is ecumenical because the Holy Spirit leads it to state the truth. Reception does not *make* it true; it *recognises* that it is. On this view the council's authority is present from the moment it speaks rightly, and reception is the Church's "amen".
2. **Reception as part of the process.** Others stress that the Church's acceptance is itself the sign by which we know the Spirit was at work, so that a council's ecumenical standing is fully established only as the Church receives it. Both views reject the idea that the people vote on doctrine.

**The 1848 encyclical.** In 1848 the Eastern Patriarchs, writing to Pope Pius IX, stated the principle that among the Orthodox neither patriarchs nor councils could introduce novelty, because **the guardian of the faith is the whole body of the Church, the people themselves** (a paraphrase of the encyclical's well-known sentence). Lesson 20 returns to it.

**The point.** **A council's authority rests on its faithfulness to the Tradition, recognised by the whole Church in the Spirit**, not on any single office or procedure.
Who counts as a Father of the Church:
The Fathers are the third great witness after Scripture and the councils. But "Father" is not an office with a fixed list.

**The term.** In the early Church a bishop was called "father" by his flock. Over time **"the Fathers"** came to mean the holy teachers whose writings the Church recognises as faithful witnesses to the apostolic faith. The study of them is **patristics** (from Latin *pater*); the Greek is *patérēs* (πατέρες).

**No closed list, and no closing date.** Some Western handbooks end the age of the Fathers with St John of Damascus (died about 750). Orthodox teaching does not. **The Church holds that the age of the Fathers has not closed**, because the same Spirit still raises up saints who teach the same faith. St Symeon the New Theologian (949–1022), St Gregory Palamas (1296–1359) and St Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain (1749–1809) are all read as Fathers.

**What makes a Father.** Orthodox writers usually name four marks:

| Mark | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Orthodoxy of teaching** | his teaching agrees with the faith of the Church |
| **Holiness of life** | he is a saint, or his life bore the fruit of the Spirit |
| **The Church's recognition** | the Church reads him, quotes him and honours him |
| **Antiquity**, in a loose sense | he stands in the line of witnesses; but this mark is the least strict |

**Some of the Fathers by region:**

| Region | Fathers |
| --- | --- |
| **Asia Minor and Constantinople** | Ignatius (of Antioch, martyred in Rome), Basil, Gregory the Theologian, Gregory of Nyssa, John Chrysostom, Maximus the Confessor |
| **Alexandria and Egypt** | Athanasius, Cyril of Alexandria, Anthony the Great and the desert fathers |
| **Syria and Palestine** | Ephrem the Syrian, John of Damascus, Isaac the Syrian |
| **The Latin West** | Irenaeus (of Lyons), Hilary of Poitiers, Ambrose, Augustine, Leo the Great, Gregory the Great |
| **The later East** | Symeon the New Theologian, Gregory Palamas, Nicholas Cabasilas, Mark of Ephesus |

**Fathers can err on single points.** A Father is not infallible. St Gregory of Nyssa speculated that all might in the end be saved; Orthodox writers differ on how to read him, but the Church has never adopted the view as her teaching. **The authority of the Fathers lies in what they hold in common**, which is the subject of the next lesson.

**Mothers too.** The Church honours holy women teachers as well, such as St Macrina the Younger (about 327–379), sister of Basil and Gregory, whom Gregory of Nyssa called "the Teacher", and the desert mothers whose sayings were collected with the fathers'.

**Stage 9** reads twelve of the Fathers in their own words.
The consensus of the Fathers:
One Father can be mistaken. What the Fathers teach together is a sure witness to the faith. This is called the consensus of the Fathers.

**The Latin phrase.** *Consensus patrum*, "the agreement of the Fathers". The Greek idea is close to *homonoia* (ὁμόνοια), "one-mindedness".

**What it means.** **Where the Fathers, in different times and places, teach the same thing as the faith of the Church, that agreement is a reliable witness to the apostolic Tradition.** It is the same principle by which Scripture is read in the Church: not by one private voice, but by the voice of the whole.

**What it does not mean.** It does not mean that every Father said the same thing about every question, or that the opinion of the majority wins a vote. On many questions the Fathers held different views, and the Church has left those questions open.

**The Councils appeal to it.** The Definition of Chalcedon (451) begins: **"Following the holy Fathers we teach with one voice..."** (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900). The councils did not see themselves as innovating. They stated what the Fathers before them had taught.

**How a consensus is recognised.** There is no counting machine. Orthodox teachers point to signs like these:

| Sign | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Received by a council** | Cyril's letters were accepted at Ephesus and Chalcedon |
| **Taught across regions** | Greek, Syriac and Latin Fathers teaching the same point |
| **Prayed in the services** | a teaching that has entered the hymns of the Church |
| **Lived by the saints** | the teaching bearing fruit in holiness |

**Florovsky's phrase.** Fr Georges Florovsky called the Church to a **"neo-patristic synthesis"**: to think with the "mind of the Fathers", not only to quote them. **On this view, following the Fathers means acquiring their way of seeing, which comes from the same life in the Spirit, not just repeating their sentences.** Stage 12 teaches Florovsky in full.

**A reasonable caution.** Orthodox writers differ on how far the consensus extends. Some treat it as covering a wide range of patristic teaching, including much spiritual and moral counsel. Others confine it more narrowly to the doctrines the councils defined and the teaching universally received, and treat much else as respected opinion. Both agree that the consensus is a real authority and that no single Father outweighs it.

**Next comes the classic text** on this question, written in 434 by a monk in southern Gaul.
Reading: St Vincent of Lérins on what ha:
The most famous rule for telling the true faith from novelty, read closely.

**Who.** St Vincent of Lérins (died about 445) was a monk of the island monastery of Lérins, off the south coast of Gaul, near modern Cannes. In 434 he wrote the *Commonitorium*, a "reminder" for his own use, under the pen-name Peregrinus, "the pilgrim". The Orthodox Church commemorates him on 24 May.

**The text** (*Commonitorium*, chapter 2, sections 5–6; tr. C. A. Heurtley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894):

> "Since the canon of Scripture is complete, and sufficient of itself for everything, and more than sufficient, what need is there to join with it the authority of the Church's interpretation? For this reason — because, owing to the depth of Holy Scripture, all do not accept it in one and the same sense, but one understands its words in one way, another in another; so that it seems to be capable of as many interpretations as there are interpreters."

> "Moreover, in the Catholic Church itself, all possible care must be taken, that we hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"the canon of Scripture is complete"** | Vincent does not doubt Scripture's sufficiency; he asks how it is to be rightly read |
| **"as many interpretations as there are interpreters"** | he then names heretics from Novatian to Nestorius, each quoting Scripture |
| **"the Catholic Church"** | *catholic* (καθολικός) means "according to the whole": the whole Church, not one region or party |
| **"everywhere, always, by all"** | the rule in three words: *ubique, semper, ab omnibus* |

**The three tests.** Vincent names them at once: **universality, antiquity, consent.**

1. **Universality**: the faith "which the whole Church throughout the world confesses".
2. **Antiquity**: not departing from the interpretations "held by our holy ancestors and fathers".
3. **Consent**: within antiquity, holding to "the consentient definitions and determinations of all, or at the least of almost all priests and doctors".

**How the tests work together.** In the following chapters Vincent shows they back each other up. If a new error spreads widely, appeal to antiquity. If an old error appears in one corner, appeal to universality and consent: what an ancient council decided, or what the Fathers taught together.

**Why it matters for the Orthodox.** **This is the rule the Orthodox Church still lives by: truth is what agrees with the faith of the whole Church in all ages.** It is not a new rule invented by Vincent; he says he received it from many holy and learned men.
Growth without change: St Vincent on dev:
If the faith never changes, does the Church's understanding never grow? St Vincent answers in the same book.

**The question.** In chapter 23 of the *Commonitorium* Vincent asks: "Shall there, then, be no progress in Christ's Church?" His answer (tr. C. A. Heurtley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894):

> "Certainly; all possible progress. ... Yet on condition that it be real progress, not alteration of the faith. For progress requires that the subject be enlarged [i]n itself, alteration, that it be transformed into something else."

**The image of the body.** Vincent compares the faith to a person growing up: "An infant's limbs are small, a young man's large, yet the infant and the young man are the same." **The growth he allows is growth in the same doctrine, "in the same sense, and in the same meaning."**

**What this means in practice.** The Church's understanding grows chiefly in three ways:

| Kind of growth | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **New words for old truth** | *homoousios* at Nicaea (325); *Theotokos* at Ephesus (431) |
| **Clearer distinctions** | "one essence, three persons" made precise by the Cappadocians in the 370s |
| **Answers to new questions** | the two wills of Christ (681); the veneration of icons (787); the uncreated energies (1340s) |

In each case the Church held that she was saying what she had always believed, in words that shut out a new error.

**What Vincent rules out.** **A doctrine that contradicts what was believed before, or adds something foreign to it, is alteration, not growth.** The Orthodox Church applies this test strictly. It is one reason she has not accepted later Western definitions that she sees as additions, such as the addition of the *filioque* to the Creed (Stage 2 explains the issue briefly).

**Orthodox writers on "development".** Some Orthodox theologians are wary of the word *development* itself, because in the nineteenth century it came to suggest that later teaching could unfold things the early Church did not know. They prefer to speak of **the same faith expressed more fully** as heresies forced the Church to speak. Others are comfortable with Vincent's word *progress* as long as it means only what he means. Both positions hold that the content of the faith does not change.

**A sentence to remember.** **The Church's speech about the faith grows; the faith itself does not change.** A council adds no new truth; it adds a new fence around the old one.
The services as theology: the rule of pr:
The Orthodox Church teaches her doctrine most fully not in textbooks but in her worship. Her services are a great body of sung theology.

**The principle.** A fifth-century writer, Prosper of Aquitaine, argued that the Church's prayer establishes her belief. His phrase, shortened in Latin to ***lex orandi, lex credendi***, means in paraphrase that **the rule of prayer sets the rule of belief**. The Orthodox Church lives by the same principle without needing the Latin tag: what the Church prays is what she believes.

**Doctrine was prayed before it was defined.** Christians baptised "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 28:19, KJV) long before the councils defined the Trinity. They worshipped Christ as God before Nicaea said *homoousios*. They called Mary *Theotokos* in prayer before Ephesus. **The councils defended what the Church already prayed.**

**What the services contain.** The Orthodox services are vast. Some of the books:

| Book | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| **The Horologion** | the fixed parts of the daily services, the Hours |
| **The Octoechos** | hymns in eight tones (*ēchos*, ἦχος), sung in an eight-week cycle |
| **The Menaion** | the hymns for each fixed feast and saint, one volume for each month |
| **The Triodion** | the services of Great Lent and the weeks before it |
| **The Pentecostarion** | from Pascha to the Sunday after Pentecost |
| **The Typikon** | (*Typikón*, Τυπικόν) the rule that tells how to combine them all |

**Theology in the hymns.** The Sunday hymns of the Octoechos set out the Resurrection in every tone. The *Dogmatika*, hymns to the Theotokos at Saturday evening Vespers, state the doctrine of the Incarnation in verse. The hymns of Nativity and Theophany teach Christology and the Trinity line by line. Much of this hymnography was written by Fathers: St Romanos the Melodist, St Andrew of Crete, St John of Damascus, St Theodore the Studite.

**How to use the services as a source.** Orthodox teachers give two cautions:

1. **The central texts weigh more than the margins.** The Creed, the anaphora of the Liturgy and the hymns of the great feasts carry the Church's whole authority. A line in a little-used canon to a local saint carries less.
2. **Poetry is poetry.** Hymns use images and exclamations. They are read as the Church reads them, not pressed for technical definitions.

**Why it matters.** **Every Orthodox Christian who attends the services is taught theology every week, whether he notices or not.** Stage 6 walks through the services themselves.
Icons and the lives of the saints as wit:
The faith is not only spoken and sung. The Church also shows it in images and lives it in her saints, and both are witnesses to what she believes.

**Icons as theology.** *Eikṓn* (εἰκών) means "image". The Orthodox Church calls icons **theology in line and colour**. An icon of the Nativity shows the doctrine of the Incarnation; an icon of the Resurrection, Christ raising Adam and Eve from Hades, shows what Christ's death and rising achieved. Icon painters follow the Church's patterns closely, so that the image teaches what the Church teaches.

**Why icons are possible at all.** The Seventh Ecumenical Council (Nicaea II, 787) defended icons on Christological grounds: **because God the Word became man and was seen, He can be depicted.** The honour given to an icon passes to the person shown. The Church celebrates this victory every year on the first Sunday of Great Lent, the **Sunday of Orthodoxy**, which recalls the restoration of icons in 843. Stage 6 and Stage 8 teach icons in full.

**The saints as witnesses.** A saint (*hágios*, ἅγιος, "holy one") is someone in whom the Holy Spirit has borne visible fruit. **The lives of the saints are the faith in action**, and the Church reads them in her services and her homes.

| Kind of saint | What their witness shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Martyrs** | that Christ is worth more than life itself |
| **Confessors** | that the faith is kept under persecution without death |
| **Hierarchs** | the faith taught and defended by bishops |
| **Monastics** | the Gospel lived to the full |
| **Holy fools** | that the world's wisdom is folly before God |
| **New martyrs** | the same witness in modern times, under the Ottomans and the Soviet state |

**The saints confirm doctrine.** When a teaching produces saints, the Church sees its truth confirmed. **St Gregory Palamas was defended not only by argument but by the holiness of the monks whose experience he described.** When a teaching produces pride, division and despair, the Church is suspicious of it.

**Relics and the bodies of saints.** The Church honours the relics of saints, because the body of a saint was a temple of the Holy Spirit. Their veneration also teaches the resurrection of the body (Stage 4).

**Glorification.** The Orthodox Church does not make saints; she **recognises** them. The process, called glorification, usually follows long popular veneration, the testimony of a holy life, and often miracles, after which a synod of bishops adds the saint to the calendar and composes services. Local practice differs between churches, but the principle is the same everywhere: the Church glorifies those whom God has already glorified.
The holy canons: akriveia and oikonomia:
Alongside her dogma the Church has a body of law for her life and order. Applying it requires both strictness and mercy.

**The word.** *Kanṓn* (κανών), "rule" or "measuring rod", is the same word used for the canon of Scripture. The **holy canons** are the rules of church order and discipline issued by the apostles' tradition, the ecumenical and local councils, and certain Fathers.

**Where they come from.** The main body, received in the East, includes:

| Source | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **The Apostolic Canons** | 85 canons, ancient, attributed to the apostles |
| **The ecumenical councils** | e.g. Nicaea I on the date of Pascha and the order of the great sees |
| **The Council in Trullo** (692) | also called the Quinisext, it issued the canons that the fifth and sixth councils had not; the East counts them as ecumenical |
| **Local councils** | Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Carthage and others, received by the whole Church |
| **Canonical letters of the Fathers** | Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, Athanasius and others |

**The Rudder.** The best-known Greek collection with commentary is the ***Pedalion*** (Πηδάλιον, "The Rudder"), prepared by St Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain and Hieromonk Agapios and published in 1800. Russian and Serbian churches use their own collections, including the Slavonic *Kormchaya Kniga*, also "the pilot's book".

**Canons are not dogma.** A dogma states unchanging truth. **A canon applies that truth to the Church's life, and it serves the salvation of persons.** Some canons are no longer kept literally because the situation they addressed no longer exists, and the Church may apply them differently today.

**Akriveia and oikonomia.** Two Greek words guide how canons are applied:

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| ***Akríveia*** (ἀκρίβεια) | "exactness": applying the rule strictly, as written |
| ***Oikonomía*** (οἰκονομία) | "household management": applying it with pastoral flexibility for a person's salvation |

A bishop or confessor may use *oikonomia* to relax a penance for someone in weakness, or to receive a convert in a certain way. **Oikonomia does not change the rule; it bends its application for love, in a particular case.**

**Where Orthodox differ.** The use of *oikonomia* is one of the live questions among Orthodox churches. Some apply it widely, for example in receiving converts from other Christian bodies by chrismation rather than baptism, or in second marriages. Others hold that it has been stretched too far and call for more *akriveia*, especially some monasteries of Mount Athos and the Old Calendarist communities. Both sides appeal to the canons and the Fathers. Stage 11 returns to this.

**The aim.** The canons exist **to heal**, not to punish. St Basil and the Fathers treated penances as medicine, with the confessor as physician.
Dogma, theologoumenon and private opinio:
Not every teaching found among Orthodox writers has the same weight. The Church distinguishes three levels, and knowing them prevents both rigidity and looseness.

**The three levels:**

| Level | Greek | What it is | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Dogma** | *dógma* (δόγμα), "what seemed good", a decision | teaching the whole Church holds as revealed truth, usually defined by a council or universally received | the Trinity; Christ one person in two natures; the Theotokos; the resurrection of the body |
| **Theologoumenon** | *theologoúmenon* (θεολογούμενον), "something theologised" | a theological opinion held by a Father or by many writers, compatible with dogma but not defined | the exact order of the angelic ranks; how the soul is united to the body |
| **Private opinion** | — | the view of an individual writer, not widely received | a speculation by one modern author |

**Dogma is not dry.** In Orthodox use *dogma* is not a rule imposed from above. **It is a fence around a mystery**: it says what must not be denied, so that the Church can go on living in the truth. The Creed is the first and greatest statement of dogma.

**Why the distinction matters.** If every opinion is treated as dogma, Orthodox Christians end up condemning one another over questions the Church has left open. If dogma is treated as opinion, the faith dissolves. **The Church binds where she has bound, and leaves free where she has left free.** The often-repeated maxim, of uncertain origin, is: in essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity.

**Disputed examples.** Some questions are held differently by Orthodox writers. These lessons will flag them as they come. Two examples:

1. **The toll-houses** (*telōnia*, τελώνια): the teaching that the soul after death passes demonic "customs posts". Some Orthodox teachers, such as St Ignatius Brianchaninov in the nineteenth century and Fr Seraphim Rose in the twentieth, held it to be the Church's teaching, found in many Fathers and services. Others, such as Archbishop Lazar Puhalo, have argued it is a later image, not dogma, and must not be taken literally. Stage 4 presents both.
2. **The details of the "last things"**: the Church holds as dogma the resurrection, the judgement and life everlasting. Much about the state of souls before the resurrection is less defined.

**How to tell which is which.** Ask: **Has a council defined it? Is it in the Creed or the central services? Have the Fathers taught it with one voice?** If yes, it is dogma. If it rests on some Fathers and is widely held but undefined, it is a theologoumenon. If it rests on one modern writer, it is an opinion, however attractive.

**A note of humility.** Even theologoumena carry weight when they come from great saints. The distinction is not a license to dismiss them, but a way to hold each teaching at its proper weight.
Bishops and apostolic succession: Ignati:
The Church keeps the apostolic faith not as a library but as a living community with an order. At the centre of that order stands the bishop.

**The three orders.** From very early, the Church has had three ordained orders:

| Order | Greek | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Bishop** | *epískopos* (ἐπίσκοπος), "overseer" | head of the local church, guardian of the faith, presides at the Eucharist |
| **Priest** | *presbýteros* (πρεσβύτερος), "elder" | celebrates the Mysteries under the bishop |
| **Deacon** | *diákonos* (διάκονος), "servant" | assists at the Liturgy and serves the community |

**St Ignatius of Antioch.** Bishop of Antioch, martyred in Rome early in the second century (about 107–110), he wrote seven letters on his way to death. To the Christians of Smyrna he wrote (Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 8; tr. Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885):

> "Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church."

**This is the earliest surviving use of the phrase "Catholic Church".** For Ignatius the local church gathered around its bishop at the Eucharist is the whole Church in that place.

**St Irenaeus of Lyons.** Born in Asia Minor, a hearer of St Polycarp, who had known the apostle John, Irenaeus (about 130–about 202) became bishop of Lyons in Gaul. Against the Gnostics, who claimed secret teachings handed down privately, he wrote (*Against Heresies* 3.3.1; tr. Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885):

> "It is within the power of all, therefore, in every Church, who may wish to see the truth, to contemplate clearly the tradition of the apostles manifested throughout the whole world; and we are in a position to reckon up those who were by the apostles instituted bishops in the Churches..."

**What succession means.** **Apostolic succession is the unbroken line of bishops from the apostles, and it guards the unbroken faith.** Irenaeus's argument is public: if the apostles had had secret teachings, they would have given them to the bishops they appointed, and those bishops taught nothing like the Gnostics.

**Succession and faith go together.** In Orthodox teaching, succession is not a mechanical chain of hands. **A bishop who abandons the Orthodox faith loses the authority his succession was meant to guard.** The Church therefore looks for both: the line of ordination, and faithfulness to what was handed down.

**Conciliarity.** No bishop rules the Church alone. Bishops of a region meet in synod, and the whole Church acts through councils. The Russian word ***sobornost*** (соборность), from *sobor*, "council" or "gathering", was used by nineteenth-century Russian writers, especially Alexei Khomiakov, for this quality of the Church: unity in freedom and love, the many acting as one. Stage 4 develops it.
The mind of the Church: phronema and the:
Councils, Fathers and bishops all speak for something they share with every faithful member of the Church: a common mind.

**The word.** *Phrónēma* (φρόνημα), "mind" or "outlook". Orthodox writers speak of the **"mind of the Church"** or the **"Orthodox phronema"**: the way of thinking, praying and judging that comes from living within the Church's Tradition. St Paul writes: "But we have the mind of Christ" (1 Corinthians 2:16, KJV), and the Church understands this mind as given to the whole body.

**Every member shares in it.** At baptism and chrismation each Christian receives the Holy Spirit. **The Church teaches that the whole people of God, not the clergy alone, are bearers of the truth.** The bishops have a special responsibility to teach and to judge, but they do so as members of the body, not as owners of the faith.

**The 1848 encyclical.** The Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs of 1848, signed by the patriarchs of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem and their synods, said in effect (here paraphrased) that **the guardian of the true faith is the whole body of the Church, the people themselves**, who want their faith kept unchanged. Orthodox writers often cite this as a classic statement of the principle.

**Examples from history:**

| When | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **The Arian crisis, 4th century** | many bishops wavered; monks and laypeople in Alexandria and elsewhere held to Nicaea with St Athanasius |
| **Iconoclasm, 8th–9th centuries** | emperors and many bishops attacked icons; monks such as St Theodore the Studite and lay people kept venerating them |
| **Florence, 15th century** | delegates signed a union; clergy, monks and people refused it |

**How the phronema is formed.** No one acquires the mind of the Church by reading alone. It grows from **the Eucharist, the services, prayer, fasting, confession, obedience to a spiritual father, and reading the Scriptures and the Fathers**. This is why converts are often told to "go slowly": the mind is formed by living, not by argument.

**A guard against two errors.** The mind of the Church guards against **private judgement** on the one side, where each person decides doctrine for himself, and against **mere authority** on the other, where truth is whatever an office says. **The truth is held by the whole Church, in the Spirit, with the bishops as its appointed witnesses.**

**Where it can be misused.** Orthodox teachers warn that "the mind of the Church" can be invoked to dress up one's own preferences. The test is always the same as St Vincent's: agreement with what has been believed everywhere, always and by all, and with the Scriptures, councils and Fathers.
The Church in one map: the patriarchates:
The Orthodox Church is one Church, made of self-governing local churches in communion with each other. This lesson draws the map.

**Autocephaly.** *Autokephalía* (αὐτοκεφαλία), "being one's own head". An **autocephalous** church elects its own primate and governs itself, while sharing one faith and one communion with the others. An **autonomous** church governs most of its affairs but its primate is confirmed by a mother church.

**The ancient patriarchates.** The early Church recognised great sees in order of honour; Rome was first until the break between East and West (Stage 8). The four ancient Eastern patriarchates remain:

| Church | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Constantinople** (the Ecumenical Patriarchate) | first in honour among the Orthodox; seat in Istanbul; also oversees churches in the diaspora, Crete, the Dodecanese and Mount Athos |
| **Alexandria** | Patriarch "of Alexandria and all Africa"; a fast-growing mission in sub-Saharan Africa |
| **Antioch** | seat in Damascus since the fourteenth century; Arabic-speaking; a large diaspora in the Americas |
| **Jerusalem** | guardian of the holy places; includes the autonomous Church of Sinai |

**The other churches**, in the usual order of Constantinople's diptychs (*díptycha*, the list of primates commemorated at the Liturgy):

| Church | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Moscow** (Russia) | patriarchate since 1589; the largest Orthodox church by numbers |
| **Serbia** | autocephalous since St Sava in 1219; a patriarchate, restored in 1920 |
| **Romania** | autocephaly recognised 1885; patriarchate 1925 |
| **Bulgaria** | patriarchate restored 1953 |
| **Georgia** | ancient; its autocephaly was recognised by Constantinople in 1990 |
| **Cyprus** | autocephalous since the Council of Ephesus (431) |
| **Greece** | autocephalous since 1850 |
| **Poland** | 1924 |
| **Albania** | 1937; refounded after communism by Archbishop Anastasios |
| **The Czech Lands and Slovakia** | autocephaly from Moscow 1951; from Constantinople 1998 |

**The order is not identical everywhere.** The Russian Church's diptychs place Georgia higher, after Moscow.

**Two churches whose status is disputed:**

1. **The Orthodox Church in America (OCA)** received autocephaly from Moscow in 1970. Some churches recognise it; Constantinople and several others do not, and treat the Americas as diaspora territory.
2. **The Orthodox Church of Ukraine** received a tomos of autocephaly from Constantinople in January 2019. As of November 2026 a few churches recognise it, and most, including Moscow, do not. Stage 12 sets out each side's case.

**Autonomous churches** include Finland and Estonia (under Constantinople), Sinai (under Jerusalem), and Japan (under Moscow).

**What holds them together.** Not one central office but **one faith, one Eucharist, and conciliar fellowship among bishops.** Stage 11 tells how each of these churches came to be.
Looking back: how the Church knows:
This stage asked how the Orthodox Church knows what she believes. Here is the answer gathered into one place.

**The core.** **God reveals Himself, most fully in Jesus Christ; the Holy Spirit keeps the Church in that truth; and the Church hands it on as one living Tradition.** Every witness to the faith is a voice within that Tradition, not a separate source competing with the others.

**The witnesses, and what each gives:**

| Witness | What it gives | Key text in this stage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Scripture** | the inspired word, the heart of Tradition | 2 Thessalonians 2:15 |
| **Unwritten tradition** | practices and confessions kept by all the churches | Basil, *On the Holy Spirit* 27 |
| **Councils** | definitions that fence the mystery | Acts 15:28; the seven councils |
| **The Fathers** | the faith taught by saints, above all in agreement | Chalcedon's "Following the holy Fathers" |
| **The services** | doctrine prayed and sung | the rule of prayer |
| **Icons and saints** | the faith seen and lived | Nicaea II; the Sunday of Orthodoxy |
| **The canons** | the faith applied to life, with *akriveia* and *oikonomia* | the *Pedalion* |
| **The bishops** | guardians in succession from the apostles | Ignatius; Irenaeus |
| **The whole people** | bearers of the mind of the Church | the 1848 encyclical |

**The test.** St Vincent gave it in 434: **"that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all."** Universality, antiquity and consent together point to the apostolic faith.

**The conditions of knowing.** Theology is knowledge of God, and it is given to those who pray and are being purified. **The saints are the surest theologians.** Gregory the Theologian's warning stands over all study: not before every audience, nor at all times, nor on all points.

**What is fixed and what is open.** Dogma, defined by councils and universally received, binds. Theologoumena carry the weight of the Fathers who held them. Private opinions are only opinions. Where Orthodox writers differ, the Church has left room, and these lessons will set out each view.

**The Church as she stands.** One faith, held by self-governing local churches, from Constantinople and Alexandria to Moscow, Belgrade, Tbilisi and the Americas, in communion through the Eucharist and the councils of bishops. Some questions of status, like the OCA's and Ukraine's, are disputed and will be treated fairly in Stage 12.

**Questions to test yourself:**

1. Why does the Orthodox Church speak of one Tradition rather than "Scripture and Tradition"?
2. What are Vincent's three tests, and how do they support each other?
3. Why were Ephesus 449 and Florence rejected though they called themselves councils?
4. What is the difference between *akriveia* and *oikonomia*?
5. How would you tell a dogma from a theologoumenon?

**Next.** Stage 2 turns to the content of the faith, beginning where the Creed begins: "I believe in one God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906).
Context: the Creed and why the Church sa:
Stages 2 to 4 follow the Creed article by article. This stage covers its first part: the one God, the Holy Trinity, and creation.

**The Creed.** The Orthodox Church calls it the **Symbol of Faith**, from Greek *sýmbolon* (σύμβολον), a token that matches its other half. A *symbolon* was the half of a broken object that proved who you were. **The Creed is the sign by which Orthodox Christians recognise one another's faith.**

**Where it comes from.** Its first part was drawn up at the **First Ecumenical Council, Nicaea, in 325**; it was completed at the **Second, Constantinople, in 381**. It is therefore called the **Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed**. Its text was read out and confirmed at **Chalcedon in 451**, and the Church has said it ever since without change.

**Where it is said.**

| Occasion | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **The Divine Liturgy** | sung or said by all the people before the Eucharistic prayer, after the deacon's call "The Doors! The Doors! Wisdom! Let us attend" (Hapgood's *Service Book*, 1906) |
| **Baptism** | said by the person being baptised, or by the godparent for an infant |
| **Daily prayer** | at the Midnight Office and Small Compline, and in many people's morning prayers |

**"We" and "I".** The councils wrote "We believe" (*Pisteúomen*, Πιστεύομεν), the voice of the bishops confessing together. In the Liturgy and at baptism the Church says **"I believe"** (*Pisteúō*, Πιστεύω): each person confesses the faith of the whole Church as his own.

**Its shape follows the Trinity.**

| Part | Subject | Stage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Article 1** | God the Father, maker of all | this stage |
| **Articles 2–7** | the Son: His divinity, Incarnation, cross, resurrection, ascension and coming again | Stage 3 |
| **Article 8** | the Holy Spirit | Stage 4 |
| **Articles 9–12** | the Church, baptism, the resurrection and the life to come | Stage 4 |

**This stage covers**: faith; the knowledge of God; the one God and the Father; the Trinity and its terms, *ousía* and *hypóstasis*; the Cappadocian Fathers; the procession of the Spirit; how God is known and unknown (apophatic and cataphatic theology); the essence and energies of God; creation from nothing; the angels; and the human person as made in God's image.

**Why the Trinity first.** **The Trinity is not one doctrine among many. It is who God is**, and every other teaching, about Christ, the Church, salvation and prayer, flows from it. Christians are baptised into the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and every service begins and ends by glorifying the Three.

**Point across.** The **Philosophy** curriculum covers the Greek ideas of being and substance (Aristotle, Plotinus) from which the Fathers took their words. The **Greek** curriculum covers the words themselves.
The Symbol of Faith: the text of Nicaea:
Before studying the Creed article by article, read it whole.

**The text** (Creed of the Council of Constantinople, 381; tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900):

> "We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth and of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only begotten Son of God, begotten of his Father before all worlds, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten not made, being of one substance with the Father, by whom all things were made. Who for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven and was incarnate by the Holy Ghost and the Virgin Mary, and was made man, and was crucified also for us under Pontius Pilate. He suffered and was buried, and the third day he rose again according to the Scriptures, and ascended into heaven, and sits at the Right Hand of the Father. And he shall come again with glory to judge both the quick and the dead. Whose kingdom shall have no end."

> "And [we believe] in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and Giver-of-Life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified, who spoke by the prophets. And [we believe] in one, holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church. We acknowledge one Baptism for the remission of sins, [and] we look for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. Amen."

**What Nicaea (325) wrote and Constantinople (381) added.**

| Nicaea 325 | Added or changed in 381 |
| --- | --- |
| the Father, maker of all things visible and invisible | "maker of **heaven and earth**" added |
| the Son "of the substance of the Father", *homoousios* | "begotten **before all worlds**"; the Incarnation "by the Holy Ghost and the Virgin Mary"; "under Pontius Pilate"; "whose kingdom shall have no end" |
| "And in the Holy Ghost" (and no more) | the whole article on the Spirit: **Lord, Giver of life, proceeding from the Father, worshipped and glorified with the Father and Son** |
| anathemas against Arius' phrases | the anathemas dropped; the articles on the Church, baptism and the resurrection added |

**Key terms in the Greek:**

| Phrase | Greek | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **"of one substance"** | *homooúsios* (ὁμοούσιος) | of the same essence as the Father (Lesson 11) |
| **"begotten not made"** | *gennēthénta ou poiēthénta* | the Son is not a creature |
| **"Giver of life"** | *zōopoión* (ζωοποιόν) | the Spirit gives life as only God does |
| **"Catholic"** | *katholikḗn* (καθολικήν) | "according to the whole" |

**One change the Orthodox Church does not accept.** In the West the words "and the Son" (Latin *filioque*) were later added to the article on the Spirit. The Orthodox Church keeps the Creed as the councils left it. Lesson 16 explains the question briefly.

**How to use this text.** **Learn the Creed by heart, in your own church's liturgical translation**, since that is how the Church prays it. The Percival translation above is the councils' text in older English; parish versions differ slightly in wording but not in sense.
Faith: what \"I believe\" means:
The Creed begins with a verb. Before asking what the Church believes, ask what it means to believe.

**The word.** *Pístis* (πίστις) means faith, trust and faithfulness at once. The verb *pisteúō* (πιστεύω) is to trust, to rely on, to believe. **In the Creed, "I believe in" means "I put my trust in", not merely "I hold the opinion that".**

**Two sides of faith.**

| Side | What it is | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Trust** | giving oneself to God as a person | Abraham leaving his country at God's word |
| **Assent** | holding true what God has revealed | confessing the Trinity, the Incarnation, the resurrection |

The two belong together. To trust God and refuse what He reveals is not trust. To assent to doctrines while not trusting God is the faith of which James says "the devils also believe, and tremble" (James 2:19, KJV).

**Faith is a gift and a response.** The Church teaches that faith is **given by God's grace** and **freely accepted by the person**. God does not force belief, and no one comes to faith by his own power alone. This cooperation of grace and freedom, called *synergeia* (συνέργεια), runs through all Orthodox teaching on salvation (Stage 3).

**Faith and knowledge.** St Basil the Great, answering an opponent, said he knew that God exists but held God's essence to be beyond understanding. He asked how, then, he is saved, and answered: "Through faith. It is faith sufficient to know that God exists, without knowing what He is" (Letter 234; tr. Blomfield Jackson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 8, 1895). **Faith does not wait for full comprehension; it trusts the One it cannot comprehend.**

**Faith grows.** In the Orthodox tradition faith begins as trust in what one has heard, and grows through prayer and the commandments into a living knowledge of God. The spiritual writers speak of the faith that comes by hearing and the faith that comes by seeing, the second given to those purified by grace.

**Faith is confessed with the Church.** In the Liturgy the Creed is preceded by this exchange (Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906): the deacon says, "Let us love one another, that with one accord we may confess", and the choir answers, "Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the Trinity, one in Essence and undivided." **Faith in Orthodoxy is personal but never private: each believes with the whole Church.**

**Doubt.** The Fathers did not treat honest struggle as unbelief. The father in Mark 9 who cried "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief" (Mark 9:24, KJV) is the patron of every believer. Orthodox spiritual fathers counsel the doubter to keep praying, keep coming to the services and keep the commandments, because faith is strengthened by living it more than by argument.
Can God be known? Creation, conscience a:
The Fathers teach that God can be known in some ways by everyone, and fully only by His own self-revelation.

**What anyone can know.** St Paul writes: "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead" (Romans 1:20, KJV). **From the order and beauty of the world, the human mind can know that God exists and is powerful and wise.** This is called **natural knowledge of God**.

**The arguments the Fathers used.** St John of Damascus, in his *Exposition of the Orthodox Faith* (Book 1, chapter 3), gives classic arguments: from change (everything changeable must have a cause that does not change), from order (the harmony of the world points to a mind that orders it), and from preservation (the world holds together though made of opposing elements). The Philosophy curriculum examines these arguments as arguments.

**Conscience.** Paul also says that the Gentiles "shew the work of the law written in their hearts" (Romans 2:15, KJV). The sense of right and wrong found in every people is, for the Fathers, a second witness to God.

**The limits of natural knowledge.**

| Can be known from creation | Known only by revelation |
| --- | --- |
| that God exists | that God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit |
| that He is powerful, wise, good | that the Son became man |
| that He is one | that God is love to the point of the Cross |
| that we owe Him worship | how we are saved and what awaits us |

**Knowing about and knowing.** The Fathers draw a further line. Natural knowledge gives knowledge *about* God. **Revelation, received in faith and prayer, leads to knowing God Himself**, as person to person. The Damascene opens his book by saying that the Deity is "ineffable and incomprehensible", and that no one has known God "save he to whom He revealed Himself" (Book 1, chapter 1; tr. E. W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series vol. 9, 1899).

**The heart.** Orthodox spiritual writers locate the knowledge of God not only in reasoning but in the **heart** (*kardía*, καρδία), the deep centre of the person, and in the ***nous*** (νοῦς), the spiritual intellect that perceives directly. Reason works step by step; the purified *nous* sees. Stage 10 teaches this in full.

**Why many do not know Him.** St Paul says the knowledge is plain, and yet people "glorified him not as God" (Romans 1:21, KJV). The Fathers teach that **the obstacle is not lack of evidence but the passions**, which darken the mind. This is why purification comes before vision.

**The key sentence.** **God may be known from His works, but He is known as He is only when He reveals Himself, and that knowledge is received by a heart made pure.**
One God: the faith of Israel and the Chu:
"I believe in one God" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906). The first word of the Creed's content is the oneness of God, received from Israel.

**The Shema.** The great confession of Israel: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD" (Deuteronomy 6:4, KJV). Christ Himself named it the first commandment (Mark 12:29). **The Church inherits Israel's faith in one God and never abandons it.** The doctrine of the Trinity is not three gods; it is the one God of Israel revealed as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

**What "one" means.** God is one not as one item among many, as there is one apple on a table. **God is one in a way that admits no second**: no other god, no rival principle of evil equal to Him, no division within Him. St John of Damascus gives the reasoning (*Exposition* Book 1, chapter 5): if there were many gods, there would be difference among them, and then one would lack what the other has, and so would not be perfect, and so would not be God.

**Monotheism among the nations.** In the ancient world many peoples worshipped many gods. Some philosophers spoke of one highest principle, but usually with lesser divinities beneath it. The faith of Israel was unusual: one God, Creator of all, who is personal, speaks, makes covenants, and forbids images of Himself made from the creation (Exodus 20:4).

**Against dualism.** Some religions in the Fathers' time, like the Manichaeans, taught two eternal principles, one good and one evil. **The Church teaches there is one God, wholly good; evil has no independent existence** but is a turning away from the good by free creatures. Lesson 23 returns to this.

**The divine attributes.** The Fathers list what can be said of the one God. St John of Damascus gives a long list, beginning "without beginning, without end, eternal and everlasting, uncreate, unchangeable" (Book 1, chapter 2; tr. Watson and Pullan, NPNF 2nd series vol. 9, 1899). The main ones:

| Attribute | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Eternal** | without beginning or end, outside time |
| **Uncreated** (*ágenētos*) | not brought into being by anything |
| **Unchangeable** | not subject to change or passion |
| **Simple** | not made of parts |
| **Infinite** | without limit |
| **Omnipresent** | present everywhere, contained by nothing |
| **Almighty** | able to do all that He wills |
| **Good** | the source of all goodness |

**Oneness is not loneliness.** The Christian claim, which the next lessons unfold, is that the one God is a communion of Persons. **The unity of God is not undone by the Trinity; it is the Trinity's unity.** "I and my Father are one" (John 10:30, KJV).
God the Father: the monarchy of the Fath:
"I believe in one God the Father Almighty" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906). The Creed names the one God first as Father. This lesson explains why.

**The Father is the source.** In Orthodox teaching, the Father is **the source** (*pēgḗ*, πηγή, "spring") and **cause** (*aitía*, αἰτία) of the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Son is begotten of the Father; the Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Father is from no one.

**The monarchy of the Father.** *Monarchía* (μοναρχία) means "single source" or "one rule". **The Orthodox Church teaches that the unity of the Trinity is grounded in the Father**: there is one God because there is one Father, who eternally begets the Son and brings forth the Spirit, sharing with them His whole divine nature. The Cappadocian Fathers made this point against those who accused them of teaching three gods: three gods would need three sources, and there is only one.

**Why the Creed begins "one God, the Father".** In the New Testament, "God" (*ho Theós*) usually means the Father: "one God, the Father, of whom are all things" (1 Corinthians 8:6, KJV). This does not make the Son and Spirit less divine. It shows the order (*táxis*, τάξις) within the Trinity: **from the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit.**

**Father from eternity.** God did not become a Father at some point. St Gregory the Theologian says the Father had no beginning, and so did not begin to be a Father: "He did not then become a Father after He began to be, for His being had no beginning" (Third Theological Oration, section 5; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894). **Fatherhood is eternal in God, because the Son is eternal.**

**Father of Christ and our Father.** God is Father **by nature** of the eternal Son, and Father **by adoption and grace** of those who are united to the Son in baptism. This is why Christians dare to say "Our Father". In the Liturgy the priest introduces the Lord's Prayer: "And vouchsafe, O Lord, that boldly and without condemnation we may call upon thee, God the heavenly Father, and say" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906).

**Fatherhood is not about gender.** The Fathers stress that God is beyond male and female, and that "Father" and "begetting" are used without any bodily sense. Gregory says the Father begets "without passion of course, and without reference to time, and not in a corporeal manner." The Church nonetheless keeps the names Father, Son and Holy Spirit as revealed names, given by Christ, not as metaphors to be replaced.

**The image of the Father.** The Church generally does not paint the Father as an old man in icons, since the Father was not incarnate and was never seen. Images of the Father as "the Ancient of Days" do exist in some later Russian and Greek churches; the Great Moscow Council of 1666–1667 forbade them, and Orthodox iconographers still differ on how strictly to apply that ruling.
Almighty: God the Pantokrator:
"The Father Almighty." The Greek word behind "almighty" says more than "able to do anything".

**The word.** *Pantokrátōr* (Παντοκράτωρ), from *pan*, "all", and *kratéō*, "to hold, to rule". **The Pantokrator is the One who holds all things.** It is not first about raw power but about God holding the whole creation in being, ruling it and keeping it from falling back into nothing.

**In the Septuagint.** The Greek Old Testament uses *Pantokrator* to translate the Hebrew titles "Lord of hosts" and *Shaddai*. The book of Revelation uses it nine times of God, as in "Lord God Almighty" (Revelation 4:8, KJV).

**The icon of Christ Pantokrator.** In the dome of an Orthodox church one usually sees **Christ Pantokrator**: Christ holding the Gospel book and blessing, looking down on the assembly. The Creed applies "Almighty" to the Father, and the icon gives the title to Christ. **There is no conflict: the Son shares all that the Father has, including His rule over all.** The oldest surviving Pantokrator icon, at St Catherine's Monastery on Sinai, dates from the sixth century.

**What almighty means, and what it does not.**

| It means | It does not mean |
| --- | --- |
| God can do all that He wills | God does what is self-contradictory (making a square circle) |
| nothing can thwart His purposes in the end | God wills evil or is its author |
| He holds every creature in being at every moment | God overrides the freedom He has given |
| the world depends wholly on Him | God is distant from what He made |

**Almighty and free creatures.** The Fathers teach that God's greatest act of power is to create beings who can freely love Him, and therefore who can freely refuse Him. **God's almightiness includes the power to limit Himself for the sake of love**, which the Incarnation and the Cross reveal most fully (Stage 3). St Gregory of Nyssa notes, in his *Catechetical Oration*, that God's descent to humility shows His power more than great miracles do.

**Almighty in prayer.** Many of the Church's prayers address God as Lord God Almighty. The title expresses both reverence and trust: **the One who holds all things holds us too**, so we can ask for what we need.

**The Pantokrator and providence.** Because God holds all things, nothing happens outside His knowledge and care. This is the doctrine of **providence** (Lesson 25). God's rule is not that of a tyrant pulling strings but of a Father ordering all things toward the good, while respecting the freedom of His creatures.

**Point across.** The **Greek** curriculum shows how *pantokrator* is built and how compounds with *pan-* work. The Philosophy curriculum treats the philosophers' arguments about omnipotence and its paradoxes.
The divine Name: \"I am THE BEING\":
At the burning bush God gave Moses His name. How the Greek Bible renders it has shaped Orthodox theology and iconography.

**The text.** Moses asks God's name. In the Septuagint (tr. Sir Lancelot Brenton, 1851):

> "And God spoke to Moses, saying, I am THE BEING; and he said, Thus shall ye say to the children of Israel, THE BEING has sent me to you." (Exodus 3:14)

The King James Version, translating the Hebrew, reads: "I AM THAT I AM" (Exodus 3:14, KJV).

**The Greek.** The Septuagint has *Egṓ eimi ho Ṓn* (Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ Ὤν), "I am the One who is." ***Ho Ōn*** (ὁ Ὤν) means "the One who is", "He who exists". The Fathers read it as saying that **God's being is not received from another**: He simply *is*, while everything else exists by sharing in being from Him.

**On every icon of Christ.** Look at the halo of Christ in any Orthodox icon: inside the cross are three Greek letters, **Ο Ω Ν**, *ho Ōn*. **The Church writes the name from the burning bush on the halo of Christ**, because the One who spoke to Moses was, the Fathers taught, the eternal Word, who later became man. This is one of the clearest everyday statements of Christ's divinity.

**The burning bush as a type.** The bush that burned but was not consumed (Exodus 3:2) is read by the Church as a type of the **Theotokos**, who bore God in her womb and was not consumed. Hymns of the Nativity and the Annunciation use the image, and the icon of the "Unburnt Bush" shows her within it.

**How the Fathers read the Name.** Two lines of interpretation, both found among the Fathers, complement each other:

| Reading | Emphasis |
| --- | --- |
| **God is Being itself** | God is the source of all existence; creatures have being by participation |
| **God is beyond being** | the Name refuses a definition; "I am who I am" means God cannot be captured by any name. St Gregory Palamas says God's essence is beyond even "being" as we know it |

Dionysius the Areopagite (about 500) speaks of God as "beyond being" (*hyperoúsios*, ὑπερούσιος). The two readings meet in apophatic theology (Lesson 18).
