**The Name in Jewish and Christian worship.** In Hebrew the name was written with four letters (YHWH) and not pronounced. The Septuagint renders it *Kýrios* (Κύριος), "Lord". **When the New Testament calls Jesus "Lord", it uses the word that stands for the divine Name.** Paul applies Old Testament texts about YHWH directly to Christ (compare Philippians 2:10–11 with Isaiah 45:23).

**Christ's own "I am".** In John's Gospel Christ says, "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58, KJV), and in Greek *egō eimi* recurs throughout that Gospel. The Fathers heard in it the Name from the bush.
The Trinity revealed: Scripture, the The:
The Church did not invent the Trinity by reasoning. She received it from God's self-revelation, chiefly in Christ.

**The Old Testament: hints and shadows.** The Fathers saw the Trinity foreshadowed but not yet revealed:

| Text | What the Fathers saw |
| --- | --- |
| "Let us make man according to our image and likeness" (Genesis 1:26, Brenton 1851) | God speaking in the plural within Himself |
| Abraham's three visitors at Mamre (Genesis 18) | three who are addressed as one Lord |
| the threefold "Holy, holy, holy" of the seraphim (Isaiah 6:3) | praise of the Three-in-One |
| the Word and the Spirit (breath) of God at creation (Psalm 33:6; Genesis 1:2) | the Son and the Spirit at work with the Father |

**The New Testament: revealed in Christ.** **The Trinity is revealed by the coming of the Son and the sending of the Spirit.** Christ speaks of the Father who sent Him, and promises "the Comforter... whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father" (John 15:26, KJV). He sends the apostles to baptise "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 28:19, KJV): one name, three Persons.

**The Theophany.** At Christ's baptism in the Jordan the Father's voice speaks from heaven, the Son stands in the water, and the Spirit descends as a dove (Matthew 3:16–17). The Church calls the feast **Theophany** (*Theopháneia*, Θεοφάνεια, "appearance of God"), kept on **6 January**. Its troparion, the hymn of the feast, reads (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906):

> "When in Jordan thou wast baptized, O Lord, the worship of the Trinity was made manifest. For the voice of the Father bare witness unto thee, calling thee his beloved Son, and the Spirit, in the form of a Dove, confirmed the steadfastness of that word: O Christ our God, who didst manifest thyself, and dost enlighten the world, glory to thee."

**The Hospitality of Abraham.** The Church's best-known image of the Trinity is the icon of **the three angels at Mamre**. The most famous version was painted by **St Andrei Rublev** in the early fifteenth century for the Trinity monastery of St Sergius near Moscow. It does not depict the divine essence; it shows the three visitors whom Abraham welcomed, and through them points to the Trinity. A Moscow council of 1551, the Stoglav, held up this kind of image as the model for icons of the Trinity.

**Pentecost.** The Spirit's descent on the apostles, fifty days after Pascha, completes the revelation. **The Orthodox Church calls Pentecost "Trinity Sunday"**, because with the Spirit's coming the whole Trinity is made known and the Church is born. Stage 4 teaches Pentecost.

**From revelation to doctrine.** The New Testament gives the Father, the Son and the Spirit, each spoken of as God, together with the faith in one God. It does not give the technical terms. **The terms came later, when the Church had to explain how both are true at once without falling into error.** The next lessons teach them.
Ousia and hypostasis: the words for one:
To say how God is one and three, the Fathers used two Greek words. Getting them right is the key to the whole doctrine.

**The two words.**

| Greek | English | What it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ***Ousía*** (οὐσία) | essence, substance, being | **what** God is |
| ***Hypóstasis*** (ὑπόστασις) | person, subsistence | **who** God is |

**The formula.** **God is one *ousia* in three *hypostases*: one essence, three Persons.** *Mía ousía, treís hypostáseis.* The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each fully God, not a third of God each, and are one God.

**An analogy and its limit.** The Cappadocians used an analogy: Peter, James and John share one human nature, yet are three persons. Likewise Father, Son and Spirit share one divine nature. **The limit is crucial**: three men are three separate beings who act separately and can be counted as three men. The three divine Persons are not separated; they share one will, one action, one life, and are one God. St Gregory of Nyssa's short work *To Ablabius: That There Are Not Three Gods* explains why the analogy works only partly.

**Why two words were needed.** Before about 360, *ousia* and *hypostasis* were often used as near-synonyms. The Creed of Nicaea itself, in its anathemas, treated them as the same. That caused confusion:

| If you said | Some heard |
| --- | --- |
| "three hypostases" | three separate beings, three gods |
| "one hypostasis" | one Person wearing three masks |

**The settlement.** At a council in Alexandria in 362 under St Athanasius, both usages were examined and found to be Orthodox when correctly meant. Over the following years **St Basil the Great** and the two Gregories fixed the terms: *ousia* for what is common, *hypostasis* for what is particular.

**A third word: *prosopon*.** *Prósōpon* (πρόσωπον), "face" or "person", is also used of the three. It had been suspected because the heretic Sabellius used it to mean a mere role or mask. Once *hypostasis* was fixed, *prosopon* was used alongside it, meaning a real person, not a mask.

**The Latin side.** In Latin, the Church spoke of *una substantia, tres personae*. *Substantia* is literally the same as *hypo-stasis* ("standing under"), which made translation confusing: Greeks heard "one hypostasis" in the Latin, and Latins heard "three substances" in the Greek. St Gregory the Theologian noted that the two sides meant the same faith and should not quarrel over words.

**What the terms do not do.** **They do not explain the Trinity; they guard it.** *Ousia* says the Three are equally God. *Hypostasis* says they are truly three, not one in disguise. The mystery remains, now protected on both sides.

**Point across.** The **Philosophy** curriculum's lesson on Aristotle's *Categories* shows where *ousia* came from; the Fathers changed its meaning in using it of God.
Homoousios: of one essence with the Fath:
One word, chosen at Nicaea in 325, became the badge of Orthodox faith in the divinity of the Son.

**The word.** *Homooúsios* (ὁμοούσιος), from *homós*, "same", and *ousía*, "essence". **The Son is of the same essence as the Father**: not of a similar essence, not of a lesser one, but the same.

**Why it was needed.** Arius, a priest of Alexandria (about 256–336), taught that the Son was the first and greatest of God's creatures, made before time but not eternal. His slogan was: **"there was when He was not."** He could accept almost any biblical phrase about the Son, such as "image of God" or "from God", because all creatures are from God in some sense. **The bishops at Nicaea needed a word Arius could not accept.** *Homoousios* was that word.

**The text of Nicaea.** The Creed of 325 confesses "one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten of his Father, of the substance of the Father, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten (γεννηθέντα), not made, being of one substance (ὁμοούσιον, consubstantialem) with the Father" (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900).

**The fight after Nicaea.** The word was resisted for over fifty years. Some objected that it was not in Scripture; others feared it blurred the Father and Son. Parties formed:

| Party | Their phrase | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nicene** (St Athanasius) | *homoousios* | of the same essence |
| **Homoiousians** | *homoioúsios* (ὁμοιούσιος) | of a *like* essence; many came over to Nicaea later |
| **Homoeans** | *hómoios* | "like" the Father, without saying how |
| **Anomoeans** (Aetius, Eunomius) | *anómoios* | **unlike** the Father in essence |

The difference between *homoousios* and *homoiousios* is one letter, the iota. It was not a quarrel about trifles. **One says the Son is God; the other, as its strict opponents used it, left room for Him to be something less.**

**St Athanasius.** Bishop of Alexandria (about 296–373), exiled five times for the Nicene faith, St Athanasius argued that **only God can save**: if the Son were a creature, He could not unite us to God (Stage 3). He was called "Athanasius against the world". His feasts are 18 January and 2 May.

**The Spirit too.** At Constantinople in 381 the Church confessed the Spirit as worshipped and glorified with the Father and Son. The Fathers drew the conclusion that the Spirit is likewise *homoousios*. St Gregory the Theologian asked in his Fifth Theological Oration: "Is the Spirit God? Most certainly. Well then, is He Consubstantial? Yes, if He is God" (Oration 31, section 10; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894).

**In the Liturgy.** Before the Creed the choir answers the deacon's call to confess with **"Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the Trinity, one in Essence and undivided"** (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906): *homoousios*, put into prayer.
The Cappadocian Fathers and the settleme:
Three friends and relatives from central Asia Minor gave the Church the language in which she still speaks of the Trinity.

**Who they were.**

| Father | Dates | Role | Feast |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **St Basil the Great** | about 330–379 | bishop of Caesarea; organiser and defender of the Nicene faith; *Against Eunomius*, *On the Holy Spirit* | 1 January |
| **St Gregory of Nazianzus** (the Theologian) | about 329–390 | Basil's friend; the *Theological Orations* (380); presided for a time at the Council of 381 | 25 January |
| **St Gregory of Nyssa** | about 335–about 395 | Basil's younger brother; the deepest speculative mind of the three; *Against Eunomius*, *To Ablabius* | 10 January |

**Cappadocia** is a region of central Anatolia, today in Turkey. Their sister **St Macrina** and their family formed a household of saints.

**What they faced.** After Nicaea, the Anomoeans **Aetius and Eunomius** argued that God's essence is "unbegottenness". Since the Son is begotten, they said, He must be of a different essence. Others, the **Pneumatomachians** ("fighters against the Spirit"), accepted the Son's divinity but denied the Spirit's.

**What they did:**

1. **Fixed the terms.** *Ousia* for what the Three share; *hypostasis* for what distinguishes them (Lesson 10).
2. **Named the distinguishing properties.** The Father is **unbegotten**, the Son **begotten**, the Spirit **proceeding** (Lesson 13). These describe relations of origin, not differences of nature.
3. **Answered Eunomius.** **"Unbegotten" is not God's essence; it is a property of the Father's person.** God's essence cannot be defined at all, and Eunomius' claim to know it was itself the error (Lesson 18).
4. **Defended the Spirit's divinity.** Basil's *On the Holy Spirit* and Gregory's Fifth Theological Oration.
5. **Grounded unity in the Father.** One God, because one Father, the single source (Lesson 6).

**The Council of 381.** The Second Ecumenical Council, held in Constantinople under the Emperor Theodosius I, completed the Creed and confirmed Nicaea. Basil had died two years before, but the council's faith was his. **This is the "Cappadocian settlement": one essence, three hypostases, the Spirit worshipped with the Father and the Son.**

**How they are honoured.** St Basil and St Gregory the Theologian, with St John Chrysostom, are the **Three Holy Hierarchs**, kept together on **30 January**. The Liturgy of St Basil is still served ten times a year, including on the Sundays of Great Lent.

**Point across.** The **Philosophy** curriculum's lesson "Athens and Jerusalem: Justin, Clement, Origen and the Cappadocians" treats their use of Greek philosophy. Stage 9 of this curriculum reads Basil, Gregory and Gregory of Nyssa in their own words.
Begotten and proceeding: what distinguis:
If the Three share one essence, what makes them three? The Fathers answer: only their relations of origin.

**The three properties.** Each Person has one property that belongs to Him alone, called a **hypostatic property** (*idíōma*, ἰδίωμα):

| Person | Property | Greek |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The Father** | unbegotten, without origin | *agennēsía* (ἀγεννησία) |
| **The Son** | begotten of the Father | *génnēsis* (γέννησις) |
| **The Holy Spirit** | proceeding from the Father | *ekpóreusis* (ἐκπόρευσις) |

**Everything else is common.** Goodness, power, wisdom, eternity, will, glory: all of these belong to the one essence and so to each Person equally. **The Persons differ only in how they are related to one another, never in what they are.** St John of Damascus states the rule: everything the Father has belongs to the Son, except being unbegotten; everything belongs to the Spirit, except being unbegotten and begotten.

**Begetting and proceeding are different.** The Son is begotten; the Spirit is not a second Son. But how begetting differs from procession, the Fathers decline to say. St Gregory the Theologian, in his Fifth Theological Oration (Oration 31, section 8; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894), answers an opponent who demands an account of it:

> "What then is Procession? Do you tell me what is the Unbegottenness of the Father, and I will explain to you the physiology of the Generation of the Son and the Procession of the Spirit, and we shall both of us be frenzy-stricken for prying into the mystery of God."

**Without beginning in time.** These relations are eternal. The Son did not come into being at a moment; the Spirit did not begin to proceed. **"Begotten" here has no sense of before and after.** Gregory gives the image of the sun and its light: the sun is not prior to its light, though the light is from the sun (Third Theological Oration, section 3; quoted in the reading lesson).

**The Father as cause, without inferiority.** The Fathers say the Father is "greater" than the Son only as cause (John 14:28, KJV: "my Father is greater than I"), not in nature. St Gregory the Theologian, in his Oration on Holy Baptism, says he would like to call the Father the greater "because from him flows both the Equality and the Being of the Equals" (Oration 40, section 43; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894). **To be the source of equals is not to be superior to them.**

**What the names mean.**

| Name | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| **Father** | the One from whom the others are, and who is from none |
| **Son** / **Word** (*Lógos*) / **Image** | the One begotten, who expresses and reveals the Father |
| **Spirit** (*Pneûma*, "breath") | the One who proceeds, and who rests on the Son and is sent into the world |

**Why it matters.** If the Persons were distinguished by different natures, there would be three gods. If they were not distinguished at all, there would be one Person with three names. **Relations of origin keep both truths: one God, three real Persons.**
Reading: St Gregory the Theologian, Thir:
In 380, in his small chapel of the Anastasis ("Resurrection") in Constantinople, while the city's churches were in Arian hands, St Gregory preached the five *Theological Orations*. The third, Oration 29, is **On the Son**. These two sections hold the Trinity in a few lines.

**The text** (Oration 29, sections 2–3; tr. Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894):

> "The three most ancient opinions concerning God are Anarchia, Polyarchia, and Monarchia. The first two are the sport of the children of Hellas, and may they continue to be so."

> "But Monarchy is that which we hold in honour. It is, however, a Monarchy that is not limited to one Person ... but one which is made of an equality of Nature and a Union of mind, and an identity of motion, and a convergence of its elements to unity — a thing which is impossible to the created nature — so that though numerically distinct there is no severance of Essence. ... This is what we mean by Father and Son and Holy Ghost. The Father is the Begetter and the Emitter; without passion of course, and without reference to time, and not in a corporeal manner. The Son is the Begotten, and the Holy Ghost the Emission."

> "When did these come into being? They are above all When. But, if I am to speak with something more of boldness — when the Father did. And when did the Father come into being. There never was a time when He was not. And the same thing is true of the Son and the Holy Ghost."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"Anarchia, Polyarchia, and Monarchia"** | no ruling principle, many, or one. *Anarchy* here is literally "no source". Polytheism, he says, ends in disorder |
| **"a Monarchy that is not limited to one Person"** | one God, but not a solitary Person: the monarchy is the Father's, shared fully with the Son and Spirit (Lesson 6) |
| **"equality of Nature... Union of mind... identity of motion"** | the Three share one nature, one will and one action. Among creatures this cannot happen |
| **"numerically distinct... no severance of Essence"** | three Persons who can be counted, one essence not divided |
| **"the Begetter and the Emitter"** | the Father begets the Son and brings forth the Spirit: the relations of origin (Lesson 13) |
| **"without passion... without reference to time... not in a corporeal manner"** | the words "beget" and "proceed" carry no bodily or temporal meaning |
| **"They are above all When"** | the Three are eternal. To "when?" Gregory answers "when the Father did", and the Father has no beginning |

**"There never was a time when He was not."** **This is Arius' slogan turned around.** Arius said of the Son, "there was when He was not". Gregory says of each Person that there never was such a time.

**The sun and its light.** In the same section Gregory explains how the Son and Spirit are from the Father yet not after Him: "the Cause is not necessarily prior to its effects, for the sun is not prior to its light."

**Why it matters.** **In a few sentences Gregory states the monarchy of the Father, the equality of the Three, their distinction by origin, and their eternity.**
One will, one action: perichoresis and t:
The three Persons are not three agents cooperating. They act as one, and they dwell in one another.

**One will, one action.** **The Trinity has one will, one power and one action (*enérgeia*, ἐνέργεια), because these belong to the one essence.** Whatever God does toward the world, creating, sustaining, saving, sanctifying, is done by the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit: one act, from the Father, through the Son, completed in the Spirit.

**St Gregory of Nyssa's argument.** In *To Ablabius* Gregory says that among men, each person acts separately, so we count them as many men. **But every action of God toward creation begins with the Father, passes through the Son and is completed in the Holy Spirit.** There is no action of one Person apart from the others. So we do not speak of three gods.

**Perichoresis.** *Perichṓrēsis* (περιχώρησις), "moving around" or "interpenetration". St John of Damascus used it for the Trinity: **each Person dwells in the others without confusion and without separation.** Christ says: "I am in the Father, and the Father in me" (John 14:10, KJV). The Persons are not side by side like three men; each is wholly in each.

**Gregory the Theologian's vision.** In his Oration on Holy Baptism (Oration 40, section 41; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894), Gregory describes how his mind moves between the One and the Three:

> "No sooner do I conceive of the One than I am illumined by the Splendour of the Three; no sooner do I distinguish Them than I am carried back to the One. ... When I contemplate the Three together, I see but one torch, and cannot divide or measure out the Undivided Light."

**Distinct roles without division.** Scripture and the Fathers still speak of particular things as belonging to one Person: **the Father sends, the Son becomes incarnate, the Spirit descends at Pentecost.** Only the Son became man. These are not three separate actions but the one divine action showing each Person's distinctive place:

| Act | Father | Son | Spirit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Creation** | the source who wills | the Word through whom all was made | the Spirit who gives life and perfection |
| **Salvation** | sends the Son | becomes man, dies, rises | makes Christ present in the Church |
| **Sanctification** | adopts us as children | unites us to Himself | dwells in us |

**The Trinity and the Church.** Orthodox writers draw a lesson for human life: **the Trinity is the pattern of communion**, many persons one in love, without losing who each is. Some twentieth-century Orthodox theologians, notably Metropolitan John Zizioulas (1931–2023), built a whole theology of personhood on this. Others, while agreeing that the Trinity is the source of communion, have warned against reading human social models back into God, since the divine Persons share one essence in a way human persons never do. Stage 12 takes up the discussion.

**In prayer.** The Divine Liturgy opens: "Blessed is the kingdom of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906).
The procession of the Holy Spirit and th:
The Creed says the Spirit "proceeds from the Father". A later Western addition to this phrase became one of the main points of division between East and West.

**What the Creed says.** In 381 the Council confessed the Holy Spirit "who proceeds from the Father" (Creed of Constantinople; tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900). The words echo Christ's own: "the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father" (John 15:26, KJV).

**What Orthodox teaching holds.** **The Holy Spirit has His eternal origin from the Father alone, as the single source in the Trinity.** This follows the monarchy of the Father (Lesson 6). The Father is the one cause of both the Son and the Spirit.

**The Spirit and the Son.** The Orthodox Church does not separate the Spirit from the Son. The Fathers say the Spirit **rests on the Son**, **shines forth through the Son**, and is **sent by the Son** into the world (John 15:26, KJV: "whom I will send unto you from the Father"). St Gregory of Cyprus, Patriarch of Constantinople, at the Council of Blachernae in 1285, distinguished the Spirit's **eternal origin**, from the Father alone, from His **eternal manifestation through the Son**. This distinction became standard Orthodox teaching.

**The Western addition.** In Latin churches the words ***filioque***, "and from the Son", were added to the Creed. Spain did so in the sixth century (the Third Council of Toledo, 589, is usually cited). The practice spread under the Franks, and **Rome adopted it in the Creed sung at Mass in the early eleventh century, usually dated 1014.** Stage 8 tells the history, with St Photios and 1054.

**Why the Orthodox object.** Orthodox writers give two kinds of reason:

| Kind | Objection |
| --- | --- |
| **Canonical** | the Creed of an ecumenical council cannot be changed by one part of the Church alone; Ephesus (431) forbade composing a "different faith" |
| **Theological** | making the Son a co-source of the Spirit's being seems to confuse the persons of Father and Son, or to make two sources in God |

St Photios of Constantinople set out the theological case in his *Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit* in the 880s; St Mark of Ephesus restated it at Florence.

**Where Orthodox writers differ.** All Orthodox agree that the Creed should be said without the addition. They differ on how grave the doctrine itself is:

1. **A heresy.** Many Orthodox, following Photios and Mark of Ephesus, and later writers such as St Justin Popović, judge the *filioque* as a doctrine to be a serious error about the Trinity.
2. **A theologoumenon, wrongly elevated.** Others, following the Russian historian Vasily Bolotov (1898), have argued that "from the Father through the Son", which some Fathers taught, can be held as a legitimate opinion, and that the fault lies chiefly in imposing it as dogma and adding it to the Creed.

**This lesson's point is positive.** **The Orthodox Church confesses the Spirit as proceeding from the Father, and keeps the Creed in the words of the councils.** The answer to other churches belongs to a separate curriculum.
Errors the Church rejected about the Tri:
The Church defined the Trinity by refusing errors that made it simpler and smaller. Knowing them shows what the doctrine protects.

**Two ways to go wrong.** Every error about the Trinity loses either the oneness or the threeness:

| Error | What it lost | What it taught |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Modalism** (Sabellianism) | the three Persons | one God who appears in three modes or roles, like masks, Father in creation, Son in redemption, Spirit in sanctification |
| **Subordinationism** / **Arianism** | the equal divinity of Son and Spirit | the Son and Spirit are lesser, created beings |
| **Tritheism** | the oneness | three separate gods sharing a kind of nature |

**Modalism.** Taught in the early third century by Noetus, Praxeas and **Sabellius**, it held that Father, Son and Spirit are one Person under three names. **The Church answered that the Father sends the Son, the Son prays to the Father, the Spirit is sent: they are really three.** At the Theophany, all three are present at once.

**Arianism.** Arius (about 256–336) taught that the Son was created. Nicaea (325) answered with *homoousios*. A later stream, the **Pneumatomachians**, also called Macedonians, accepted the Son's divinity but denied the Spirit's; Constantinople (381) answered them.

**Eunomianism.** Eunomius of Cyzicus (died about 394) claimed that God's essence is "unbegottenness" and that he could know it exactly. The Cappadocians answered that **God's essence is unknowable**, and that "unbegotten" names the Father's person, not the divine essence.

**Tritheism.** In the sixth century John Philoponus, an Alexandrian philosopher, was accused of teaching that the three Persons were three individual instances of divinity, and so three gods. The Church rejected this. (The **Philosophy** curriculum covers Philoponus on other questions.)

**Why the errors were attractive.** Each made the faith easier to grasp:

- Modalism kept God's oneness simple.
- Arianism kept God remote from the world and gave a tidy chain of being.
- Tritheism made the Persons easy to imagine as individuals.

**The Orthodox doctrine is harder because it refuses to give up either truth.** God is truly one; the Three are truly three.

**How the errors still appear.** Teachers of the faith warn of them in everyday speech:

| Careless phrase | Error it suggests |
| --- | --- |
| "God is like water, ice and steam" | modalism: one thing in three states |
| "The Son is God's first creation" | Arianism |
| "The Trinity is a committee of three" | tritheism |
| "The Spirit is God's power, not a Person" | denial of the Spirit's personhood |

**The lesson for prayer.** The Church prays to the Father, to the Son and to the Spirit, and to the Trinity together, and glorifies them as one. **Right worship is the best guard against wrong doctrine.**
Apophatic theology: knowing God by unkno:
The Orthodox Church holds that God, in His essence, is beyond every concept. The way of theology that honours this is called apophatic.

**The word.** *Apóphasis* (ἀπόφασις), "denial" or "negation". **Apophatic theology speaks of God by saying what He is not**: not limited, not changing, not visible, not comprehensible. Its opposite, *katáphasis* (κατάφασις), "affirmation", is cataphatic theology (next lesson).

**Why negation.** Every concept the mind forms is drawn from created things. **God is not a created thing, so no concept fits Him exactly.** St Gregory the Theologian, in his Second Theological Oration, says: "It is difficult to conceive God but to define Him in words is an impossibility... But in my opinion it is impossible to express Him, and yet more impossible to conceive Him" (Oration 28, section 4; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894).

**St John of Damascus** puts it in one sentence: **"God then is infinite and incomprehensible and all that is comprehensible about Him is His infinity and incomprehensibility"** (*Exposition*, Book 1, chapter 4; tr. Watson and Pullan, NPNF 2nd series vol. 9, 1899).

**The darkness of Sinai.** The Fathers read Moses' ascent of Mount Sinai as the pattern. He first saw God in light at the burning bush; later "Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was" (Exodus 20:21, KJV). **St Gregory of Nyssa**, in his *Life of Moses*, teaches that the closer one comes to God, the more one knows that He is beyond knowing: the darkness is not ignorance but a knowledge beyond knowledge.

**Dionysius.** The writings under the name of **Dionysius the Areopagite**, St Paul's convert in Athens (Acts 17:34), appeared about 500; the Church receives them as a faithful expression of the tradition. His *Mystical Theology* teaches the ascent by negation into the divine darkness. (The **Philosophy** curriculum's lesson on Pseudo-Dionysius treats this as philosophy.)

**Apophasis is not agnosticism.** It does not mean we know nothing of God, or that all statements about Him are equally good. **It means that our true statements about God point beyond themselves**, to a reality greater than they can hold. It is a discipline of humility, and it leads to worship.

**Apophasis and the Persons.** Lossky, in *The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church*, argued that apophatic theology does not lead to an impersonal abyss but to the living Trinity. **The God beyond concepts is not an "it" but the Father, the Son and the Spirit**, met in prayer.

**In the Liturgy.** The Anaphora of St John Chrysostom addresses the Father: "for thou art God ineffable, incomprehensible, invisible, inconceivable; thou art from everlasting and art changeless, thou, and thine Only-begotten Son, and thy Holy Spirit" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906). **The Church prays apophatic theology every Sunday.**

**Why it matters.** Apophatic theology protects against two errors: **idolatry of concepts**, which confuses our idea of God with God, and **rationalism**, which supposes theology can be completed like a science. Lossky and many Orthodox writers called it the fundamental character of Eastern theology.
Cataphatic theology: the names of God:
If God is beyond concepts, can anything positive be said of Him? Yes: through the names He has revealed and the works He has done.

**The word.** *Katáphasis* (κατάφασις), "affirmation". **Cataphatic theology speaks of God by affirming what is true of Him**: that He is good, wise, loving, just, living, light.

**Where the names come from.** The names are drawn from:

| Source | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **God's self-revelation in Scripture** | "God is love" (1 John 4:8, KJV); "God is light" (1 John 1:5, KJV) |
| **His works in creation** | Creator, Almighty, Wise |
| **His acts in history** | Saviour, Deliverer, Shepherd |
| **The revelation of the Trinity** | Father, Son, Holy Spirit |

**Dionysius' *Divine Names*.** In *The Divine Names* Dionysius the Areopagite examines the names Scripture gives God: Good, Being, Life, Wisdom, Power, One. Each is true, he says, but God possesses it **in a way beyond our understanding**: He is not good as a good man is good, but as the source of all goodness, "super-good".

**Three steps.** The tradition often uses three steps together, especially in Dionysius:

1. **Affirm**: God is wise.
2. **Deny**: God is not wise as creatures are wise.
3. **Exceed**: God is beyond wisdom, *hypersophos*, the source of all wisdom.

**Cataphatic and apophatic together.** **The two are not rivals; they correct each other.** Without the cataphatic, theology would fall silent; without the apophatic, it would mistake its words for God. St John of Damascus notes that names like good and just tell "not God's nature but only the qualities of His nature" (*Exposition* Book 1, chapter 4; tr. Watson and Pullan, NPNF 2nd series vol. 9, 1899).

**What the names refer to.** Orthodox teaching, made fully explicit by St Gregory Palamas, is that **the names of God refer to His energies**, His real presence and action toward us, not to His essence (next lesson). When we call God good, we name a real, uncreated goodness that we can meet. It is not a mere human projection.

**The highest cataphatic statements.** Some names have special weight:

| Name | Why it weighs |
| --- | --- |
| **Father, Son, Holy Spirit** | revealed by Christ; names of the Persons, not of God's acts |
| **He who is** (*ho Ōn*) | given from the burning bush (Lesson 8) |
| **Love** | "God is love": the Fathers read it as revealing the life of the Trinity itself |

**Images in Scripture.** Scripture speaks of God's hand, eyes, anger and repentance. The Fathers read these as **condescension** (*synkatábasis*, συγκατάβασις): God speaking in human terms so that we can understand. St John of Damascus devotes a chapter (Book 1, chapter 11) to explaining such bodily language.

**In worship.** Orthodox hymns pile up names of God and the Theotokos in long litanies, such as the Akathist hymns. **This is cataphatic theology turned into praise**: no single name suffices, so the Church multiplies them.
Essence and energies: God unknown and kn:
How can God be beyond knowing and yet truly known and shared? Orthodox teaching answers with the distinction between God's essence and His energies.

**The two terms.**

| Term | Greek | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Essence** | *ousía* (οὐσία) | what God is in Himself: wholly beyond creatures, never known or shared |
| **Energies** | *enérgeiai* (ἐνέργειαι), "operations", "activities" | God's real, uncreated presence and action toward creation: His life, grace, light, love, power |

**St Basil already said it.** In Letter 234 (tr. Blomfield Jackson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 8, 1895), answering Eunomius' followers, Basil writes:

> "The operations are various, and the essence simple, but we say that we know our God from His operations, but do not undertake to approach near to His essence. His operations come down to us, but His essence remains beyond our reach."

"Operations" here translates *energeiai*.

**St Gregory Palamas.** In the fourteenth century the monks of Mount Athos who practised the Jesus Prayer, the **hesychasts** (from *hēsychía*, ἡσυχία, "stillness"), said they saw in prayer the uncreated light of God, the light of Christ's Transfiguration on Mount Tabor. Barlaam of Calabria mocked them: either they saw God's essence, which is impossible, or they saw a created light. **St Gregory Palamas** (1296–1359), monk of Athos and later Archbishop of Thessalonica, answered that there is a third possibility: **they saw God's uncreated energy, which is truly God, though not His essence.**

**The councils.** Councils in Constantinople in **1341, 1347 and 1351** upheld Palamas. Their teaching was added to the **Synodikon of Orthodoxy**, read on the first Sunday of Lent. Palamas is commemorated on the **second Sunday of Great Lent** and on 14 November.

**What the distinction protects:**

1. **God's transcendence.** We never become God by essence; the Creator–creature line is never crossed.
2. **Real union.** What we receive in grace is not a created gift but **God Himself in His energies**. This is what makes *theosis* possible (Stage 3).
3. **God's simplicity.** The energies are not parts of God or lesser gods. **God is wholly present in each of His energies.**

**Uncreated grace.** It follows that **grace is not a created thing but God's own life shared**. This is one of the distinctive emphases of Orthodox teaching.

**How to describe the distinction.** All Orthodox hold the distinction as the Church's teaching. Theologians differ on how to describe it: some, following Palamas' language closely, call it a **real distinction** in God, though not a separation; others stress that it is a distinction **without division**, which the human mind cannot model, and warn against treating essence and energies as two "things". Both reject both separation and mere verbal difference.

**Point across.** The **Philosophy** curriculum's lesson "Palamas and Barlaam: the hesychast controversy and the essence–energies distinction" treats the arguments. Stage 8 tells the history; Stage 10 the hesychast practice.
Creation from nothing:
"Maker of heaven and earth and of all things visible and invisible" (Creed of 381, tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900). The Church teaches that God made everything that exists, not from pre-existing matter but from nothing.

**The phrase.** *Ex nihilo* in Latin; in Greek *ex ouk óntōn* (ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων), "from things that are not". **Before creation, nothing existed but God. God did not shape an eternal matter; He gave existence itself.**

**In Scripture.** The clearest statement is the mother of the seven martyrs in Maccabees: "I beseech thee, my son, look upon the heaven and the earth, and all that is therein, and consider that God made them of things that were not; and so was mankind made likewise" (2 Maccabees 7:28, KJV Apocrypha). Genesis 1:1, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth", is read the same way.

**Against the Greek view.** Plato's *Timaeus* describes a craftsman shaping pre-existing chaos; Aristotle held the world to be without beginning. **The Fathers rejected both: only God is without beginning.** Early Christian writers such as Theophilus of Antioch and St Irenaeus, in the late second century, stated creation from nothing explicitly.

**Creation is by will, not by nature.** This is a key Orthodox distinction. St John of Damascus says that in God, **begetting** "is without beginning and everlasting, being the work of nature and producing out of His own essence", whereas **creation**, "being the work of will, is not co-eternal with God. For it is not natural that that which is brought into existence out of nothing should be co-eternal with what is without beginning and everlasting" (*Exposition* Book 1, chapter 8; tr. Watson and Pullan, NPNF 2nd series vol. 9, 1899).

| | **Begetting** (the Son) | **Creating** (the world) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **From** | the Father's essence | nothing |
| **By** | nature | will |
| **When** | eternally | with a beginning |
| **Result** | God from God | a creature, not God |

**Why God created.** Not from need: the Trinity lacks nothing. **God created out of goodness and love, freely, so that others might share in His goodness.** St John of Damascus says that because God is good, He was not content to contemplate Himself, but willed that there should be beings to benefit from His goodness (*Exposition* Book 2, chapter 2, in paraphrase).

**The Trinity creates.** The Father creates through the Son, the Word "by whom all things were made", in the Holy Spirit (Psalm 33:6).

**What this means for the world.** Because the world comes from nothing, **it depends on God at every moment**: if He withdrew, it would fall back into nothing. Because it comes from His goodness, **it is good**: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31, KJV). Matter is not evil.

**Creation and science.** Orthodox writers differ on how to relate Genesis to modern science. Some read the six days literally, as Fr Seraphim Rose argued; others hold that Genesis teaches the meaning of creation, not its mechanics, and accept an ancient universe. Both affirm creation from nothing by the one God.
Created and uncreated: the great divide:
The deepest line in Orthodox theology does not run between spirit and matter, but between the uncreated God and everything He made.

**The two kinds of existence.**

| Uncreated (*áktistos*, ἄκτιστος) | Created (*ktistós*, κτιστός) |
| --- | --- |
| the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit | angels, souls, bodies, the material world |
| God's essence and His energies | every creature, visible and invisible |
| without beginning, unchangeable | brought from nothing, changeable |
| exists by itself | exists by sharing in God's gift |

**Spirit is not divine by being spirit.** Many ancient philosophies treated the soul as a fragment of the divine, trapped in matter. **Orthodox teaching rejects this: angels and human souls are as much creatures as stones.** They are higher creatures, but they come from nothing and depend on God. The line between God and creation is absolute.

**Why the divide matters.** Almost every heresy about the Trinity and Christ, the Fathers observed, blurred this line:

| Error | How it blurred the line |
| --- | --- |
| **Arianism** | made the Son a creature, yet worshipped Him |
| **Origenism** (as condemned in 553) | treated souls as pre-existing, falling into bodies |
| **Pantheism** | treats the world as part of God |

**Change is the mark of the creature.** Created things came from non-existence to existence, so their very being involves change. St Gregory of Nyssa saw this as good: **the creature's changeability is what allows it to grow without end toward God**, moving "from glory to glory" (2 Corinthians 3:18, KJV). Created nature is not a prison; it is a road.

**The energies cross the divide.** The great divide does not leave creation far from God. **God's uncreated energies are present everywhere in the creation, holding it in being and calling it to Him.** Christ, the eternal Word, is the one in whom created and uncreated are united without confusion (Stage 3). Through Him creatures can share in the uncreated life of God by grace, while remaining creatures.

**Not a hierarchy of being.** Neoplatonist philosophy described reality as a ladder of emanations from the One down to matter, each lower level less divine. The Fathers took over some of its language but **rejected emanation**: creatures do not flow out of God's essence. **Between God and the highest angel there is no gradual slope, only the gulf crossed by God's free love.** The **Philosophy** curriculum's lessons on Plotinus show the system the Fathers corrected.

**Matter is honoured.** Because matter is God's good creation, and because God the Word took a material body, Orthodox worship uses matter fully: water, oil, bread, wine, wood, paint, incense. **St John of Damascus, defending icons, wrote that he would not cease to honour matter, through which his salvation was worked** (in paraphrase, from his treatises on the icons).

**The key sentence.** **Only God is uncreated; all else was made from nothing; and the uncreated God, by His energies and in Christ, unites Himself to what He made without either ceasing to be what it is.**
The invisible creation: the angels:
"Of all things visible and invisible." The invisible creation, the Church teaches, includes the angels, created spirits who serve God and minister to us.

**The word.** *Ángelos* (ἄγγελος) means "messenger". It names their task, not their nature. Their nature, St John of Damascus says, is spiritual and created.

**What the Church teaches.** St John of Damascus gives the classic definition (*Exposition* Book 2, chapter 3; tr. Watson and Pullan, NPNF 2nd series vol. 9, 1899):

> "An angel, then, is an intelligent essence, in perpetual motion, with free-will, incorporeal, ministering to God, having obtained by grace an immortal nature: and the Creator alone knows the form and limitation of its essence."

**Key points:**

| Point | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Created** | angels came from nothing, like all creatures; they are not divine |
| **Spiritual** | without bodies as we have them, though "incorporeal" is relative: only God is wholly so |
| **Free** | they chose, and some fell |
| **Immortal by grace** | not by nature; God sustains them |
| **Ministering** | they praise God and serve His purposes toward the world |

**The nine ranks.** Following Dionysius the Areopagite's *Celestial Hierarchy*, the Church speaks of nine orders in three triads: **Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones; Dominions, Powers, Authorities; Principalities, Archangels, Angels.** The names come from Scripture (Isaiah 6, Ezekiel 10, Colossians 1:16, Ephesians 1:21). The precise arrangement is a theologoumenon, an opinion of great weight, not a dogma.

**Feasts of the angels.** The chief is the **Synaxis of the Archangel Michael and the other bodiless powers** on **8 November**. Every Monday in the weekly cycle of services is dedicated to the angels. The Annunciation (25 March) celebrates the Archangel Gabriel's message to the Virgin.

**Guardian angels.** The Church teaches that **each Christian is given a guardian angel**, often said to be received at baptism. Christ says of "these little ones" that "in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father" (Matthew 18:10, KJV). Orthodox prayer books contain prayers to one's guardian angel in the morning and evening prayers.

**The fallen angels.** The devil (*diábolos*, διάβολος, "slanderer") and the demons were created good and **fell by their own free choice, through pride**. Evil is not a power equal to God; it is a created will turned away. St John of Damascus devotes the next chapter of his book to the devil and demons. Their defeat by Christ is part of Stage 3.

**Angels in worship.** The Liturgy joins the angels' worship. **The Cherubic Hymn**, sung at the Great Entrance, begins (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906): "Let us, the Cherubim mystically representing, and unto the Life-giving Trinity the thrice-holy chant intoning, all cares terrestrial now lay aside." The assembly joins the angels' praise. The *Sanctus*, "Holy, holy, holy", is the seraphim's hymn from Isaiah 6:3.

**Why angels matter.** The created order is larger than the visible world. **The human being stands between the angels and the material world**, sharing in both: the subject of the next lesson.
The human person: made in the image and:
The crown of creation, in Scripture and the Fathers, is the human person, made in God's image. The Church's teaching on man follows from her teaching on God.

**The text.** "And God said, Let us make man according to our image and likeness" (Genesis 1:26, Brenton's Septuagint, 1851). In Greek: *kat' eikóna hēmetéran kai kath' homoíōsin* (κατ᾽ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν).

**Image and likeness.** Many Fathers distinguish the two words:

| Term | Greek | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Image** | *eikṓn* (εἰκών) | what is given: reason, freedom, the capacity for God |
| **Likeness** | *homoíōsis* (ὁμοίωσις) | what is to be attained: becoming like God in virtue, by grace and freedom |

**St John of Damascus** puts it plainly: "For the phrase after His image clearly refers to the side of his nature which consists of mind and free will, whereas after His likeness means likeness in virtue so far as that is possible" (*Exposition* Book 2, chapter 12; tr. Watson and Pullan, NPNF 2nd series vol. 9, 1899). **The image is the starting point; the likeness is the goal.** The goal, in its fullness, is *theosis* (Stage 3).

**Not every Father uses the distinction.** Some, such as St Athanasius, use "image" and "likeness" almost interchangeably. The distinction is widely taught, especially from St Irenaeus onward, but the teaching beneath it is common to all: **the human being is made for communion with God and growth toward Him.**

**Man as a microcosm and mediator.** The Fathers say the human person unites the visible and invisible creation: **a body from the earth and a soul breathed by God** (Genesis 2:7). St Gregory the Theologian and St Maximus the Confessor describe man as a "little world" (*mikrókosmos*) and as the one called to unite all creation and offer it to God, as a priest of creation.

**Body and soul together.** St John of Damascus insists that body and soul "were formed at one and the same time, not first the one and then the other, as Origen so senselessly supposes" (*Exposition* Book 2, chapter 12). **The human person is not a soul in a body but the unity of both.** This is why the Church teaches the resurrection of the body (Stage 4).

**Where the image is.** The Fathers locate the image chiefly in the mind and freedom, sometimes in the soul's rule over the body, sometimes in the whole person. **The image is not lost by sin**, the Church teaches, but darkened and wounded. Stage 3 begins with the fall.

**Persons, not only natures.** Modern Orthodox writers, among them Lossky, Zizioulas and Yannaras, have stressed that the image of God is above all **personhood**: the human being, like the persons of the Trinity, is made for communion, not isolation. Other Orthodox theologians accept the emphasis while warning against reading modern ideas of the person into the Fathers. Both agree that the human person is irreducible, free and made for love.

**Why every person matters.** Every human being bears the image of God. **To honour a person is to honour the image; to despise one is to despise it.** In the Liturgy the deacon censes the icons and then the people, because they too are icons of God.
Providence: God's care for his creation:
God did not create the world and leave it. He holds it, cares for it and guides it. The Church calls this providence.

**The word.** *Prónoia* (πρόνοια), "forethought", "care". St John of Damascus defines it: "Providence, then, is the care that God takes over existing things" (*Exposition* Book 2, chapter 29; tr. Watson and Pullan, NPNF 2nd series vol. 9, 1899).

**What the Church teaches.** **God knows all things, holds all things in being, and orders all things toward the good**, while respecting the freedom of His rational creatures. Christ says that a sparrow shall not "fall on the ground without your Father" and that "the very hairs of your head are all numbered" (Matthew 10:29–30, KJV).

**Two kinds of providence.** St John of Damascus distinguishes:

| Kind | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **God's good pleasure** (*eudokía*) | what God wills directly: all that is good |
| **God's permission** (*synchṓrēsis*) | what God allows but does not will: the evil choices of free creatures and their consequences |

**God is not the author of evil.** **Evil is not a creature or a substance; it is the absence or corruption of the good**, brought about by the free turning away of angels and men. St Basil preached a homily, *That God Is Not the Author of Evil*, on exactly this. God permits evil because He will not destroy freedom, and He can bring good out of it, as He brought salvation out of the Cross. (The **Philosophy** curriculum's lessons on Plotinus and Augustine examine evil as privation as an argument.)

**Foreknowledge is not compulsion.** St John of Damascus says God foreknows all things but **does not predetermine the free choices of His creatures**. His foreknowledge does not cause them (*Exposition* Book 2, chapter 30). Orthodox teaching has never accepted a doctrine of predestination in which God chooses some for damnation regardless of their freedom.

**Suffering.** The Fathers do not explain every suffering. They teach that suffering can be **permitted for healing**, **for testing**, **for the sake of others**, or simply in a fallen world where death reigns, and that God is with the sufferer. **The Cross is the Church's deepest answer: God does not stand outside suffering but enters it.** Job's friends gave tidy explanations and were rebuked (Job 42:7).

**Providence in the life of the Christian.** The Orthodox spiritual tradition teaches **trust in providence** as a virtue. The common prayer of the Optina Elders, a nineteenth-century Russian monastic tradition, asks to accept everything that comes in the day with peace, and to believe that all is under God's care (here given in paraphrase). Saints such as St Paisios of Mount Athos counselled people in hardship to give thanks, believing God turns all things to good for those who love Him (Romans 8:28).

**Providence and history.** The Church reads the history of Israel, of the Church and of nations as under God's providence, without claiming to read every event. **Providence is a matter for trust more than for calculation.**
Looking back: God and the Trinity:
This stage covered the first article of the Creed and the doctrine of God. Here is the whole in one place.

**The core.** **There is one God, the Father, who eternally begets the Son and brings forth the Holy Spirit, sharing with them His one divine essence. The Three are one God, distinct in their relations of origin, one in will and action. This God, beyond all knowing in His essence, is truly known and shared in His uncreated energies. Out of goodness He made all things from nothing, visible and invisible, and made the human person in His image, for likeness to Him.**

**The terms, in one table:**

| Term | Greek | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Essence** | *ousía* | what God is: one |
| **Person** | *hypóstasis* / *prósōpon* | who God is: three |
| **Of one essence** | *homooúsios* | the Son and Spirit are God as the Father is |
| **Monarchy** | *monarchía* | the Father as single source |
| **Begetting** / **procession** | *génnēsis* / *ekpóreusis* | how the Son and Spirit are from the Father |
| **Interpenetration** | *perichṓrēsis* | each Person in the others |
| **Energies** | *enérgeiai* | God's uncreated presence and action |
| **Apophatic** / **cataphatic** | *apóphasis* / *katáphasis* | knowing by negation / by affirmation |
| **Image** / **likeness** | *eikṓn* / *homoíōsis* | the gift / the goal |
| **Providence** | *prónoia* | God's care for creation |

**The witnesses.** Scripture (Deuteronomy 6:4; Exodus 3:14; Matthew 28:19; John 15:26); the councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381), and the hesychast councils (1341–1351); the Fathers: Athanasius, Basil, Gregory the Theologian, Gregory of Nyssa, Dionysius, John of Damascus, Gregory Palamas.

**What the Church rejected.** Modalism, Arianism, the Pneumatomachians, Eunomius' claim to know God's essence, tritheism, dualism, emanation.

**Where Orthodox writers differ, as set out here:**

1. How grave the *filioque* is as doctrine, while all reject the addition to the Creed.
2. How to describe the essence–energies distinction, while all hold it.
3. How far to build a theology of personhood on the Trinity.
4. How to read Genesis alongside modern science.

**Questions to test yourself:**

1. Why did Nicaea need the word *homoousios*?
2. What is the difference between *ousia* and *hypostasis*, and why were both needed?
3. What makes the Son different from the Spirit?
4. Why does apophatic theology lead to worship rather than to agnosticism?
5. What did Palamas answer to Barlaam, and how does Basil's Letter 234 anticipate it?
6. Why is creating different from begetting?

**Next.** Stage 3 turns to the second article of the Creed: "And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906).
Context: the second article of the Creed:
Most of the Creed is about one Person: Jesus Christ. This stage follows the Creed's second article from the eternal Son to His coming again.

**The text** (Creed of Constantinople, 381; tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900):

> "And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only begotten Son of God, begotten of his Father before all worlds, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten not made, being of one substance with the Father, by whom all things were made. Who for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven and was incarnate by the Holy Ghost and the Virgin Mary, and was made man, and was crucified also for us under Pontius Pilate. He suffered and was buried, and the third day he rose again according to the Scriptures, and ascended into heaven, and sits at the Right Hand of the Father. And he shall come again with glory to judge both the quick and the dead. Whose kingdom shall have no end."

**The shape of the article, and of this stage:**

| Clause | Subject | Lessons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "begotten of his Father before all worlds" | the eternal Son, the Word | 6–7 |
| "for us men and for our salvation" | why He came: the fall and its healing | 2–5, 9 |
| "was incarnate... and was made man" | the Incarnation, the Theotokos, the two natures | 8–17 |
| "was crucified... suffered and was buried" | the Cross and the descent into Hades | 19–21 |
| "the third day he rose again" | the Resurrection | 22 |
| (what it achieves) | salvation and *theosis* | 23–25 |
| "ascended... shall come again" | the Ascension and Second Coming | 27 |

**The question behind it all.** **Who is Jesus Christ?** The Church answers: **He is the eternal Son of God, one of the Holy Trinity, who became truly man without ceasing to be God, so that man might be united to God.** Every council from Nicaea (325) to Constantinople III (681) was fought over some part of that answer.

**Why it matters for salvation.** The Fathers argued about Christ not from curiosity but because **salvation depends on who He is**. If He were not truly God, He could not unite us to God. If He were not truly man, He would not have united *us*. If He were two persons, God and man would only stand side by side. St Gregory the Theologian puts the rule in one sentence, which this stage will meet again: "that which He has not assumed He has not healed."

**Christology and the Theotokos.** Orthodox teaching about Mary flows from teaching about Christ. She is called *Theotokos*, "the one who gave birth to God", because her Son is God. Lessons 13 and 14 teach this.

**Point across.** The **Philosophy** curriculum's lesson on Maximus the Confessor and the natural will treats the two-wills question as philosophy of action. Stages 7 and 8 of this curriculum tell the history of the councils; this stage teaches what they defined.

**A word for this stage.** *Oikonomía* (οἰκονομία), which in Stage 1 meant pastoral flexibility, has an older meaning: **God's "economy", His plan of salvation**, above all the Incarnation. The Fathers distinguish *theología*, God in Himself (Stage 2), from *oikonomía*, God's saving work in the world (this stage).
The fall: what happened in Paradise:
"For us men and for our salvation." Salvation presupposes something to be saved from. Scripture tells it in the story of Adam and Eve.

**The story.** In Genesis 2–3, God places the first human beings in Paradise, gives them every tree but one, and warns that eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil will bring death. Tempted by the serpent, they eat. They hide from God, are sent out of Paradise, and become subject to toil, pain and death.

**What the Fathers saw in it.**

| Element | Patristic reading |
| --- | --- |
| **Paradise** | a life of communion with God, not yet complete but growing |
| **The commandment** | a training in obedience and love, given for growth |
| **The serpent** | the devil, a fallen angel, envying man (Wisdom 2:24) |
| **The eating** | turning from God to the creature, seeking godhood without God |
| **The hiding** | the first fruit of sin: shame, fear and broken communion |
| **Expulsion and death** | not mainly a punishment imposed from outside but the consequence of turning from the source of life |

**Adam was created good but not yet perfect.** St Irenaeus of Lyons taught that the first humans were like children, meant to grow into the likeness of God. **The fall was a turning aside from the path of growth, choosing to grasp at what God meant to give as a gift.** This is one reason the Orthodox Church speaks of salvation as the completion of man's original calling, not only the repair of damage.

**Death as separation.** God is life. **To turn away from God is to turn toward death**, as a branch cut from a vine withers. St Athanasius teaches that human nature, made from nothing, would fall back toward nothing apart from God's grace (Lesson 4).

**The devil's part.** The Church teaches that the devil, a fallen angel, deceived the first humans and gained a kind of hold over them through sin and death. **Christ's work is therefore also a victory over the devil** (Lesson 20).

**How literally to read Genesis 2–3.** Orthodox writers differ here as on Genesis 1 (Stage 2). Some read it as straightforward history, with a first human pair in a real garden. Others read it as a God-given account told in images, teaching true things about humanity's origin, its turning from God and its need of healing, without requiring each detail to be literal. **Both agree on the theology**: humanity was made good, turned from God by its own free choice, and fell under death, from which only God can rescue it.

**The first gospel.** Even in the curse, God promises a remedy: the woman's seed will strike at the serpent (Genesis 3:15). The Fathers call this the ***Protoevangelium***, "the first gospel" (Lesson 5).
Ancestral sin: what we inherit from Adam:
What does Adam's sin mean for his descendants? The Orthodox answer differs in emphasis from the Western one, and Orthodox writers state it in more than one way.

**The text at the centre.** "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned" (Romans 5:12, KJV).

**What all Orthodox hold:**

1. **Death entered through Adam, and all his descendants are born mortal and subject to corruption** (*phthorá*, φθορά).
2. **Human nature is wounded**: the mind is darkened, the will weakened, and the passions disordered, so that every person is inclined to sin.
3. **Every person who sins does so freely** and is responsible for his own sins.
4. **The image of God is not destroyed**, and freedom remains.
5. **Baptism heals and renews** the fallen nature, and infants are baptised "for the remission of sins", as the Creed says of baptism.

**The term "ancestral sin".** Many modern Orthodox writers prefer ***propatorikón amártēma*** (προπατορικὸν ἁμάρτημα), **"ancestral sin"**, to the Western "original sin". The emphasis: **we inherit the consequences of Adam's sin, above all death and corruption, but not Adam's personal guilt.** Guilt belongs to the person who sins.

**The question of Romans 5:12.** The last phrase, Greek *eph' hō pántes hḗmarton* (ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον), was read in the Latin Bible as "in whom (Adam) all sinned", which supported the idea of inherited guilt. Many Greek Fathers read it as "because all sinned", or even, in one line of interpretation, "because of which (death) all sinned": **mortality itself breeds fear and selfishness, and so sin.**

**Two Orthodox emphases.** Orthodox writers state the teaching in two ways, and the difference is real though not a division:

| View | Held by | Emphasis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ancestral sin as inherited mortality, not guilt** | Fr John Romanides, whose 1957 dissertation *The Ancestral Sin* shaped Greek theology; Fr John Meyendorff | sharp contrast with Augustine; we inherit death and corruption, from which sin follows |
| **Inherited sinfulness as a real condition** | the older Orthodox catechisms, such as St Peter Mogila's *Orthodox Confession* (1640) and St Philaret of Moscow's *Catechism* (1823), which used the term "original sin"; some later writers who defend that usage | we are born not only mortal but in a state of sin needing cleansing, though not personally guilty of Adam's act |

The second group warns that reacting against Augustine can understate the depth of the fall; the first warns that importing juridical guilt distorts the Fathers. **Both deny that a newborn is personally guilty of Adam's act, and both affirm that every person needs Christ's healing.**

**Why it matters.** **In Orthodox teaching the fall is above all a sickness of nature and a captivity to death, and salvation is above all healing and life.** That shapes everything that follows in this stage.
Death and corruption: St Athanasius on t:
Before explaining the Incarnation, St Athanasius describes the problem it solves. His account is the classic Orthodox statement of what the fall did.

**The book.** St Athanasius' *On the Incarnation of the Word* is an early work, dated by most scholars between about 318 and the mid-330s. It is read in this stage's reading lesson. Here are his chapters 4–7.

**Made from nothing, held by grace.** Athanasius says God made man "out of nothing" and gave him, by the grace of the Word, a life in fellowship with God. Men were "by nature corruptible", but would have escaped that natural state, had they remained good (section 5; tr. Archibald Robertson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892).

**The fall as a slide back toward nothing.** When man turned from God, he began to return to his natural state. In Robertson's translation (section 4):

> "For transgression of the commandment was turning them back to their natural state, so that just as they have had their being out of nothing, so also, as might be expected, they might look for corruption into nothing in the course of time."

**Corruption.** The Greek is *phthorá* (φθορά): decay, dissolution, the undoing of a thing. **For Athanasius the human problem is not first a legal debt but a mortal disease**: human nature was wasting away toward non-existence, and sin multiplied as it went. He describes the spread of sin through the world in vivid terms in section 5.

**God's dilemma.** Athanasius then sets out what he calls the "dilemma" of God (section 6), in which two things seem to pull against each other:

| On one side | On the other |
| --- | --- |
| **God's goodness**: "it were not worthy of God's goodness that the things He had made should waste away" | **God's truth**: God had said that transgression would bring death, and "God would not be true, if, when He had said we should die, man died not" |

**Why repentance was not enough.** Could God simply call men to repent? Athanasius answers (section 7) that **repentance does not call men back from what is their nature; it merely stays them from acts of sin.** "Now, if there were merely a misdemeanour in question, and not a consequent corruption, repentance were well enough." But nature itself had been corrupted, and needed to be restored.

**The answer, in outline.** Only the Word who first made man from nothing could re-create him. **"None could renew but He Who had created"**, as Robertson's chapter summary puts it. The Word would take a body capable of death, die in the place of all, and by His own life overcome corruption from within. Lessons 9 and 10 read his answer.

**Why this passage matters.** It shows why Orthodox teaching speaks of salvation as **life from death, incorruption from corruption, and re-creation**, and why it insists that only God Himself could save.
The promise: Christ foretold in the Old:
The Church reads the whole Old Testament as pointing to Christ. Some passages promise Him outright; others foreshadow Him in figures.

**The first gospel.** After the fall God says to the serpent (Genesis 3:15, Brenton's Septuagint, 1851):

> "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman and between thy seed and her seed, he shall watch against thy head, and thou shalt watch against his heel."

The Fathers read the woman's seed as Christ, born of a woman, and the wound to the serpent's head as His victory over the devil. St Irenaeus already reads it this way in the second century.

**The sign of the virgin.** Isaiah 7:14, in Brenton's Septuagint:

> "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb, and shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name Emmanuel."

The Septuagint's *parthénos* (παρθένος) means "virgin". Matthew 1:23 quotes this text of the birth of Christ. *Emmanuel* means "God with us".

**Prophecy and type.** The Church reads the Old Testament in two ways:

| Kind | What it is | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Prophecy** | words that foretell Christ | Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 53, the suffering servant; Micah 5:2, Bethlehem; Psalm 22, the crucifixion |
| **Type** (*týpos*, τύπος) | a person, event or thing that foreshadows Him | Adam; Isaac carried wood up the mountain; the Passover lamb; Jonah in the whale three days; the bronze serpent lifted up (John 3:14) |

**Christ Himself read Scripture so.** After the Resurrection He explained to the disciples "in all the scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27, KJV). **The Orthodox Church reads the Old Testament through this lens: Christ is its key.** Stage 5 teaches typology in full.

**Types of the Theotokos.** The Church also sees Mary foreshadowed: the burning bush that was not consumed (Exodus 3), the ladder of Jacob joining heaven and earth (Genesis 28), the closed gate of Ezekiel 44, through which only the Lord passes. These readings appear in the Old Testament readings at Vespers of her feasts.

**The Messiah.** Israel awaited a **Messiah** (Hebrew *Mashiach*, "anointed"; Greek *Christós*, Χριστός): a king from David's line, a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), a priest after the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4). **The Church confesses that Jesus fulfils all three, in a way beyond what was expected** (Lesson 26).

**Why the Old Testament matters.** The Gospel did not arrive out of nowhere. **The God who became man in Christ is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the whole history of Israel is the preparation for His coming.** The Fathers called this the *praeparatio evangelica*, the preparation for the Gospel.
\"One Lord Jesus Christ\": the names and:
Each name the Creed and Scripture give Christ teaches something about who He is.

**The main names and titles:**

| Name | Origin | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Jesus** | Hebrew *Yeshua*, Greek *Iēsoûs* (Ἰησοῦς) | "the Lord saves"; given by the angel (Matthew 1:21) |
| **Christ** | Greek *Christós*, Hebrew *Mashiach* | "the Anointed One", the Messiah |
| **Lord** | Greek *Kýrios* (Κύριος) | the Septuagint's word for the divine Name (Stage 2) |
| **Son of God** | | the eternal Son, of one essence with the Father |
| **Only-begotten** | Greek *monogenḗs* (μονογενής) | the unique Son, not one son among many |
| **Son of Man** | Daniel 7:13 | Christ's own favourite title: the heavenly figure who receives the Kingdom, and the one who truly shares our humanity |
| **Word** | Greek *Lógos* (Λόγος) | the eternal Word of the Father (next lesson) |
| **Emmanuel** | Isaiah 7:14 | "God with us" |

**On every icon.** An icon of Christ carries the letters **IC XC**, the first and last letters of *Iēsoûs Christós*, and on the halo **Ο Ω Ν**, "the One who is". The two together say: **this man, Jesus, is the Messiah, and He is God.** The words **IC XC NIKA**, "Jesus Christ conquers", are stamped on the Eucharistic bread.

**Peter's confession.** At Caesarea Philippi Christ asked the apostles who they said He was. Peter answered: "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:16, KJV). **The Church's whole Christology is the unfolding of that sentence.**

**"One Lord".** The Creed says *one* Lord Jesus Christ. The word guards against a later error (Lesson 13): that the eternal Son and the man Jesus were two different subjects. **There is one Lord, and He is both the eternal Son and the man born of Mary.**

**The Jesus Prayer.** The names are prayed as well as confessed. The **Jesus Prayer**, which in its usual form asks the Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, to have mercy on me, a sinner, gathers the main titles into one sentence: Lord, Jesus, Christ, Son of God. Stage 10 teaches it in full. **To pray it is to confess the whole of Christology in a breath.**

**The Name of Jesus.** The Church honours the Name itself, following Philippians 2:10, "at the name of Jesus every knee should bow" (KJV). She keeps the feast of the Circumcision of Christ, when He was named, on 1 January. How far the Name itself is to be venerated became a dispute among Russian monks on Mount Athos in 1912–1913, the "name-glorifiers" (*imiaslavie*) controversy; Orthodox writers still differ in their judgement of it, and it is treated in Stage 11.
The eternal Word: \"In the beginning was:
Before He was born of Mary, the Son existed eternally with the Father. St John's Gospel calls Him the Word.

**The text.** "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1, KJV).

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| **"In the beginning"** | echoes Genesis 1:1; the Word was already there when all things began |
| **"was the Word"** | *was*, not *came to be*: the Word did not begin |
| **"with God"** | Greek *pros ton Theón*, "toward God": distinct from the Father, in relation to Him |
| **"the Word was God"** | the Word is truly God |

**The Greek.** *Lógos* (Λόγος) means "word", "reason", "account". Greek philosophers, beginning with Heraclitus, used it for the rational order of the cosmos, and Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish thinker of the first century, for God's agent in creation. **St John uses the word his readers knew and fills it with a meaning none of them had: the Logos is a Person, is God, and became flesh.** (The **Philosophy** curriculum's lessons on Heraclitus and on Philo show the background.)

**Begotten before all ages.** The Creed says the Son is "begotten of his Father before all worlds". **His begetting is eternal**: there was never a time when the Father was without His Word (Stage 2). The Word is begotten as a word is spoken, without passion or division, the Fathers say, and the Father is never "wordless".

**Through Him all things were made.** "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" (John 1:3, KJV). **The Word is the Father's agent in creation**, as the Spirit is its perfecter. This is why St Athanasius insists that **the one who saves us is the same one who made us**.

**The Word in the Old Testament.** The Fathers taught that the appearances of God in the Old Testament, to Abraham at Mamre, to Moses in the bush, to Isaiah in the Temple, were appearances of the Word before His Incarnation. This is why icons write *ho Ōn* on Christ's halo.

**The Image of the Father.** St Paul calls Christ "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15, KJV), and Hebrews "the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person" (Hebrews 1:3, KJV). The Fathers took *image* (*eikṓn*) here in the fullest sense: **the Son is the perfect Image of the Father, equal to Him.** Humanity is made "according to" this Image (Stage 2).

**"And the Word was made flesh."** John 1:14 turns from eternity to history. **The same eternal Word became man.** The next lesson begins there.
\"Was incarnate and was made man\": the:
"And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" (John 1:14, KJV). This is the centre of the Christian faith.

**The words.** The Creed uses two verbs:

| Greek | English | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *sarkōthénta* (σαρκωθέντα) | "was incarnate" | took flesh; from *sárx*, flesh |
| *enanthrōpḗsanta* (ἐνανθρωπήσαντα) | "was made man" | became fully human; from *ánthrōpos*, human being |

**The second verb was added for a reason.** "Flesh" could be misread as a body only, as if the Word had taken a body without a human soul. **"Was made man" says He became a complete human being**, body, soul and mind (Lesson 12).

**Who became man.** **The Person who became man is the eternal Son, one of the Holy Trinity.** Not the Father, not the Spirit, not the divine essence in general. The Son did not cease to be God; He did not change into a man as water changes into steam. St Gregory the Theologian puts it: **"What He was He continued to be; what He was not He took to Himself"** (Third Theological Oration, section 19; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894).

**By the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.** The Creed of 381 adds that He "was incarnate by the Holy Ghost and the Virgin Mary". **The Incarnation is the work of the whole Trinity**: the Father sends, the Spirit overshadows, the Son takes flesh. Mary's free consent, "be it unto me according to thy word" (Luke 1:38, KJV), is part of the event. The Church celebrates it on the **Annunciation, 25 March**.

**The self-emptying.** St Paul writes that Christ, "being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men" (Philippians 2:6–7, KJV). The Greek for "made himself of no reputation" is *ekénōsen*, "emptied Himself", from which comes ***kénōsis*** (κένωσις). **The Fathers read the self-emptying not as the Word giving up His divinity, but as His humbling Himself to take our lowly state.**

**The Nativity.** The Church celebrates the birth of Christ on **25 December**. St Gregory the Theologian's Christmas sermon (Oration 38) opens: "Christ is born, glorify Him. Christ from heaven, go out to meet Him. Christ on earth; be exalted" (tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894). These words open St Cosmas the Hymnographer's Nativity canon, sung from 21 November onward.

**A hymn of the Incarnation.** At every Divine Liturgy the Church sings the hymn "Only-begotten Son", attributed to the Emperor Justinian in the sixth century (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906):

> "O Only-begotten Son and Word of God! Thou who art immortal yet didst deign for our salvation to become incarnate of the Holy Birth-giver of God and ever-virgin Mary; and without change of essence wast made man; who also wast crucified for us, O Christ our God, trampling down Death by death; who art one of the Holy Trinity, and art glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit: Save us."

**It is a whole Christology in one hymn.**
Why God became man: St Athanasius and St:
The Creed says He came down "for us men and for our salvation". The Fathers explain what that salvation is, and why only the Incarnation could bring it.

**The answer of St Irenaeus.** In the second century St Irenaeus of Lyons wrote that the Word of God "did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself" (*Against Heresies* Book 5, preface; tr. Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885).

**He explains why** (*Against Heresies* 3.19.1, same translation):

> "For it was for this end that the Word of God was made man, and He who was the Son of God became the Son of man, that man, having been taken into the Word, and receiving the adoption, might become the son of God. For by no other means could we have attained to incorruptibility and immortality, unless we had been united to incorruptibility and immortality."

**The answer of St Athanasius.** A century and a half later Athanasius says the same in fewer words: **"For He was made man that we might be made God"** (*On the Incarnation* 54.3; tr. Archibald Robertson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892). This is the most quoted sentence in Orthodox theology on salvation.

**What "made God" means.** It does not mean becoming God by nature, or becoming a fourth person of the Trinity. **It means sharing by grace in the divine life: incorruption, immortality, holiness, love.** The Church calls this *theosis* (Lessons 24–25).

**Why the Incarnation, and not some other way.** The Fathers give several reasons, which complement each other:

| Reason | Explanation |
| --- | --- |
