| **Only life can overcome death** | corruption is a disease of nature; it must be healed from inside by union with incorruptible life |
| **Only the Creator can re-create** | the Word who made man from nothing can make him anew (Athanasius) |
| **Union requires both natures** | to unite man to God, the Saviour must be both |
| **Recapitulation** | Christ goes through every stage of human life and gathers it up, undoing Adam's disobedience by His obedience (Irenaeus' *anakephalaíōsis*, ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, "summing up") |
| **Revelation** | He shows us the invisible Father in a visible face (Athanasius 54.3) |

**Recapitulation.** **Christ is the new Adam**: where the first Adam disobeyed at a tree, the second obeyed on a tree; where Eve listened to the fallen angel, Mary listened to Gabriel. Irenaeus pairs Eve and Mary in exactly this way.

**Would the Word have become man without the fall?** Orthodox writers differ. Some, following hints in St Maximus the Confessor, hold that **union of God and man was God's purpose from the beginning**, so the Incarnation was willed before and apart from sin, though the Cross was made necessary by it. Others, with the many Fathers who speak only of the actual history, hold the question idle: the Incarnation was "for our salvation", as the Creed says. Both agree that God's love, not the fall, is the deepest reason for it.

**The point to keep.** **The Incarnation is not a rescue plan bolted on to creation. It is the union of God and man in one Person, which heals what was broken and fulfils what was begun.**
Reading: St Athanasius, On the Incarnati:
Two passages from the classic treatise on why God became man, read closely.

**Who.** St Athanasius of Alexandria (about 296–373), bishop for forty-five years and five times exiled for the faith of Nicaea, wrote *On the Incarnation of the Word* as a young man, perhaps before the Arian controversy broke out, perhaps in the 330s. It was written for a friend, to explain the faith simply. In the twentieth century C. S. Lewis wrote a well-known introduction to a modern translation, but the version quoted here is the public-domain Victorian one.

**The text** (section 8.2–4; tr. Archibald Robertson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892):

> "He took pity on our race, and had mercy on our infirmity, and condescended to our corruption, and, unable to bear that death should have the mastery — lest the creature should perish, and His Father's handiwork in men be spent for nought — He takes unto Himself a body, and that of no different sort from ours. For He did not simply will to become embodied, or will merely to appear."

> "And thus taking from our bodies one of like nature, because all were under penalty of the corruption of death He gave it over to death in the stead of all, and offered it to the Father — doing this, moreover, of His loving-kindness..."

**And the summary** (section 54.3, same translation):

> "For He was made man that we might be made God; and He manifested Himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father; and He endured the insolence of men that we might inherit immortality."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"had mercy on our infirmity"** | the motive is compassion; the human condition is a sickness |
| **"unable to bear that death should have the mastery"** | the enemy is death and corruption |
| **"of no different sort from ours"** | a real human body, not a phantom |
| **"not simply will to become embodied, or... merely to appear"** | against those who said Christ only seemed human (Docetism) |
| **"in the stead of all"** | He dies on behalf of all, in their place |
| **"offered it to the Father"** | the death is a sacrifice, offered in love |
| **"He was made man that we might be made God"** | the purpose: *theosis* |
| **"that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father"** | the Incarnation reveals the Father |
| **"that we might inherit immortality"** | the fruit: incorruption, life |

**The image of the king.** In section 9 Athanasius gives a comparison: when a great king enters a city and lives in one house, the whole city is honoured and protected from bandits. **"So, too, has it been with the Monarch of all"**: by dwelling in one human body, the Word has protected the whole race.

**Why this text matters.** **It shows that, for the Fathers, the Incarnation, the Cross and theosis are one act of love**: the Word takes our nature to die our death and give us His life.
Truly God: the divinity of Christ:
The first thing the Church confesses about Christ is that He is God, of one essence with the Father. This lesson gathers the evidence and the reasons.

**The witness of Scripture:**

| Text | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| "the Word was God" (John 1:1, KJV) | the Word is God |
| "I and my Father are one" (John 10:30, KJV) | unity with the Father |
| "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58, KJV) | eternal existence, and the divine Name |
| "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28, KJV) | Thomas' confession after the Resurrection |
| "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily" (Colossians 2:9, KJV) | the whole Godhead in Christ |
| "in the form of God... equal with God" (Philippians 2:6) | equal with the Father before the Incarnation |

**The witness of His acts.** Christ forgives sins, which only God can do (Mark 2:7). He accepts worship. He commands the wind and sea. He raises the dead by His own word. He speaks of the angels as "his" angels. **No prophet ever acted so.**

**The witness of worship.** From the beginning Christians prayed to Christ. In about 112 a Roman governor, Pliny the Younger, reported to the Emperor Trajan that the Christians met before dawn and sang a hymn to Christ as to a god (a paraphrase of his letter). The first Christians, Jews who knew that only God may be worshipped, worshipped Him.

**Why it matters for salvation.** St Athanasius' chief argument against Arius was this: **if Christ were a creature, He could not unite us to God, because a creature cannot give what it does not possess by nature.** Only one who is God can make us partakers of God. The divinity of Christ is not an extra honour; it is the ground of our salvation.

**One of the Holy Trinity.** The Fifth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople II, 553) put it sharply in the tenth of its anathemas (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900):

> "If anyone does not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ who was crucified in the flesh is true God and the Lord of Glory and one of the Holy Trinity: let him be anathema."

**The one who hung on the Cross is God the Son.** This is why the Church sings on Holy Friday of the Creator hanging on the tree, and why the Theotokos is the Mother of God.

**Divinity is not diminished by the Incarnation.** St Gregory the Theologian, in his Third Theological Oration (section 20; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894), sets Christ's human and divine acts side by side:

> "He hungered — but He fed thousands; yea, He is the Bread that gives life, and That is of heaven. He thirsted — but He cried, If any man thirst, let him come unto Me and drink."

**The pattern of the whole passage.** Each human weakness is matched by a divine act. **The same Christ hungers as man and feeds thousands as God**, which is the doctrine of Lesson 16.
Truly man: a human body, soul and mind:
Christ is not God disguised as a man, nor God in a human body without a human soul. He is fully, truly human.

**Two errors the Church rejected:**

| Error | Teacher | What it held |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Docetism** (*dokéō*, "to seem") | various groups in the 1st–2nd centuries | Christ only *seemed* to have a body and to suffer |
| **Apollinarianism** | Apollinaris of Laodicea (about 310–about 390) | Christ had a human body and lower soul, but **the divine Word took the place of the human mind** (*nous*) |

**Against Docetism.** The apostles insisted they had seen, heard and touched Him (1 John 1:1). St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom early in the second century, argued that if Christ only seemed to suffer, his own suffering for Christ was pointless. **Christ was born, ate, slept, wept, bled and died. His body was real.**

**Against Apollinaris: the great rule.** Apollinaris thought a human mind would make Christ changeable and sinful. St Gregory the Theologian answered him in his first Letter to Cledonius (Letter 101; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894):

> "For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved. If only half Adam fell, then that which Christ assumes and saves may be half also; but if the whole of his nature fell, it must be united to the whole nature of Him that was begotten, and so be saved as a whole."

**The principle.** **Whatever part of human nature Christ did not take, He did not heal.** The mind is where sin begins; if He had no human mind, our minds would be unhealed. So Christ has everything human: body, soul, mind, will, emotions. The Council of Constantinople (381) condemned Apollinarianism.

**What Christ's humanity included:**

| Human feature | In the Gospels |
| --- | --- |
| **Growth** | He "increased in wisdom and stature" (Luke 2:52, KJV) |
| **Emotion** | He wept at Lazarus' tomb (John 11:35); was moved with compassion |
| **Bodily need** | hunger, thirst, weariness, sleep |
| **Suffering** | agony in Gethsemane; scourging; the Cross |
| **A human will** | "not my will, but thine, be done" (Luke 22:42, KJV): Lesson 17 |
| **Death** | He truly died, His soul separated from His body |

**Like us in all things but sin.** "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15, KJV). **Sin is not part of human nature as God made it; it is its corruption.** So Christ, being sinless, is not less human than we are but more fully human, humanity as it was meant to be.

**Blameless passions.** The Fathers distinguish **"blameless passions"**, hunger, tiredness, grief, fear of death, which Christ took on, from **sinful passions**, which He did not. He accepted the first freely, for our sake.

**Why it matters.** **The whole of our humanity, body and mind, is healed because the whole of it was taken by God.** This is the reason Orthodox spirituality never despises the body, and why it hopes for the resurrection of the body.
The Theotokos: Ephesus (431) and the Mot:
The title the Church gives the Virgin Mary is a statement about Christ. It was defended at the Third Ecumenical Council.

**The word.** *Theotókos* (Θεοτόκος), from *Theós*, "God", and *tíktō*, "to give birth": **"she who gave birth to God"**, usually rendered "Mother of God" or "Birth-giver of God". The title was in use well before the fifth century, in prayer and in the Fathers.

**Already in Scripture.** Elizabeth greets Mary: "And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" (Luke 1:43, KJV). "My Lord" here is the title of God.

**The dispute.** In 428 **Nestorius** became Archbishop of Constantinople. He objected to *Theotokos*: Mary, he said, gave birth to the man Jesus, in whom God the Word dwelt, not to God. He proposed *Christotókos*, "Christ-bearer". **St Cyril of Alexandria** (died 444) saw at once what was at stake: **if Mary did not give birth to God, then the one she bore was not God; and then the man Jesus and the eternal Word are two subjects, two sons, side by side.**

**The council.** The **Council of Ephesus (431)** deposed Nestorius and received Cyril's teaching. Cyril's first anathema states it (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900):

> "If anyone will not confess that the Emmanuel is very God, and that therefore the Holy Virgin is the Mother of God (Θεοτόκος), inasmuch as in the flesh she bore the Word of God made flesh [as it is written, The Word was made flesh] let him be anathema."

**What the title says, and what it does not:**

| It says | It does not say |
| --- | --- |
| the one she bore **is God**, the eternal Son | that Mary is the source of the divine nature |
| there is **one subject** in Christ, God the Word made flesh | that Mary existed before God |
| she gave birth to Him **in the flesh** | that Mary is divine |

**A safeguard of Christology.** **The title Theotokos is first a confession about Christ: one person, truly God, truly born.** Honour to Mary follows from it.

**In worship.** Almost every Orthodox service ends with a hymn to the Theotokos, and her name is joined to Christ's in the litanies: "Calling to remembrance our most holy, undefiled, most blessed and glorious Lady, the Birth-giver of God and ever-virgin Mary, with all the Saints, let us commend ourselves, and each other, and all our life unto Christ our God" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906). The best known hymn to her, sung at every Liturgy and in Matins, reads (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906):

> "More honourable than the Cherubim, and beyond compare more glorious than the Seraphim, thou who without defilement barest God the Word, true Birth-giver of God, we magnify thee."

**The icon of the Theotokos.** She is almost always shown holding Christ. The letters **ΜΡ ΘΥ** (*Mḗtēr Theoû*, "Mother of God") mark her icon. **She is never shown alone as the centre; she points to her Son**, as in the *Hodigitria* ("she who shows the way") icon, where her hand directs the viewer to Him.
The Ever-Virgin Mary in Orthodox teachin:
The Church honours the Theotokos as ever-virgin, all-holy, and the first of the saints. This lesson sets out what is dogma, what is universal tradition, and where Orthodox writers differ.

**Ever-virgin.** *Aeipárthenos* (ἀειπάρθενος), "ever-virgin". **The Church teaches that Mary was a virgin before, during and after the birth of Christ.** The Fifth Ecumenical Council (553) speaks of "the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary" (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900), and the title is in every Liturgy.

**The "brothers of the Lord".** The Gospels mention Christ's brothers (Mark 6:3). The common Eastern explanation, found in St Epiphanius of Salamis in the fourth century and in the Protoevangelium of James, is that they were **Joseph's children by an earlier marriage**. Another, found in St Jerome, is that they were cousins. Both keep the ever-virginity.

**All-holy.** The Church calls her ***Panagía*** (Παναγία), "all-holy", and sings of her as "most pure" and "spotless". **The common Orthodox teaching is that she never committed a personal sin**, by her own free cooperation with grace. A few early Fathers, among them St John Chrysostom, spoke of small human failings in her; the Church's hymnography as a whole speaks of her as without sin.

**Born under the ancestral condition.** The Orthodox Church teaches that Mary was born **subject, like all Adam's descendants, to mortality**, and was purified and prepared by the Holy Spirit, above all at the Annunciation. **The Orthodox Church does not accept the Roman Catholic dogma of the Immaculate Conception defined in 1854**, which concerns her conception free from original sin. The difference rests partly on the different understandings of ancestral sin (Lesson 3).

**The Dormition.** The Church celebrates the **Dormition**, *Koímēsis* (Κοίμησις), "falling asleep", on **15 August**. **The tradition, expressed in the feast's hymns and icon, is that she truly died, was buried, and was taken up in body to her Son.** This is universal Orthodox tradition, taught in the services; it has not been defined by a council, and the Orthodox Church has not made it a dogma in the way Rome did in 1950.

**Her feasts.** Four of the Twelve Great Feasts are hers:

| Feast | Date |
| --- | --- |
| **Nativity of the Theotokos** | 8 September |
| **Entry of the Theotokos into the Temple** | 21 November |
| **Annunciation** (also a feast of Christ) | 25 March |
| **Dormition** | 15 August |

The Slavic churches also keep the **Protection** (*Pokrov*) on 1 October.

**Why the Church honours her.** **She is the one through whom God became man, the first to receive Christ, and the image of what every Christian is called to be: a person entirely given to God.** St Irenaeus called her the new Eve, whose obedience undid Eve's disobedience. "From henceforth all generations shall call me blessed" (Luke 1:48, KJV).

**Honour, not worship.** The Church distinguishes **worship** (*latreía*, λατρεία), given to God alone, from **veneration** (*proskýnēsis*, προσκύνησις), given to saints and icons. Mary receives the highest veneration, but never the worship due to God.
The Definition of Chalcedon (451): one p:
After Ephesus, a new error arose from the opposite side. The Fourth Ecumenical Council answered it with the most precise statement of who Christ is.

**The new error.** **Eutyches** (about 380–456), an archimandrite in Constantinople, eager to defend Christ's unity against Nestorius, taught that after the union Christ had **one nature only**, the human as if swallowed up in the divine. This is called **Monophysitism** in its extreme form, or Eutychianism.

**The Tome of Leo.** Pope Leo's letter to Archbishop Flavian, the *Tome*, set out two natures in one person; the Robber Council (449) refused it and Chalcedon received it.

**The Definition** (Council of Chalcedon, 451; tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900):

> "Following the holy Fathers we teach with one voice that the Son [of God] and our Lord Jesus Christ is to be confessed as one and the same [Person], that he is perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, very God and very man, of a reasonable soul and [human] body consisting, consubstantial with the Father as touching his Godhead, and consubstantial with us as touching his manhood; made in all things like us, sin only excepted..."

> "This one and the same Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son [of God] must be confessed to be in two natures, unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably [united], and that without the distinction of natures being taken away by such union, but rather the peculiar property of each nature being preserved and being united in one Person and subsistence..."

**The four adverbs.** The heart of the Definition is four Greek words, two against each error:

| Greek | English | Against |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ***asynchýtōs*** (ἀσυγχύτως) | unconfusedly | Eutyches: the natures are not mixed |
| ***atréptōs*** (ἀτρέπτως) | immutably, unchangeably | Eutyches: neither nature changes into the other |
| ***adiairétōs*** (ἀδιαιρέτως) | indivisibly | Nestorius: there are not two persons |
| ***achōrístōs*** (ἀχωρίστως) | inseparably | Nestorius: the natures are never apart |

**Two *homoousioi*.** **Christ is *homoousios* with the Father in His divinity and *homoousios* with us in His humanity.** Nicaea's word is used twice.

**Natures and person.** The Definition uses Stage 2's vocabulary: *phýsis* (φύσις), "nature", is what Christ is (divine and human); *hypóstasis* and *prósōpon*, "person", is who He is (the one Son). **In the Trinity: one nature, three persons. In Christ: two natures, one person.**

**The churches that did not receive Chalcedon.** The Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Syriac and Malankara churches did not accept the Definition, chiefly because they held St Cyril's formula "one incarnate nature of God the Word" and feared Chalcedon's "in two natures" leaned toward Nestorius. They also rejected Eutyches. Stage 7 tells this history and Stage 12 the modern dialogues between them and the Orthodox Church, which have produced agreed statements but not union.

**The point.** **Chalcedon does not explain the mystery of Christ. Like Nicaea, it fences it on both sides**: not two sons, not one mixed nature, but one Christ, truly God and truly man.
The hypostatic union and the exchange of:
How can one person be both God and man? The Church calls the union "hypostatic", and draws out a rule for how to speak of Christ.

**The hypostatic union.** *Hypostatikḗ hénōsis* (ὑποστατικὴ ἕνωσις), "union in the hypostasis". **The divine and human natures are united in the one Person, or hypostasis, of God the Word.** It is not a union of two persons by agreement or love, as between friends, nor a mixture of two natures into a third, but the eternal Son making a human nature His own.

**Who the Person is.** **The one Person in Christ is the eternal Son of God.** He did not join Himself to an existing man; from the moment of conception, the humanity He took existed only as His. Later writers, among them St John of Damascus, said Christ's humanity is ***enhypóstatos*** (ἐνυπόστατος), "having its existence in a hypostasis": it is real and complete, but it exists in the Person of the Word, not as a separate human person.

**The Fifth Council's emphasis.** Constantinople II (553) read Chalcedon through St Cyril: **the subject of all Christ did and suffered is God the Word.** Its fifth anathema says: "For since one of the Holy Trinity has been made man, viz.: God the Word, the Holy Trinity has not been increased by the addition of another person or hypostasis" (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900).

**The exchange of properties.** Because there is one Person, what belongs to either nature can be said of that Person. The Fathers call this ***antídosis tōn idiōmátōn*** (ἀντίδοσις τῶν ἰδιωμάτων), the **exchange** or **communication of properties**, Latin *communicatio idiomatum*.

| We may say | Because |
| --- | --- |
| **"God was born"** | the Person born of Mary is God |
| **"God died on the Cross"** | the Person who died in the flesh is God the Son |
| **"The man Jesus is eternal"** | the Person who is this man is eternal |
| **"The Lord of glory was crucified"** | St Paul's own phrase (1 Corinthians 2:8) |

**The rule has a limit.** We say "God died" *in the flesh*; we do not say the divine nature died or suffered. **Properties are exchanged between the natures in speech about the one Person, not merged in the natures themselves.**

**The paradoxes in hymns.** Orthodox hymnography lives by this rule. St Gregory the Theologian's sermon gives the pattern: "He was born — but He had been begotten: He was born of a woman — but she was a Virgin. The first is human, the second Divine" (Third Theological Oration, section 19; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894). The Holy Week hymns sing of the Creator hanging upon the tree.

**The deification of Christ's humanity.** In the union, Christ's human nature is not absorbed, but it is **penetrated by the divine energy and glorified**, as iron in fire glows with the fire's heat while remaining iron. This image, used by St John of Damascus and others, appears again in theosis (Lesson 25). **What happens to Christ's humanity is what is offered to ours.**

**Why it matters.** **The hypostatic union means that God has not only visited humanity but made a human nature His own forever.** The Son remains man, risen and ascended, and our humanity is now at the right hand of the Father.
Two wills and two energies: St Maximus a:
In the seventh century the Church had to decide whether Christ has one will or two. The answer came through the witness of a monk who suffered for it.

**The question.** If Christ is one person, does He have one will? An imperial compromise of the 630s, meant to reconcile those who had rejected Chalcedon, said He had **one energy** (*Monoenergism*) and then **one will** (*Monothelitism*, from *thélēma*, θέλημα, "will"). Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople and Emperor Heraclius promoted it; the *Ekthesis* of 638 made it imperial policy.

**St Maximus the Confessor.** St Maximus (about 580–662), a monk, saw that **one will would mean one nature**, and so deny Chalcedon by the back door. **Will belongs to nature, not to person.** Christ has a divine nature and a human nature, so He has a divine will and a human will. A human nature without a human will would be incomplete, and what is not assumed is not healed. For refusing to accept the imperial doctrine, Maximus had his tongue cut out and his right hand cut off, and died in exile in 662. The Church honours him as **the Confessor**, with feasts on 21 January and 13 August. St Sophronius of Jerusalem and Pope Martin I of Rome also suffered for the same faith.

**Gethsemane.** The key text: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done" (Luke 22:42, KJV). **Maximus reads this as Christ's human will, with its natural shrinking from death, freely and fully submitting to the divine will**, which is His own as God.

**The council.** The **Sixth Ecumenical Council, Constantinople III (680–681)**, decreed (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900):

> "We likewise declare that in him are two natural wills and two natural operations indivisibly, inconvertibly, inseparably, inconfusedly, according to the teaching of the holy Fathers. And these two natural wills are not contrary the one to the other (God forbid!) as the impious heretics assert, but his human will follows and that not as resisting and reluctant, but rather as subject to his divine and omnipotent will."

**Note the four adverbs again**, applied now to the wills and energies.

**The natural will and the gnomic will.** Maximus distinguished the **natural will** (*thélēma physikón*), the human faculty of willing what is good for one's nature, from the **gnomic will** (*gnṓmē*, γνώμη), the deliberating, hesitating choice of a person who does not clearly see the good. **Christ has a natural human will, but no gnomic will**, because He never hesitates between good and evil. (The **Philosophy** curriculum's lesson "Maximus the Confessor: the natural will and the deliberating will" treats this as philosophy of action.)

**Why it matters.** **Our salvation includes the healing of our will.** In Christ a human will for the first time is perfectly united to God's will, freely. That is the pattern of our own freedom being healed: not abolished, but brought into harmony with God.
Christ revealed: the Nativity and the Tr:
Two feasts of Christ show His divinity shining through His humanity: His birth, hidden and humble, and His Transfiguration, bright and glorious.

**The Nativity, 25 December.** God enters the world as a child in a cave, laid in a manger. **The Nativity icon** shows this: the Child in swaddling clothes like grave-cloths, in a dark cave like a tomb, with the ox and the ass of Isaiah 1:3, the shepherds, the Magi, and Mary lying beside Him. Joseph sits apart, troubled, tempted by doubt. **The icon already points to the Cross and the Resurrection.** The feast is prepared by a forty-day fast from 15 November.

**The Nativity and the Theophany.** In the East the Nativity and Theophany were once kept together on 6 January; Constantinople adopted 25 December for the Nativity in the late fourth century, and St Gregory the Theologian's Oration 38 (380 or 381) is one of the earliest witnesses there. Theophany (Stage 2) now reveals the Trinity at the Jordan.

**The Transfiguration, 6 August.** Christ took Peter, James and John up a high mountain, which tradition identifies as **Mount Tabor**. "And his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light" (Matthew 17:2, KJV). Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets, appeared and talked with Him, and the Father's voice spoke from a bright cloud.

**The hymns of the feast** (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906). The troparion:

> "Thou wast transfigured upon the Mount, O Christ-God, revealing unto thy disciples thy glory in so far as they were able to bear it. Let thy light everlasting illumine us sinners also; through the prayers of the Birth-giver of God. O Light-giver, glory to thee!"

And the kontakion:

> "Upon the Mount wast thou transfigured, and thy disciples, in so far as they were qualified, beheld thy glory, O Christ-God; that when they should see thee crucified they might comprehend that thy suffering was voluntary..."

**What the Transfiguration teaches:**

| Truth | How |
| --- | --- |
| **Christ's divinity** | the light is His own, not reflected like Moses' face |
| **His humanity glorified** | His human body shines with divine light |
| **The Passion is voluntary** | the disciples see His glory before they see Him crucified |
| **Our destiny** | the light He shows is the glory promised to the saints |

**The uncreated light.** The Fathers taught that the light of Tabor was not a created light, but **the uncreated glory of God**, shining through Christ's humanity. Christ did not change; **the disciples' eyes were opened**, "in so far as they were able". St Gregory Palamas made this the centre of his teaching on the energies (Stage 2). The hesychast saints said they saw the same light in prayer.

**The feast of first fruits.** On 6 August grapes and other fruit are blessed in church. **The fruits of the earth are offered as a sign that the whole creation is to be transfigured.**

**Why the two belong together.** **At the Nativity, God hides His glory in our poverty; at the Transfiguration, He shows our nature filled with His glory.** Both are the same mystery of the Incarnation.
The Cross: the voluntary Passion:
"And was crucified also for us under Pontius Pilate. He suffered and was buried." The Church sees the Cross not as a defeat reversed by the Resurrection but as itself the place of victory.

**The facts.** Jesus was crucified outside Jerusalem under **Pontius Pilate**, Roman prefect of Judaea from 26 to 36. The Creed names Pilate to fix the event in history. The Gospels place the crucifixion on a Friday at Passover; scholars most often date it to AD 30 or 33.

**Voluntary.** Christ says: "No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again" (John 10:18, KJV). **The Passion is voluntary**, the Transfiguration kontakion says. Christ is not a victim overtaken by events but the one who freely goes to death.

**Who suffered.** By the exchange of properties (Lesson 16), **God the Son suffered and died in the flesh**, while the divine nature remained impassible. The Church does not shrink from saying, with the hymn "Only-begotten Son", that "one of the Holy Trinity" was crucified.

**Why the Cross?** The Fathers give many answers together, the subject of Lesson 20. In brief: **on the Cross the Son offers His perfect obedience and love to the Father on behalf of all, takes death into Himself, and overthrows the devil's hold on mankind.**

**"It is finished."** Christ's last word in John's Gospel: "It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost" (John 19:30, KJV). The Greek *tetélestai* (τετέλεσται) means "it has been completed, brought to its goal": the work for which He came.

**The Cross in Orthodox worship:**

| Occasion | What the Church does |
| --- | --- |
| **Every Wednesday and Friday** | fasting, remembering the betrayal and the Cross |
| **Holy Friday** | the Passion Gospels read at Matins; the *Epitaphios*, the embroidered image of Christ in the tomb, carried in procession |
| **The Exaltation of the Cross**, 14 September | recalls the finding of the Cross by St Helen in Jerusalem in the fourth century; a strict fast day |
| **The Sunday of the Cross** | the third Sunday of Great Lent, at the midpoint of the fast |
| **The sign of the cross** | made by every Orthodox Christian many times a day (Stage 1, Basil's unwritten traditions) |

**The life-giving Cross.** The Church calls the Cross **"life-giving"**, not only "holy". The tree of death in Paradise is answered by the tree of life on Golgotha. **The Cross is venerated because it was the instrument of the victory over death.**

**The Cross and the Christian.** "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Galatians 2:20, KJV). The Christian takes up the Cross by self-denial, repentance and love. **Orthodox spirituality joins Cross and Resurrection**: the Great Lent leads to Pascha, the fast to the feast.
Ransom, sacrifice, victory and healing::
Scripture and the Fathers describe what Christ's death achieved in many images. The Orthodox Church holds them together rather than reducing them to one theory.

**The main images:**

| Image | Scripture | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ransom** | "to give his life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45, KJV) | we were captive, and Christ set us free at the cost of His life |
| **Sacrifice** | "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (John 1:29, KJV) | Christ is the true Passover lamb and the true High Priest, offering Himself |
| **Victory** | "that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil" (Hebrews 2:14, KJV) | Christ defeats death and the devil |
| **Healing** | "with his stripes we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5, KJV) | Christ cures the sickness of human nature |

**Ransom paid to whom?** St Gregory of Nyssa's *Catechetical Oration* pictures the devil taking the bait of Christ's humanity and caught on the hook of His divinity. **St Gregory the Theologian refused to say the ransom was paid either to the devil or to the Father.** In his Second Oration on Pascha he asks (Oration 45, section 22; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894):

> "To Whom was that Blood offered that was shed for us, and why was It shed? ... Is it not evident that the Father accepts Him, but neither asked for Him nor demanded Him; but on account of the Incarnation, and because Humanity must be sanctified by the Humanity of God, that He might deliver us Himself, and overcome the tyrant, and draw us to Himself by the mediation of His Son..."

**Victory over death.** The Paschal troparion, sung dozens of times at Pascha, puts the victory in one line (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906): **"Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down Death by death, and upon those in the tomb bestowing life."** Many modern writers see this victory as the centre of the Orthodox view.

**Legal language and where Orthodox differ.** In the West, St Anselm of Canterbury (in *Why God Became Man*, 1098) developed the idea of Christ making **satisfaction** to God's honour; later Protestant theology stressed **penal substitution**. Orthodox writers differ in how they treat such legal language:

1. **Some reject juridical theories as foreign to the Fathers.** Metropolitan Antony Khrapovitsky in the early twentieth century, and later Fr John Romanides and others, argued that the Orthodox view is about healing, love and victory, not satisfying divine justice.
2. **Others hold that legal and sacrificial language belongs to the tradition too**, when kept in place. St Athanasius himself says that Christ by His death "satisfied the debt" (*On the Incarnation* 9.2; tr. Archibald Robertson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892), and the services speak of the debt paid and the handwriting of sin torn up (Colossians 2:14). So did older catechisms such as Philaret's (1823).

Both agree that **God is not appeased by suffering for its own sake, and that the Cross is God's love in action.**

**No single image captures the mystery.** Each, taken alone and pressed too hard, distorts. The Church prays them all.
The descent into Hades:
Between His death and Resurrection, the Church teaches, Christ descended into Hades and set free those held there. It is the subject of the Orthodox icon of the Resurrection.

**Hades.** *Háidēs* (ᾍδης), in the Septuagint the word for Hebrew *Sheol*: **the realm of the dead**, where all who died before Christ awaited redemption, righteous and unrighteous alike. It is not the same as the final hell of the Last Judgement.

**Scripture.** "For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit: By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison" (1 Peter 3:18–19, KJV). Peter's Pentecost sermon says God raised Him, "having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it" (Acts 2:24, KJV). Ephesians 4:9 speaks of His descent "into the lower parts of the earth" (KJV).

**What happened.** **Christ's human soul, united to His divinity, went down to Hades while His body, also united to His divinity, lay in the tomb.** There He proclaimed the Gospel, broke the gates of Hades, and brought out the righteous of the Old Covenant, beginning with Adam and Eve.

**The icon of the Resurrection.** The Orthodox Church's icon of Pascha, the ***Anástasis*** (Ἀνάστασις, "Resurrection"), does not show Christ stepping out of the tomb. It shows:

| Detail | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Christ in white and gold**, in a mandorla of light | the risen Lord, shining with divine glory |
| **The broken gates of Hades** beneath His feet, in the shape of a cross | death's prison destroyed |
| **Scattered locks, keys and nails** | the bonds of death undone |
| **A bound figure in the darkness** | Death, or Hades, chained |
| **Adam and Eve** pulled from their tombs by the wrists | Christ raising fallen humanity, not by their strength but by His |
| **David, Solomon, John the Baptist** and others | the righteous of the Old Testament awaiting Him |

**Holy Saturday.** The Church calls Holy Saturday the "Blessed Sabbath", the day of Christ's rest in the tomb and His descent into Hades. **At its Vesperal Liturgy the dark vestments are changed for white.**

**St John Chrysostom's Paschal homily**, read at the end of Paschal Matins, describes Hades as embittered when it met Christ below, because it took a body and met God (a paraphrase; the homily is not in the public-domain books used here). **The descent is the moment death swallows what it cannot hold.**

**Who was saved?** The Fathers agree that Christ freed the righteous of the Old Testament. Whether His preaching in Hades offered salvation to others, and to whom, is a question **on which they differ**. Some, like St Gregory the Theologian and St Maximus, suggest that those who received His preaching were saved; the Church's hymns sometimes speak of Hades being emptied. **The Church holds the descent and the liberation as her teaching, and has not defined how widely it extended.**

**Why it matters.** **No place, not even death, is outside Christ's reach.** The Resurrection begins in the depths.
The Resurrection on the third day:
"And the third day he rose again according to the Scriptures." The Resurrection is the centre of Orthodox faith and the feast of feasts.

**The earliest witness.** St Paul, writing in the 50s, hands on what he had received: "For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3–4, KJV). He lists the witnesses, Peter, the Twelve, over five hundred at once, James, and himself.

**What the Church teaches:**

| Truth | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **A bodily resurrection** | the same body, now glorified: the tomb was empty; He ate and was touched |
| **A transformed body** | it passes through closed doors and is not always recognised: a body made fully alive by the Spirit |
| **Not a return to mortal life** | "Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him" (Romans 6:9, KJV); unlike Lazarus, who would die again |
| **The first fruits** | "now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept" (1 Corinthians 15:20, KJV): the beginning of the general resurrection |
| **By His own power** | He rose as God, and the Father raised Him; both are said in Scripture |

**The first witnesses.** **The Myrrh-bearing Women**, coming to anoint the body, were the first to find the empty tomb and to hear the angel. St Mary Magdalene, to whom Christ first appeared (John 20), is called **"equal to the apostles"** in the Orthodox Church. The Sunday of the Myrrh-bearers, two weeks after Pascha, honours them.

**Pascha.** The Orthodox Church calls the feast **Pascha** (Πάσχα), from the Hebrew *Pesach*, Passover: **Christ is the true Passover, passing from death to life and bringing us with Him.** It is the "feast of feasts", above even the Twelve Great Feasts. The Paschal troparion is sung over and over from the midnight service through the forty days to Ascension (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906):

> "Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down Death by death, and upon those in the tomb bestowing life."

**The Paschal greeting.** For forty days Orthodox Christians greet one another with the words Christ is risen, and answer that He is truly risen, in every language of the Church. The date of Pascha and the calendar question belong to Stage 6 and Stage 11.

**Every Sunday a little Pascha.** Sunday is the Lord's Day, the "eighth day", the day of the Resurrection. **The Sunday services of the Octoechos all celebrate the Resurrection**, in each of the eight tones, so that every week is shaped by Pascha.

**Why it matters.** "And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14, KJV). **The Resurrection shows that death is defeated, that Christ is who He said, and that human nature, body and soul, is destined for eternal life.** Stage 4 teaches the general resurrection that it promises.
Salvation in Orthodox teaching: grace, f:
What does it mean to be saved? The Orthodox answer is that salvation is union with God, begun now and completed in the age to come, by God's grace and our free cooperation.

**Salvation as a process and a gift.** The Greek *sōtēría* (σωτηρία) means rescue, safety and health. **In Orthodox teaching salvation is not only a verdict but a healing and a transformation**: being freed from sin, death and the devil, and being brought into communion with God. It has a beginning, baptism; a path, the life of the Church; and a fulfilment, the Kingdom.

**Past, present and future.** The New Testament speaks of salvation in all three tenses, and the Church keeps all three:

| Tense | Text | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **We have been saved** | Ephesians 2:8 | Christ has done all that is needed; in baptism we are united to Him |
| **We are being saved** | 1 Corinthians 1:18 | the healing goes on through the life of the Church |
| **We shall be saved** | Romans 5:9–10 | it is completed at the resurrection and judgement |

**Grace.** *Cháris* (χάρις), "grace", in Orthodox teaching is **God's own uncreated energy, His life given to us** (Stage 2). It is not a created substance, nor merely God's favourable attitude. **To receive grace is to receive God Himself.** Salvation is entirely His gift: no one can save himself.

**Synergy.** But God does not save anyone against his will. *Synergeía* (συνέργεια), "working together", names the **cooperation of divine grace and human freedom**. St Paul says: "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure" (Philippians 2:12–13, KJV). **God's work comes first and does almost everything; our part is to consent, to turn, to keep turning.** The Fathers' image is of a sick man who must still take the medicine he could never make.

**Faith and works.** Orthodox teaching does not set faith against works. **Faith is a living trust that acts**, and works are faith's fruit, done by grace. Prayer, fasting, almsgiving and the keeping of the commandments are not ways of earning salvation but the means by which we cooperate with God's healing.

**The Church and the Mysteries.** Salvation is received **in the Church**, the Body of Christ, above all through the Mysteries (sacraments): baptism, chrismation and the Eucharist (Stage 4). **To be saved is to be in Christ, and Christ is found in His Body.**

**Assurance and humility.** Orthodox Christians do not usually speak of being "already saved" as a settled possession. They hope with confidence in God's mercy, while remaining watchful, because freedom remains and one can turn away. **The saints called themselves the first of sinners**, because the nearer the light, the clearer one's own darkness.

**Who can be saved?** The Church teaches that Christ is the only Saviour and that salvation is given through Him and His Church. How God deals with those who never knew Christ is not defined; Orthodox writers commonly say, in a saying of uncertain origin, that **we know where the Church is, but do not presume to say where she is not**. This question is taken up again in Stage 4.
Theosis: becoming by grace what God is b:
The goal of salvation, in Orthodox teaching, is not only forgiveness but deification: union with God so close that the Fathers dared to say that man becomes god by grace.

**The word.** *Théōsis* (θέωσις), "deification", or *theopoíēsis*. **Theosis is the participation of the whole human person in the life of God, by grace, while remaining a creature.**

**Scripture.** St Peter writes: "Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust" (2 Peter 1:4, KJV). Christ quotes Psalm 82:6: "I said, Ye are gods" (John 10:34, KJV). St Paul speaks of being changed "from glory to glory" into Christ's image (2 Corinthians 3:18, KJV) and of Christians as "joint-heirs with Christ" (Romans 8:17, KJV).

**The Fathers, in one voice:**

| Father | Words |
| --- | --- |
| **St Irenaeus** (about 180) | the Word "did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself" (tr. Roberts and Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885) |
| **St Athanasius** (4th century) | "For He was made man that we might be made God" (tr. Robertson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892) |
| **St Gregory the Theologian** (380) | Christ's humanity was united to God "in order that I too might be made God so far as He is made Man" (Oration 29.19; tr. Browne and Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894) |
| **St Maximus the Confessor** (7th century) | in paraphrase: God and man are patterns of each other; as far as God became man out of love, so far man is made god by grace |

**The rule: by grace, not by nature.** **We become by grace what God is by nature**: a common formula in Orthodox teaching, drawn from St Maximus and others. God remains God; we remain creatures. What is given is participation in His life, holiness, incorruption and love, never His essence (next lesson).

**Theosis is Christ's life in us.** Theosis is not a separate project beside salvation; **it is salvation in its fullness.** It happens because in Christ the divine and human natures were united; what His humanity received in the union, ours receives by being joined to Him.

**How it happens.** Through:

1. **Baptism and chrismation**: union with Christ and the gift of the Spirit.
2. **The Eucharist**: receiving the deified Body and Blood of Christ.
3. **The commandments and the virtues**: love, humility, purity, mercy.
4. **Prayer**: above all the prayer of the heart.
5. **Repentance and ascetic struggle**: purification of the passions.

These follow Stage 1's three stages: **purification, illumination, deification.**

**Theosis begins now.** The saints are those in whom it is visible already. The light seen around St Seraphim of Sarov (died 1833) by his disciple Nicholas Motovilov, who recorded it, is often cited as a modern witness. **Theosis is not only for monks**; every Christian is called to it.

**Theosis has no end.** St Gregory of Nyssa taught that because God is infinite, union with Him is an eternal growth: ***epéktasis*** (ἐπέκτασις), "stretching forward" (Philippians 3:13). **Even in the Kingdom, the saints go from glory to glory forever.**
Theosis without confusion: union with Go:
If man becomes god by grace, is the line between Creator and creature erased? Orthodox teaching answers no, and explains why with the distinction of essence and energies.

**The danger.** Many religions and philosophies speak of union with the divine as absorption: the drop merges into the ocean, the self dissolves. **Orthodox theosis is not that.** The human person remains a person and a creature, forever.

**Why there is no confusion.** Stage 2 taught that God's essence is unknowable and unshareable, while His uncreated energies are truly God and truly given. **We are united to God in His energies, never in His essence.** So:

| What is shared | What is not |
| --- | --- |
| God's life, glory, holiness, light, love | God's essence |
| real divine life, uncreated grace | becoming a fourth Person of the Trinity |
| union with God in Christ | ceasing to be a creature |

**The model is Christ.** In Christ the two natures are united **without confusion, without change** (Chalcedon), and His human nature is filled with divine glory without ceasing to be human. **Theosis is the same pattern extended to us by grace**: we are united to God without our nature being changed into His.

**Iron in the fire.** The Fathers' favourite image, used by St Maximus, St John of Damascus and St Gregory Palamas: **iron placed in fire glows, burns and gives light like fire, but remains iron.** The fire's energy penetrates the iron; the iron does not become the fire's nature. So the deified human being shines with God's light while remaining human.

**The person is not lost.** Lossky stressed that theosis concerns **the person**: the unique, free human being called by name, who meets God face to face. **Union with God does not dissolve the person but completes it.** The saints in the Kingdom are more themselves, not less.

**Uncreated grace.** Because grace is uncreated energy, **what deifies us is God Himself, not a created gift standing between us and Him.** This is one of the reasons the hesychast councils of the fourteenth century mattered so much: they defended the reality of theosis.

**Theosis and the body.** The Transfiguration showed it; the relics of saints are a sign of it; the resurrection will complete it (Stage 4). **Orthodox theosis is never an escape from the body but its glorification.**

**Theosis and love.** The content of theosis is above all **love**, since "God is love". St Maximus taught that through love man becomes by grace what God is. A deified person is not someone with special powers but someone in whom **the love of God has become his own**, extending even to enemies. St Silouan the Athonite (1866–1938), canonised in 1987, made love for enemies the test of the Holy Spirit's presence. Stage 12 teaches him.

**Emphases, not divisions.** Some Orthodox writers describe theosis chiefly as **participation in the energies**; others stress **communion of persons** with the Trinity in Christ, and warn against speaking of the energies as a substance to acquire.

**The key sentence.** **We become gods by grace, by union with God's uncreated energies in Christ, without ceasing to be human, without becoming His essence, and without end.**
Christ the Prophet, Priest and King:
The name "Christ" means anointed. In Israel, three kinds of person were anointed, and the Church confesses that Christ fulfils all three.

**The three offices.** Orthodox catechisms, such as St Philaret of Moscow's *Catechism* (1823), teach Christ's work under three headings. **"Christ" means "the Anointed"**, and in the Old Testament prophets, priests and kings were anointed:

| Office | Old Testament | Christ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Prophet** | Moses promised "a Prophet... like unto me" (Deuteronomy 18:15, KJV) | Christ reveals the Father and teaches the way of life; He is the Word Himself |
| **Priest** | Aaron and the priests offered sacrifices for the people | Christ offers Himself as the one perfect sacrifice and intercedes for us |
| **King** | David and his line ruled God's people | Christ rules over all, and His kingdom "shall have no end" |

**Prophet.** Christ is more than a prophet: prophets bring God's word; **He is God's Word.** He teaches with authority, "not as the scribes" (Matthew 7:29, KJV), and His teaching is completed by His life.

**Priest.** The Letter to the Hebrews is the great text: "Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession" (Hebrews 4:14, KJV). **Christ is both the priest and the offering.** The Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, in the priest's prayer during the Cherubic Hymn, says to Christ: "For it is thou who offerest and art offered, who receivest and art thyself received, O Christ our God" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906). Every Orthodox priest serves as an icon of Christ the one High Priest.

**One Mediator.** "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5, KJV). **Christ is the one Mediator because in His one Person God and man are united.** The prayers of the saints do not compete with this; they share in it, as members of His body.

**King.** Christ is King not as worldly rulers are. "My kingdom is not of this world" (John 18:36, KJV). He is crowned with thorns and enthroned on the Cross; Pilate's inscription read "JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS" (John 19:19, KJV). **His kingship is revealed in self-giving, and will be manifest to all at His coming in glory.** The Liturgy begins: "Blessed is the kingdom of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906).

**The Christian shares the three offices.** At chrismation each Christian is anointed with holy myron, and so shares in Christ's anointing: **prophet**, by confessing the faith; **priest**, by offering prayer and his own life to God; **king**, by ruling his passions. St Peter calls the Church "a royal priesthood" (1 Peter 2:9, KJV).

**Why this teaching helps.** It gathers Christ's work into one picture. **Christ teaches us (prophet), reconciles us (priest), and rules and protects us (king)**, and through Him we are made His people.
The Ascension and the Second Coming:
"And ascended into heaven, and sits at the Right Hand of the Father. And he shall come again with glory to judge both the quick and the dead. Whose kingdom shall have no end."

**The Ascension.** Forty days after Pascha, Christ led the apostles out to the Mount of Olives, blessed them, and was taken up into heaven. The angels said: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven" (Acts 1:11, KJV). The Church keeps the feast on the **Thursday forty days after Pascha**.

**What the Ascension means.** **The Son, who came down without leaving the Father, returns to the Father without leaving us, and takes our human nature with Him.** A hymn of the feast says that Christ "graciously hast borne on high our fallen nature, and hast sat down with the Father" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906).

**Not an absence.** The kontakion of the Ascension says (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906):

> "When thou hadst accomplished thy dispensation to usward, and hadst united things earthly with things heavenly, thou didst ascend into glory, O Christ our God, yet in no wise departing but abiding uninterruptedly with us, and crying unto those who love thee: I am with you, and none shall prevail against you."

**He remains with the Church in the Holy Spirit and the Eucharist.** The Ascension prepares for Pentecost, ten days later, when the Spirit is sent (Stage 4).

**"Sits at the right hand of the Father."** The right hand means honour and power, not a place. **A human nature, ours, is now enthroned in the life of the Trinity.** This is the pledge of our own glorification.

**The Second Coming.** *Parousía* (παρουσία), "presence" or "arrival". **Christ will come again visibly, in glory, to judge the living and the dead, to raise the dead and to bring in the Kingdom in its fullness.** "When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory" (Matthew 25:31, KJV).

**The Judge is the Saviour.** The one who will judge is the one who died for all. The icon of the Last Judgement, on the west wall of many churches, shows Christ enthroned and a river of fire flowing from His throne. Many Fathers taught that **the same divine love will be experienced as light by those who love Him and as fire by those who hate Him.** Stage 4 teaches the judgement and the life to come.

**No date.** Christ said that of that day and hour "knoweth no man" (Mark 13:32, KJV). **The Orthodox Church has never set dates or built systems of the end-times.** She asks for watchfulness: the hymn of the Bridegroom who comes at midnight (Matthew 25:6), sung at Matins of the first days of Holy Week.

**Facing east.** Orthodox churches face east, and Christians pray toward the east **awaiting Christ's coming**, one of St Basil's unwritten traditions (Stage 1).

**"Whose kingdom shall have no end."** These words were added at Constantinople in 381 against Marcellus of Ancyra, who taught that Christ's reign would end. **Christ's kingdom, and His humanity, are eternal.**
Looking back: Christ:
This stage followed the Creed's second article. Here is the whole of Orthodox Christology in one place.

**The core.** **Jesus Christ is the eternal Son and Word of God, one of the Holy Trinity, who for our salvation became truly man of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, the Theotokos. He is one Person in two natures, divine and human, unconfused and undivided, with two wills in harmony. He died on the Cross by His own will, descended into Hades, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come again in glory. He became man that we might become god by grace.**

**The councils, in one table:**

| Council | Year | What it confessed about Christ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nicaea I** | 325 | He is *homoousios* with the Father: truly God |
| **Constantinople I** | 381 | He became truly man, with a human mind (against Apollinaris); His kingdom shall have no end |
| **Ephesus** | 431 | one Person; Mary is *Theotokos* |
| **Chalcedon** | 451 | one Person in two natures, unconfused, unchanged, undivided, inseparable |
| **Constantinople II** | 553 | the one Person is God the Word, "one of the Holy Trinity" |
| **Constantinople III** | 680–681 | two natural wills and energies, the human freely obedient to the divine |

**The key terms:** *oikonomía*, *kénōsis*, *Theotókos*, *aeipárthenos*, *phýsis* and *hypóstasis*, the hypostatic union, the exchange of properties, *anakephalaíōsis*, *phthorá*, *synergeía*, *théōsis*, *epéktasis*, *parousía*.

**The rule of the whole stage.** St Gregory the Theologian: **"that which He has not assumed He has not healed."** Christ took all of human nature, so all of it can be healed.

**The fall and salvation, in Orthodox emphasis.** The fall is above all a **sickness of nature and a captivity to death**; salvation is **healing, victory, life and union with God**, received by grace and free cooperation in the Church.

**Where Orthodox writers differ, as set out here:**

1. How to state **ancestral sin**: inherited mortality only, or a real inherited sinful condition.
2. How to treat **legal and satisfaction language** for the Cross.
3. Whether the Incarnation would have happened **without the fall**.
4. How widely Christ's preaching in **Hades** saved.
5. Whether to read **Genesis 2–3** as straightforward history or as history told in images.

**Questions to test yourself:**

1. Why did Cyril insist on the title *Theotokos*?
2. What do the four adverbs of Chalcedon guard against?
3. Why must Christ have a human mind and a human will?
4. What does "He was made man that we might be made God" mean, and what does it not mean?
5. How does the essence–energies distinction keep theosis from becoming absorption into God?
6. Why does the Orthodox icon of the Resurrection show Christ in Hades?

**Next.** Stage 4 turns to the third part of the Creed: "And in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and Giver of Life" (tr. Isabel Hapgood, *Service Book*, 1906), the Church, the Mysteries and the life to come.
Context: the third part of the Creed:
Stages 2 and 3 covered the first two parts of the Creed: God the Father, maker of all things, and the Son, who became man for our salvation. This stage takes the rest, from the Holy Spirit to "the life of the world to come".

**The text.** The Creed's last articles, in the translation Isabel Hapgood printed in her *Service Book* (1906), as they are sung at every Divine Liturgy:

> "And in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and Giver of Life, Who proceedeth from the Father, Who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified. Who spake by the Prophets. In one Holy Catholic and Apostolic Church. I acknowledge one Baptism for the remission of sins. I look for the Resurrection of the dead. And the Life of the world to come. Amen."

**Where it comes from.** The first part of the Creed was set out at the **First Council of Nicaea (325)**. The Second Ecumenical Council, **Constantinople I (381)**, expanded the article on the Holy Spirit and added the articles that follow. That is why the full text is called the **Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed**, or in Orthodox use simply the **Symbol of Faith** (Greek *Sýmvolon tís Písteos*). A *symbolon* was a token broken in two, so that the halves could be fitted together to prove who you were. The Creed is the token by which Orthodox Christians recognise one another. Its text has been fixed since 381, and the Orthodox Church recites it without addition.

**The shape of the articles:**

| Article | Subject | Lessons in this stage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8 | the Holy Spirit | the Spirit, Pentecost, the procession, the gifts |
| 9 | the Church | the Body of Christ, the four marks, bishops and councils |
| 10 | one Baptism | the Mysteries, baptism, chrismation, the Eucharist |
| 11 | the resurrection of the dead | death, the intermediate state, the toll-houses, resurrection |
| 12 | the life of the world to come | judgement, heaven and hell |

**Why these belong together.** The Creed moves from God to God's work in us. **The Spirit makes the Church; the Church gives the Mysteries; the Mysteries prepare us for the resurrection.** Pentecost, the parish, the font and the grave are one story. The Church calls it the *oikonomía* (economy): God's "household plan" for the world's salvation.

**How this stage is taught.** Most of what follows was settled by councils and is believed by every Orthodox Christian: the divinity of the Spirit, the Church as Christ's Body, baptism, the resurrection of the body. A few questions are still open among Orthodox writers, above all **what the soul experiences between death and the Last Judgement**. Where that is so, each lesson says it plainly and sets out each view in its strongest form.

**One reading.** Halfway through comes a close reading of St Basil the Great's *On the Holy Spirit*, written in 375 and the book that prepared the ground for 381.
The Holy Spirit in the Creed: \"the Lord:
Every phrase of the Creed's eighth article was chosen with care. Read slowly, it makes a complete theology of the Spirit.

**Why the article was needed.** In the 360s and 370s, after Nicaea had confessed the Son "of one essence with the Father", some bishops accepted the Son's divinity but denied the Spirit's. They treated the Spirit as a creature, a ministering power, perhaps a higher kind of angel. Their opponents called them **Pneumatomachi**, "fighters against the Spirit" (also *Macedonians*, after Bishop Macedonius of Constantinople, though his link to them is uncertain). The Council of 381 answered them.

**The article, phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it teaches |
| --- | --- |
| **"the Lord"** (*tò Kýrion*) | the Spirit has the title the Septuagint uses for God. He rules; he is not ruled |
| **"the Giver of Life"** (*tò Zōopoión*) | the Spirit gives life, as only God can: at creation, in the Incarnation, at baptism, at the resurrection |
| **"Who proceedeth from the Father"** | his origin. The words come from John 15:26. Lesson 5 covers what "proceeds" means |
| **"Who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified"** | he receives the same worship as the Father and the Son. Only God is worshipped, so the Spirit is God |
| **"Who spake by the Prophets"** | the same Spirit inspired the Old Testament. The Church's God is the God of Israel |

**Notice what the council did not say.** It never calls the Spirit "God" or "of one essence" (*homooúsios*) in so many words, although that is what it means. The council chose biblical and liturgical language that every faithful bishop could accept. In 382 the bishops wrote that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit have one Godhead, power and essence. **The Church's teaching that the Spirit is fully God is universally received, and it is defined by the Second Ecumenical Council.**

**A person, not a force.** The Spirit is not the Father's energy or mood. He is a divine **hypostasis** (*hypóstasis*, a concrete person: Stage 2): he speaks (Acts 13:2), can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30), intercedes (Romans 8:26), and distributes gifts "as he will" (1 Corinthians 12:11). Orthodox prayer addresses him directly. Nearly every service begins with the prayer to the Spirit. In Hapgood's translation:

> "O heavenly King, the Comforter, Spirit of Truth, who art in all places and fillest all things; Treasury of good things and Giver of life: Come and take up thine abode in us, and cleanse us from every stain; and save our souls, O Good One."

**"Comforter"** translates *Paráklētos*, the **Paraclete**, John's word (John 14:16): advocate, helper, one who is called alongside. Because the prayer belongs to Pentecost, it is not said from Pascha until Pentecost; the Church waits for the Spirit as the apostles did.

**The key sentence:** the Spirit is the Lord, equal in honour, the giver of all life, and a person to whom Orthodox Christians pray. For the Cappadocian argument behind 381, see Stage 2, and the Philosophy curriculum's lesson on the Cappadocians.
The Spirit in the Old Testament and the:
The Spirit did not first arrive at Pentecost. Scripture shows him at work from the first verse, and the Fathers read his story as one revelation unfolding in stages.

**The word.** Hebrew *rûaḥ* and Greek *pneûma* both mean **breath, wind and spirit**. The image is of the invisible power that moves things and gives life, as breath gives life to a body.

**In the Old Testament:**

| Where | What the Spirit does |
| --- | --- |
| **Creation** (Genesis 1:2) | "the Spirit of God moved over the water" (Brenton): the Fathers read this as the Spirit brooding over creation, bringing order and life |
| **The breath of life** (Genesis 2:7) | God breathes into Adam, and he becomes a living soul |
| **The judges and kings** | the Spirit "comes upon" Gideon, Samson, Saul and David, for a task |
| **The prophets** | the Spirit speaks through them: "Who spake by the Prophets" |
| **The promise** | Joel promises that the Spirit will be poured out "upon all flesh"; Ezekiel sees dry bones given breath (Ezekiel 37) |

In the Old Testament the Spirit rests on **chosen individuals for a time**. The promise is that he will be given to all God's people for good.

**In the Gospels the Spirit surrounds Christ:**
- At the **Annunciation**: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee" (Luke 1:35). The Incarnation is the Spirit's work.
- At the **Baptism in the Jordan**: the Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father's voice is heard. Theophany is the feast of the Trinity revealed (Stage 6).
- In the **desert**: the Spirit leads Christ to be tempted.
- At **Nazareth**: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me" (Isaiah 61, read by Christ in Luke 4:18).
- At the **Last Supper**: Christ promises "another Comforter", "the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father" (John 14–16).
- After the **Resurrection**: "he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost" (John 20:22, KJV).

**One revelation in stages.** St Gregory the Theologian explained why the Spirit's divinity was revealed last, in his *Fifth Theological Oration* (Oration 31, delivered in 380), §26, translated by Browne and Swallow in the NPNF (1894):

> "The Old Testament proclaimed the Father openly, and the Son more obscurely. The New manifested the Son, and suggested the Deity of the Spirit. Now the Spirit Himself dwells among us, and supplies us with a clearer demonstration of Himself."

**Why this matters.** It explains why the Church's teaching on the Spirit was defined late (381) without being invented late. **God revealed himself step by step, as people could bear it**, and the full knowledge of the Spirit belongs to the age of the Church, in which the Spirit lives in believers. The Philosophy curriculum covers Gregory's arguments as philosophy; here he is the Church's teacher, honoured with the title *Theologian*, which Orthodoxy gives to only three saints: John the Evangelist, Gregory, and Symeon the New Theologian.
Pentecost: the feast and the event:
Fifty days after Pascha, the Spirit came. The Church calls this her birthday, and keeps it as one of the twelve great feasts.

**The event** (Acts 2:1–4, King James Version):

> "And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance."

**The Jewish feast behind it.** *Pentēkostḗ* is Greek for "fiftieth". It was the feast of Weeks (Hebrew *Shavuot*), fifty days after Passover: a harvest festival, later linked with the giving of the Law at Sinai. The Fathers saw both meanings fulfilled: **the first harvest of the Church** (three thousand baptised that day), and **the new Law written not on stone but on hearts** (Jeremiah 31; 2 Corinthians 3).

**Babel undone.** At Babel (Genesis 11) God confused the languages and scattered the nations. At Pentecost the apostles speak, and every nation in Jerusalem hears in its own tongue. The kontakion of the feast draws exactly this contrast. **Pentecost does not abolish the languages; it makes them carry one faith.** This is why the Orthodox Church has always served in the languages of the peoples: Greek, Syriac, Coptic, Georgian, Slavonic, Romanian, Arabic, English, Swahili.

**How the feast is kept:**

| Day | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **Sunday of Pentecost** | Greek usage stresses the descent of the Spirit; Slavic usage calls it **Trinity Sunday**, since this is when the Trinity was fully revealed. Churches are decked with green branches and grass |
| **Kneeling Vespers** | held on Sunday evening (often straight after the Liturgy). The first kneeling since Pascha; three long prayers attributed to St Basil, the third including prayer for the departed |
| **Monday of the Holy Spirit** | in Greek and Antiochian usage, the Spirit himself is honoured. Slavic usage calls it Spirit Day |
| **The week after** | a fast-free week |
| **The Sunday after** | **All Saints**: the fruit of the Spirit is holiness. Slavic churches keep their own national saints on the Sunday after |

**The icon.** The apostles sit in a curve, with Paul among them although he was not there. That is a sign that the icon shows the Church, not a snapshot. Below, in a dark arch, stands a crowned old man holding twelve scrolls: **Kosmos**, the world, waiting for the apostles' preaching.

**The key sentence:** Pentecost is not only something that happened once. The Spirit given then is given to each Christian at **chrismation** (lesson 16), and the feast is the Church remembering what she is.
The procession of the Spirit and the fil:
The Creed says the Spirit "proceedeth from the Father". In the West a word was added: *filioque*, "and from the Son". This is the one doctrinal difference this curriculum names in detail, because without it the history of 1054 cannot be understood.

**What the Orthodox Church teaches.** **The Father is the one source (*aitía*, cause; *archḗ*, principle) of the Son and the Spirit.** The Son is *begotten* of the Father; the Spirit *proceeds* (*ekporeúetai*) from the Father. These are two different ways of coming from the Father, and both are eternal. Neither is a creation.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Monarchy of the Father** (*monarchía*) | the Father as the single source within the Trinity. It guarantees one God, not three |
| **Generation** (*génnēsis*) | the Son's eternal origin from the Father |
| **Procession** (*ekpóreusis*) | the Spirit's eternal origin from the Father |
| **Sending** (*pémpsis*) | the Spirit's mission into the world, *in time*, which is from the Father **through the Son** (John 15:26: "whom I will send unto you from the Father") |

The distinction in the last row is the key. Orthodox theology happily says the Spirit is **sent** by the Son, **rests on** the Son, shines forth **through** the Son, and is the Spirit **of** the Son (Galatians 4:6). What it does not say is that the Son is a second source of the Spirit's eternal being.

**The history, briefly.**
- **589**: the Third Council of Toledo, in Visigothic Spain, recites the Creed with *filioque*, against Arian views of the Son.
- **800s**: the addition spreads in the Frankish church. Pope Leo III, about 809–810, refused to add it to the Creed in Rome and had the original text engraved on silver shields in St Peter's.
- **About 886**: **St Photios** of Constantinople, in the *Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit*, sets out the Orthodox objection at length (Stage 8).
- **1014**: Rome adopts the Creed with *filioque* at the coronation of Emperor Henry II.

**The Orthodox objections, stated positively:**
1. **The text of the Creed belongs to the whole Church.** It was fixed by ecumenical councils, and the Council of Ephesus (431) forbade composing "another faith". Only the whole Church can change it.
2. **The monarchy of the Father.** The Father alone is the source in the Trinity; making two sources blurs the persons, as if what Father and Son have in common (their essence) produced the Spirit.
3. **The Spirit's place.** The Spirit is not a bond the other two produce but a person in his own right.

**Where Orthodox theologians differ.** All reject the addition to the Creed. They differ on how far the Western teaching can be read in an Orthodox sense. Some, following **St Maximus the Confessor** (who in the 640s explained the Roman "and the Son" as meaning "through the Son"), think it can, if understood as sending or manifestation. Others, following St Photios and **St Mark of Ephesus** at the Council of Florence (1438–39), hold that the Western doctrine itself, not just the wording, is mistaken. That debate continues in the official dialogues, covered in Stage 12.
Acquiring the Holy Spirit: gifts and fru:
The Spirit is not only a doctrine to confess. Orthodox teaching holds that the goal of the Christian life is to be filled with him.

**St Seraphim of Sarov (1754–1833; some sources give his birth as 1759)** was a Russian monk, hermit and elder, glorified as a saint in 1903. In **November 1831** he spoke at length with a landowner he had healed, **Nicholas Motovilov**, who wrote the conversation down; it was published in 1903. Its central teaching, in paraphrase:

> Prayer, fasting, vigils and almsgiving are good, but they are not the aim of the Christian life. They are means. **The true aim is the acquiring of the Holy Spirit of God.** Every good deed done for Christ's sake gives us the Spirit, as a merchant gains capital by trading.

During the conversation, Motovilov reports, Seraphim's face shone brighter than the sun in the winter forest, and Motovilov felt warmth, peace and joy. This is the uncreated light of Tabor in a modern witness (Stage 2's essence and energies; Stage 10's hesychasm).

**The gifts of the Spirit.** Isaiah 11:2–3 in the Septuagint lists seven: wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, godliness and the fear of God. St Paul lists *charísmata*, gifts of grace, for building up the Church (1 Corinthians 12): wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues, interpretation. **Every member has some gift, and no one has all of them.**

**The fruit of the Spirit** (Galatians 5:22–23, KJV): "love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance". Gifts are given for service; fruit is the Spirit's own character growing in a person. **The fruit, not the spectacular gifts, is the sign of holiness.**

| | Gifts (*charísmata*) | Fruit (*karpós*) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What** | abilities given to serve the Church | the virtues of Christ formed in us |
| **Who** | distributed, each differently | meant for every Christian |
| **Test** | can exist without holiness (Matthew 7:22–23) | cannot exist without it |

**Grace and synergy.** Orthodox teaching speaks of *synergeía*, **synergy**, "working together". God's grace (*cháris*) does the work of salvation, and human freedom must cooperate with it. The Spirit does not override the will; he heals and frees it. Prayer, the Mysteries and the commandments are where that cooperation happens.

**Discernment.** The Fathers warn that not every spiritual experience comes from God. St Paul says to "try the spirits" (1 John 4:1). The Orthodox tradition is cautious about visions and ecstasies and trusts humility, obedience and peace as signs of the Spirit. Stage 10 takes this up.

**The key sentence:** the Spirit given at baptism and chrismation is meant to be "acquired", made one's own, through a whole life of prayer and repentance. The aim of the Christian life is not to be good but to be filled with God.
Reading: St Basil, On the Holy Spirit 9,:
St Basil the Great (about 330–379), Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, wrote *On the Holy Spirit* in **375** for his friend Bishop Amphilochius of Iconium. It began with a quarrel about a doxology: Basil was attacked for praying "glory to the Father **with** the Son **together with** the Holy Spirit". The book defends the Spirit's equal honour, and laid the ground for the Council of 381.

**The text.** Chapter 9, §23, in Blomfield Jackson's translation (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 8, 1895):

> "Shining upon those that are cleansed from every spot, He makes them spiritual by fellowship with Himself. Just as when a sunbeam falls on bright and transparent bodies, they themselves become brilliant too, and shed forth a fresh brightness from themselves, so souls wherein the Spirit dwells, illuminated by the Spirit, themselves become spiritual, and send forth their grace to others. Hence comes foreknowledge of the future, understanding of mysteries, apprehension of what is hidden, distribution of good gifts, the heavenly citizenship, a place in the chorus of angels, joy without end, abiding in God, the being made like to God, and, highest of all, the being made God."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it teaches |
| --- | --- |
| **"those that are cleansed from every spot"** | purification comes first. Just before this, Basil says the Spirit draws near not by moving through space but as the soul is freed from the passions and the "Royal Image" in it is cleaned |
