| **"a sunbeam falls on bright and transparent bodies"** | the image. Glass in sunlight does not become the sun, yet it truly shines, with the sun's own light |
| **"send forth their grace to others"** | the holy person becomes a source of light for others. This is why Orthodox Christians seek out holy elders |
| **"a place in the chorus of angels"** | the life of the Spirit is already heavenly: the Liturgy is shared with the angels (Stage 6) |
| **"the being made like to God"** | likeness (*homoíōsis*), the goal of Genesis 1:26 |
| **"the being made God"** | Basil's Greek is *Theòn genésthai*. This is **theosis** (*théōsis*, deification), taught in Stage 3 |

**Why the image of light is exact.** Glass shines with the sun's light, not its own, yet the light is really in it. That is the Orthodox teaching on grace: the Christian is made god **by grace and participation**, not by nature. Man never becomes the divine essence. He shares God's uncreated energies (*enérgeiai*), as glass shares the sunlight without becoming the sun. Basil states in a single image what St Gregory Palamas defined in the fourteenth century (Stage 8).

**What the passage proves about the Spirit.** Only God can make someone God. A creature cannot give what it does not have. **If the Spirit deifies, the Spirit is God.** That is Basil's argument for the Spirit's divinity, made not from abstract reasoning but from what Christians experience of him.

**The surrounding chapter.** §22, just before, lists the Spirit's titles and calls him "in essence simple, in powers various, wholly present in each and being wholly everywhere", and compares him to sunlight that falls on each person "as though it shone for him alone". Read §§22–23 together on CCEL; they are among the finest pages of the Fathers on the Spirit.
The Church as the Body of Christ:
The ninth article of the Creed reads: "In one Holy Catholic and Apostolic Church." Before asking what the Church does, Orthodox teaching asks what the Church is.

**The word.** *Ekklēsía* is Greek for "assembly", from *ek-kaléō*, "to call out". In the Septuagint it translates Israel gathered before God. **The Church is the people God has called together.** Modern Greek still uses *ekklisía* for both a church building and the Church (the Greek curriculum).

**What the Church is not.** Not a voluntary society of people who share opinions, and not mainly an institution that dispenses services. **The Church is the Body of Christ, a living reality made by the Spirit.**

> "Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular." (1 Corinthians 12:27, KJV)

**The images Scripture uses:**

| Image | Where | What it teaches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Body** | 1 Corinthians 12; Ephesians 1:22–23 | Christ is the head; the members are joined to him and to one another; each has a different function |
| **Bride** | Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 21 | the Church is loved and cleansed by Christ; "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church" (Ephesians 5:32) |
| **Temple** | 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:20–22 | built of living stones, on the foundation of apostles and prophets, inhabited by the Spirit |
| **Vine** | John 15 | life flows from Christ into the branches |
| **Flock** | John 10 | Christ the Good Shepherd, and the shepherds he appoints |
| **People of God** | 1 Peter 2:9 | "a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation" |

**Christ and the Spirit together.** Orthodox theology stresses that the Church is made by **both** the Son and the Spirit. Christ is her head and the content of her life; the Spirit gives her life and makes Christ present in her. St Irenaeus of Lyons (about 130–202) put it this way in *Against Heresies* III.24.1, translated by Roberts and Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885):

> "For where the Church is, there is the Spirit of God; and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church, and every kind of grace; but the Spirit is truth."

**Visible and invisible.** The Church has bishops, parishes, canons and buildings. She is also the communion of the living and the departed, the saints and the angels. These are not two Churches. **The one Church is both a historical community and a mystery of God**, as Christ is both man and God. The Orthodox Church does not speak of an "invisible church" of true believers separate from the visible one.

**"Outside the Church."** St Cyprian of Carthage (died 258) wrote in *On the Unity of the Church* §6, translated by Wallis (ANF vol. 5, 1886): "He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother." Orthodox teaching affirms that **the Church is where salvation is given**. Most Orthodox writers add, with Fr Thomas Hopko and Metropolitan Kallistos Ware, that we know where the Church is but **cannot say where she is not**; God's judgement of those outside her visible bounds belongs to him. Others stress Cyprian's words more strictly. Both views claim the Fathers, and the Church has not defined the fate of those outside.

**The key sentence:** to be a Christian is to be a member of a body. Orthodoxy knows no Christianity of the individual alone. The Russian theologian Khomiakov put it this way (a paraphrase): when anyone falls, he falls alone; but no one is saved alone.
One, holy, catholic and apostolic: the f:
The Creed gives the Church four marks. Each one is a gift of God before it is a task for Christians.

**One** (*mía*). There is one Church because there is one Christ and one Body. **Orthodox teaching holds that the Church's unity is never lost**, because Christ is never divided. What can be lost is a person's or a group's communion with her. Unity is not a federation: it is the same faith, the same Mysteries and the same bishops in communion, in every place. The many local churches (Constantinople, Moscow, Belgrade, Bucharest, Antioch and the rest) are not branches of a larger body but **the one Church present in each place**.

**Holy** (*hagía*). The Church is holy because Christ her head is holy and the Spirit lives in her, not because her members are sinless. They plainly are not. **The Church is holy with sinners in her, as a hospital is a place of health that is full of the sick.** St John Chrysostom often calls the Church a hospital (*iatreíon*). Every Liturgy prays for the forgiveness of those who serve and those who receive.

**Catholic** (*katholikḗ*). From *kath' hólou*, "according to the whole". The word appears first in **St Ignatius of Antioch** (martyred about 107), *To the Smyrnaeans* §8, translated by Roberts and Donaldson (ANF vol. 1, 1885):

> "Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church."

Orthodox teaching gives the word two meanings:

| Sense | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Wholeness** | the Church has the whole faith and the whole life in Christ, lacking nothing. Each local church gathered around its bishop at the Eucharist is fully the Church, not a part of it |
| **Universality** | the Church is for every people, place and age |

The first sense is the deeper one in Orthodox writing. It is why Slavic churches translated *katholikḗ* in the Creed as *sobornaya*, "conciliar, gathered" (lesson 11), not by a word meaning "worldwide".

**Apostolic** (*apostolikḗ*). The Church is built on the apostles in three ways:
1. **Faith**: she keeps the apostles' teaching unchanged (Jude 3: "the faith which was once delivered unto the saints").
2. **Succession**: her bishops stand in an unbroken line of ordination from the apostles (next lesson).
3. **Mission**: like the apostles, she is *sent* (*apostéllō*, "I send") to all nations.

**The Orthodox claim.** The Orthodox Church confesses that she **is** the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church of the Creed. She is not one denomination among many, nor a branch of a divided Church. It is said positively, as a confession of faith, and it does not mean every Orthodox Christian is holy or every Orthodox practice perfect. How the Orthodox Church relates to other Christians is one of the questions Orthodox writers answer differently (ecumenism, in Stage 12).

**A card to keep:** one in faith and communion; holy by Christ's holiness; catholic, lacking nothing, in every place; apostolic in faith, succession and mission.
Bishops, apostolic succession and the eu:
The Church has a shape, and it was there from the beginning. At its centre is the bishop at the altar, surrounded by his clergy and people.

**The three orders.** By the early second century the Church everywhere had the threefold ministry still kept today:

| Order | Greek | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Bishop** | *epískopos*, "overseer" | presides at the Eucharist, teaches, ordains, keeps the faith and unity of the local church |
| **Priest** | *presbýteros*, "elder" | celebrates the Mysteries in the bishop's name, in parishes the bishop cannot reach in person |
| **Deacon** | *diákonos*, "servant" | serves at the altar, leads the litanies, and of old cared for the poor |

St Ignatius of Antioch, writing on his way to martyrdom about 107, already says of the Smyrnaeans' church that no Eucharist is valid "which is [administered] either by the bishop, or by one to whom he has entrusted it" (ANF, as in the previous lesson).

**Apostolic succession.** Every Orthodox bishop was ordained by other bishops, who were ordained by others, in a line reaching back to the apostles. St Irenaeus, about 180, listed the bishops of Rome from the apostles to his own day to show that the true teaching had been handed on openly. **In Orthodox teaching succession is not a mechanical chain of hands.** It is succession in the **faith** and in the **local church**: a bishop is ordained to a real flock and must confess the apostolic faith. A bishop who falls into heresy does not keep the Church's authority by holding the office.

**The eucharistic assembly.** Ignatius's picture is of one altar, one bishop and one people. **The Church is most fully herself when she gathers for the Eucharist.** In the twentieth century Fr Nicholas Afanasiev (1893–1966) and Metropolitan John Zizioulas (1931–2023) developed this as **eucharistic ecclesiology**: each local church gathered around its bishop at the Eucharist is the whole Church. Other Orthodox theologians accepted the insight but warned against overstating it; they stress that local churches must also be bound by the same faith and in conciliar communion, and that the Church's unity has a universal dimension too. Stage 12 takes up these writers.

**The laity.** *Laós* is the people of God. The laity are not passive. They are an order in the Church, made so at baptism and chrismation (1 Peter 2:9, the "royal priesthood"). Every Liturgy needs the people's "Amen", and the laity are the guardians of the faith with the bishops. The Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs of **1848** said that among the Orthodox the guardian of religion is the very body of the Church, that is, the people themselves.

**How the churches are arranged.** Bishops of a region form a **synod** under a **primate** (a patriarch, archbishop or metropolitan). A church that elects its own primate is **autocephalous** (*autoképhalos*, "self-headed"). The Patriarch of Constantinople has a **primacy of honour** among Orthodox primates, as "first among equals". Exactly what that primacy involves, and who may grant autocephaly, are live questions among the churches today (Stages 11 and 12).
Conciliarity: sobornost and the councils:
The Orthodox Church has no single bishop who decides for all. She decides together. This way of life is called **conciliarity**.

**The word.** Greek *synodikótēs* or Russian *sobornost'* (from *sobor*, "council" or "gathering", the same root as the Slavonic word used for "catholic" in the Creed). The idea was made famous by the Russian lay theologian **Alexei Khomiakov (1804–1860)**, who described the Church as a free unity of believers in love, where truth is held by the whole body, not by any one office.

**The pattern is apostolic.** In **Acts 15** (about AD 49), the apostles and elders met in Jerusalem to decide whether Gentile converts must keep the Law of Moses. They debated, heard testimony, reached a common mind and wrote: "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us" (Acts 15:28, KJV). That formula, the Spirit and the assembly speaking together, is the model for every later council.

**Levels of council:**

| Council | Who gathers | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Parish assembly** | priest and people | the life of a local community |
| **Diocesan assembly** | bishop, clergy and laity | the life of a diocese |
| **Local synod** | the bishops of one church | elects bishops, judges, keeps order. Apostolic Canon 34 says the bishops of each nation should recognise the first among them, and he should do nothing without them |
| **Pan-Orthodox council** | the autocephalous churches | the Holy and Great Council of Crete (2016) is the most recent attempt (Stage 12) |
| **Ecumenical council** | the bishops of the whole Church | defines doctrine for all. The Orthodox Church recognises **seven** (325 to 787) |

**How a council becomes ecumenical.** Not by size, nor by who summoned it. Some large councils were later rejected, like the "Robber Council" of Ephesus in 449. **A council is ecumenical when the whole Church receives its teaching as the faith she has always held.** This is called **reception**. It is the work of the Spirit in the whole body, clergy and people, over time.

**Orthodox views on more councils.** Some Orthodox writers count further councils as having ecumenical authority, especially the council of **879–880** under St Photios and the **hesychast councils** of 1341–1351 that confirmed St Gregory Palamas. Others keep the number at seven while recognising those later councils' teaching as binding Orthodox faith. Both views agree on the content of the teaching; they differ on the title.

**Conciliarity in a parish.** Conciliarity is not only for bishops. The Liturgy itself is conciliar: the people answer, sing, say "Amen" and receive together. Orthodox Christians speak of the **mind of the Church** (*phrónēma*), the common sense of the faith formed by the services, the Fathers and life in the Church. Stage 1 explained how the Church knows; this is the same thing seen as a way of governing.

**The key sentence:** in the Orthodox Church, authority belongs to the truth, which the Spirit gives the whole Church; bishops in council speak it, and the whole body receives it.
The Mysteries: what a sacrament is in Or:
The Creed confesses "one Baptism for the remission of sins". Baptism is the first of the Church's **Mysteries**, the acts in which God gives his grace through visible means.

**The word.** Greek *mystḗrion* means something hidden that has been revealed. St Paul uses it of God's plan in Christ, "the mystery which hath been hid from ages" (Colossians 1:26). Latin writers translated it *sacramentum*, giving English "sacrament". **Orthodox Christians usually prefer "Mystery"**, because it says that what happens is God's own act, beyond full explanation.

**What a Mystery is.** In each Mystery:

| Element | Example in baptism |
| --- | --- |
| **A visible sign** from creation | water |
| **A word of prayer** in the Church | "The servant of God, N., is baptized, in the name of the Father..." |
| **The invocation of the Spirit** (*epíklēsis*) | the blessing of the water |
| **A real gift of grace** | death to sin, new birth, membership of Christ's Body |

**Why matter.** Because of the Incarnation. God the Word took flesh, so created things can carry divine life. **Water, oil, bread, wine and human hands are not obstacles to grace but its instruments.** St John of Damascus defended icons with the same argument (Stage 6). The Mysteries extend the Incarnation into the life of every Christian: what Christ did in his body, he now does through his Body, the Church.

**Who acts.** Orthodox prayers make it plain that **the true celebrant is Christ**. The priest's prayer before the Great Entrance says to Christ, in Hapgood's translation: "For it is thou who offerest and art offered, who receivest and art thyself received, O Christ our God." In baptism the priest says "the servant of God is baptized" rather than "I baptize you": the passive form keeps the focus on God. The worthiness of the priest does not make the Mystery; a sinful priest's Eucharist is still Christ's. Yet the Mysteries are always celebrated **within the Church**, by her bishops and those they appoint, and the Church decides where her Mysteries are.

**Faith and freedom.** The Mysteries are not magic. Grace is truly given, but it must be received. A person who receives Communion without faith or repentance receives, in St Paul's words, "damnation to himself" (1 Corinthians 11:29). The Mysteries meet human freedom; they do not replace it (lesson 6's *synergy*).

**The Mysteries and the Church.** Each Mystery is an act of the whole Church, not a private transaction. Baptism makes a member of the community; marriage is crowned in the assembly; even confession, though private, reconciles a person with the Church. **The Eucharist is the Mystery in which the Church becomes what she is**, and all the others lead to it or flow from it (lesson 18).

**Where this goes next.** The next lesson asks how many Mysteries there are; then come baptism, chrismation, the reception of converts and the Eucharist. The other four are taught with the services, in Stage 6.
How many Mysteries? Seven, and the sacra:
Orthodox catechisms list seven Mysteries. Orthodox theologians add that the number is a teaching device, not a fence around grace.

**The seven, as most Orthodox catechisms give them:**

| Mystery | Greek | Stage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Baptism** | *Váptisma* | this stage |
| **Chrismation** | *Chrísma* | this stage |
| **Eucharist** | *Eucharistía*, "thanksgiving" | this stage, and the Liturgy in Stage 6 |
| **Confession (Repentance)** | *Metánoia*, *Exomológēsis* | Stage 6 |
| **Marriage** | *Gámos* | Stage 6 |
| **Holy Unction** | *Euchélaion*, "prayer-oil" | Stage 6 |
| **Holy Orders** | *Hierōsýnē*, *Cheirotonía* | Stage 6 |

**Where the number came from.** The early Fathers never counted the Mysteries. St Dionysius the Areopagite (a writer of about 500 who wrote under the name of Paul's convert) describes six rites: illumination (baptism), the synaxis (Eucharist), the consecration of myron, ordination, monastic tonsure and the rites for the dead. The list of exactly seven became common in Orthodox writing from the thirteenth century, and was fixed in the confessions of the seventeenth century: the *Orthodox Confession* of **Metropolitan Peter Mogila of Kiev** (approved by the Eastern patriarchs in **1643**) and the **Synod of Jerusalem (1672)**.

**Two Orthodox approaches.** Both are found in good Orthodox teaching, and they are complementary rather than opposed:

- **The catechism approach** (strong in Russian, Greek and Romanian school theology): the seven are the Mysteries Christ instituted, each conveying a particular grace, and other blessings are lesser **sacramentals**. This approach gives clarity and guards against confusion.
- **The patristic approach** (Schmemann, Hopko, Kallistos Ware and many others): **the whole life of the Church is sacramental.** The seven are the chief moments of it, but monastic tonsure, the funeral, the great blessing of water at Theophany and the consecration of a church are also true acts of God's grace. Some writers call monastic tonsure a "second baptism". This approach guards against seeing the Mysteries as isolated rites.

**Why the list should not be held too tightly.** The rites are not equal. Baptism and the Eucharist stand at the centre and are necessary for every Christian; marriage and ordination are vocations, and not everyone receives them. Unction and confession are given again and again. **A ranked list of seven can hide how the Mysteries flow into one another**: baptism, chrismation and first Communion were one rite in the early Church, and still are in Orthodox practice.

**One Church, one life.** Hopko's way of putting it is worth keeping: the Mysteries are not things the Church *has*, but what the Church *is*, the life of God given to people.

**The key sentence:** seven Mysteries are taught, and all seven are received; but Orthodoxy's whole life, from the blessing of a house to the burial of the dead, is a single sacramental life in the Spirit.
Baptism: dying and rising with Christ:
"I acknowledge one Baptism for the remission of sins." Baptism is the door into the Church and the beginning of the Christian life.

**The word.** *Baptízō* is Greek for "I plunge, immerse". Orthodox baptism is by **threefold immersion**: the person is plunged under the water three times, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Church also calls it **Illumination** (*phōtismós*), because the newly baptised are "enlightened".

**The command.** "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 28:19, KJV). And to Nicodemus: "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God" (John 3:5).

**What baptism does.** Orthodox teaching names several gifts, all given at once:

| Gift | Scripture |
| --- | --- |
| **Dying and rising with Christ** | "buried with him by baptism into death... we also should walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:4). The immersion is a burial; coming up from the water is a resurrection |
| **Forgiveness of sins** | Acts 2:38 |
| **New birth** | John 3:5; Titus 3:5, "the washing of regeneration" |
| **Putting on Christ** | "as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ" (Galatians 3:27), sung at every baptism and at the Liturgy on great feasts |
| **Membership of the Body** | 1 Corinthians 12:13 |
| **Freedom from the devil** | the exorcisms and renunciation before baptism |

**Ancestral sin.** Orthodox teaching speaks of **ancestral sin** (*propatorikḗ hamartía*). In Adam humanity fell into mortality and corruption, and every person is born into a fallen world, prone to sin. Baptism frees the person from death's dominion and joins them to Christ's risen life. Orthodox writers usually say that infants do not bear **personal guilt** for Adam's sin; they are baptised so they may be joined to Christ and receive life, not because they are guilty. Some older Orthodox catechisms use the term "original sin" and speak more strongly of an inherited guilt; this is a difference of emphasis among Orthodox writers. The Philosophy curriculum's lessons on Augustine show the Western debate in which the stronger language took shape.

**Infant baptism.** The Orthodox Church baptises infants, as she has done since at least the second and third centuries (St Hippolytus and Origen speak of it). Infants are baptised into the faith of the Church and of their **godparents** (*anádochos*, "sponsor"), who answer for them and promise to raise them in the faith. Baptised infants are chrismated and given Communion straight away.

**Once only.** Because there is one death and resurrection of Christ, there is **one baptism**. It is never repeated. Sins after baptism are healed by repentance and confession, which the Fathers called a "second baptism" of tears.

**Who may baptise.** Normally a bishop or priest. **In danger of death, any Orthodox Christian may baptise**, by immersing or pouring water three times with the words of the rite. If the person lives, a priest completes the rest. This shows that baptism belongs to the whole Church.

**Martyrs.** The Church has always held that martyrs who die for Christ before baptism are baptised in their own blood. St Basil says so in *On the Holy Spirit* 15.36.
The rite of baptism step by step:
The Orthodox rite of baptism is one of the oldest services the Church has, and its parts teach what baptism means.

**Before the service**, the person becomes a **catechumen** (*katēchoúmenos*, "one being instructed"). In the early Church the catechumenate lasted up to three years, and Pascha was the great day of baptism. The Vesperal Liturgy of Holy Saturday still reflects that (Stage 6).

**1. The prayers of the catechumen.** The priest breathes on the person three times, signs them with the cross, and prays that they be enrolled in Christ's flock.

**2. The exorcisms.** Three prayers command the devil to depart. They are among the most ancient texts the Church uses. Orthodox teaching takes evil seriously: baptism is a rescue from a real enemy.

**3. The renunciation.** The person, or the godparent for an infant, **turns to face west**, the direction of darkness, and is asked three times. In Hapgood's translation (1906):

> "Dost thou renounce Satan, and all his Angels, and all his works, and all his service, and all his pride?"

They answer "I do renounce him", and are told to blow and spit on him.

**4. The union with Christ.** They **turn east**, toward the rising sun and Christ, and are asked three times whether they unite themselves to Christ. Then they **recite the Creed**. Baptism follows confession of the faith.

**5. The blessing of the water.** The great prayer over the font recalls creation, the Jordan and the gift of the Spirit, and asks God to sanctify the water. The priest breathes on the water and signs it.

**6. The anointing with the oil of gladness.** The person is anointed with blessed olive oil on brow, breast, ears, hands and feet, as athletes were anointed before a contest. The Christian life is a struggle.

**7. The immersion.** Facing east, the person is plunged three times, while the priest says, in Hapgood's version:

> "The servant of God, N., is baptized, in the name of the Father, Amen. And of the Son, Amen. And of the Holy Spirit, Amen."

**8. The white garment.** The newly baptised is clothed in white, "the robe of righteousness". The ancient name for Bright Week (the week after Pascha) recalls the newly baptised in white.

**9. Chrismation** follows immediately (next lesson).

**10. The procession and readings.** The priest, godparents and newly baptised walk three times around the font while all sing "As many as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. Alleluia" (Hapgood). The Epistle is Romans 6:3–11 and the Gospel Matthew 28:16–20.

**11. The tonsure.** A few hairs are cut in the form of a cross: the first offering of the new Christian to God.

**12. Communion.** The newly baptised receives the Eucharist at the next Liturgy, or at once if the rite is joined to it. In some places the old rites of washing after seven days and churching are still done.

**The key sentence:** **every gesture says one thing.** The Christian has left darkness for light, died with Christ, risen with him, and been clothed in him.
Chrismation: the seal of the gift of the:
Straight after baptism comes the second Mystery. Baptism joins a person to Christ's death and resurrection; chrismation gives them the Spirit of Pentecost.

**The word.** *Chrísma* is Greek for "anointing", and the oil is the **holy myron** (*mýron*, perfumed oil, sometimes called chrism). It is from the same root as *Christós*, "the Anointed One". **The Christian is anointed, a little Christ**, as kings, priests and prophets were anointed in Israel.

**In Scripture.** In Acts 8:14–17, Peter and John went to Samaria and laid hands on the newly baptised, "and they received the Holy Ghost". St Paul writes that God "hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts" (2 Corinthians 1:22, KJV). The apostles laid on hands; the Church soon anointed with myron instead, so that the apostles' successors could give the Spirit everywhere without being present in person.

**The rite.** After a prayer, the priest anoints the newly baptised with myron on brow, eyes, nostrils, lips, ears, breast, hands and feet, and at each anointing says, in Hapgood's 1906 translation:

> "The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. Amen."

Every sense and every part of the body is sealed: what one sees, smells, says, hears, loves, does and where one goes.

**The myron itself.** Myron is made of olive oil, wine and **dozens of aromatic substances**. It is consecrated, usually in Holy Week, by the primate of an autocephalous church. The **Ecumenical Patriarch** consecrates it for Constantinople and for several other churches; some autocephalous churches, among them the Russian, Romanian and Georgian, consecrate their own. Because only the bishop consecrates myron, **every chrismation by a priest is an act of the bishop**, and of the Church's unity.

**What it gives.** Orthodox teaching describes chrismation as **a personal Pentecost**. At baptism a person is born; at chrismation they receive the breath of the Spirit to live. Chrismation makes them a full member of the **royal priesthood**, the laity, able to offer their life to God and receive the Eucharist.

**How it differs from the Western practice.** Many Western churches separate baptism and confirmation by years. **Orthodoxy keeps baptism, chrismation and first Communion together as one rite**, given at once to infants and adults alike. A baptised Orthodox baby receives the Spirit and the Body and Blood of Christ on the day of her baptism.

**Chrismation used alone.** Chrismation is also used, in many Orthodox churches, to receive converts who were baptised in the name of the Trinity in another Christian body. The next lesson explains why practice differs here.

**Other anointings.** Kings were once anointed with myron at coronation in Byzantium and Russia. The altar of a newly consecrated church is anointed with it too. In each case the anointing means: **this belongs to God and is filled with his Spirit.**
Receiving converts: akriveia and oikonom:
How is someone already baptised in another Christian body received into the Orthodox Church? Here Orthodox churches genuinely differ, and the difference rests on two principles every Orthodox Christian should know.

**The two principles:**

| Term | Greek | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Akriveia** | *akríveia*, "exactness, strictness" | applying the canons and the Church's norm in full |
| **Oikonomia** | *oikonomía*, "household management, stewardship" | a bishop's or synod's pastoral decision to relax the strict norm, for the salvation of souls, without changing the teaching |

*Oikonomia* is not a loophole. It is the steward's care that the household be saved, and it is used by bishops, not by private choice. It does not alter what is true; it alters what is done in a particular case.

**The three ways of reception**, all found in Orthodox practice:
1. **By baptism.**
2. **By chrismation** (with renunciation of former error and confession of the Orthodox faith).
3. **By confession of faith alone**, with the bishop's permission, for those already chrismated in some way. This is mainly used for clergy of churches with apostolic succession, such as the Non-Chalcedonians in some places.

The canonical basis is old. **Canon 95 of the Council in Trullo (692)** lists different ways of receiving different groups, and St Basil's First Canonical Epistle discusses the question.

**The view of strictness.** Some Orthodox hold, from St Cyprian and the Apostolic Canons, that there is no true baptism outside the Church. A rite performed elsewhere is a form without the grace, and the convert should be **baptised**. When converts were received by chrismation, it was by *oikonomia*, filling the empty form with grace. In **1755** Patriarch Cyril V of Constantinople and the patriarchs of Alexandria and Jerusalem required the baptism of Latin and Protestant converts. Many Greek monasteries, Mount Athos, some ROCOR parishes and many converts today follow this practice. Its strength: it makes plain that the Church's Mysteries are found in the Church, and it gives the convert a clear, full beginning.

**The view of economy as norm.** Others hold that a baptism in the name of the Trinity, with water, performed by other Christians, has a real form which the Church can recognise and complete by chrismation. The **Russian Church** has received Roman Catholics and many Protestants by chrismation since the Moscow Council of **1667**. The Antiochian Archdiocese, the OCA and most Greek Orthodox parishes in the diaspora usually do the same. Its strength: it reflects long practice, respects the faith of those coming in, and treats the Trinitarian name as something holy wherever it is invoked.

**What both views share.** Both affirm one baptism and the Church as the place of the Mysteries. Both regard the decision as the bishop's. Neither is a private opinion: each is the official practice of real Orthodox churches. **A convert follows the practice of the bishop who receives them**, and Orthodox churches recognise one another's converts.

**The key sentence:** Orthodox churches agree on what baptism is, and differ on how to judge rites done outside the Church; *akriveia* and *oikonomia* are both Orthodox, and each guards something true.
The Eucharist: the Mystery of the Church:
Every Mystery leads to one table. The Eucharist is the Mystery in which the Church receives Christ himself and becomes his Body.

**The word.** *Eucharistía* is Greek for "thanksgiving". At the Last Supper Christ "gave thanks" (*eucharistḗsas*) over the bread. The Orthodox Church also calls it **Holy Communion** (*Theía Koinōnía*), the **Holy Gifts**, and the **Divine Liturgy** (the service, in Stage 6).

**The institution.** Christ took bread and said, "Take, eat; this is my body", and the cup, "this is my blood of the new testament" (Matthew 26:26–28). In John 6 he had already said, "Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you" (John 6:53).

**What the Church teaches.** **The bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Christ.** It is not a symbol, a reminder, or a spiritual presence alongside unchanged bread. Before Communion the priest prays, in Hapgood's translation (1906): "And I believe that this is, of a truth, thine all-pure Body, and that this is thine own precious Blood." Yet the bread and wine still look, feel and taste as they did.

**How it happens.** The Fathers use the words *metabolḗ* (change) and *metapoíēsis* (re-making). The Liturgy prays that the Father "send thy Holy Spirit upon us, and upon these Gifts here spread forth", and the priest blesses the Gifts with the words "**Transmuting them by thy Holy Spirit**" (Hapgood). Orthodox teaching places the moment of change in the **epiclesis** (*epíklēsis*, invocation of the Spirit), together with the whole anaphora.

**How far the Church explains.** Here Orthodox writers have spoken in different ways. The **Synod of Jerusalem (1672)** used the word *metousiōsis* (a Greek equivalent of the Latin "transubstantiation") to state the reality of the change firmly, while saying the manner is beyond understanding. Many Orthodox writers since, such as Schmemann, Kallistos Ware and Hopko, prefer not to use a term borrowed from Latin philosophy and simply say "change", leaving the manner a mystery. **All agree on the reality: the Gifts are the true Body and Blood of Christ.**

**Why the Eucharist makes the Church.** St Paul: "we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread" (1 Corinthians 10:17, KJV). **Communion with Christ is communion with one another.** That is why Communion is given only to Orthodox Christians, who share the one faith, and why Orthodox Christians receive only in the Orthodox Church. It is not a judgement of others' sincerity; it is the Church's understanding that the common cup expresses a unity of faith that already exists.

**A sacrifice.** The Liturgy calls the Eucharist a "**reasonable and unbloody service**" (Hapgood's translation; the Greek *latreía* is the worship due to God alone), and the Fathers call it a sacrifice (*thysía*). It is not a new sacrifice of Christ, nor a repetition of the Cross. It is **the one sacrifice of Christ made present**, offered by the risen Christ himself. "Thine own, of thine own, we offer unto thee", says the priest (Stage 6's reading).

**A foretaste.** The Eucharist is also the **Kingdom made present** now. Schmemann called the Liturgy "the sacrament of the Kingdom". The Church gathers, ascends to the heavenly altar, and tastes the life of the world to come. This links the Eucharist to the last articles of the Creed, the subject of the rest of this stage.
The communion of saints:
The Church is not only the believers alive now. She is one family in heaven and on earth, and death does not divide it.

**One Church, living and departed.** Christ "is not the God of the dead, but of the living" (Matthew 22:32), "for all live unto him" (Luke 20:38). The saints who have died are alive in Christ, and still members of his Body. Hebrews 12:1 calls them "so great a cloud of witnesses", surrounding the runners in the race. **The Church on earth and the Church in heaven are one Church**, sometimes called the Church militant and the Church triumphant.

**Who is a saint.** In the New Testament "the saints" (*hágioi*, "holy ones") are all believers (Romans 1:7). Every Christian is called to holiness. The Church gives the title in a special sense to those **in whom God's holiness has been shown plainly**, and whom she glorifies and asks to pray.

**The kinds of saints.** Orthodox service books name classes of saints, each honoured in its own way:

| Class | Who |
| --- | --- |
| **Apostles** | the Twelve, the Seventy, Paul |
| **Equal-to-the-Apostles** (*isapóstoloi*) | those who brought whole peoples to Christ: Mary Magdalene, Constantine and Helen, Nino of Georgia, Cyril and Methodius, Vladimir and Olga |
| **Prophets** | Moses, Elijah, John the Forerunner |
| **Martyrs** | those killed for Christ, from Stephen to the new martyrs of the twentieth century |
| **Hierarchs** | holy bishops: Nicholas, Basil, Chrysostom, Spyridon, Savva of Serbia |
| **Venerables** (*hósioi*) | holy monastics: Antony, Seraphim, Paisios |
| **Unmercenaries** (*anárgyroi*) | healers who took no fee: Cosmas and Damian, Panteleimon |
| **Righteous** | holy laypeople, including the Old Testament righteous and Joachim and Anna |
| **Fools for Christ** | who hid holiness under apparent madness: Xenia of Petersburg, Basil of Moscow |

**How the Church recognises saints.** The early Church honoured martyrs at their tombs; holiness was recognised by the faithful first. Today each autocephalous church **glorifies** (*agiokatátaxis*, "enrolment among the saints") its saints by decision of its synod, after the life, the people's veneration and often miracles are examined. The Ecumenical Patriarchate, for example, glorified St Paisios of Mount Athos in 2015 and St Porphyrios in 2013. A saint glorified by one church is usually received by the others in time. **The Church does not make saints; she recognises those God has glorified.**

**Mutual prayer.** In the Body of Christ all pray for all. Christians on earth pray for each other and for the departed; the saints pray for the Church on earth. "The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much" (James 5:16, KJV). Death removes the saint from sight, not from love.

**The key sentence:** to be Orthodox is to live among a great family; the Church gathered for the Liturgy includes, in every service, the Theotokos, the angels and all the saints.
The Theotokos and the saints in prayer::
Orthodox Christians ask the saints for their prayers, venerate their icons and relics, and honour the Mother of God above them all. This lesson explains what that honour is and is not.

**Two kinds of honour.** The Seventh Ecumenical Council, **Nicaea II (787)**, distinguished them. Its definition, translated by Henry Percival (NPNF, Second Series, vol. 14, 1900), says that images should be given "due salutation and honourable reverence (*aspasmòn kaì timētikḕn proskýnēsin*), not indeed that true worship of faith (*latreían*) which pertains alone to the divine nature."

| Term | Meaning | Given to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Latreia** (*latreía*) | adoration, worship | **God alone**: Father, Son and Holy Spirit |
| **Proskynesis** (*proskýnēsis*), **timetike** | veneration, honour, bowing, kissing | the saints, their icons and relics, the Cross, the Gospel book |
| **Hyperdulia** (a Western term some Orthodox use) | the highest veneration | the Theotokos |

**Why the saints are honoured.** Not as rivals of God but as his work. **To honour a saint is to honour the God who made them holy.** Brenton's Septuagint renders Psalm 67:36 "God is wonderful in his holy places", and notes the alternative "among his holy ones": the Church sings this verse at the feasts of saints.

**The Theotokos.** Stage 3 taught why Mary is called **Theotokos** (*Theotókos*, "God-bearer"), defined at Ephesus in 431. Her place in prayer follows from it. She is commemorated in every service, most of all in the Liturgy, straight after the consecration: "Especially our most holy, all-undefiled, most blessed and glorious Lady, the Birth-giver of God and ever-virgin Mary" (Hapgood). The hymn that follows calls her "More honourable than the Cherubim, and beyond compare more glorious than the Seraphim". **She is honoured above all creatures because she is the one in whom God became man**, and Orthodox writers call her the first of the redeemed and the image of the Church.

**Asking the saints to pray.** Orthodox prayers to saints end, in essence, with "pray to God for us". To the Theotokos the Church sings, in Hapgood's translation, "O most holy Birth-giver of God, save us", meaning save us by your prayers. **No Orthodox prayer treats a saint as a source of grace apart from God.**

**Relics** (*leípsana*, "remains"). The bodies of saints are honoured because the Holy Spirit dwelt in them and they will rise. In Scripture a dead man touched Elisha's bones and came to life (4 Kingdoms 13:21, LXX; 2 Kings in the KJV), and cloths that touched Paul healed the sick (Acts 19:12). The church of Smyrna gathered the bones of St Polycarp (martyred about 155–156) "as being more precious than the most exquisite jewels, and more purified than gold" (*Martyrdom of Polycarp* 18, tr. Roberts and Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885), and early Christians celebrated the Eucharist at martyrs' tombs. To this day every Orthodox altar has relics of a martyr sewn into the **antimension** (*antimínsion*, the cloth on which the Liturgy is served), or sealed under the altar.

**Incorrupt relics and myrrh.** Some saints' bodies have not decayed, and some relics exude fragrant oil (St Demetrius in Thessaloniki, St Nicholas in Bari). The Church receives these as signs, not as the test of holiness: many great saints' bodies have decayed normally.

**The key sentence:** God alone is worshipped; the saints are honoured as his friends, asked to pray as family; and that honour, says Nicaea II, "passes on to that which the image represents".
Death and the departure of the soul:
"I look for the Resurrection of the dead." Before the resurrection comes death. Orthodox teaching neither denies death nor makes peace with it.

**What death is.** Death is **the separation of the soul from the body**. God made the human person as **one being of soul and body together**: neither is the whole person alone. Death tears apart what God joined. **Death is not natural to humanity as God made it. It is the enemy**, "the last enemy that shall be destroyed" (1 Corinthians 15:26). It came into the world through sin (Romans 5:12), and Christ came to destroy it.

**The soul.** The soul (*psychḗ*) is created by God, and it does not die with the body. Orthodox teaching holds it is not immortal by its own nature, as Plato taught, but **by the gift of God**, who keeps it in being. The Philosophy curriculum's lessons on the *Phaedo* and on Aristotle's *On the Soul* show the arguments the Fathers inherited and changed: Christians teach not just an immortal soul but the resurrection of the whole person.

**Christ has changed death.** Christ did not remove death from this life; he entered it and broke it from inside. The Paschal troparion, sung hundreds of times each Pascha, says it in one sentence (Hapgood): "Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down Death by death, and upon those in the tomb bestowing life." **For a Christian, death is now a passage, a "falling asleep" in the hope of resurrection.** That is why the departed are said to have "fallen asleep" (*koímēsis*, from which "cemetery", *koimētḗrion*, a sleeping-place).

**Preparing for death.** The Church teaches Christians to keep **the remembrance of death** (*mnḗmē thanátou*), not from gloom but to live soberly. The Liturgy prays at every celebration, in Hapgood's translation, for "A Christian ending to our life, painless, blameless, peaceful; and a good defence before the dread Judgment Seat of Christ". The dying receive confession, unction and Communion. The priest reads the **Canon at the Parting of the Soul**, prayers for the soul as it leaves the body.

**The funeral.** The body is washed, dressed and laid in the church, often with an icon in the hands and a paper band on the forehead showing Christ, the Theotokos and the Forerunner. The service is full of grief and of hope. Its most famous hymn, the kontakion, in Hapgood's version:

> "With the Saints give rest, O Christ, to the soul of thy servant, where there is neither sickness, nor sorrow, nor sighing, but life everlasting."

At the end, the mourners give the **last kiss** to the departed. The body is buried, facing east, to await the resurrection. **The Orthodox Church buries her faithful and does not permit them to choose cremation**, because the body is a temple of the Spirit and will rise.

**Christian grief.** St Paul does not forbid grief, only grief without hope: "that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13, KJV). The Orthodox funeral weeps and hopes at once.
The intermediate state and prayer for th:
Between death and the Last Judgement, the soul waits for the resurrection. The Church calls this the **intermediate state**, and she prays for her departed throughout it.

**The particular judgement.** "it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment" (Hebrews 9:27, KJV). Orthodox teaching holds that **after death each soul receives a foretaste of its final state**: the righteous a foretaste of the Kingdom's joy, sinners a foretaste of its suffering. This is the **particular judgement**, distinguished from the **general judgement** at Christ's Second Coming. The parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31) is the Church's main image of it: Lazarus in "Abraham's bosom", the rich man in torment, both conscious, both waiting.

**Not yet complete.** The joy or pain of the soul now is **partial**. The soul is without its body, and the history of the world is not yet finished. **Full blessedness and full condemnation come only at the resurrection.** Hebrews 11:39–40 says the Old Testament saints "received not the promise: God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect".

**Prayer for the departed.** The Church prays for her dead constantly, and teaches that **these prayers help them**. The practice is very old: Judas Maccabeus made an offering for the dead "that they might be delivered from sin" (2 Maccabees 12:45). The Liturgy remembers them at the Proskomedia, in the anaphora, and with the particles placed on the paten for the departed. The funeral prayer asks God to give rest to the departed "in a place of brightness, a place of verdure, a place of repose" and to "pardon every transgression" (Hapgood).

**How the Church prays for the dead:**

| When | What |
| --- | --- |
| **3rd, 9th and 40th days** after death | memorial services. The 40th recalls the Ascension on the 40th day |
| **Anniversaries** | memorials yearly |
| **Memorial Saturdays** (*Psychosávvata*, "Saturdays of souls") | the Saturdays before Meatfare Sunday and Pentecost, and in Lent; in Slavic use also Demetrius Saturday in autumn |
| **Every Saturday** | the day of the week dedicated to the departed (Stage 6) |
| **Kollyva** | boiled wheat with sugar and spices, blessed at memorials: "except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die" (John 12:24) |
| **Memory eternal** | sung at the end of every memorial (*Aiōnía hē mnḗmē*; Slavonic *Vechnaya pamyat'*) |

**How the prayers help.** The Church has not defined it. Orthodox writers say that love is not stopped by death, that the dead are still members of the Body and benefit from its prayer, and that God, who is not bound by time, hears prayers for them. The Fathers mention almsgiving and the Liturgy offered for them as the most powerful help.

**Without purgatory.** The Orthodox Church does not teach a **purgatorial fire** that pays off temporal punishment for sins, as later medieval Western theology did. At the Council of Florence (1438–39) **St Mark of Ephesus** explained the Orthodox view: the departed are helped by the Church's prayer and God's mercy, not purified by a material fire of satisfaction. This is mentioned only to make the Orthodox teaching clear.

**What remains open.** The Church has said much less about the details of the intermediate state than about the resurrection. One particular question has divided Orthodox writers in recent decades: what happens to the soul in the first hours and days after death. That is the next lesson.
The toll-houses: a question among Orthod:
Does the soul, after death, pass through a series of trials in the air where demons accuse it of its sins? This is the teaching of the **aerial toll-houses** (Greek *telṓnia*, Slavonic *mytarstva*). Orthodox writers of real authority hold it, and Orthodox writers of real authority reject or reinterpret it. **The Church has not settled it by council.** This lesson gives each side in its strongest form.

**What the teaching says.** After death the soul, accompanied by angels, rises through the air. At a series of "toll-stations", demons accuse it of particular sins (lies, anger, pride, lust and so on). Angels answer with its good deeds and repentance. A soul with unrepented sins may be seized; one cleansed by repentance passes freely.

**Where it comes from.** The image is old. **St Athanasius's *Life of Antony* (§65, written about 360)** reports a vision, in Ellershaw's translation (NPNF, Second Series, vol. 4, 1892): Antony "saw himself, as it were, from outside himself, and that he was led in the air by certain ones. Next certain bitter and terrible beings stood in the air and wished to hinder him from passing through." Similar images are found in homilies attributed to St Macarius and St Cyril of Alexandria, in the **Life of St Basil the New** (tenth century) with its vision of the blessed Theodora's twenty toll-houses, and in some prayers of the service books.

**The view that the toll-houses are real.** Its defenders include **St Ignatius (Brianchaninov) (1807–1867)**, who defended it at length in the 1860s; **St Theophan the Recluse (1815–1894)**; **St John (Maximovitch) of Shanghai and San Francisco (1896–1966)**; and **Fr Seraphim Rose (1934–1982)**, whose *The Soul After Death* (1980) brought the teaching to English-speaking Orthodox. In 2017 a large collection of patristic texts in support, *The Departure of the Soul*, was published by St Anthony's Monastery in Arizona. **The strongest form of the case:** the teaching is found across many centuries, in many Fathers, saints' lives and service texts; it gives a vivid sense of the seriousness of sin and of the need for repentance and Communion before death; the Bible speaks of "the prince of the power of the air" (Ephesians 2:2); and Fr Seraphim wrote that the details are images, but the reality of a testing of the soul is the Church's teaching.

**The view that the toll-houses are not doctrine.** **Lev Puhalo**, then a deacon in ROCOR and later Archbishop Lazar of the OCA, answered Fr Seraphim's book in *The Soul, the Body and Death* (also 1980), and **Fr Michael Azkoul** wrote *The Toll-House Myth* in the 1990s. Many other Orthodox theologians who did not join the dispute treat the toll-houses as **an imaginative tradition rather than dogma**. **The strongest form of the case:** the teaching is not in Scripture, the Creed or any council; the texts that describe it in detail are visions and saints' lives, which the Church does not treat as dogmatic sources; the picture of demons with authority to judge a soul seems hard to square with Christ's victory over the devil and with judgement belonging to Christ alone; and the images can frighten believers instead of leading them to trust God's mercy.

**What the Church did.** In the 1980s the Synod of ROCOR, where the quarrel began, ordered the dispute to stop in its journals. It did not define the teaching as dogma, and later rejected the claim that the toll-houses were a Gnostic idea. Outside the English-speaking world many Orthodox, especially in Russian and Greek monastic piety, take the toll-houses for granted, while many others never meet the teaching at all.

**Common ground.** Both sides agree that the soul **faces a particular judgement** after death; that **repentance, confession and Communion** prepare us for it; that the departed are helped by **the Church's prayer**; and that **Christ is the judge**, merciful to those who turn to him. They differ on whether the toll-house picture describes that reality literally, as an image of it, or not at all.

**What would settle it.** An authoritative statement by a pan-Orthodox council; or, short of that, a clear consensus among the autocephalous churches' synods. Neither exists as of 2026.
The resurrection of the body and the Las:
The Creed's eleventh article: "I look for the Resurrection of the dead." Christian hope is not for souls escaping bodies, but for **whole persons raised in glory**.

**The Second Coming.** Christ "shall come again with glory to judge both the quick and the dead" (the Creed). The **Parousia** (*parousía*, "presence, arrival") will be visible, sudden and universal (Matthew 24:27, 30). No one knows the day (Matthew 24:36). **Orthodox teaching refuses to calculate dates**; the Church's attitude is watchfulness, not prediction.

**The general resurrection.** At Christ's coming **all the dead will rise**, "they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation" (John 5:29, KJV). Souls will be reunited with their bodies. Christ's resurrection is the first-fruits, and the pattern (1 Corinthians 15:20).

**What the risen body will be.** St Paul (1 Corinthians 15:42–44, KJV):

> "So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body."

**"Spiritual" does not mean ghostly.** It means **wholly filled by the Spirit**. The risen Christ ate fish and was touched (Luke 24:39–43), yet passed through closed doors (John 20:19). The risen body is **the same body, transfigured**: continuous with this one, as a plant is with its seed (1 Corinthians 15:37), but no longer subject to death, decay or need. The Fathers, from Irenaeus on, defended this against those who wanted to save only souls.

**The renewal of creation.** Not only humanity but the whole world will be transfigured: "new heavens and a new earth" (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1). "the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption" (Romans 8:21). **Orthodox hope includes the whole created world.**

**The Last Judgement.** Christ will judge all people (Matthew 25:31–46). The parable of the sheep and the goats sets the measure: what we did, or did not do, to "the least of these my brethren". **Judgement is by love shown to Christ in the neighbour.** The Gospel is read on **Meatfare Sunday**, the Sunday of the Last Judgement, a week before Lent.

**The icon of the Last Judgement.** Painted on the west wall of many churches, so the faithful see it as they leave. Christ is enthroned in the centre, with the Theotokos and John the Forerunner interceding at his sides. A river of fire flows from his throne. The righteous are on his right, sinners on his left. Adam and Eve kneel beneath, and at the bottom are the angels with the scales.

**Who judges.** "the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son" (John 5:22). **The Judge is the One who died for those he judges.** Orthodox hymns hold fear and confidence together: the Judge is terrible because he is holy, and merciful because he became man.

**The key sentence:** the Christian looks for the resurrection of the whole person, soul and body, in a renewed creation, and for judgement by Christ according to love.
Heaven, hell and the hope for all:
The Creed's last article: "And the Life of the world to come." What is that life, what is its opposite, and may we hope that all will share it?

**The Kingdom.** The life to come is **eternal life with God**: seeing God (Matthew 5:8), the wedding feast (Revelation 19:9), the Kingdom prepared "from the foundation of the world" (Matthew 25:34). It is **endless growth**. **St Gregory of Nyssa** (about 335–about 395) taught that even in the Kingdom the soul goes on "from glory to glory" (2 Corinthians 3:18) forever, because God is infinite; he called this *epéktasis*, "stretching forward" (Philippians 3:13). Heaven is never boredom; it is love that never ends.

**Hell.** Christ speaks plainly of "everlasting fire" (Matthew 25:41), "outer darkness" and "weeping and gnashing of teeth". **The Orthodox Church teaches that hell is real**, and its services warn of it often. It is not the absence of God, since God is everywhere.

**The fire of love.** Many Orthodox writers explain heaven and hell as **one reality, God's love, experienced in two ways**. The same divine glory that is light and joy to those who love God is torment to those who have hardened themselves against him. **St Isaac the Syrian** (seventh century), in his *Homilies*, writes in essence (this is a paraphrase) that those in Gehenna are scourged by the scourge of love: to know one has sinned against love is the bitterest suffering. **God does not torment anyone; people refuse the love that is offered.** This view is common among modern Orthodox writers. Others stress more strongly, from the Gospel and the Fathers, that hell is also God's just judgement and not only a subjective state.

**Apokatastasis.** Will all, in the end, be saved? The word *apokatástasis* ("restoration") comes from Acts 3:21.

- **What the Church condemned.** Origen (about 185–about 254) and later Origenist monks taught a restoration of all spirits, including the devil, connected to a belief in the pre-existence of souls. **Fifteen anathemas against Origenist teaching**, including this restoration, are linked to the Fifth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople II, 553). Scholars debate whether they were formally voted by the council itself or by a synod just before it; the Church has received them as condemning the Origenist system.
- **The view that the Church teaches eternal hell.** Most Fathers and the services teach that hell is everlasting, as Christ said "everlasting punishment" (Matthew 25:46); the condemnation of 553 rules out teaching that all must be saved; and **a universal salvation preached as certain would empty human freedom and repentance of their seriousness.** This is the view of the great majority of the Fathers and of Orthodox catechisms.
- **The view that the Church may hope for all.** St Gregory of Nyssa, who is honoured as a Father of Fathers, wrote of a final restoration in which evil is wholly removed, and St Isaac the Syrian expressed hope that God's love would not abandon any creature. Writers such as Sergius Bulgakov, and, in more cautious form, Metropolitan Kallistos Ware, held that **we may pray and hope that all will be saved**, while not teaching it as doctrine. The strongest form: God "will have all men to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:4); the third kneeling prayer at Pentecost Vespers prays even for those held in Hades; hope is not a doctrine and is not condemned.

**Where the views meet.** All Orthodox writers agree that **hell is a real possibility for every person, including oneself**, that human freedom is real, and that the Church may pray for the salvation of all. They differ on whether hope for universal salvation is permitted. **What would settle it**: a clear common judgement of the Orthodox churches on what exactly the anathemas of 553 condemn.

**The last word.** The Creed ends not with hell but with "the Life of the world to come. Amen." Orthodox eschatology is mostly joy. The services keep returning to the same hope: the Kingdom that has no end, already tasted at every Liturgy.
Looking back: the Spirit, the Church and:
This stage covered the last five articles of the Creed: the Spirit, the Church, baptism, the resurrection and the life of the world to come. Here is the whole of it in one view.

**The Holy Spirit.** **The Spirit is Lord and Giver of life, proceeding from the Father, worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son** (Constantinople I, 381). He is a person, revealed last and now dwelling in the Church (St Gregory the Theologian). He came at **Pentecost**, the Church's birthday, and is given to every Christian at chrismation. The aim of the Christian life, St Seraphim taught, is to acquire him. St Basil shows what that means: like glass in sunlight, a cleansed soul shines with God's own light and is made god by grace.

**The filioque.** The Orthodox Church confesses the Creed as written. The Father is the one source of the Spirit's eternal procession; the Son sends the Spirit into the world. The Western addition is the doctrinal difference behind 1054. Orthodox writers differ on how far the Western teaching can be read in an Orthodox sense.

**The Church.** The Church is **the Body of Christ, made by the Spirit**: one, holy, catholic and apostolic. Each local church gathered around its bishop at the Eucharist is the whole Church. She is governed **conciliarly**, from the parish to the ecumenical council, and teaching is confirmed by **reception**. The Orthodox Church confesses that she is the Church of the Creed.

**The Mysteries.** God gives grace through created things because the Word became flesh. Seven Mysteries are taught, and the whole of the Church's life is sacramental. **Baptism** by threefold immersion is death and resurrection with Christ; **chrismation** is the seal of the Spirit; **the Eucharist** is the true Body and Blood of Christ, which makes the Church one. The reception of converts follows *akriveia* or *oikonomia*, and Orthodox churches differ in practice.

**The communion of saints.** The living and the departed are one family. **God alone is worshipped (*latreia*); the Theotokos and the saints are venerated (*proskynesis*).** Their relics are holy because the Spirit dwelt in them.

**The last things:**

| Moment | Orthodox teaching | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Death** | separation of soul and body; an enemy Christ has overcome | taught by all |
| **Particular judgement** | a foretaste of one's final state | taught by all |
| **Prayer for the departed** | it helps them; no purgatorial fire | taught by all |
| **Toll-houses** | a testing of the soul in the air | **an open question among Orthodox writers** |
| **Resurrection** | of the whole person, in a transfigured body | defined (the Creed) |
| **Last Judgement** | by Christ, according to love | defined (the Creed) |
| **Hell** | real, and experienced as the refusal of God's love | taught by all; its explanation varies |
| **Apokatastasis** | the Origenist teaching condemned; whether one may hope for all is debated | partly settled, partly open |

**What links it all.** The Spirit came at Pentecost, makes the Church, sanctifies the water of baptism and the bread and wine of the Eucharist, and will raise the dead at the last day. **The same Spirit who spoke by the prophets fills the font, the chalice and the grave.**

**What comes next.** Stage 5 turns to the Spirit's other work in the Church: the Scriptures he inspired, and how the Church reads them. Stage 6 then shows how all of this is prayed: in the Divine Liturgy, the daily services and the Church's year.
Context: the Bible as the Church's book:
Stage 1 called Scripture the first witness of Tradition. This stage looks at the book itself: what is in it, how the Church came to recognise it, and how she reads it.

**The Bible is the Church's book.** It was written within God's people, recognised by the Church, and is read in the Church's worship. **The Church did not invent Scripture, and Scripture did not create the Church**: both come from the same Spirit, and they belong together. The Creed says the Spirit "spake by the Prophets"; the same Spirit leads the Church into all truth (John 16:13).

**Where the Bible lives.** For most of Christian history most believers did not own a Bible. They **heard** it, and they still do:

| Where | How Scripture is present |
| --- | --- |
| **The Divine Liturgy** | an Epistle and a Gospel every time |
| **Vespers and Matins** | the Psalms every day, whole psalms and verses woven into hymns; Old Testament readings on feasts |
| **The hymns** | Orthodox hymnography is made almost entirely of biblical phrases and images |
| **The icons** | painted Gospel: feasts, parables, miracles |
| **The altar** | the Gospel book is enthroned on the altar, kissed and carried in procession, as Christ himself |

**The Gospel book on the altar says it all.** The written Word lies on the same table where the Eucharist is offered. Orthodox Christians stand for the Gospel, and the deacon cries "Wisdom! Let us attend." **Scripture is heard as the voice of Christ in the assembly.**

**Inside the Church, not over it or under it.** In the Orthodox understanding, Scripture is the **highest written witness** within Tradition. It is not set against Tradition, as if one could read the Bible without the Church, and not placed beneath the Church, as if the Church could change it. The Fathers, the councils and the services are the Church's way of reading Scripture rightly. St Irenaeus, about 180, compared heretics who rearrange biblical texts to someone who takes "a beautiful image of a king... constructed by some skilful artist out of precious jewels" and rearranges the gems into "the form of a dog or of a fox" (*Against Heresies* I.8.1, tr. Roberts and Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885). **The pieces are all Scripture; the picture comes from the Church's faith.**

**The plan of the stage.**

| Lessons | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| 2–5 | the canon: Old Testament, Septuagint, New Testament, inspiration |
| 6–8 | how to read: the senses of Scripture, typology, and a reading of Genesis 22 |
| 9–14 | the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, the Psalter, the prophets, Wisdom, types of the Theotokos |
| 15–24 | the New Testament: the Gospels, Acts, Paul, the Catholic Epistles, Revelation |
| 25–27 | the Fathers as interpreters, the lectionary, and reading the Bible today |

**A word on translations.** Quotations here come from public-domain translations: **Brenton's Septuagint (1851)** for the Old Testament, which follows the Church's Greek text, and the **King James Version (1611)** for the New. The Philosophy curriculum has a lesson on hermeneutics (Gadamer and Ricoeur): the modern philosophy of interpretation. This stage is about the Church's older art of the same thing.
The canon of the Old Testament and the r:
Which books belong in the Old Testament? Orthodox Bibles contain more books than the Hebrew Bible, and Orthodox writers describe their status in two ways.

**The word.** *Kanṓn* is Greek for "rule" or "measuring rod". The **canon** of Scripture is the list of books the Church receives as the rule of faith.

**Two collections.** The Jewish Scriptures existed in two forms in the time of Christ: the **Hebrew** collection, later fixed by the rabbis, and the **Greek** collection, the Septuagint, which contained further books, some written in Greek, some translated from Hebrew or Aramaic. The apostles and the early Church used the Greek.

**What Orthodox Bibles contain.** All the books of the Hebrew Bible, plus:

| Book | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **1 Esdras** (Greek *Esdras A*) | a parallel account of the return from exile |
| **Tobit**, **Judith** | stories of faithfulness |
| **Additions to Esther** | prayers of Mordecai and Esther, among others |
| **1, 2 and 3 Maccabees** | the revolt against Antiochus IV; 4 Maccabees in an appendix in Greek Bibles |
| **Wisdom of Solomon**, **Wisdom of Sirach** | wisdom books, much read in the services |
| **Baruch**, **Letter of Jeremiah** | attached to Jeremiah |
| **Additions to Daniel** | the Song of the Three Children, Susanna, Bel and the Dragon |
| **Prayer of Manasseh** | read at Great Compline |
| **Psalm 151** | David's psalm after the Psalter |

Slavonic Bibles also include **3 Esdras** (an apocalypse, called 4 Ezra in the West).

**The name.** Orthodox tradition often calls these books *anaginōskómena*, "**the readable books**", or books "worthy to be read". St Athanasius in his **Thirty-Ninth Festal Letter (367)** distinguished books "included in the Canon" from others "appointed by the Fathers to be read by those who newly join us", listing among them Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith and Tobit (tr. NPNF, Second Series, vol. 4, 1892).

**Two Orthodox views of their status.** Both are held by Orthodox writers in good standing:

- **They are fully Scripture.** The **Synod of Jerusalem (1672)** named Wisdom, Judith, Tobit, the history of the Dragon, Susanna, the Maccabees and Sirach as genuine parts of Scripture. The Council in Trullo (692) received older canon lists that include several of them. The strongest form: the Church has always read them in worship as Scripture; the New Testament echoes them (Hebrews 11:35 recalls 2 Maccabees 7); and the Septuagint is the Church's Bible.
- **They are a second rank, "readable" but not canonical in the strict sense.** This view is found in Athanasius, in St John of Damascus's list, and in nineteenth-century Russian catechisms, such as St Philaret of Moscow's. The strongest form: the Fathers distinguished the two groups, and doctrine is drawn primarily from the books of the narrower canon.

**What both agree on.** The books are **read in church**, are **edifying**, and belong in the Orthodox Bible. **The Church has never produced a Bible without them.** The difference concerns their rank, not whether Orthodox Christians should read them. Many Orthodox writers today speak of the **wider canon**, honouring both.

**Why it matters for the services.** Wisdom 3:1 ("the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God") is read at the feasts of martyrs. The Song of the Three Children is the source of the seventh and eighth odes of Matins canons. Removing these books would remove part of the Church's prayer.
The Septuagint: the Old Testament of the:
The Orthodox Church reads the Old Testament in the Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Christ. This choice shapes her doctrine, hymns and liturgy.

**The name.** *Septuaginta* is Latin for "**seventy**", often written **LXX**. The name comes from the **Letter of Aristeas** (probably 2nd century BC), which tells how 72 Jewish scholars translated the Law in Alexandria for King **Ptolemy II Philadelphus** (reigned 283–246 BC). The story is legend in its details, but the core is accepted: **the Torah was translated into Greek in Alexandria in the third century BC**, and the other books over the next two centuries.

**Why it was made.** Alexandria had a large Greek-speaking Jewish community, many of whom no longer read Hebrew. The Septuagint was their Bible, and the Bible of Jews across the Greek world, including Philo of Alexandria (the Philosophy curriculum covers him in its lesson on Middle Platonism).

**The Bible of the apostles.** Most Old Testament quotations in the New Testament follow the Septuagint's wording. When the Gospel of Matthew quotes Isaiah 7:14, it follows the Greek *parthénos*, "virgin". The Greek Fathers all read it, and the Orthodox hymns were written from it.

**Where it differs from the Hebrew (Masoretic) text.** The **Masoretic Text**, standardised by Jewish scholars (the Masoretes) between about the 7th and 10th centuries AD, underlies most modern translations. The Septuagint often reflects an older or different Hebrew original. The Dead Sea Scrolls (found from 1947) show that some Septuagint readings go back to Hebrew manuscripts.

| Passage | Septuagint (Brenton, 1851) | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Isaiah 7:14** | "behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb" | *parthénos*, the reading Matthew uses; the Hebrew *ʿalmāh* means "young woman" |
| **Psalm 39:6** (40:6 in English Bibles) | "a body hast thou prepared me" (also quoted in Hebrews 10:5) | Hebrews follows the Greek |
| **Jeremiah** | about one-eighth shorter, arranged differently | a different edition of the book |
| **Psalm numbering** | mostly one lower than in Hebrew-based Bibles, from Psalm 10 to 147 | Orthodox service books use the LXX numbers |

**The Church's teaching on the text.** The Orthodox Church receives the Septuagint as **inspired**, used by the apostles and the Fathers. The Church of Greece uses it as her official Old Testament text. The Church Slavonic Bible (the Elizabeth Bible of 1751) follows it, as do Romanian and Arabic Orthodox Bibles. **Orthodox writers do not regard the Hebrew text as wrong**: St Jerome's translation from the Hebrew was respected, and the nineteenth-century **Russian Synodal Bible** (completed 1876) translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew, inserting the extra books from the Greek. Orthodox scholars disagree about how much weight to give the Hebrew where the two differ; all agree that **the Septuagint is the Church's own text** and the one her worship is built on.

**The key sentence:** the Church's Old Testament is the Greek Bible of the apostles; it is why the Creed, the hymns and the Fathers sound as they do, and why the Orthodox Psalter is numbered differently.
The canon of the New Testament:
The New Testament has 27 books. The Church recognised them gradually, over about three centuries, and that process is itself a lesson in how the Church knows.

**The books:**

| Group | Books |
| --- | --- |
| **Gospels** | Matthew, Mark, Luke, John |
| **History** | Acts of the Apostles |
| **Catholic (general) Epistles** | James; 1–2 Peter; 1–3 John; Jude |
| **Pauline Epistles** | Romans to Philemon, and Hebrews: fourteen in Orthodox counting |
| **Prophecy** | Revelation (the Apocalypse) |

Orthodox Bibles, following the Greek manuscripts, usually place the **Catholic Epistles straight after Acts**, before Paul.

**How the canon formed.**
- **By about 150**: the four Gospels and Paul's letters were read in church everywhere. St Justin Martyr (about 155) describes the "memoirs of the apostles" read at the Sunday Eucharist.
- **About 180**: St Irenaeus insists there are **exactly four** Gospels.
- **Third and fourth centuries**: some books are still disputed in some places: Hebrews (in the West), James, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude, and Revelation (in the East).
- **367**: St Athanasius's **Thirty-Ninth Festal Letter** gives the first list of exactly our 27 books. Of them he writes, in the NPNF translation (Second Series, vol. 4, 1892):

> "These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these."

- **Later**: Western councils (Hippo 393, Carthage 397) confirm the same list; the Council in Trullo (692) receives the earlier canon lists for the East.

**How the Church decided.** Not by a vote that created a Bible, but by **recognition**. The tests the Fathers used:

| Test | Question |
| --- | --- |
| **Apostolic origin** | does it come from an apostle or his close companion? |
| **Orthodoxy** | does it agree with the rule of faith handed down? |
| **Use** | has it been read in the churches, widely and from early on? |

Books that failed, such as the *Gospel of Thomas* or the *Gospel of Peter*, were not suppressed by force; they simply were not read in the Liturgy and faded. **The canon is the result of the Church's worship and reception**, the same process by which councils are received (Stage 4).

**Revelation's late acceptance.** In the East, Revelation was accepted more slowly than any other book. St Cyril of Jerusalem (about 350) omits it from his list, and the canon list attributed to the Council of Laodicea does too. It was accepted fully by the Byzantine period, but **to this day it is not read in the Divine Liturgy**. Lesson 24 explains how the Church reads it.

**Hebrews.** Orthodox tradition counts Hebrews as St Paul's. Fathers from Origen on noticed that its Greek differs from his other letters; Origen said that God alone knows who wrote it down, while the thoughts are Paul's. Orthodox Christians receive it as fully canonical; its authorship is an open historical question.

**The key sentence:** the New Testament was **recognised, not invented**: the books that the churches read at the Eucharist, from apostolic sources and in the apostolic faith, became the canon.
Inspiration: the Spirit who spoke by the:
The Creed says the Spirit "spake by the Prophets". What does it mean to call Scripture inspired, and how does Orthodox teaching understand the human authors' part?

**The word.** *Theópneustos*, "**God-breathed**", is St Paul's word: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness" (2 Timothy 3:16, KJV). St Peter: "holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost" (2 Peter 1:21, KJV).

**What Orthodox teaching affirms.**
1. **Scripture is truly God's word.** God speaks through it, and it is without error in what it teaches for salvation.
2. **The human authors were truly authors.** They wrote in their own language, style and culture, used sources (Luke 1:1–4 says so), and had their own characters. Mark's Greek is rough; Luke's is polished; Paul dictates and corrects himself.
3. **The two belong together as in Christ.** Many Orthodox writers compare Scripture to the Incarnation: **as Christ is fully God and fully man, Scripture is fully God's word in fully human words.** Inspiration is a **synergy**, not dictation.

**What it is not.** Orthodoxy does not teach a **mechanical dictation**, as if the authors were pens. Nor does she treat inspiration as a property only of the original manuscripts. **The Spirit who inspired the writers also inspires the Church that reads**, so inspiration is not only something that happened once.

**Inspiration and the Church.** The same Spirit works in three moments:

| Moment | Work of the Spirit |
| --- | --- |
| **Writing** | moving the prophets and apostles to write |
| **Recognition** | leading the Church to receive the canon |
| **Reading** | opening the understanding of those who read in faith, as Christ did on the road to Emmaus: "Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures" (Luke 24:45) |
