**The Bible is the Church's book.** Written in the Church, recognised by her, read in her worship, and interpreted by her Fathers. **Scripture and Tradition are not rivals**: Scripture is the highest written witness within Tradition. Irenaeus's image is the key: the gems of Scripture rightly arranged make the portrait of the King.

**The canon.**

| | Orthodox teaching |
| --- | --- |
| **Old Testament** | the Hebrew books plus the readable books (*anaginōskómena*) of the Septuagint. Orthodox writers differ on whether these are fully canonical or a second rank; all read them in church |
| **Text** | the **Septuagint**, the Greek Bible of the apostles, with LXX psalm numbers |
| **New Testament** | 27 books, first listed exactly by **Athanasius in 367**; recognised by use, apostolic origin and orthodoxy |
| **Inspiration** | **God-breathed**, through real human authors: a synergy, not dictation |

**How to read.** Begin with the letter. Then read **in Christ**, as he taught on the road to Emmaus. **Typology** sees real events foreshadowing Christ: Isaac carrying the wood, the ram in the thicket, the Passover lamb, the Red Sea. Alexandria and Antioch gave the Church two emphases, and she kept both. The **rule of faith** is the boundary of interpretation.

**The Old Testament in the Church.** Genesis gives the doctrine of creation and the fall (how literally to read its days is open); the Exodus is the Old Testament Pascha; the **Psalter** is the Church's prayer book in twenty kathismata; the **prophets** speak of Christ (Isaiah 7:14 and 53); **Wisdom** is read as the Son (Hagia Sophia); and the **types of the Theotokos** (bush, ladder, gate, house) are the readings of her feasts.

**The New Testament in the Church.** Four Gospels, symbolised by man, lion, ox and eagle; the **Synoptics** with their characters; **John** the Theologian's Gospel of the eternal Word; parables and miracles as signs of the Kingdom; the **Beatitudes** as a ladder; **Acts** as the Church's own beginning; **Paul**, read with Chrysostom, on grace and a living faith working by love; the **Catholic Epistles** with theosis and the faith once delivered; **Revelation**, unread at the Liturgy but everywhere in it.

**The lectionary:**

| Season | Gospel | Epistle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pascha to Pentecost | John | Acts |
| Summer | Matthew | Romans onward |
| Autumn to the Triodion | Luke | Paul |
| Lent | Mark (weekends) | Hebrews (Sundays) |

**Open questions in this stage.** The status of the readable books; the weight of the Hebrew text where it differs from the Septuagint; how literally to read Genesis 1; the order in which the Synoptics were written; and how far modern biblical scholarship helps. **On none of these has the Church spoken through a council**, and Orthodox writers hold different views in good faith.

**What links it all.** The Gospel book lies on the altar. **The Word read and the Word received in the Eucharist are one Christ.** The Bible is heard in the assembly, in the hymns, and in the icons.

**What comes next.** Stage 6 enters the services in which all of this is heard: the Divine Liturgy step by step, the daily and yearly cycles, the feasts, the fasts, the temple and its icons, and the other Mysteries.
Context: worship as theology:
Stages 2 to 5 set out what the Church believes. This stage shows where she says it most fully: in her worship. **For the Orthodox Church, worship is not one activity among others. It is where the faith lives.**

**The law of prayer.** An old Western saying, from the fifth-century writer Prosper of Aquitaine, is often quoted by Orthodox writers as well: *lex orandi, lex credendi*, "**the rule of prayer is the rule of belief**". The Church's doctrine was first prayed before it was defined. St Basil defended the Spirit's divinity from the doxology and from the ancient lamp-lighting hymn (Stage 4 and lesson 18 below). The Creed is sung at every Liturgy. **If you want to know what the Orthodox Church believes, go to her services.**

**Theology as prayer.** A saying attributed to **Evagrius of Pontus** (345–399), from his *Chapters on Prayer*, sums up the Orthodox view (this is a paraphrase): a theologian is one who prays truly, and one who prays truly is a theologian. Stage 1 began with it. Worship is not the decoration of theology but its home.

**Heaven on earth.** The Russian Primary Chronicle tells how Prince Vladimir of Kiev, about 987, sent envoys to see the worship of different peoples. Of the Liturgy in Hagia Sophia in Constantinople they reported, in paraphrase, that they did not know whether they were in heaven or on earth, and that God dwells there among men. Whatever the history behind the story, it says what the Orthodox Church believes her worship is: **the Kingdom of heaven made present**, where the Church on earth joins the angels.

**The marks of Orthodox worship:**

| Mark | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Liturgical** | the services follow fixed texts and an order, not improvised prayer. The word *leitourgía* means "the work of the people" |
| **Corporate** | the whole Church prays together; even private prayer uses the Church's words |
| **Sung** | nearly everything is chanted or sung; there are no musical instruments in most Orthodox churches |
| **Physical** | standing, bowing, prostrations, the sign of the cross, kissing icons, candles, incense: **the body prays too** |
| **Biblical** | the texts are woven from Scripture (Stage 5) |
| **Cyclical** | the services follow the day, the week and the year |
| **In many languages** | Greek, Church Slavonic, Arabic, Romanian, Georgian, English, Swahili and others, from the same books |

**The plan of the stage.**

| Lessons | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| 2–5 | the temple, icons, the clergy and the three Liturgies |
| 6–16 | the **Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, step by step**, with the Reading (the anaphora) at lesson 12 |
| 17–21 | the daily, weekly and yearly cycles, and the service books |
| 22–26 | the twelve great feasts, Great Lent, Holy Week and Pascha, the fasts |
| 27–29 | confession, marriage, unction and ordination |

**One translation throughout.** The service texts quoted here are from **Isabel Florence Hapgood's *Service Book of the Holy Orthodox-Catholic Apostolic (Greco-Russian) Church* (1906)**, the first full English Orthodox service book, made with the interest and practical help of St Tikhon, then Archbishop of North America, whom her preface thanks. It is public domain and is quoted from the 1906 scan. Modern translations in parishes differ in wording, but the order of service is the same.
The temple: narthex, nave, iconostasis a:
An Orthodox church building is itself a statement of the faith. Its shape says where the worshipper stands and where he is going.

**The word.** Orthodox Christians often call the building a **temple** (Greek *naós*, Slavonic *khram*), because it is a house of God, as the Temple in Jerusalem was. It is consecrated by a bishop, with relics placed in the altar and the altar anointed with myron.

**Facing east.** Churches are built, where possible, with the altar at the **east**, toward the rising sun, the symbol of Christ, "the Dayspring from on high" (Luke 1:78), who will come from the east (Matthew 24:27). **The whole congregation faces east with the priest.**

**The three parts:**

| Part | Greek | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Narthex** | *nárthēx* | the entrance porch. Of old, the place of catechumens and penitents. Candles are lit and icons venerated here |
| **Nave** | *naós* | the body of the church, where the faithful stand. "Nave" is from Latin *navis*, ship: the Church as the ark of salvation |
| **Sanctuary** | *hierón*, *vḗma* | the altar area behind the iconostasis, entered by clergy and servers |

**The iconostasis** (*eikonostásion*, "icon-stand"). A screen of icons separates the nave from the sanctuary. **It does not hide heaven; it shows it**: the saints are the window through which the faithful see the Kingdom. It has three doors:

- **The Royal Doors** (or Holy Doors) in the centre, used only by clergy at certain moments, usually painted with the **Annunciation** and the **four evangelists**: the gospel is the door into the Kingdom.
- **The deacons' doors** at the north and south, usually with archangels or holy deacons.

On either side of the Royal Doors: **Christ** on the right (as one faces the screen), the **Theotokos** with the Child on the left. Beyond them, usually **St John the Forerunner** and the **patron saint or feast** of the church. In Russian churches, from about the fifteenth century, the iconostasis grew into several tiers: the Deisis (Christ with intercessors), the feasts, the prophets and the patriarchs. Greek iconostases are usually lower.

**In the sanctuary:**

| Object | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **The Holy Table** (*Hagía Trápeza*, the altar) | square, consecrated, holding the antimension, the Gospel book, a cross and the tabernacle. Only clergy touch it. It is Christ's tomb and the throne of God |
| **The antimension** | the cloth with relics on which the Liturgy is served (Stage 4) |
| **The tabernacle** (*artophórion*) | holds the reserved Gifts for the sick |
| **The Table of Oblation** (*próthesis*) | on the north side, where the bread and wine are prepared |
| **The High Place** | behind the altar, the bishop's throne, flanked by seats for the priests |

**The dome.** In Byzantine churches the dome shows **Christ Pantocrator** (*Pantokrátōr*, "Ruler of all"), looking down, with the prophets and apostles below, and the evangelists in the four pendentives. The apse above the altar usually shows the **Theotokos**, "wider than the heavens", because she contained the uncontainable. **Above is heaven, below is earth, and the church joins them.**

**The key sentence:** the temple faces east, is divided into narthex, nave and sanctuary, and its iconostasis shows heaven rather than hiding it; at its centre is the Holy Table, Christ's tomb and God's throne.
Icons: the theology of the image:
Icons are not decorations. The Orthodox Church teaches that they are a confession of the Incarnation, and the Seventh Ecumenical Council defined their veneration.

**The word.** *Eikṓn* is Greek for "**image**". An icon is a holy image of Christ, the Theotokos, the angels, the saints or the feasts, painted (Orthodox say **written**, from *graphḗ*) according to tradition.

**The argument from the Incarnation.** The Old Testament forbade images of God, because God had not been seen (Deuteronomy 4:12–16). **In Christ, the invisible God became visible.** St John of Damascus (about 675–749), defending icons against the iconoclast emperors, wrote in his *First Apology against Those Who Attack the Divine Images*, translated by Mary H. Allies (1898):

> "Now, however, when God is seen clothed in flesh, and conversing with men, I make an image of the God whom I see. I do not worship matter, I worship the God of matter, who became matter for my sake, and deigned to inhabit matter, who worked out my salvation through matter."

**To refuse the icon of Christ is to deny that he truly became man.** That is the Orthodox argument, and it is why the restoration of icons is called the **Triumph of Orthodoxy**.

**The council.** **Nicaea II (787)**, the Seventh Ecumenical Council, defined that icons should be set up and venerated, and explained why, in Percival's translation (NPNF, Second Series, vol. 14, 1900):

> "For the honour which is paid to the image passes on to that which the image represents, and he who reveres the image reveres in it the subject represented."

The council drew this principle from **St Basil**, who wrote in *On the Holy Spirit* 18.45 that "the honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype" (tr. Jackson, NPNF II.8, 1895). Basil was speaking of the Son as the image of the Father; the council applied it to painted images. The distinction between **veneration** (*proskýnēsis*) and **worship** (*latreía*) is the council's (Stage 4).

**The history, briefly.** **Iconoclasm** ("image-breaking") began under Emperor Leo III about 726–730, was condemned in 787, returned in 815, and was ended finally in **843** under Empress Theodora. The restoration is kept on the **first Sunday of Great Lent**, the **Sunday of Orthodoxy**, with a procession of icons. Stage 8 tells the full history.

**How icons are made.** Iconographers follow traditional patterns (the Russian *podlinnik*, pattern books), pray and often fast, and work with egg tempera on wooden boards, with gold for the light of heaven. The style is not naturalism. **Icons show the world transfigured**: no shadows (the light comes from within), reverse perspective (the lines open toward the viewer, drawing him in), large eyes and ears, small mouths (the senses open to God, the passions stilled).

**How icons are used.** Orthodox Christians **kiss** icons, light candles and lamps before them, bow and cross themselves, carry them in procession, and keep an **icon corner** at home, facing east where possible, where the family prays. Many icons are honoured as **wonder-working**: the Vladimir icon in Russia, the Kazan icon, the Iveron icon of Mount Athos (and its copies), the Kykkos icon in Cyprus. **The icon is a meeting-place, not an idol.** One prays not to wood and paint but to the person shown, who is present to the one praying.

**The key sentence:** because God became visible in Christ, he can be painted; the honour given to the icon passes to the person it shows (Nicaea II, 787); and refusing icons would deny the Incarnation.
Clergy, servers and vestments:
Orthodox worship is served by an ordered assembly. Each person has a place, and the vestments say what each is doing.

**Who serves.** The three major orders (Stage 4): **bishop**, **priest** and **deacon**. Below them are the minor orders: **subdeacon** (*hypodiákonos*), who assists the bishop, and **reader** (*anagnṓstēs*), who reads the Epistle and the Psalms; a **chanter** (*psáltēs*) leads the singing in Greek use, and a choir in Slavic use. Laymen and boys serve in the altar as **altar servers**, carrying candles and the censer.

**The deacon's role.** In the full Liturgy the **deacon** leads the people's prayer: he sings the litanies, reads the Gospel, censes, and calls the people to attention. He stands between the altar and the people, as a bridge. Many parishes have no deacon, and the priest takes his parts.

**Vestments.** Orthodox vestments descend from the formal dress of the late Roman world and have kept their meaning since. Each is put on with a verse from the Psalms.

| Vestment | Worn by | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sticharion** (*sticharion*) | all orders, and servers | the long tunic: the garment of salvation, like the baptismal robe |
| **Orarion** | deacon | a long stole over the left shoulder, raised when he leads prayer: an angel's wing, in the old image |
| **Epitrachelion** | priest and bishop | the stole round the neck, falling in front: **no priest serves any Mystery without it** |
| **Zone** | priest and bishop | the belt |
| **Epimanikia** | all major orders | the cuffs: the hands of God that shaped the world |
| **Phelonion** | priest | the large cape: the robe of righteousness |
| **Epigonation** | bishop, and some priests as an award | the diamond-shaped cloth at the knee: the sword of the Spirit |
| **Sakkos** | bishop | the tunic of the Byzantine emperors, given to bishops |
| **Omophorion** | bishop | the broad stole over the shoulders: **the lost sheep carried by the Good Shepherd** |
| **Mitre** | bishop (and some priests as an award) | the crown |
| **Panagia** | bishop | a round icon of the Theotokos on the breast |

**Colours.** There is no single fixed scheme. Common practice: **gold** for ordinary Sundays; **white** at Pascha (in Greek usage), Theophany and the Transfiguration; **red** for martyrs (and at Pascha in Russian usage); **blue** for feasts of the Theotokos (Slavic usage); **green** at Pentecost and Palm Sunday (Slavic); **purple** or **dark red** in Lent and on feasts of the Cross; **black** in Lent in some Slavic usage. Local traditions differ.

**Monastics and married clergy.** Priests and deacons may be married, if they married before ordination to the diaconate (lesson 29). **Bishops are chosen from the monastics**, or from widowed clergy who take monastic vows. Monastic clergy wear black robes and, on some occasions, the *klobuk* or *kamilavka* with a veil.

**The people.** The laity are not spectators. They sing the responses (directly, or through the choir), say "Amen", make the sign of the cross at the name of the Trinity, bow, light candles, venerate icons, bring the bread and wine (and the names for commemoration), and receive Communion. Stage 4 called them the **royal priesthood**: the Liturgy is their work too.

**The key sentence:** bishop, priest and deacon, with readers, chanters and servers, serve a whole assembly; their vestments, inherited from late Roman dress, say who they are, and above all the epitrachelion and the omophorion carry the meaning of priestly and pastoral care.
The three Liturgies: Chrysostom, Basil a:
The Orthodox Church celebrates the Eucharist in a few forms. All have the same shape, and they differ mostly in the priest's prayers.

**The word.** *Leitourgía* is Greek for "**public work**", a work done on behalf of the people. In Orthodox use "the Divine Liturgy" (*Theía Leitourgía*) means the Eucharist.

**The four in use:**

| Liturgy | When | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **St John Chrysostom** | **most days of the year** | the usual Liturgy. Its anaphora is attributed to Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople from 398 to 404 (died 407) |
| **St Basil the Great** | **ten times a year** | longer anaphora. The five Sundays of Lent (first to fifth), Holy Thursday, Holy Saturday, the eves of the Nativity and Theophany (or the feasts themselves, in certain years), and St Basil's feast on 1 January |
| **The Presanctified Gifts** | Wednesdays and Fridays of Great Lent, and the first three days of Holy Week | not a full Liturgy but Vespers with Communion from Gifts consecrated the previous Sunday. Attributed to **St Gregory the Dialogist** (Pope Gregory I of Rome, 590–604) |
| **St James** | on the feast of St James (23 October), and in some places on other days | the ancient Liturgy of Jerusalem, revived in modern times |

**Who wrote them.** The attribution of a liturgy to a Father means he shaped its central prayer, the anaphora. **St Basil's anaphora is very probably his own work**, a revision of an older Cappadocian prayer. **The Chrysostom anaphora** is related to older Antiochene prayers; the liturgical scholar **Robert Taft** argued from its language that Chrysostom himself was very likely its author or reviser. The rest of the service (litanies, hymns, entrances) grew up in Constantinople between the fifth and the twelfth centuries and is shared by both.

**Why the Liturgy of Chrysostom displaced Basil's.** In the early Byzantine period Basil's was the main Liturgy of Constantinople. From about the eleventh century the shorter Chrysostom anaphora became the usual one, and Basil's was kept for the great days. **The structure of the service is the same**; only the priest's prayers change, so the people hardly notice the difference except in the length of the anaphora and the hymn to the Theotokos ("In thee rejoiceth" in Basil's).

**The shape of the Divine Liturgy:**

| Part | Content | Lessons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Proskomedia** (Preparation) | the bread and wine are prepared at the Table of Oblation | 6 |
| **Liturgy of the Catechumens** (of the Word) | litanies, antiphons, Little Entrance, Trisagion, Epistle, Gospel, sermon | 7–9 |
| **Liturgy of the Faithful** (of the Eucharist) | Great Entrance, Creed, anaphora, Communion, dismissal | 10–15 |

**The Liturgy is served once a day on one altar**, by one priest, as a general rule: the Eucharist is the assembly of the whole community, not a private devotion. A church may have side altars for a second Liturgy on great feasts.

**Days without the Liturgy.** The full Liturgy is not served on the weekdays of Great Lent (Monday to Friday), because its joy does not fit the fast; on Wednesdays and Fridays the Presanctified is served instead. **On Great Friday no Liturgy at all is served**: the Church stands at the Cross.

**The Philosophy curriculum** has nothing to say about liturgies; this is a place where Orthodox theology is simply prayer.

**The key sentence:** the Chrysostom Liturgy is the everyday form, Basil's is served ten times a year, the Presanctified on Lenten weekdays; all share one shape, from the Proskomedia through the Word to the Eucharist.
The Divine Liturgy 1: the Proskomedia:
Before the public Liturgy begins, the priest prepares the gifts at the Table of Oblation. This **Proskomedia** (*proskomidḗ*, "offering", also called the *Prothesis*) is a whole theology in actions.

**When.** Before the Liturgy, usually during the Hours, often while the people are arriving. The priest has already said the **entrance prayers** before the iconostasis, kissed the icons, and vested.

**The bread.** Orthodox Christians use **leavened bread**, called *prósphora* ("offering"). Each loaf is stamped with a seal: a cross with the letters **IC XC NIKA** ("Jesus Christ conquers"). The faithful bake or bring the prosphora, with lists of names of the living and the dead to be remembered. Russian usage uses **five** prosphora (for the five loaves of the feeding of the five thousand); Greek usage often uses one large loaf.

**The Lamb.** The priest cuts the central square of the seal out of the loaf with the **spear** (*lónchē*), a small knife. This square is the **Lamb** (*Amnós*), which will become the Body of Christ. As he cuts, he says the words of Isaiah 53, in Hapgood's translation (1906):

> "He was led as a sheep to the slaughter. And as a spotless lamb before his shearers is dumb, so opened he not his mouth."

He then pierces the side of the Lamb with the spear, and pours wine and water into the chalice, saying John 19:34: "one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out blood and water". **The Proskomedia re-enacts the Passion in miniature.**

**The particles.** Around the Lamb on the **diskos** (the paten) the priest places small particles cut from the other prosphora:

| Position | For whom |
| --- | --- |
| **To the right of the Lamb** (one triangular particle) | **the Theotokos**: "the queen stood by on thy right hand" (Psalm 44:10, Brenton) |
| **To the left, in three rows of three** | **the nine ranks of saints**: John the Forerunner, the prophets, the apostles, the hierarchs, the martyrs, the monastic saints, the unmercenaries, Joachim and Anna with the saint of the day, and the author of the Liturgy |
| **Below** | **the living**: the bishop, the clergy, and the names the people have brought |
| **Below again** | **the departed** |

**The whole Church on one plate.** On the diskos lie Christ, his Mother, the saints, the living and the dead. This is the Church as Stage 4 described it: **one Body, gathered around the Lamb**. At the end of the Liturgy, after Communion, the particles for the living and dead are put into the chalice, with the prayer, in Hapgood, "Wash away, O Lord, the sins of all who are here commemorated, by thy precious Blood, through the prayers of thy Saints."

**The covers.** The priest places the **asterisk** (a folding star over the diskos, recalling the star of Bethlehem), and covers the diskos and chalice with veils and a large veil, the **aër** (air). He censes them and says the **prayer of offering**. **The Proskomedia also recalls the Nativity**: the Table of Oblation is the cave of Bethlehem, the diskos the manger.

**The prosphora and the antidoron.** What remains of the prosphora is cut up and blessed, and given to the people at the end of the Liturgy as the **antidoron** (*antídōron*, "instead of the gift"), a blessed bread. It is not Communion, and in many places it is offered to visitors and non-Orthodox too.

**The key sentence:** in the Proskomedia the priest cuts the Lamb with Isaiah's words, pierces it, and places around it the Theotokos, the saints, the living and the dead: the whole Church gathered on the diskos, awaiting the Spirit.
The Divine Liturgy 2: \"Blessed is the k:
The public Liturgy begins. Its first words announce where the Church is going: into the Kingdom.

**The opening blessing.** The deacon asks, "Bless, Master". The priest lifts the Gospel book and makes the sign of the cross with it over the altar, saying, in Hapgood's translation:

> "Blessed is the kingdom of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, now, and ever, and unto ages of ages."

The people answer: "Amen." **The Liturgy begins not with "Let us pray" but with the Kingdom already present.** Fr Alexander Schmemann made this opening the key to his book *The Eucharist: Sacrament of the Kingdom*: the Liturgy is the Church's journey into the Kingdom of the Trinity, and its first words state the destination.

**The Great Litany.** A *litany* (Greek *ektenḗs* or *synaptḗ*; Slavonic *ektenia*) is a series of petitions led by the deacon, each answered by the people with **"Lord, have mercy"** (*Kýrie eléēson*; Slavonic *Gospodi pomiluy*). The **Great Litany**, also called the **Litany of Peace**, opens almost every service. In Hapgood:

> "In peace let us pray to the Lord.
> For the peace that is from above, and for the salvation of our souls, let us pray to the Lord.
> For the peace of the whole world; for the welfare of God's holy Churches, and for the union of them all..."

**What the Great Litany prays for, in order:**

| Petition | For |
| --- | --- |
| **Peace** | in our hearts, from above, in the whole world |
| **The Church** | the holy churches, their unity, this temple and those who enter it with faith |
| **The clergy** | the patriarch or synod, the bishop, the clergy, all the people |
| **The civil authorities** | the country and those who govern it |
| **The city and the world** | this city, every city and land, and those who live in them |
| **The weather and the harvest** | good seasons, abundance of the fruits of the earth |
| **Travellers, the sick, the suffering, captives** | and their salvation |
| **Deliverance** | from all tribulation, wrath and need |
| **The Theotokos and the saints** | remembering them, "let us commend ourselves, and each other, and all our life unto Christ our God" (Hapgood) |

**Peace first.** The first three petitions are about peace. The Fathers taught that **no one can pray rightly without peace**: peace with God, with one's neighbour, within oneself. The deacon does not invite the people to pray for peace only, but **in peace**.

**"Lord, have mercy."** The Orthodox response is not a cry of despair. *Éleos* (mercy) is related in sound to *élaion*, olive oil, and the Fathers liked the connection: mercy is God's healing, poured out like oil on a wound. "Lord, have mercy" asks for God's loving-kindness in everything.

**The commemoration.** The litany ends with the Theotokos and all the saints, then, in Hapgood: "let us commend ourselves, and each other, and all our life unto Christ our God." The people answer, "To thee, O Lord." **The litany ends in self-offering.** Then the priest's exclamation: "For unto thee are due all glory, honour and worship, to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit."

**The pattern.** Every litany has the same three parts: the **deacon's petitions**, the **people's response**, and the **priest's exclamation** (*ekphṓnēsis*), a doxology to the Trinity. Meanwhile the priest says a **quiet prayer** at the altar, which the exclamation concludes. Since about the sixth century many of these prayers have been said quietly, though some churches today say them aloud.

**The key sentence:** the Liturgy opens by blessing the Kingdom of the Trinity, and the Great Litany prays in peace, for peace and for the whole world, before the people commit themselves to Christ.
The Divine Liturgy 3: the antiphons and:
After the Great Litany come three antiphons and the first procession of the Liturgy, with the Gospel book.

**The antiphons.** *Antíphōnos* means "sounding in response": psalms sung by two choirs in turn, as in the old processions of Constantinople. Between them come two short litanies and prayers. **Their content varies by day and by local usage:**

| Day | First antiphon | Second | Third |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Ordinary Sunday** (Slavic usage) | **Psalm 102** (LXX): "Bless the Lord, O my soul" (Brenton) | **Psalm 145**: "My soul, praise the Lord" (Brenton) | **the Beatitudes** |
| **Ordinary Sunday and weekdays** (Greek usage) | Psalm verses with the refrain "Through the prayers of the Birth-giver of God, O Saviour, save us" (Hapgood) | verses with a refrain asking the Son of God to save "us who sing unto thee: Alleluia" (Hapgood) | Psalm verses with the troparion of the day |
| **Great feasts** | psalm verses with special refrains for the feast | | |

**"O Only-begotten Son."** After the second antiphon the Church always sings this hymn, traditionally attributed to **Emperor Justinian I** (reigned 527–565). In Hapgood's translation:

> "O Only-begotten Son and Word of God! Thou who art immortal yet didst deign for our salvation to become incarnate of the Holy Birth-giver of God and ever-virgin Mary; and without change of essence wast made man; who also wast crucified for us, O Christ our God, trampling down Death by death; who art one of the Holy Trinity, and art glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit: Save us."

**It is the Creed of Christ in one breath**: the Son is God, became man of the Theotokos "without change of essence" (against confusing the natures, Stage 3), was crucified, destroyed death, and is one of the Trinity. The phrase "one of the Holy Trinity" answered a sixth-century controversy about whether one may say "one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh".

**The Beatitudes.** The third antiphon on Sundays in Slavic usage (and on some days in Greek usage), introduced with the good thief's prayer: "In thy Kingdom remember us, O Lord, when thou comest into thy Kingdom" (Hapgood). Stage 5 read them as a ladder of ascent.

**The Little Entrance.** During the third antiphon the priest and deacon come out through the north door, carrying the **Gospel book**, with candles, and stand before the Royal Doors. The deacon raises the Gospel and cries, in Hapgood's translation, "**Wisdom, O believers!**" (the Greek *Sophía! Orthoí!* means literally "Wisdom! Upright!", that is, stand up), and all sing the entrance hymn, in Hapgood: "O come, let us worship and fall down before Christ." **The Gospel book is Christ coming among his people to teach them.** The clergy enter the sanctuary through the Royal Doors.

**The history.** In early Constantinople the Little Entrance was **the actual entry of clergy and people into the church**, after a procession through the city during which the antiphons were sung. It is now a symbolic procession, but its name and meaning remain: **the Church enters the Kingdom.** At a bishop's Liturgy the bishop stands in the middle of the church until this entrance, and enters the sanctuary only then.

**The troparia and kontakia.** After the entrance the choir sings the **troparion** and **kontakion** of the day: short hymns of the Resurrection (on Sundays), the feast, the saint of the day and the church's patron. **These hymns tell the people what the Church is celebrating today.**

**The key sentence:** three antiphons of psalms and hymns, "O Only-begotten Son" with its whole Christology, and the Little Entrance with the Gospel book, in which the Church enters the Kingdom to hear the Word.
The Divine Liturgy 4: the Trisagion, the:
The Liturgy of the Word reaches its climax: the thrice-holy hymn of the angels, and then the readings from the Apostle and the Gospel.

**The Trisagion.** *Trisághios* means "**thrice-holy**". The choir sings three times or more, in Hapgood's translation:

> "O Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal One, have mercy upon us."

The hymn is very old. It was sung by the bishops at the **Council of Chalcedon (451)**, according to the council's acts, and Byzantine tradition tells that it was revealed to a boy in Constantinople during an earthquake in the fifth century. It echoes the seraphim's song in Isaiah 6:3. **The three "Holy"s address the Trinity**: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and the singular "have mercy" the one God. On certain great feasts, which were once days of baptism (Nativity, Theophany, Lazarus Saturday, Pascha and Bright Week, Pentecost), it is replaced by "As many as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ" (Galatians 3:27), and on feasts of the Cross by a hymn venerating the Cross and glorifying the Resurrection.

**The Prokeimenon.** *Prokeímenon*, "**that which is set before**": a psalm verse sung before the Epistle, with one or two further verses. Each day and tone has its own. It sets the theme.

**The Epistle.** The reader stands in the middle of the church and chants the **Epistle** (the *Apóstolos*), from Acts or the Letters (Stage 5's lectionary). The priest blesses: "Peace be with thee" (Hapgood). The reader answers, "And with thy spirit."

**The Alleluia.** The choir sings **"Alleluia"** (Hebrew, "praise the Lord") with psalm verses, while the deacon censes the altar, the iconostasis, the clergy and the people. The incense rises before the Gospel.

**The prayer before the Gospel.** The priest prays, in Hapgood's version (Stage 5): "Illumine our hearts, O God who lovest mankind, with the pure light of thy divine knowledge."

**The Gospel.** The deacon (or priest) comes out to the ambo with the Gospel book. The call and response:

| Who | Says (Hapgood, 1906) |
| --- | --- |
| Priest | "Wisdom, O believers! Let us listen to the Holy Gospel." |
| Priest | "Peace be with you all." |
| People | "And with thy spirit." |
| Deacon | "The Lesson from the Holy Gospel according to N." |
| People | "**Glory to thee, O Lord; glory to thee.**" |
| Priest | "Let us attend." |

All **stand**, as for Christ himself. At the end the priest says "Peace be unto thee, who hast announced the good tidings", and the people sing again "Glory to thee, O Lord; glory to thee." The Gospel book is often then given to the faithful to kiss.

**The homily.** The sermon (*homilía*) belongs here, after the Gospel, as it did in the time of the Fathers: Chrysostom's homilies on Matthew and John were preached at this point. (In many parishes the sermon is given at the end of the Liturgy instead, for practical reasons.) **The preacher explains the Gospel just read.**

**"Wisdom!"** The deacon's repeated cry, *Sophía*, calls attention to the holiest moments: before the readings, the Creed and other key points. **Wisdom is Christ himself**, the Word (Stage 5's lesson on the Wisdom books). The people are told: what follows is Christ speaking; stand up and attend.

**The key sentence:** after the Trisagion of the angels, the Church hears the Apostle and then the Gospel, standing and with "Glory to thee, O Lord", and the homily explains the Word: Christ the Wisdom of God speaking in the assembly.
The Divine Liturgy 5: the catechumens an:
After the Word comes the Eucharist. In between, the Church dismisses the catechumens and carries the gifts to the altar in the Great Entrance.

**The Litany of Fervent Supplication** (*ektenḗs*, "intense"). Petitions with a threefold "Lord, have mercy", for the Church, the authorities, the living and the departed by name. Here families' names are read.

**The Litany for the Catechumens.** Prayer for those preparing for baptism: that the Lord will have mercy on them, reveal to them the Gospel, and unite them to his holy Church (in paraphrase). Then, in Hapgood's translation:

> "Depart, all ye Catechumens, depart. Depart, all ye Catechumens: let no Catechumen remain: but let us who are in the faith again, yet again, in peace pray unto the Lord."

**Why the dismissal remains.** In the early Church the unbaptised really left at this point, because only the baptised could witness the Eucharist and pray its prayers. Today catechumens usually stay, but the words remain. They remind the faithful that **what follows is the Mystery of the baptised**, and they mark the beginning of the **Liturgy of the Faithful**.

**The Litanies of the Faithful.** Two short litanies and two prayers for the faithful: that they may stand without blame before the altar.

**The priest's prayer.** While the choir sings the Cherubic Hymn, the priest says a long quiet prayer, unworthy to approach. It ends, in Hapgood's translation:

> "For it is thou who offerest and art offered, who receivest and art thyself received, O Christ our God."

**Christ is the priest, the offering and the one who receives it.** No human priest offers the Eucharist on his own authority (Stage 4).

**The Cherubic Hymn.** *Cheroubikón*. Introduced in Constantinople in the **570s**, under Emperor Justin II, it is sung slowly, in long melodies. Hapgood's translation:

> "Let us, the Cherubim mystically representing, and unto the Life-giving Trinity the thrice-holy chant intoning, all cares terrestrial now lay aside. That we may raise on high the King of all, like conqueror on shield and spears, by the Angelic Hosts invisibly up-borne."

**Read it phrase by phrase.** "**Mystically representing the Cherubim**": the people on earth stand where the angels stand in heaven. "**All cares terrestrial now lay aside**": the moment to leave the world behind. "**Raise on high the King of all**": the image is of a Roman emperor lifted on his soldiers' shields at his proclamation; Christ is carried in, invisibly, by angels. **The earthly assembly joins the heavenly one.**

**The Great Entrance.** During the hymn the priest and deacon go to the Table of Oblation, take the diskos and chalice, and process out through the north door, round into the nave and back through the Royal Doors. They commemorate the patriarch, the bishop, the clergy, the authorities, the people and all Orthodox Christians, asking the Lord God to remember them all in his kingdom. The gifts are placed on the altar and covered with the aër.

**What the Great Entrance is not.** **The gifts are not yet consecrated.** The faithful bow because these are the gifts offered to God and about to become Christ's Body and Blood, and because the procession is an icon of Christ going to his Passion, and of his burial (the priest says the hymns of Joseph of Arimathea as he lays them on the altar). Liturgical scholars warn against treating the unconsecrated gifts as though they were already the Body and Blood.

**On Holy Thursday and Holy Saturday** the Cherubic Hymn is replaced by others: "Of thy Mystical Supper" and "Let all mortal flesh keep silence".

**The key sentence:** the catechumens are dismissed, the faithful pray, and in the Great Entrance, as the Cherubic Hymn is sung, the gifts are carried to the altar, the people standing in the place of the angels.
The Divine Liturgy 6: the kiss of peace:
Before the anaphora, the faithful are reconciled and confess one faith. **Love and faith come first, then the offering.**

**The Litany of Supplication.** A litany in which the people answer each petition by asking the Lord to grant it: for an angel of peace, a faithful guide and guardian of soul and body, for pardon, for "A Christian ending to our life" (Hapgood), and others.

**"Peace be with you all."** The priest blesses the people. Then the deacon, in Hapgood's translation:

> "Let us love one another, that with one accord we may confess"

and the people complete the sentence:

> "Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the Trinity, one in Essence and undivided."

**This is the hinge of the Liturgy.** **Love leads to the confession of the Trinity.** The Trinity is a communion of love, and only those who love one another can confess the God who is love.

**The kiss of peace.** In the early Church all the faithful exchanged a kiss at this point (Romans 16:16: "Salute one another with an holy kiss"). Today, in most places, **only the clergy at the altar exchange it**, kissing the gifts, the altar and each other on the shoulders, in Hapgood's form:

> "Christ is in the midst of us." "He is and shall be."

Some parishes have restored the kiss among the people. The principle comes from Christ: "if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift... first be reconciled to thy brother" (Matthew 5:23–24, KJV).

**"The doors! The doors!"** The deacon cries, in Hapgood, "The Doors! The Doors! Wisdom! Let us attend." In the early Church this was an order to the doorkeepers to close the doors, so that no unbaptised person entered during the Mystery. **The doors are now the doors of the heart**: the faithful are told to shut out everything foreign to what follows.

**The Creed.** All sing or say the **Symbol of Faith**: "I believe in one God the Father Almighty..." (Stage 4's opening lesson quotes Hapgood's text of its last articles). It was introduced into the Liturgy at Constantinople in the early **sixth century**. During it, the priest waves the aër over the gifts, the trembling of the Spirit. **The Church confesses her faith before she offers.** Only those who share this faith share the cup (Stage 4).

**"Let us stand aright."** The deacon, in Hapgood's translation:

> "Let us stand aright, let us stand with fear, that we may offer in peace the Holy Oblation."

and the people answer:

> "A mercy of peace, a sacrifice of praise."

**What the response means.** The Eucharist is "**a mercy of peace**": God's mercy, which brings peace, and also the peace (reconciliation) that is our offering, following the kiss. And it is "**a sacrifice of praise**" (Hebrews 13:15): the thanksgiving that is the Church's offering. The Greek is *éleon eirḗnēs, thysían ainéseōs*.

**The order is the teaching:**

| Step | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Peace** | reconciliation with God and neighbour |
| **Love one another** | the communion of the Church |
| **The kiss** | love made visible |
| **The doors** | the heart closed to everything else |
| **The Creed** | one faith confessed |
| **Stand aright** | attention and awe |
| **A mercy of peace, a sacrifice of praise** | the offering ready |

**The key sentence:** before the anaphora the Church is reconciled in love, confesses the Trinity with one mouth, shuts the doors of the heart, and stands ready to offer "a mercy of peace, a sacrifice of praise".
Reading: the anaphora of St John Chrysos:
This is the heart of the Divine Liturgy, the great eucharistic prayer, read closely in the translation of the first full English Orthodox service book.

**The text.** From Isabel Florence Hapgood's *Service Book* (1906), pages 101–105, the Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, abridged:

> **Priest.** The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, be with you all.
> **Choir.** And with thy spirit.
> **Priest.** Lift up your hearts.
> **Choir.** We lift them up unto the Lord.
> **Priest.** Let us give thanks unto the Lord.
> **Choir.** Meet and right is it that we should adore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the Trinity, one in Essence and undivided.
>
> *The Priest, secretly:* "It is meet and right that we should laud thee, bless thee, praise thee, give thanks unto thee, and adore thee in all places of thy dominion: for thou art God ineffable, incomprehensible, invisible, inconceivable; thou art from everlasting and art changeless, thou, and thine Only-begotten Son, and thy Holy Spirit. Thou from nothingness hast called us into being; and when we had fallen away from thee, thou didst raise us up again; and thou hast not ceased to do all things until thou hadst brought us back to heaven, and hadst endowed us with thy kingdom which is to come. For all which things we give thanks unto thee... for all the things whereof we know, and whereof we know not..."
>
> **Choir.** Holy, holy, holy, Lord of Sabaoth; heaven and earth are full of thy glory: Hosanna in the highest: Blessed is he that cometh in the Name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.
>
> **Priest.** Take, eat, this is my Body which is broken for you, for the remission of sins... Drink ye all of this: for this is my Blood of the New Testament, which is shed for you, and for many, for the remission of sins.
>
> *The Priest, secretly:* "Bearing in remembrance, therefore, this commandment of salvation, and all those things which came to pass for us; the Cross, the Grave, the Resurrection on the third day, the Ascension into Heaven, the Sitting on the right hand, the Second and glorious Coming-again:"
> **Priest.** Thine own, of thine own, we offer unto thee, in behalf of all, and for all.
> **Choir.** We praise thee, we bless thee, we give thanks unto thee, O Lord, and we pray unto thee, O our God.
>
> *The Priest, secretly:* "Again we offer unto thee this reasonable and unbloody service. And we beseech and implore thee, and offer our supplications unto thee, that thou wilt send thy Holy Spirit upon us, and upon these Gifts here spread forth."

**The parts of the anaphora.** *Anaphorá* means "**lifting up, offering**".

| Part | Greek | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dialogue** | | "Lift up your hearts": the Church ascends |
| **Thanksgiving** | *eucharistía* | for God himself, for creation, for the fall reversed, for the Kingdom: **"all the things whereof we know, and whereof we know not"** |
| **Sanctus** | | the angels' song from Isaiah 6, and the crowd's from Palm Sunday |
| **Institution** | | Christ's words at the Last Supper |
| **Anamnesis** | *anámnēsis*, remembrance | the whole saving work, **including the Second Coming**, remembered as present |
| **Offering** | | "Thine own, of thine own" |
| **Epiclesis** | *epíklēsis*, invocation | the Father is asked to send the Spirit "upon us, and upon these Gifts" |

**Three things to notice.**

1. **The prayer is addressed to the Father**, through the Son, in the Spirit. It is the prayer of the whole Trinity's work, and the first thing it says of God is apophatic: "ineffable, incomprehensible, invisible, inconceivable" (Stage 2).
2. **The anamnesis remembers the future.** "The Second and glorious Coming-again" is listed among things "which came to pass for us". **In the Liturgy the Kingdom is already present**, so even what is still to come can be remembered.
3. **"Thine own, of thine own."** The bread and wine are God's creation, given back to him. **Nothing is offered that was not first received.** The phrase echoes David's prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:14. The deacon lifts the diskos and chalice crossed over the altar as it is said: the offering is "in behalf of all, and for all", the whole of creation.

**The epiclesis.** The prayer for the Spirit continues in the next lesson. **Orthodox teaching holds that the consecration is completed at the epiclesis**: the Father sends the Spirit, and the gifts become Christ's Body and Blood. The words of institution are recited as Christ's command and the ground of the prayer, not as a formula that consecrates by itself.

**Read it slowly at home.** Most of this prayer is said quietly by the priest while the choir sings. Hapgood's book, and modern service books, print it in full, and many Orthodox Christians read it in preparation for the Liturgy.
The Divine Liturgy 7: the epiclesis and:
The anaphora reaches its climax in the prayer to the Spirit, and then turns to the whole Church, living and departed, with the Theotokos first.

**The epiclesis completed.** After asking the Father to send the Spirit "upon us, and upon these Gifts here spread forth" (Hapgood), the priest blesses the bread and the cup. The dialogue with the deacon, in Hapgood's translation:

| Deacon | Priest |
| --- | --- |
| "Bless, Master, the Holy Bread." | "**And make this bread the precious Body of thy Christ.**" |
| "Amen. Bless, Master, the holy chalice." | "**And make that which is in this chalice the precious Blood of thy Christ.**" |
| "Amen. Master, bless both." | "**Transmuting them by thy Holy Spirit.**" |
| "Amen, amen, amen." | |

**This is the moment of consecration.** The clergy make a prostration to the earth. **From here on the bread and wine are the Body and Blood of Christ** (Stage 4).

**The troparion of the Third Hour.** Before the blessing, many service books insert a prayer three times: "O Lord, who at the Third Hour didst send down upon thine Apostles thy Holy Spirit: Take not the same from us, O Good One, but renew it in us who make our supplications unto thee" (Hapgood), with verses of Psalm 50. It is a later insertion into the anaphora, found in Hapgood's Russian-based text and in many Greek books; some modern editions, Greek and Slavic, omit it as an interruption of the prayer. **Orthodox practice varies here.**

**What the Gifts are for.** The priest continues: that they may be "unto soberness of soul, unto the remission of sins, unto the fellowship of thy Holy Spirit, unto the fulfilling of the kingdom of Heaven, and unto boldness toward thee; and not unto judgment or unto condemnation" (Hapgood).

**The commemorations.** The Eucharist is offered "for all thy servants departed this life before us in the faith; for our ancestors, fathers, the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, Preachers, Evangelists, Martyrs, Confessors, Ascetics; and for every righteous soul who hath died in the faith". **The Church offers the Eucharist even for the saints**: not because they need forgiveness, but because the Eucharist is thanksgiving for them and union with them.

**The Theotokos.** Then aloud, in Hapgood: "**Especially our most holy, all-undefiled, most blessed and glorious Lady, the Birth-giver of God and ever-virgin Mary**". The choir sings the hymn to her, the *Axion estin* ("It is truly meet"), in Hapgood's version:

> "Meet is it, in truth, to bless thee, the Birth-giver of God, ever-blessed, and all-undefiled, and the Mother of our God. More honourable than the Cherubim, and beyond compare more glorious than the Seraphim..."

The first part of this hymn, by Athonite tradition, was taught by the Archangel Gabriel to a monk on **Mount Athos** in the tenth century; the second part ("More honourable than the Cherubim") is by **St Cosmas the Hymnographer** (eighth century). On great feasts and in the Liturgy of St Basil another hymn replaces it.

**The living.** The priest then prays for the bishops (in Hapgood: "Among the first have in remembrance, O Lord, the Most Holy Governing Synod (or Patriarch)", then the diocesan bishop), the clergy, the city, travellers, the sick, the suffering, captives, and all. **The diptychs** (*díptycha*, "folded tablets"), the lists of the living and the dead read at this point, were in early centuries the sign of communion: to be named was to be in communion; to be struck off was to be out of it. Today the commemoration of one's bishop, and his commemoration of his primate, still marks communion between the churches.

**The anaphora ends** with a doxology, in Hapgood: "And grant that with one mouth and one heart we may glorify and praise thine all-honourable and majestic Name, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit". The people answer: "Amen." **The whole Church, heaven and earth, has been gathered into one prayer.**

**The key sentence:** the priest asks the Spirit to make the bread and wine the Body and Blood of Christ, "transmuting them by thy Holy Spirit"; then the Church offers the Gifts for the saints, the departed and the living, with the Theotokos first of all.
The Divine Liturgy 8: the Lord's Prayer,:
After the anaphora, the Church prepares to receive. The climax is the elevation of the Lamb and the Communion of clergy and people.

**The Litany before the Lord's Prayer.** Petitions for the precious Gifts now offered and sanctified, and that God may send down on the faithful his divine grace and the gift of the Holy Spirit (in paraphrase).

**The Lord's Prayer.** All sing or say "Our Father". The priest asks that we may "dare" (*katarxíōson*) to call God Father: **only by grace can a creature call God "Father"**, and the Liturgy says so before the prayer. The priest's exclamation closes it: "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit."

**"Holy things unto the Holy."** The priest lifts the Lamb above the diskos and proclaims, in Hapgood's translation:

> "Holy things unto the Holy."

and the people answer:

> "One only is holy, one only is the Lord, Jesus Christ, in the glory of God the Father. Amen."

**Read it carefully.** The priest's words seem to say that only the holy may receive. The people's answer says that **no one is holy except Christ**. Together they say: **the holy things are given to those who are made holy by them, and their holiness is Christ's.** No one receives because they are worthy; all receive because Christ is holy and makes them so.

**The fraction.** The priest breaks the Lamb into four parts, arranged in a cross on the diskos, saying, in Hapgood: "Broken and divided is the Lamb of God, which is broken, yet not disunited; which is ever eaten, yet never consumed, but sanctifieth those who partake thereof."

**The zeon.** The priest puts one piece (marked IC) into the chalice, and the deacon pours in a little **hot water** (*zéon*, "boiling"), with the words, in Hapgood, "The warmth of faith, full of the Holy Spirit. Amen." **The warmth is the warmth of life**: the Body and Blood given are those of the living, risen Christ. This is a distinctively Byzantine custom.

**The clergy's Communion.** The clergy receive at the altar, first the Body, then the Blood, separately. Before receiving they say the prayer of St John Chrysostom, in Hapgood's translation:

> "I believe, O Lord, and I confess, that thou art, in very truth, the Christ, the Son of the living God, who didst come into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief. And I believe that this is, of a truth, thine all-pure Body, and that this is thine own precious Blood."

**The people's Communion.** The Royal Doors open. The deacon comes out with the chalice and calls, in Hapgood:

> "In the fear of God and with faith draw near."

The people answer, "Blessed is he that cometh in the Name of the Lord; God is the Lord and hath revealed himself unto us." The faithful come forward, cross their arms on their breasts, and say the same prayer, "I believe, O Lord, and I confess". The priest gives **both the Body and the Blood together from the chalice, with a spoon** (*labís*), saying the communicant's baptismal name, in Hapgood: "The servant of God, N., partaketh of the precious and holy Body and Blood of our Lord, and God, and Saviour, Jesus Christ, unto the remission of his (or her) sins, and unto life everlasting." A server holds a red cloth under the chin. **Infants receive from the day of their baptism.**

**What is required.** Only **Orthodox Christians** receive, who have **prepared** by fasting, prayer and usually confession, according to their tradition and their spiritual father's guidance (lesson 16). Those who do not receive may take the antidoron at the end.

**The particles of the saints and of the living and the dead** are then poured into the chalice, with the prayer that their sins be washed away.

**The key sentence:** after "Our Father", the priest lifts the Lamb, "Holy things unto the Holy", the people answer that one only is holy, Jesus Christ, and they receive his Body and Blood together from the spoon, confessing "I believe, O Lord, and I confess".
The Divine Liturgy 9: thanksgiving and d:
After Communion the Church gives thanks and is sent out. The Liturgy does not just end; **it sends the faithful into the world**.

**"We have beheld the true Light."** The priest blesses the people with the words of Psalm 27:9 (LXX), asking God to save his people and bless his inheritance. The choir sings, in Hapgood's translation:

> "We have beheld the true Light; we have received the heavenly Spirit; we have found the true faith. Let us bow down in worship to the Trinity Undivided, for it hath saved us."

In the Paschal season "Christ is risen" is sung instead. **This hymn is the Pentecost hymn of Vespers**, and its words are those of the Church after Communion: light, the Spirit, the true faith, the Trinity. (Because it speaks of having "received the heavenly Spirit", it is omitted from Pascha to Pentecost.)

**The gifts are taken away.** The priest censes, saying, in Hapgood, "Be thou exalted in heaven, O God, and thy glory above all the earth" (the Ascension psalm verse), and carries it to the Table of Oblation. **The movement from altar to Table of Oblation is an icon of the Ascension**: Christ, who was present, ascends, remaining with his Church.

**The thanksgiving.** The deacon calls the people to give thanks, having received the divine, immortal and life-giving Mysteries of Christ (in paraphrase). The priest's prayer thanks God for the gift, and asks that it may make our path straight and keep our life.

**"Let us depart in peace."** The priest says, in Hapgood, "Let us depart in peace"; the people answer, "In the Name of the Lord."

**The Prayer before the Ambo.** The priest comes out to the ambo (the platform before the iconostasis) and reads aloud, in Hapgood:

> "O Lord, who blessest those who bless thee, and sanctifiest those who put their trust in thee: Save thy people and bless thine inheritance. Preserve the fulness of thy Church; sanctify those who love the beauty of thy house..."

It continues: "Give peace to thy world, and to thy Churches, and to thy Priests" (Hapgood), and ends with James 1:17, "every good gift and every perfect gift is from above". **The prayer is the Liturgy's summary**, said out among the people.

**"Blessed be the Name of the Lord."** The choir sings, in Hapgood, "Blessed be the Name of the Lord henceforth and forever" (Psalm 112:2), three times; in Slavic use Psalm 33 is sung while the antidoron is given.

**The dismissal** (*apólysis*). The priest blesses, in Hapgood's form: "May Christ, our true God, through the prayers of his most-holy Mother; of Saint N. (the saint of the day); and of all the Saints, have mercy upon us and save us, in that he is gracious and loveth mankind." In practice the dismissal also names the church's patron and the author of the Liturgy, St John Chrysostom.

**The antidoron and the cross.** The faithful come forward to kiss the hand cross the priest holds, and receive the **antidoron** (lesson 6). In many places they greet the priest and one another. Some stay for memorials, blessings or coffee.

**"The liturgy after the Liturgy."** Orthodox missiologists of the twentieth century, among them Fr Ion Bria and Archbishop Anastasios of Albania (1929–2025), used this phrase for the life of service and mission that should follow from the Eucharist. **The dismissal is a sending**: the people who received the Kingdom go out to live it.

**The key sentence:** the Church sings that it has seen the true Light, the gifts return to the Table of Oblation as at the Ascension, and the people are dismissed in peace, blessed and fed with the antidoron, to live "the liturgy after the Liturgy".
Preparing for Communion: fasting, confes:
How should an Orthodox Christian prepare to receive the Body and Blood of Christ, and how often should he receive? The tradition is clear on the reverence required. On frequency and on the link with confession, Orthodox practice genuinely differs.

**What all Orthodox practice shares:**

| Preparation | What it involves |
| --- | --- |
| **The Eucharistic fast** | **no food or drink from midnight** before the Liturgy (or from the evening before, or from waking, in some places). The sick and infants are excused |
| **Prayer** | the **Prayers before Holy Communion** in the prayer book: a canon, psalms and prayers by St Basil, St John Chrysostom, St Symeon the New Theologian and others, said the evening before and the morning of |
| **Reconciliation** | being at peace with one's neighbour (Matthew 5:23–24) |
| **Repentance** | examining one's conscience, and confessing serious sins before receiving |
| **Attending Vespers or the Vigil** | the evening before, where possible |

**"In the fear of God and with faith draw near."** St Paul warns: "whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 11:27, KJV). **No one is worthy; the question is whether one approaches with repentance and faith.** The prayers before Communion say this again and again: the communicant is a sinner, and approaches because Christ calls sinners.

**The question of frequency.** In the early Church all the faithful received at every Liturgy. St Basil (Letter 93) says that in Caesarea Christians received four times a week. Over the Byzantine centuries lay Communion became rare, and in many places Christians received only a few times a year, after long preparation.

**Two Orthodox views, both with deep roots:**

- **Frequent Communion.** In the eighteenth century the **Kollyvades** movement on Mount Athos called for a return to frequent Communion. **St Nikodemos the Hagiorite** and **St Makarios of Corinth** published the book *On Frequent Communion* (1783). In the twentieth century the eucharistic revival, associated with Russian émigré theologians in Paris and with movements in Greece, spread frequent Communion widely. **Its strength**: the Liturgy is the Church's common meal, and every prayer in it assumes that the people will receive; abstaining for months contradicts the service itself.
- **Less frequent Communion, with fuller preparation.** Many Orthodox, especially in Russian and other Slavic traditions and in many monasteries, receive less often (monthly, or in each fasting season), after several days of fasting, confession and prayer. **Its strength**: it guards the reverence due to the Mystery, prevents Communion becoming routine, and links it to repentance.

**Confession before Communion.**
- In **Russian and much Slavic practice**, confession before each Communion is the norm.
- In **Greek, Antiochian, Romanian and much diaspora practice**, the faithful confess regularly (perhaps in each fasting season) but not necessarily before each Communion, with the blessing of their spiritual father.

Both are Orthodox, and both rest on the same principles: **repentance and Communion belong together, and the spiritual father guides the individual**.

**What would settle it.** There is no council on the question. The Holy and Great Council of Crete (2016) did not legislate on it. Practice is set by the local churches and by each person's confessor.

**Women.** In many places women do not receive Communion during menstruation, by old custom based on purity laws. Other Orthodox bishops and theologians hold that this custom has no place in Christian teaching on the body, and do not ask women to abstain. **Practice varies by church and by spiritual father**, and Orthodox writers argue both sides.

**The key sentence:** every Orthodox Christian fasts, prays and repents before Communion; how often to receive, and whether to confess before each Communion, differ between Orthodox churches and are set by one's spiritual father.
The daily cycle of services: from Vesper:
The Orthodox Church prays through the whole day in a cycle of services. **The liturgical day begins at sunset**, as in Genesis: "the evening and the morning were the first day" (Genesis 1:5, KJV).

**The cycle:**

| Service | Greek | When | Theme |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Vespers** | *Hesperinós* | sunset | creation, the fall, the evening sacrifice, the coming of Christ, the light that does not set |
| **Compline** | *Apódeipnon*, "after supper" | before sleep | protection through the night; death and repentance |
| **Midnight Office** | *Mesonyktikón* | midnight | Christ the Bridegroom coming at midnight (Matthew 25:6) |
| **Matins** | *Órthros*, "dawn" | before dawn | the Resurrection, the light rising |
| **First Hour** | *Prṓtē Hṓra* | about 7 a.m. | the beginning of the day's work |
| **Third Hour** | | about 9 a.m. | the descent of the Spirit (Acts 2:15) |
| **Sixth Hour** | | noon | the Crucifixion |
| **Ninth Hour** | | about 3 p.m. | the death of Christ |
| **Divine Liturgy** | | in the morning, usually after the Third and Sixth Hours | the Eucharist |

**Why sunset.** The Jewish day began at sunset (Genesis 1:5), and the Church kept that reckoning. **Every feast begins with Vespers the evening before.** Sunday begins on Saturday evening; Christmas on Christmas Eve.

**The Hours.** Each of the four Hours is short (about fifteen minutes): three psalms, troparia, a few prayers and the **Prayer of the Hours**, which begins, in Hapgood: "Thou who, at all times, and at every hour, both in heaven and on earth, art worshipped and glorified, O Christ our God". They sanctify the times of the day by the events of Christ's Passion and the descent of the Spirit.

**The All-Night Vigil.** On the eves of Sundays and feasts, **Vespers, Matins and the First Hour** are joined into one service, the **Vigil** (*agrypnía*; Slavonic *vsenoshchnoe bdenie*, "all-night vigil"). In monasteries, especially on Mount Athos, it can last all night. In Russian parishes it is served on Saturday evening and lasts about two hours. **Greek parish practice** usually serves Vespers on Saturday evening and Matins on Sunday morning, directly before the Liturgy.

**Who serves the daily cycle.** In **monasteries**, the full cycle is served every day. In most **parishes**, Vespers (or the Vigil) on Saturday evening and the eves of feasts, and Matins and the Liturgy on Sunday morning. The faithful who cannot attend pray parts of it at home, from the **Horologion** (Book of Hours) or a prayer book: morning and evening prayers are drawn from Matins, Compline and the Hours.

**A day sanctified.** The cycle teaches that **all time belongs to God**. St Paul's "Pray without ceasing" (1 Thessalonians 5:17) is answered by the Church in two ways: the services that cover the day, and the Jesus Prayer that covers the heart (Stage 10).

**The key sentence:** the Orthodox day begins at sunset with Vespers and runs through Compline, the Midnight Office, Matins and the four Hours, each tied to an event of salvation; on Sunday and feast eves Vespers and Matins become the Vigil.
Vespers and Matins: the evening and morn:
Vespers and Matins are the two great services of the daily cycle. Together they tell the whole story of salvation, from creation to the Resurrection.

**Vespers.** The order of a Saturday-evening or feast-eve Vespers:

| Part | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **"O come, let us worship"**, and **Psalm 103** (LXX), "Bless the Lord, O my soul" | **Creation**: the world in its first beauty. In a Vigil the priest censes the whole church with the Royal Doors open: **Paradise** |
| **The Great Litany** | the doors close: **the fall** and our prayer from outside Paradise |
| **A kathisma** (on Saturday evening, "Blessed is the man", Psalms 1–3) | the way of the righteous |
| **"Lord, I have cried"** (Psalms 140, 141, 129, 116), with **stichera** (hymns) of the day | the evening sacrifice: "Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice" (Psalm 140:2, Brenton). Incense rises as it is sung |
| **The Entrance** with the censer | the coming of Christ into the world |
| **"O Gladsome Light"** | Christ the light of the Father |
| **The Prokeimenon** | the theme of the day |
| **Old Testament readings** (on feasts) | the types (Stage 5) |
| **Litanies, "Vouchsafe, O Lord"** | prayer for the night |
| **Aposticha** | more hymns of the day |
| **The Song of Simeon** | "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace" (Luke 2:29): the Old Testament meeting Christ |
| **Trisagion prayers, troparion, dismissal** | |

**"O Gladsome Light"** (*Phōs hilarón*). One of the oldest Christian hymns still sung, sung at the lighting of the lamps. In Hapgood's translation (1906):

> "O gladsome radiance of the holy glory of the Father immortal, heavenly, holy, blessed, Jesus Christ! In that we now are come unto the setting of the sun, and behold the light of even, we hymn thee, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, God."

**St Basil already called it ancient** in 375. In *On the Holy Spirit* 29.73 (tr. Jackson, NPNF II.8, 1895) he wrote: "Who was the author of these words of thanksgiving at the lighting of the lamps, we are not able to say. The people, however, utter the ancient form, and no one has ever reckoned guilty of impiety those who say We praise Father, Son, and God's Holy Spirit." **Basil used the hymn as evidence for the Spirit's divinity.**

**Matins.** The order of Sunday Matins, in outline:

| Part | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **The Six Psalms** (*Hexápsalmos*) | read in near darkness, lights dimmed: humanity waiting for the dawn |
| **The Great Litany** | |
| **"God is the Lord, and hath revealed himself unto us"** (Psalm 117) | the light breaks through; the troparia of the Resurrection |
| **Kathismata** | |
| **The Polyeleos** (on feasts: Psalms 134–135, "for his mercy endureth for ever") and the **Evlogitaria** of the Resurrection (on Sundays: the myrrh-bearing women at the tomb) | lamps lit; the church fully lit |
| **The Gospel of the Resurrection** (one of the eleven *Eothina*, Stage 5) | read by the priest **from the altar**, as from the tomb; the Gospel book is brought out to be kissed |
| **"Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ"** | sung after the Gospel |
| **Psalm 50** | repentance |
| **The Canon** | nine odes (usually eight are sung; the second is used only in Lent), each with an *irmós* (model verse) and troparia, based on the nine biblical odes |
| **The Magnificat** (ode 9) | "My soul doth magnify the Lord", with "More honourable than the Cherubim", as the deacon censes |
| **The Praises** (Psalms 148–150) | all creation praising God |
| **The Great Doxology** | "Glory to God in the highest... and on earth peace": **sung as the day dawns** |

**The canon.** The **canon** (*kanṓn*) is the great hymnographic form of Matins, developed in Palestine in the seventh and eighth centuries by **St Andrew of Crete**, **St John of Damascus** and **St Cosmas of Maiuma**. Each canon follows the biblical odes: the Song of Moses (ode 1), the Song of Moses in Deuteronomy (ode 2), Hannah's prayer (ode 3), Habakkuk (4), Isaiah (5), Jonah (6), the three youths (7 and 8), and the Magnificat with Zacharias's prayer (9).

**The key sentence:** Vespers moves from creation through the fall to Christ the evening light; Matins moves from the darkness of the Six Psalms through the Resurrection Gospel and the canon to the Great Doxology at dawn.
The Typikon and the service books:
The Orthodox services are not improvised. They are assembled each day from several books, according to a book of rules called the Typikon.

**The Typikon.** *Typikón*, from *týpos*, "pattern": the book that **orders the services**. It tells, for every day of the year, which texts to use, from which books, in what combination, and what to do when two commemorations fall on the same day.

**Its history in three stages:**

| Typikon | Origin | Where used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The Cathedral rite of Constantinople** | Hagia Sophia, before 1204 | the "sung office" of the imperial city; largely lost after the Latin conquest |
| **The Studite Typikon** | Monastery of Stoudios in Constantinople, ninth century, under **St Theodore the Studite** | spread to Mount Athos and to Kievan Rus' in the eleventh century |
| **The Jerusalem (Sabaite) Typikon** | the Lavra of St Sabbas near Jerusalem; it prevailed from about the twelfth to the fourteenth century | **the basis of Orthodox services almost everywhere today**, Slavic and Greek |

In the nineteenth century the Church of Constantinople issued a **parish Typikon** for Greek parishes (by **George Violakis**, 1888), adapting the Sabaite order to parish life. Slavic churches mostly follow the Sabaite Typikon in its Russian form. **This is why Greek and Russian services follow the same order but differ in details.**

**The service books:**

| Book | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| **Horologion** (*Hōrológion*, Book of Hours; Slavonic *Chasoslov*) | the fixed parts of the daily services |
| **Psalter** | the Psalms, in kathismata |
| **Octoechos** (*Oktṓēchos*, "eight tones"; also *Paraklētikḗ*) | the weekly cycle of hymns in eight tones |
| **Menaion** (*Mēnaíon*, "of the month") | twelve volumes, one for each month: the hymns of the saints and feasts of the fixed cycle |
| **Triodion** (*Triṓdion*, "three odes") | the pre-Lenten weeks, Lent and Holy Week |
| **Pentecostarion** | from Pascha to the Sunday of All Saints |
| **Euchologion** (*Euchológion*; Slavonic *Sluzhebnik* and *Trebnik*) | the priest's book: the Liturgies, the Mysteries and blessings |
| **Gospel** and **Apostolos** | the readings (Stage 5) |
| **Typikon** | the rules |

**How a service is put together.** Vespers on a Saturday in October draws from the Horologion (the fixed parts), the Psalter (the kathisma), the Octoechos (the Resurrection hymns in the tone of the week), the Menaion (the saint of the day), and perhaps the Gospel. **The chanter or reader assembles it each day**, following the Typikon. This is a skilled art, and Orthodox seminaries teach it as a subject (Slavonic *ustav*).

**The Triodion and Pentecostarion.** The movable cycle around Pascha replaces the Octoechos in Lent and the Paschal season. The Triodion takes its name from the Lenten weekday canons, which have only **three odes** instead of nine.

**The calendar of saints.** The Menaion gives each day's saints. The calendar includes saints of every Orthodox people: Greek, Slavic, Romanian, Georgian, Arab, and in recent decades American, African and others. Each local church adds its own saints to its Menaion.

**In practice.** Most parishes shorten the services. The Typikon describes the full monastic order; parishes adapt it, and the degree varies. **What is kept is the structure**, so that a worshipper anywhere can follow.

**The key sentence:** the Typikon, today the Jerusalem (Sabaite) rule in its Greek and Russian forms, orders each day's services from the Horologion, Psalter, Octoechos, Menaion, Triodion, Pentecostarion and the priest's Euchologion.
The weekly cycle: the days of the week a:
Each day of the week has its own theme, and the Sundays follow a cycle of eight musical tones. Together they give every week its shape.

**The days of the week:**

| Day | Theme |
| --- | --- |
| **Sunday** (*Kyriakḗ*, "the Lord's day") | **the Resurrection**. Every Sunday is a little Pascha. No kneeling or prostrations |
| **Monday** | **the bodiless powers**, the angels |
| **Tuesday** | **St John the Forerunner**, the greatest of the prophets |
| **Wednesday** | **the Cross and the Theotokos**: the day Judas agreed to betray Christ. A **fast day** |
| **Thursday** | **the apostles** and **St Nicholas** (as the type of holy bishops) |
| **Friday** | **the Cross**: the day of the Crucifixion. A **fast day** |
| **Saturday** | **all saints and the departed**: the day Christ lay in the tomb, and the day of rest; memorials for the dead are served |

**Wednesday and Friday.** From the first century Christians have fasted on these two days. The *Didache* (late first or early second century) already says, in M. B. Riddle's translation (ANF vol. 7, 1886): "let not your fasts be with the hypocrites; for they fast on the second and fifth day of the week; but fast on the fourth day and the Preparation (Friday)" (*Didache* 8). **The Wednesday and Friday fast is kept throughout the year**, except in the fast-free weeks.

**The Lord's Day.** Sunday is the first day of the week and **the eighth day**: the day of the new creation that lies beyond the seven days of this world. The Fathers loved this image; it is why Orthodox baptismal fonts were often eight-sided.

**The eight tones** (*ēchoi*, singular *ēchos*). Orthodox chant is organised into **eight modes**, each with its own melodies. The hymns of the **Octoechos** are written in these tones, and **each week is in one tone**, from Saturday evening to the following Friday: tone 1 one week, tone 2 the next, and so on to tone 8, then back to 1. The cycle starts each year after Pascha and runs until the next Lent.

**The tones and the Resurrection.** The Octoechos gives, for each tone, a full set of Resurrection hymns for Saturday Vespers and Sunday Matins. **In eight weeks the Church sings the Resurrection in eight different ways**, and the cycle repeats. The **Sunday Resurrection troparion** in the tone of the week is sung at Vespers, Matins and the Liturgy.

**Who composed them.** Tradition attributes the Octoechos to **St John of Damascus** (about 675–749). He shaped it and wrote many of its hymns, though the eight-tone system is older and the book was expanded after him.

**The eleven Gospels.** Alongside the eight-week cycle of tones runs the **eleven-week** cycle of the Resurrection Gospels at Matins (Stage 5). The two cycles do not coincide, so the same combination returns rarely.

**Chant traditions.** The tones are sung differently in different traditions: **Byzantine chant** (Greek, Antiochian, Romanian, Bulgarian, Serbian), written in neumes, unison with a drone (*ison*); **Znamenny chant** (old Russian), unison, in its own neumes; and **Russian and Ukrainian polyphony**, harmonised for choirs since the seventeenth century. **Georgian chant** has its own ancient three-part polyphony. All use the eight-tone framework in some form.

**A week as a little year.** The week moves from the Resurrection on Sunday, through the angels, the Forerunner and the apostles, to the Cross on Wednesday and Friday and the tomb and the departed on Saturday, and back to the Resurrection. **Each week is a Holy Week ending in Pascha.**

**The key sentence:** Sunday is the Resurrection, Wednesday and Friday the Cross and fasting, Saturday the departed, with each weekday its own saints; and the Resurrection hymns rotate through eight tones, a week each.
The yearly cycle: the fixed and movable:
The Church's year has two cycles running together: the fixed, which follows the calendar date, and the movable, which follows Pascha.

**The Church New Year.** The Orthodox Church year begins on **1 September**, the **Indiction**, from the Byzantine tax year. The first great feast of the year is the **Nativity of the Theotokos (8 September)**, and the last is the **Dormition (15 August)**. **The year begins with the birth of the Mother of God and ends with her falling asleep.**

**The fixed cycle** (the Menaion): feasts on fixed dates: the Nativity (25 December), Theophany (6 January), the Dormition (15 August), and the saints of each day.

**The movable cycle** (the Triodion and Pentecostarion): everything dated from **Pascha**:

| Period | Relative to Pascha |
| --- | --- |
| **The Triodion begins** (Sunday of the Publican and Pharisee) | 10 weeks before |
| **Great Lent begins** (Clean Monday) | 48 days before |
| **Palm Sunday** | 7 days before |
| **Pascha** | |
| **Thomas Sunday** | 7 days after |
| **Mid-Pentecost** | 24 days after (the Wednesday of the fourth week) |
| **Ascension** | **40th day** (a Thursday) |
| **Pentecost** | **50th day** |
| **All Saints** | the Sunday after Pentecost |
| **The Apostles' Fast** | from the next day until 28 June |
