**How Pascha is dated.** The **First Council of Nicaea (325)** required the whole Church to keep Pascha on the same Sunday, and not to depend on the Jewish calculation. The rule that came to be followed: **Pascha is the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox**, computed by tables (the *Paschalion*), using the **Julian calendar's equinox (21 March Julian)** and a fixed lunar cycle. A further custom ensures that Pascha does not fall before the Jewish Passover. **Orthodox Pascha falls between 4 April and 8 May** in the civil calendar, in this century.

**The calendar question.** The Julian calendar (of Julius Caesar, 45 BC) is now **13 days behind** the Gregorian calendar (of Pope Gregory XIII, 1582) used in civil life. In **1923** a congress called by Ecumenical Patriarch Meletios IV adopted the **Revised Julian calendar**, which agrees with the Gregorian for the fixed feasts until the year 2800.

| Calendar for fixed feasts | Churches (as of 2026) |
| --- | --- |
| **Revised Julian** ("new") | Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Greece, Cyprus, Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, most of the OCA, and the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (since 2023) |
| **Julian** ("old") | Jerusalem, Russia, Serbia, Georgia, North Macedonia, Mount Athos, and others |

**Pascha is shared.** Almost all Orthodox churches, on either calendar, keep **Pascha and the movable cycle by the Julian Paschalion**, so all Orthodox celebrate Pascha together. (The Church of Finland is an exception, keeping the Western date.)

**What it means in practice.** On the old calendar, the Nativity on 25 December (Julian) falls on **7 January** in the civil calendar, and Theophany on 19 January. **The feast is the same; the civil date differs.**

**A question Orthodox Christians answer differently.** For some, the calendar is a matter of discipline that each church may decide; others hold that changing it in 1923–24 without a pan-Orthodox council broke liturgical unity, and some, the **Old Calendarists**, separated from their churches over it. Stage 11 sets out each position fully.

**The key sentence:** the Church year begins on 1 September; its fixed feasts follow the Menaion, its movable feasts the date of Pascha (computed by the Julian Paschalion, decided in principle at Nicaea in 325); churches differ on the calendar for fixed feasts, but almost all keep Pascha together.
The twelve great feasts: the feasts of t:
Below Pascha, the "feast of feasts", stand **twelve great feasts**. Eight are feasts of Christ, and four of the Theotokos (next lesson).

**The feasts of the Lord, in the order of the Church year:**

| Feast | Date | What is celebrated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The Elevation of the Precious Cross** | **14 September** | the finding of the Cross in Jerusalem by **St Helen** (about 326) and the dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (335). A strict fast day |
| **The Nativity of Christ** | **25 December** | the birth of Christ in Bethlehem |
| **Theophany** (Epiphany) | **6 January** | the baptism of Christ in the Jordan: the revelation of the Trinity |
| **The Meeting of the Lord** (Presentation) | **2 February** | the infant Christ brought to the Temple, received by **Simeon** and **Anna** (Luke 2:22–38) |
| **The Entry into Jerusalem** (Palm Sunday) | **the Sunday before Pascha** | Christ entering as king on a colt |
| **The Ascension** | **40 days after Pascha** | Christ ascending into heaven with his human body |
| **Pentecost** | **50 days after Pascha** | the descent of the Spirit (Stage 4) |
| **The Transfiguration** | **6 August** | Christ shining on Mount Tabor before Peter, James and John |

(The **Meeting of the Lord** is counted by some among the feasts of the Theotokos, but its subject is Christ.)

**Each feast has its days.** Most great feasts have a **forefeast** (days of preparation) and an **afterfeast** ending in an **apodosis** (*apódosis*, "giving back", the leave-taking). The Nativity's afterfeast runs to 31 December; Pascha's to the eve of the Ascension.

**The Nativity.** Preceded by a forty-day fast (from 15 November). On the eve the **Royal Hours** are read, then Vespers with the Liturgy of St Basil. The icon shows Christ in a cave, wrapped like a corpse in a manger like a tomb, with the ox and the ass (Isaiah 1:3), the Magi and the shepherds, and Joseph troubled by the devil's doubts. **The Nativity already points to the Cross and the tomb.**

**Theophany.** *Theopháneia*, "**appearance of God**". The Church celebrates not the visit of the Magi (as in the West) but the **baptism of Christ**, where the Father's voice is heard and the Spirit descends as a dove: **the first full revelation of the Trinity**. The **Great Blessing of Waters** is served on the eve and the day: the priest plunges the cross into water three times, and the faithful drink it and take it home. In many countries the cross is thrown into the sea, a river or a lake, and young men dive for it. Houses are blessed with the water in the following weeks.

**The Transfiguration.** Christ shone with the **uncreated light** (Stage 2), the light of his divinity, which St Gregory Palamas defended in the fourteenth century as the light the saints see in prayer (Stage 8). **First fruits** (grapes in Greek practice, apples in Russian) are blessed on this day: creation transfigured.

**The Ascension.** Christ ascends with his human body: **human nature is taken into God**. He does not leave his Church; he sends the Spirit and is present in the Eucharist. The Ascension icon shows the Theotokos in the centre with the apostles, as the Church on earth.

**The Elevation of the Cross.** The bishop raises the Cross to the four directions while the people sing "Lord, have mercy" a hundred times in each direction. **The Cross is lifted over the whole world.** The day is a strict fast.

**The key sentence:** the eight great feasts of the Lord are the Elevation of the Cross (14 September), the Nativity (25 December), Theophany (6 January), the Meeting (2 February), Palm Sunday, Ascension (40th day), Pentecost (50th day) and the Transfiguration (6 August).

Four of the great feasts honour the Mother of God. Above all twelve stands Pascha.

**The feasts of the Theotokos:**

| Feast | Date | What is celebrated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The Nativity of the Theotokos** | **8 September** | her birth to **Joachim and Anna**, after long childlessness |
| **The Entry of the Theotokos into the Temple** | **21 November** | her presentation in the Temple as a child, aged three |
| **The Annunciation** | **25 March** | the angel Gabriel's announcement and her "Behold the handmaid of the Lord" (Luke 1:38). **The Incarnation begins** |
| **The Dormition** | **15 August** | her **falling asleep** (*Koímēsis*; Slavonic *Uspenie*) and her being taken, body and soul, to heaven |

**Where the feasts come from.** The **Annunciation** and **Meeting** are in the Gospels. The **Nativity** and the **Entry** come from the **Protoevangelium of James** (second century), an early account of the Theotokos's childhood that the Church does not count as Scripture but whose story she received into her hymns and icons. The **Dormition** is told in traditions from the fifth century and is the Church's universal belief.

**The Annunciation.** Nine months before the Nativity. It is so joyful that it is celebrated even in Lent with a full Liturgy and fish, and if it falls on Pascha, the two are kept together (*Kyriopascha*). Its troparion calls it the beginning, the chief point, of our salvation (in paraphrase). The Greek Orthodox also keep 25 March as the national day of the Greek revolution of 1821.

**The Dormition.** Tradition says the apostles were gathered miraculously from across the world to her deathbed in Jerusalem; Thomas arrived three days late, and when the tomb was opened for him, her body was gone. **The Orthodox Church teaches that the Theotokos truly died**, and was then raised and taken into heaven by her Son. The icon shows her body on a bier, with Christ behind holding her soul as a small child in white. The feast is preceded by a **two-week fast** (1–14 August), and in many places her burial shroud is carried in procession, as Christ's is on Great Friday.

**The Entry.** The child Mary is led by her parents into the Temple and taken by the high priest Zacharias into the **Holy of Holies**. The Fathers saw in this the living Temple entering the old one: **she who would contain God enters the place where God dwelt**.

**Other feasts of the Theotokos.** Not among the twelve, but widely kept: the **Protection** (*Pokrov*, 1 October; the Greek Church of Greece keeps 28 October), her **Synaxis** (26 December), the **Placing of her Robe** (2 July) and **Sash** (31 August), and many feasts of wonder-working icons. The **Akathist Hymn** is sung on the fifth Saturday of Lent (Stage 5).

**Pascha: the feast of feasts.** *Páscha*, from Hebrew *Pesach*, Passover. **Pascha is not one of the twelve; it stands above them**, the centre of the whole year. A hymn of the Paschal canon calls it, in paraphrase, the feast of feasts and the festival of festivals. Its season lasts **forty days**, during which Orthodox Christians greet each other with **"Christ is risen!"** and the answer **"Truly he is risen!"** (Greek *Christós anésti! Alithós anésti!*, a phrase the Greek curriculum teaches as well). Lesson 25 describes the services.

**The structure of the year in one image.**

| | Fixed | Movable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Feasts of Christ** | Elevation, Nativity, Theophany, Meeting, Transfiguration | Palm Sunday, Ascension, Pentecost |
| **Feasts of the Theotokos** | Nativity, Entry, Annunciation, Dormition | |
| **Above all** | | **Pascha** |

**The key sentence:** the four great feasts of the Theotokos are her Nativity (8 September), Entry (21 November), the Annunciation (25 March) and the Dormition (15 August); above all twelve stands Pascha, the feast of feasts.
Great Lent: from the Triodion to Holy We:
Great Lent is the Church's great season of repentance: forty days of fasting and prayer preparing for Pascha. It is preceded by weeks of preparation and followed by Holy Week.

**The pre-Lenten Sundays.** The **Triodion** opens ten weeks before Pascha. Each Sunday has its own Gospel and theme:

| Sunday | Gospel | Teaching |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Zacchaeus** (Slavic usage; the Canaanite woman in some Greek usage in certain years) | Luke 19:1–10 | desire to see Christ |
| **The Publican and the Pharisee** | Luke 18:10–14 | **humility**: the Triodion begins; the next week is fast-free |
| **The Prodigal Son** | Luke 15:11–32 | **return** to the Father |
| **The Last Judgement** (Meatfare) | Matthew 25:31–46 | **love**, the measure of judgement; the last day of meat |
| **Forgiveness** (Cheesefare) | Matthew 6:14–21 | **forgiveness**, fasting and treasure in heaven; Adam expelled from Paradise; the last day of dairy |

**Forgiveness Vespers.** On the evening of Forgiveness Sunday, at the Vespers that begins Lent, **every person asks forgiveness of every other**, bowing to the ground, in words such as: forgive me, a sinner; and the answer, God forgives, and forgive me too. **Lent begins with reconciliation.**

**Clean Monday** (*Kathará Deftéra*). Lent begins on Monday. In Greece it is a public holiday, with kites and fasting food.

**The services of Lent:**
- **The Great Canon of St Andrew of Crete** (about 660–740), the longest canon in the Church's books, is read at Great Compline on the **first four evenings of Lent**, and in full at Matins on **Thursday of the fifth week**. It goes through the whole Bible, from Adam to Christ, calling the soul to repentance by every example.
- **The Prayer of St Ephrem the Syrian**, said at every weekday service with prostrations. In Hapgood's translation (1906):

> "O Lord and Master of my life, grant not unto me a spirit of slothfulness, of discouragement, of lust of power, of vain babbling. But vouchsafe unto thy servant the spirit of continence, of meekness, of patience, and of love. Yea, O Lord and King, grant that I may perceive my own transgressions, and judge not my brother. For blessed art thou unto ages of ages. Amen."

- **The Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts** on Wednesdays and Fridays (lesson 5).
- **The Akathist**, sung in sections on the Friday evenings of the first four weeks and in full on the fifth Saturday.
- **Weekday readings** from Genesis, Isaiah and Proverbs (Stage 5).

**The Sundays of Lent:**

| Sunday | Commemoration |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **the Triumph of Orthodoxy**: the restoration of icons in 843 |
| **2** | **St Gregory Palamas** (1296–1359): the uncreated light |
| **3** | **the Veneration of the Cross**: the Cross brought out, halfway through the fast |
| **4** | **St John Climacus**, author of *The Ladder of Divine Ascent* (Stage 10) |
| **5** | **St Mary of Egypt**: the harlot turned desert saint, the model of repentance |

**The end of Lent.** Lent proper ends on the Friday of the sixth week. **Lazarus Saturday** and **Palm Sunday** follow, joyful days (fish is allowed on Palm Sunday), and then Holy Week, which is a separate fast.

**What Lent is for.** Not for punishing the body but for **freeing the soul**: prayer, fasting and almsgiving together (Matthew 6:1–18). Fasting without prayer and love, the Fathers taught, is only diet. The Lenten hymns speak of the fast as a springtime (in paraphrase): **a season of joy and light, not gloom**.

**The key sentence:** Lent is prepared by five Sundays from the Publican to Forgiveness, begins with mutual forgiveness, is marked by the Prayer of St Ephrem and the Canon of St Andrew, and its Sundays honour Orthodoxy, Palamas, the Cross, St John Climacus and St Mary of Egypt.
Holy Week and Pascha:
The last week before Pascha follows Christ day by day to the Cross and the tomb. Then, at midnight, the Church bursts into the Resurrection.

**Holy Week, day by day:**

| Day | Services and theme |
| --- | --- |
| **Palm Sunday evening to Tuesday evening** | **Bridegroom Matins** (served in the evenings in parishes), whose troparion is built on Matthew 25:6, "Behold, the bridegroom cometh" (KJV); the icon of Christ the Bridegroom, mocked and crowned with thorns. Monday: Joseph the patriarch and the fig tree; Tuesday: the ten virgins; Wednesday: the sinful woman who anointed Christ, and Judas |
| **Holy Wednesday evening** | the **general unction** in many places (lesson 29) |
| **Holy Thursday** | **the Mystical Supper**: Vespers with the Liturgy of St Basil; the washing of feet in cathedrals; reserved Gifts for the sick are consecrated for the year |
| **Holy Thursday evening** | **Matins of Great Friday** with **the Twelve Passion Gospels**; the cross is carried out and set in the middle of the church |
| **Great Friday** | **the Royal Hours** in the morning; in the afternoon **Vespers of the Taking-down**, when the **epitaphios** (*epitáphios*, a cloth embroidered with the dead Christ) is laid in a tomb decorated with flowers. **No Liturgy is served** |
| **Great Friday evening** | **Matins of Holy Saturday**: the **Lamentations** (*Enkṓmia*) sung around the tomb, woven into Psalm 118; then the epitaphios is carried in procession around the church, and the faithful pass under it |
| **Holy Saturday morning** | **Vespers with the Liturgy of St Basil**, with the **fifteen Old Testament readings** (Stage 5) and, of old, the baptism of catechumens. Partway through, the dark vestments are changed for white, and the deacon (or priest) sings "Arise, O God, judge the earth" (Psalm 81:8, LXX) while bay leaves or flowers are scattered in Greek usage: the first announcement of the Resurrection, in Hades |

**The Paschal night.**
1. **The Midnight Office** with the canon of Holy Saturday, before midnight. The epitaphios is taken into the altar.
2. **The light.** All lights are put out. The priest comes from the altar with a lit candle, inviting all to come and receive the light (in Greek usage, the hymn *Défte lávete fos*), and the light spreads from candle to candle through the church. (In Jerusalem, the **Holy Fire** is received at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre on Holy Saturday.)
3. **The procession** around the church, with candles, icons and the Gospel, singing a hymn of the Resurrection. At the closed doors, the priest proclaims the Resurrection.
4. **"Christ is risen."** The Paschal troparion is sung over and over; in Hapgood's translation: "**Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down Death by death, and upon those in the tomb bestowing life.**" The doors open and all enter the lit church.
5. **Paschal Matins** with the **canon of St John of Damascus**, sung entirely, and the Paschal stichera; at the end, all embrace.
6. **The Catechetical Homily** attributed to **St John Chrysostom** is read: an invitation to all, those who fasted and those who did not, to the feast. (It is often called the homily of Chrysostom; its attribution is traditional.)
7. **The Paschal Liturgy**, with John 1:1–17 read, often in many languages, and Communion.

**After the service** the fast is broken, often at once, with red eggs, Paschal bread, cheese and meat, blessed after the Liturgy. **Red eggs** are a symbol of the Resurrection: life breaking from the tomb, coloured by the blood of Christ.

**Bright Week.** The whole week after Pascha is one day: the **Royal Doors stay open**, there is no fasting, and the services are sung in their Paschal form. The **Artos** (a blessed loaf) stands before the iconostasis all week, and is distributed on Saturday. **Thomas Sunday** closes Bright Week.

**The key sentence:** Holy Week follows Christ through Bridegroom Matins, the Mystical Supper, the Twelve Gospels, the epitaphios and the Lamentations to Holy Saturday's first announcement in Hades; then at midnight the light spreads, the doors open to "Christ is risen", and Bright Week keeps the whole week as one day.
The fasts and the rule of fasting:
The Orthodox Church fasts on about half the days of the year. The rule is demanding, but it is applied with pastoral care, and its purpose is freedom, not punishment.

**The four fasting seasons:**

| Fast | Dates | Length |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The Nativity Fast** | **15 November to 24 December** | 40 days |
| **Great Lent and Holy Week** | from Clean Monday to Holy Saturday | 48 days |
| **The Apostles' Fast** | from the Monday after All Saints Sunday to **28 June** | varies with the date of Pascha, from about one to six weeks |
| **The Dormition Fast** | **1 to 14 August** | 14 days |

**The single fast days:** every **Wednesday and Friday** (outside the fast-free weeks); the **Elevation of the Cross** (14 September); the **Beheading of St John the Baptist** (29 August); and the **Eve of Theophany** (5 January).

**The fast-free weeks:** **Bright Week**; the week after Pentecost; the days from the Nativity to the eve of Theophany; the week after the Sunday of the Publican and Pharisee. In **Cheesefare week** meat is not eaten, but dairy is.

**What the rule asks.** The strict rule, from the monastic Typikon, is to abstain from:

| Food | Strict fast days |
| --- | --- |
| **Meat** | always in a fast |
| **Dairy and eggs** | always in a fast |
| **Fish** (with a backbone) | most fast days; allowed on certain feasts (the Annunciation, Palm Sunday, the Transfiguration) and on many days of the Nativity and Apostles' fasts |
| **Wine and olive oil** | weekdays of the strict fasts; allowed on Saturdays and Sundays and on some feasts |

Shellfish, vegetables, grains, fruit, nuts and (in many usages) vegetable oils other than olive are allowed. On the strictest days (the first days of Lent, Great Friday) many eat nothing at all, or very little.

**Economy in fasting.** The rule is the standard, not a burden imposed without mercy. **The sick, the elderly, children, pregnant and nursing mothers, and those with heavy labour** are given relaxations, by their priest's guidance. Many laypeople keep a lighter rule than monastics. **Fasting is always undertaken with the blessing of one's spiritual father**, and the measure is the person's health and spiritual state, not a contest.

**Why fast.** The Orthodox Church gives several reasons, all from Scripture and the Fathers:
- **Christ fasted** (Matthew 4:2), and said his disciples would fast (Mark 2:20).
- **Fasting restores the order lost at the fall.** Adam fell by eating; the fast teaches the body to obey the soul and the soul to obey God.
- **Fasting frees** from the passions of the belly, which the Fathers saw as the gate to others.
- **Fasting makes room** for prayer and for giving: the money saved is given as alms.

**Fasting and love.** St John Chrysostom warned his flock that fasting from food while devouring one's brother by slander is no fast at all (a paraphrase). The Lenten hymns say the same: they call for a fast pleasing to the Lord, which is abstaining from evil (in paraphrase). **The fast of the stomach is the beginning; the fast of the tongue, the eyes and the heart is the point.** The Prayer of St Ephrem ends: "grant that I may perceive my own transgressions, and judge not my brother" (Hapgood).

**Not judging others' fasting.** Christ warns against fasting to be seen (Matthew 6:16–18). Orthodox Christians are taught **not to watch what others eat**, and to accept hospitality humbly when the host does not fast, rather than make a display.

**The key sentence:** four fasting seasons (Nativity, Lent, Apostles, Dormition) and the Wednesday and Friday fast make about half the year; the rule abstains from meat, dairy, fish, wine and oil, applied with economy by one's spiritual father, for the freedom of soul and body and for prayer and love.
Confession: the Mystery of repentance:
Sins committed after baptism are healed in the Mystery of confession. Orthodox teaching sees it less as a court than as a hospital.

**The words.** *Metánoia* is Greek for "**repentance**", literally "a change of mind": a turning of the whole person back to God. *Exomológēsis* means "**confession**", acknowledging one's sins openly. The Mystery is called by both names.

**In Scripture.** Christ gave the apostles authority: "Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained" (John 20:23, KJV). St James: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed" (James 5:16). In the early Church, serious sins (apostasy, murder, adultery) were confessed publicly, and the penitent was excluded from Communion for a period. Over time, especially through monastic practice, private confession to a priest or spiritual father became the norm.

**How it is done.** The penitent stands (or kneels) before an icon of Christ, usually before the iconostasis, with the priest beside him. There is no confessional box. The priest begins with prayers, and then, in the form Hapgood printed (1906), exhorts the penitent:

> "Behold, my child, Christ standeth here invisibly, and receiveth thy confession: wherefore, be not ashamed, neither be afraid, and conceal thou nothing from me... Lo, his holy image is before us: and I am but a witness, bearing testimony before him of all things which thou dost say to me... Take heed, therefore, lest, having come to the physician, thou depart unhealed."

**Christ is the one who hears; the priest is "but a witness".** And confession is coming "to the physician".

**The absolution.** The penitent confesses. The priest may give counsel, and sometimes a penance. Then the penitent bows his head, the priest lays his **epitrachelion** over it and reads the prayer of absolution. In the Greek form, the prayer asks God to forgive the penitent, recalling how he forgave David through Nathan (in paraphrase). Russian books add a further formula in the first person, in Hapgood's translation: "And I, his unworthy Priest, through the power given unto me by him, do forgive and absolve thee from all thy sins". This form came into Russian use through the Kievan service books of the seventeenth century. **Both forms say the same thing**: God forgives, through his Church.

**Penance as medicine.** A penance (*epitímion*) is not a payment for sin. **It is a medicine**: prayers, prostrations, reading, almsgiving, or a period of abstaining from Communion, fitted to the person's illness. St Basil's canons and those of St John the Faster gave periods of penance for different sins; Orthodox confessors today apply them with economy, mostly much shortened.

**The spiritual father.** Many Orthodox Christians confess regularly to one **spiritual father** (*pneumatikós*; Russian *dukhovnik*), who knows their life and guides them. In Greek practice only priests specially blessed by the bishop may hear confessions. **The relationship of spiritual father and child is one of the main ways the Orthodox spiritual life is passed on** (Stage 10 takes it up, with the elders).

**How often.** Practice varies (lesson 16): before each Communion in much Slavic practice; in each fasting season or as one's confessor advises in Greek, Antiochian and other practice. Children usually begin confession around seven.

**The seal.** What is said in confession is **absolutely secret**. A priest who reveals a confession is deposed by the canons.

**The key sentence:** confession is the Mystery of repentance and healing: the penitent stands before Christ, the priest is a witness and physician, the epitrachelion is laid over the bowed head, and God forgives through his Church.
Marriage: the crowning:
The Orthodox marriage service is called **the crowning**. It joins a man and a woman in Christ and points them toward the Kingdom.

**What the Church teaches.** Marriage is a **Mystery** (*mystḗrion*): "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church" (Ephesians 5:32, KJV). **The love of husband and wife is made an icon of Christ's love for the Church**, and a path of salvation for both. Marriage is not a contract between two parties but a union **blessed by God in the Church**, and it is meant to be **eternal**: the couple's love is not ended by death.

**The service has two parts.**

**1. The Betrothal.** In the narthex (or at the entrance), the priest blesses the couple and gives them lighted candles. He blesses the **rings** and places them on their right hands, and the rings are exchanged three times, usually by the sponsor (*koumbáros*). **The betrothal is the promise.**

**2. The Crowning.** In the nave, before a table with the Gospel book, the cross, the crowns and the common cup:
- **Psalm 127 (LXX)**, the blessing of the household.
- (In Slavic usage, the priest asks the bride and groom whether they enter the marriage **freely**. The Greek service has **no vows**: the couple's free consent is assumed, and the marriage is made by God's blessing, not by their promises.)
- Three long prayers, recalling the marriages of the Old Testament: Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Rachel, Joseph and Asenath, Moses and Zipporah, Joachim and Anna, Zacharias and Elizabeth.
- **The crowning.** The priest places crowns on their heads (in Greek usage, *stéfana*, joined by a ribbon; in Russian, metal crowns) saying, in Hapgood's translation: "The servant of God, N., is crowned unto the handmaid of God, N.: In the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." Then he blesses them three times: "**O Lord our God, crown them with glory and honour.**" (Psalm 8:5.)
- The Epistle (Ephesians 5:20–33) and the Gospel (John 2:1–11: **the wedding at Cana**, Christ's first sign).
- **The common cup.** The couple drink three times from a cup of wine: **they will share one life**, its joys and sorrows. (In the early Church, marriage was blessed at the Eucharist and the couple received Communion; the common cup recalls that.)
- **The dance of Isaiah.** The priest leads the couple three times around the table, while the hymns are sung, beginning "Rejoice, O Isaiah! A Virgin is with child, and shall bear a Son, Emmanuel" (Hapgood). **Their first steps as a couple are a procession, led by the Church, around the Gospel.**

**What the crowns mean.** Three things, the Fathers and hymns say: **royalty** (the couple are king and queen of their household, a little Church); **martyrdom** (they will lay down their lives for each other: the third hymn of the procession is to the martyrs); and **the Kingdom** (the crowns of glory to come).

**Who may be married.** Orthodox Christians, in the Orthodox Church. Most Orthodox churches permit marriage between an Orthodox Christian and a **baptised Christian** of another confession (baptised in the Trinity), by economy; marriage with the unbaptised is not blessed. Marriage is not celebrated during fasting seasons, on the eves of feasts, or from the Nativity to Theophany.

**Second marriage.** The Church blesses one marriage as the norm. **A second, and at most a third, marriage** may be blessed, after divorce or the death of a spouse, by economy, with a **penitential service** that is quieter and includes prayers for forgiveness. Divorce is granted in the Church by the **bishop**, as a concession to human weakness, for grave causes such as adultery or abandonment; practice varies by church.

**The key sentence:** the Orthodox marriage is a betrothal with rings and a crowning with crowns, the common cup and the dance of Isaiah; it is a Mystery of Christ and the Church, meant to be eternal, and a path of salvation for both.
Holy unction and ordination:
Two Mysteries remain: unction, for the healing of the sick, and ordination, for the ministry of the Church.

**Holy Unction.** *Euchélaion*, "**prayer-oil**". The Mystery of healing, for the body and the soul.

**In Scripture.** "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord: And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him" (James 5:14–15, KJV). The apostles "anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them" (Mark 6:13).

**The service.** Ideally served by **seven priests**, though one may serve it. A vessel of oil (sometimes with wine) is set in a dish of wheat, with **seven candles** and seven brushes. The priests bless the oil; then come **seven Epistles and seven Gospels**, each followed by a prayer and an anointing on the forehead, nostrils, cheeks, lips, breast and hands. At the end the Gospel book is laid open, face down, on the sick person's head, and the senior priest reads the prayer of forgiveness.

**Not only for the dying.** In the medieval West, unction came to be given mainly at death ("extreme unction"). **In Orthodox practice it is for any sickness, of body or soul**, and is not tied to death. The dying receive confession and Communion as well, and the service for the parting of the soul.

**General unction.** In Greek, Russian and many other churches, unction is given to **all the faithful who wish it**, sick or well, on **Holy Wednesday** evening (and in some places at other times), for the healing of soul and body before Pascha. **All sin is a sickness, and all are sick.**

**Ordination.** *Cheirotonía*, "**laying on of hands**". The Mystery by which a man is made a deacon, priest or bishop.

**In Scripture.** The apostles laid hands on the seven deacons (Acts 6:6); Paul reminds Timothy of "the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands" (2 Timothy 1:6, KJV).

**Each order at its own moment in the Liturgy:**

| Order | When in the Liturgy | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Bishop** | after the Trisagion, before the readings | the bishop is the teacher of the Word |
| **Priest** | after the Great Entrance, before the anaphora | the priest offers the Eucharist |
| **Deacon** | after the anaphora, before Communion | the deacon serves the Gifts to the people |

**The rite.** The candidate is led three times around the altar, kissing its corners; he kneels and lays his head on the altar. The bishop lays his hand on his head and reads aloud, in Hapgood's translation of the ordination of a deacon:

> "The grace divine, which always healeth that which is infirm, and completeth that which is wanting, elevateth, through the laying-on of hands, N., the most devout Sub-Deacon, to be a Deacon: Wherefore, let us pray for him, that the grace of the all-holy Spirit may come upon him."

**"The grace divine... completeth that which is wanting."** No one is worthy; the Spirit supplies. The new deacon or priest is vested, and at each vestment the bishop proclaims "**Axios!**" ("**He is worthy!**"), and the people and clergy answer "Axios!" three times. **The people's acclamation is part of the rite**: the clergy are ordained for and with the people.

**The rules.** A **bishop** is consecrated by **at least two or three bishops** (Apostolic Canon 1). Priests and deacons are ordained by one bishop. **Married men may be ordained deacon and priest**, but must marry before ordination to the diaconate; a clergyman whose wife dies does not remarry. **Bishops are celibate**, chosen from monastics, since the Council in Trullo (692) made this the rule. **Minor orders** (reader, subdeacon) are given by *cheirothesía*, a blessing with the hand, outside the altar.

**The ordination of women.** The ancient Church had **deaconesses**, ordained by the bishop, who assisted at the baptism of women and cared for women; the order lapsed in the Byzantine period. Their revival is discussed among Orthodox today. The Patriarchate of Alexandria voted in 2016 to revive the order, blessed women for missionary diaconal service in the Congo in **2017** (often described as subdeaconesses), and in **May 2024** a deaconess was ordained in Zimbabwe; the Church of Cyprus questioned that step, and other churches have not taken it. **Orthodox writers differ on how and whether to revive it**; the Orthodox Church does not ordain women as priests or bishops.

**The key sentence:** unction, served with seven Epistles, Gospels and anointings, heals soul and body and is given to all on Holy Wednesday; ordination, by the laying on of hands at the moment in the Liturgy proper to each order, is completed by the grace that "completeth that which is wanting", and acclaimed with "Axios!".
Looking back: worship:
This stage entered the Church's worship: the temple and its icons, the Divine Liturgy step by step, the daily, weekly and yearly cycles, the feasts and fasts, and the other Mysteries. Here it is in one view.

**Worship is theology.** The rule of prayer is the rule of belief: the Church's doctrine lives first in her services. **The Liturgy is the Kingdom made present**, where the Church joins the angels.

**The temple and the icon.** The church faces east; narthex, nave and sanctuary; the iconostasis shows heaven; the Holy Table is Christ's tomb and God's throne. **Because God became visible in Christ, he can be painted**, and "the honour which is paid to the image passes on to that which the image represents" (Nicaea II, 787).

**The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom:**

| Part | Step | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Preparation** | Proskomedia | the Lamb cut with Isaiah's words; the whole Church on the diskos |
| **Word** | "Blessed is the kingdom"; Great Litany | the destination, and prayer in peace for the world |
| | Antiphons; "O Only-begotten Son"; Little Entrance | Christology sung; the Church enters with the Gospel |
| | Trisagion; Epistle; Gospel; homily | the angels' song; Christ speaking |
| **Eucharist** | Catechumens; Cherubic Hymn; Great Entrance | the faithful in the angels' place; the gifts to the altar |
| | "Let us love one another"; Creed | love leads to faith |
| | **Anaphora** | thanks, Sanctus, institution, anamnesis (even of the Second Coming), "Thine own, of thine own" |
| | Epiclesis; commemorations | "Transmuting them by thy Holy Spirit"; the Theotokos and all |
| | Lord's Prayer; "Holy things unto the Holy"; Communion | "One only is holy"; Body and Blood from the spoon |
| | "We have beheld the true Light"; dismissal | thanksgiving and sending |

**Three Liturgies**: Chrysostom's most days, Basil's ten times a year, the Presanctified on Lenten weekdays. **Preparation for Communion**: fasting, prayer and repentance for all; frequency and the link with confession vary by church.

**The cycles.** **The day** begins at sunset: Vespers, Compline, Midnight Office, Matins, the Hours (with the Vigil on eves). **The week**: Sunday the Resurrection, Wednesday and Friday the Cross and fasting, Saturday the departed; eight tones in rotation. **The year** begins on 1 September; fixed feasts in the Menaion, movable feasts from Pascha; churches differ on the calendar but keep Pascha together. The **Typikon** orders it all.

**The feasts.** Twelve great feasts, eight of Christ and four of the Theotokos, with **Pascha above them all**. **Great Lent** begins with forgiveness and ends at Lazarus Saturday; **Holy Week** follows Christ to the tomb; **Pascha** breaks out at midnight with "Christ is risen". **Four fasting seasons** and the Wednesday and Friday fast make about half the year, kept with economy.

**The other Mysteries.**

| Mystery | Heart of the rite |
| --- | --- |
| **Confession** | Christ hears; the priest is "but a witness"; the epitrachelion over the bowed head |
| **Marriage** | betrothal and crowning; common cup; dance of Isaiah; eternal union in Christ |
| **Unction** | seven Epistles and Gospels; healing of soul and body; general unction on Holy Wednesday |
| **Ordination** | laying on of hands, at the proper moment of the Liturgy; "Axios!" |

**Open questions in this stage.** How often to receive Communion, and whether to confess each time; women's Communion during menstruation; the calendar for fixed feasts; the troparion of the Third Hour in the anaphora; the revival of deaconesses. **On none of these has the Church spoken through an ecumenical council**, and Orthodox churches and writers answer them differently in good faith.

**What links it all.** Stages 4 to 6 belong together: **the Spirit makes the Church, the Church reads the Scripture he inspired, and the Church prays.** At the centre of all three is one action: the Liturgy, where the Word is heard, the Spirit is invoked, and the faithful receive Christ.

**What comes next.** Stage 7 turns from the Church's life to her history: the apostolic age, the martyrs, and the first four ecumenical councils, where much of what this stage has sung was first defined.
Context: from Pentecost to Chalcedon:
This stage follows the Church through her first four and a half centuries: from a few hundred disciples in Jerusalem to the faith of an empire, defined at four councils the whole Church still confesses.

**Why the history belongs to theology.** The Orthodox Church does not treat her past as background. The councils, the martyrs and the Fathers are where she learned to say what she had always believed. Stages 2 to 4 gave the Creed as doctrine. This stage shows **how each clause was won**, and against what.

**The shape of the stage:**

| Period | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **About 30 to 100** | the apostolic age: Pentecost, the mission, the Council of Jerusalem, the first bishops |
| **About 100 to 250** | the Apostolic Fathers, the apologists, the martyrs; the fight with Gnosticism |
| **250 to 313** | the great persecutions, then the conversion of Constantine |
| **325** | the **First Ecumenical Council**, Nicaea: the Son is of one essence with the Father |
| **381** | the **Second**, Constantinople: the Holy Spirit is Lord and God; the Creed completed |
| **431** | the **Third**, Ephesus: Mary is the **Theotokos**, the one who gave birth to God |
| **451** | the **Fourth**, Chalcedon: one Christ in two natures |

**An ecumenical council** (from Greek *oikouménē*, "the inhabited world") is a gathering of bishops whose teaching the **whole Church afterwards receives** as her own. The Orthodox Church counts seven. Stage 1 explained why reception, not numbers or imperial summons, is what makes a council ecumenical.

**A pattern to watch.** Almost every council answers a question someone else raised. Arius asked whether the Son was a creature; Nestorius whether Mary bore God; Eutyches whether Christ's manhood was swallowed by his Godhead. **The Church defined only what had been denied**, and as little as she needed to.

**The non-Chalcedonian churches.** After 451 the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian churches did not receive Chalcedon. This stage gives their reasons in their own terms, fairly. The modern dialogues between them and the Orthodox Church belong to Stage 12.

**Point across.** The Philosophy curriculum treats the same arguments (Arius, the Cappadocians, Chalcedon) as philosophy. The Greek curriculum teaches the words: *ousía*, *hypóstasis*, *phýsis*, *homooúsios*.
The apostolic age: from Jerusalem to the:
The Church was born at Pentecost and, within one lifetime, was in every great city of the eastern Mediterranean.

**Pentecost (about AD 30 or 33).** Fifty days after the Resurrection the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles in Jerusalem (Acts 2). **The Church dates her birth from that day.** Three thousand were baptized, and "they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers" (Acts 2:42, King James Version, 1611): teaching, communion, Eucharist and prayer from the first.

**The first community** was Jewish. It met in the Temple and in houses, kept the Law, and was led by the Twelve, with **St James the brother of the Lord** soon its head. The seven deacons were ordained to serve the tables (Acts 6). **St Stephen**, one of them, became the first martyr.

**The mission outward:**

| Step | Where |
| --- | --- |
| **Persecution scatters the Church** | Judea and Samaria; Philip baptizes the Ethiopian official (Acts 8) |
| **Peter baptizes Cornelius** | the first Gentile household (Acts 10) |
| **Antioch** | the first mixed church of Jews and Gentiles; "the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch" (Acts 11:26, KJV) |
| **St Paul's journeys** | about 46 to 58: Cyprus, Asia Minor, Macedonia, Greece |
| **Rome** | a church there before Paul arrived; Peter and Paul martyred there under Nero, in the 60s |

**Where the other apostles went** is known mostly from later tradition, which the Church honours while historians weigh it. St Thomas to India; St Mark to Alexandria; St Andrew to the Black Sea and Greece, which is why Constantinople counts him its founder. The Orthodox call several saints **Equal-to-the-Apostles** (*isapóstolos*) for spreading the faith in the same way.

**The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.** The Romans destroyed the Temple. The Christians of Jerusalem had, according to Eusebius, already left for Pella across the Jordan. After 70 the Church was less and less a movement inside Judaism and more a body of her own.

**What the apostles left** was not only writings. They left **churches with bishops, presbyters and deacons**, a way of baptizing, a Eucharist on the Lord's Day, and a body of teaching handed on by mouth as well as in letters (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Stage 1 called this **Tradition** (*parádosis*, "handing over"); this is where it begins.
The Council of Jerusalem: the first coun:
The first great question the Church faced was whether Gentile converts had to become Jews. She answered it the way she would answer every later question: by meeting.

**The question.** Some believers from Judea taught at Antioch: "Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved" (Acts 15:1, King James Version, 1611). Paul and Barnabas disputed it, and the church of Antioch sent them to Jerusalem.

**The meeting, about AD 49** (Acts 15):

1. **The apostles and elders came together** to consider the matter.
2. **Peter spoke** of how God had given the Holy Spirit to Gentiles at Cornelius's house, "and put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith."
3. **Paul and Barnabas told** what God had done among the Gentiles.
4. **James gave the judgement**, from the prophets: Gentiles were not to be troubled with the Law, only asked to abstain from idol-offerings, blood, things strangled and fornication.
5. **A letter went out** to the churches.

**The formula.** The letter says: "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us" (Acts 15:28, KJV). **That sentence is the charter of every later council.** The bishops do not vote a doctrine into being. They gather, hear the witness of Scripture and experience, and recognise together what the Holy Spirit is saying.

**Why the Orthodox Church treats it as a model:**

| Feature | Later echo |
| --- | --- |
| **A question troubling the whole Church** | Arianism, Nestorianism, iconoclasm |
| **The leaders of the churches meet** | the bishops in council |
| **Testimony from experience and Scripture** | the Fathers cite Scripture and the earlier Fathers |
| **One presides and sums up** | the presidency of a council |
| **A letter to the churches** | the conciliar definitions and canons |
| **The decision is then received** | reception by the whole Church |

**It is not counted as an ecumenical council.** The seven are later and the name is technical. But the Orthodox call it **the Apostolic Council**, and the habit of deciding together, not by one voice alone, is called **conciliarity** (Slavonic *sobórnost*, from *sobor*, "council" or "gathering"). Stage 4 gave the theology; here is its first appearance.

**What it settled.** The Church would be **one body of Jews and Gentiles**, joined by faith and baptism, not by the ceremonial Law. Paul's letters to the Galatians and Romans work out the theology. Within a century most Christians were Gentiles.
The Apostolic Fathers: Clement, Ignatius:
The writers of the generation after the apostles, some of whom had known them. They are the Church's earliest witnesses outside the New Testament.

**The name** is a modern grouping, from the seventeenth century, for the earliest Christian writings after the New Testament. They are short, practical letters and handbooks, not treatises.

| Writer or work | Date | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **St Clement of Rome**, *Letter to the Corinthians* | about 96 | the church of Rome writing to Corinth, which had deposed its presbyters; order and succession from the apostles |
| **The Didache** ("Teaching of the Twelve Apostles") | late first or early second century | a church manual: the Two Ways, baptism, fasting on Wednesday and Friday, the Lord's Prayer three times a day, the Eucharist |
| **St Ignatius of Antioch**, seven letters | about 107 | the bishop, the Eucharist, the reality of Christ's flesh, the desire for martyrdom |
| **St Polycarp of Smyrna**, *Letter to the Philippians* | about 110 to 140 | faith and good works; links Ignatius and the apostles |
| **The Martyrdom of Polycarp** | soon after about 155 | the oldest account of a martyrdom outside the New Testament |
| **The Shepherd of Hermas** | second century, Rome | visions on repentance after baptism |

**Four things they already take for granted:**

1. **The threefold ministry.** By Ignatius's day each church had **one bishop** (*epískopos*, "overseer"), with presbyters (*presbýteroi*, "elders") and deacons (*diákonoi*, "servants").
2. **The Eucharist as Christ's body and blood.** Not a symbol to them but the gift itself, offered on the Lord's Day.
3. **Fasting and set prayer.** The Didache's Wednesday and Friday fast is still the Orthodox weekly rule.
4. **Unity around the bishop** as the safeguard against division and false teaching.

**Clement and succession.** Clement tells the Corinthians that the apostles appointed bishops and deacons and arranged for others to succeed them. **This is the first written statement of apostolic succession**, the handing on of oversight from the apostles.

**How the Church honours them.** Clement (25 November), Ignatius (20 December) and Polycarp (23 February) are saints of the calendar. Their writings are not Scripture, but they show what the churches founded by the apostles were actually doing a generation later.

**Read them.** They are short and free in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1. The next lesson reads Ignatius.
Reading: St Ignatius of Antioch to the S:
A bishop under armed guard, on his way to die in Rome, writes to a church he has just visited. Read closely, it holds the faith of the early second century in a few lines.

**The text** (St Ignatius, *Epistle to the Smyrnaeans*, written about 107; translated by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, *Ante-Nicene Fathers* vol. 1, 1885; the shorter recension):

> "He was truly of the seed of David according to the flesh, and the Son of God according to the will and power of God; that He was truly born of a virgin, was baptized by John, in order that all righteousness might be fulfilled by Him; and was truly, under Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch, nailed [to the cross] for us in His flesh." (chapter 1)

> "They abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father, of His goodness, raised up again." (chapter 7)

> "See that ye all follow the bishop, even as Jesus Christ does the Father, and the presbytery as ye would the apostles... Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church." (chapter 8)

The square brackets are the translators' own additions.

**Who.** Ignatius, also called *Theophóros* ("God-bearer"), was bishop of Antioch, the second or third after the apostles. Arrested under Trajan, he wrote seven letters on the road to Rome, where he was thrown to the beasts, about 107.

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"truly... truly... truly"** | the word he repeats against the **Docetists** (from *dokéō*, "to seem"), who said Christ only seemed to have a body |
| **"under Pontius Pilate"** | already the phrase of the later Creed: the faith is tied to a date and a place |
| **"the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Saviour"** | the Eucharist is Christ's own flesh, the same flesh that suffered and rose |
| **"follow the bishop, even as Jesus Christ does the Father"** | the bishop is the centre of the local church's unity |
| **"the Catholic Church"** | the **first surviving use** of the phrase. *Katholikós* means "according to the whole": complete, lacking nothing |

**What holds the passage together.** His three themes are one. If Christ's flesh is real, then the Eucharist is real; if the Eucharist is real, then the church gathered around one bishop and one altar is where Christ is. **Deny the flesh and you lose the sacrament and the Church with it.**

**Where it lives on.** The Creed's "under Pontius Pilate", the Orthodox insistence on one Eucharist under one bishop, and the word "Catholic" in the Creed's "one Holy Catholic and Apostolic Church" (Hapgood, 1906) all have their earliest written witness here. Stage 9 reads Ignatius again, from his letter to the Romans.
The martyrs: from St Stephen to St Polyc:
For three centuries to be a Christian was to risk death. The Church remembers her martyrs first among the saints, and their witness shaped her worship.

**The word.** *Mártys* is Greek for **witness**, as in a law court. A martyr is one whose death bears witness to Christ. The Church's oldest saints' days are martyrs' days, kept on the date of death, which she calls the **birthday** into heaven.

**The first martyrs:**

| Martyr | Date | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **St Stephen the Protomartyr** | about 34 | stoned in Jerusalem, praying for his killers (Acts 7); feast 27 December |
| **St James son of Zebedee** | 44 | beheaded by Herod Agrippa (Acts 12); the first apostle martyred |
| **Sts Peter and Paul** | the 60s, Rome | under Nero; feast 29 June |
| **St Ignatius of Antioch** | about 107, Rome | thrown to the beasts |
| **St Polycarp of Smyrna** | about 155 | burned; feast 23 February |
| **St Justin and companions** | about 165, Rome | beheaded |
| **The martyrs of Lyons and Vienne** | 177 | among them the slave girl St Blandina |
| **Sts Perpetua and Felicity** | 203, Carthage | a noblewoman and her slave, in the arena; feast 1 February |

**Why Rome killed Christians.** Not usually for believing in Christ as such. Rome tolerated many gods; what it would not tolerate was **refusing to honour the gods and the emperor**, which looked like atheism and disloyalty. Christians were also rumoured to eat flesh and commit incest, garbled versions of the Eucharist and the "love-feast". For two centuries persecution was **local and sporadic**: a governor, a mob, a famine blamed on the Christians.

**The Martyrdom of Polycarp.** Polycarp, a disciple of St John according to Irenaeus, was bishop of Smyrna when he was arrested in old age. Told to curse Christ, he answered, as the account reports, that he had served Christ for eighty-six years and could not blaspheme the King who saved him. **The Smyrnaean church gathered his bones** and resolved to meet each year on the day of his death. That is the earliest witness to the cult of relics and saints' feasts.

**What the martyrs gave the Church:**

- **The veneration of relics**, and later the rule that every altar holds them (in the antimension, Stage 6).
- **The calendar**: each day a commemoration.
- **A theology of witness**: the martyr imitates Christ's Passion and shares it.
- **Growth.** Tertullian, writing about 197, said the blood of Christians is seed. Persecution did not stop the Church; it spread her.

**The martyr's crown.** In the Orthodox wedding the couple are crowned, and one hymn sung there is to the holy martyrs. Marriage, monasticism and martyrdom are all one gift of the whole self.
The great persecutions: Decius, Valerian:
In the third century persecution changed from local outbreaks to empire-wide campaigns. The Church nearly broke under it, and came out stronger.

**Why it changed.** The third century was the Empire's crisis: civil wars, plague, invasion, emperors murdered one after another. Several emperors decided that **the gods' favour had to be won back**, and that Christians who refused to sacrifice were a danger to the state.

| Persecution | Dates | What it demanded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Decius** | 250 to 251 | every inhabitant to sacrifice and obtain a certificate (*libellus*) saying so |
| **Valerian** | 257 to 260 | clergy to sacrifice; Christian meetings forbidden; clergy executed |
| **The Great Persecution** (Diocletian and his colleagues) | 303 to 311 in most of the East, ending in 313 | churches destroyed, Scriptures burned, clergy arrested, then all to sacrifice |

**Decius's certificates.** Many Christians did sacrifice. Others bought false certificates. Some stood firm and were tortured; those who survived were honoured as **confessors**. After the persecution the Church faced a new question: what to do with **the lapsed** (*lapsi*), those who had given way. Lesson 12 tells how St Cyprian answered.

**Valerian's martyrs.** St Cyprian of Carthage was beheaded in 258. In Rome Pope Sixtus II and his deacons were killed, among them St Lawrence.

**The Great Persecution** was the longest and worst. It began in February 303 at Nicomedia, Diocletian's capital. Under Galerius and Maximinus Daia in the East it was savage: whole towns of Christians are reported destroyed. Many of the Church's best-loved saints come from it:

- **St George**, an officer, martyred at Nicomedia; feast 23 April.
- **St Demetrios of Thessalonica**; feast 26 October.
- **St Panteleimon**, physician, of Nicomedia; feast 27 July.
- **St Catherine of Alexandria** and **St Barbara**, by tradition of the same era.
- **The Forty Martyrs of Sebaste**, soldiers frozen on a lake, about 320 under Licinius; feast 9 March.

**How it ended.** Galerius, dying, issued an edict of toleration in 311. In 313 Constantine and Licinius agreed at Milan to restore the Christians' property and allow them to worship freely. Lesson 13 tells the story.

**What the persecutions left:**

1. **The great-martyrs.** The Orthodox title *megalomártys* is given to the most honoured of them.
2. **A question about forgiveness.** How the lapsed were received shaped the Church's practice of repentance.
3. **Schisms.** Rigorists who would not forgive the lapsed broke away: the Novatianists after 251, the Donatists in North Africa after 311.
4. **A Church that knew she could survive the Empire.** By 300 Christians were perhaps a tenth of its people.
St Justin Martyr and the apologists:
Christians of the second century wrote to explain their faith to emperors and philosophers. They were the first to set the Gospel beside Greek philosophy.

**The word.** An *apología* in Greek is a speech of defence in court, not an apology. The **apologists** were Christian writers who defended the faith in public against slander and argued that it was true.

**St Justin Martyr (about 100 to about 165).** Born in Flavia Neapolis in Samaria to a pagan family. He tried Stoic, Peripatetic, Pythagorean and Platonist teachers, then met an old man by the sea who pointed him to the prophets, and he became a Christian. He taught in Rome in the philosopher's cloak, and was beheaded there with six companions about 165. **Feast: 1 June.**

**His works:**

| Work | Date | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **First Apology** | about 155 | to Emperor Antoninus Pius: Christians are not atheists or criminals; the faith explained |
| **Second Apology** | soon after | to the Roman Senate, after an unjust execution |
| **Dialogue with Trypho** | about 160 | a long discussion with a Jew on Christ in the Old Testament |

**The seed-bearing Word.** Justin taught that Christ is the **Lógos**, the Word and Reason of God, through whom all things were made. **Every human being shares in the Word**, and the philosophers grasped seeds of truth (*lógos spermatikós*, "seed-bearing Word") wherever they spoke well. What they had in part, Christians have whole in Christ. This let the Church claim the best of Greek thought without making it her master.

**The first description of the Liturgy.** In the *First Apology*, chapters 65 to 67, Justin describes what Christians do on Sunday: the reading of the "memoirs of the apostles" and the prophets, the sermon of the president, common prayers, the kiss of peace, bread and wine mixed with water brought, the president's prayer of thanksgiving and the people's "Amen", communion taken by the deacons to the absent, and a collection for the poor. **Every element is still in the Divine Liturgy.** He says plainly that this food is "the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh" (*First Apology* 66, translated by Roberts and Donaldson, *Ante-Nicene Fathers* vol. 1, 1885).

**The other apologists:**

- **Aristides of Athens**, about 125, to Hadrian.
- **St Athenagoras of Athens**, about 177: *A Plea for the Christians* and *On the Resurrection*.
- **St Theophilus of Antioch**, about 180: the first to use the word *triás*, "Trinity", for God.
- **The Letter to Diognetus**, second or third century: Christians "dwell in their own countries, but simply as sojourners" (chapter 5, Roberts and Donaldson, 1885), and are to the world what the soul is to the body.

**Why they matter.** They gave the Church a language for speaking to the world and showed that the faith can give reasons. The Philosophy curriculum treats Justin and the Logos more fully as an argument.
Gnosticism and St Irenaeus of Lyons:
The second century's gravest threat came from inside: teachers who said Christ brought a secret knowledge. The Church's answer, through St Irenaeus, set the shape of Orthodox theology.

**Gnosticism.** From *gnōsis*, "knowledge". Not one church but many schools: Valentinus, Basilides, Marcion (strictly a separate case), and others, flourishing about 130 to 200. **Their common ideas:**

| Gnostic claim | What it implied |
| --- | --- |
| **The material world is a mistake**, made by a lesser god (the *dēmiourgós*, "craftsman") | the God of the Old Testament is not the true God |
| **Salvation is escape** of a divine spark from the body | the body is not saved; no resurrection of the flesh |
| **Christ only seemed to be human** | no real birth, cross or Resurrection |
| **Saving knowledge is secret**, passed to an elite | the bishops and the open Scriptures are for simpler people |

**St Irenaeus (about 130 to about 202).** Born in Asia Minor, he heard Polycarp preach as a boy, so he stands **two links from St John**. He went to Gaul, was a presbyter at Lyons during the persecution of 177, and became its bishop after the martyred Pothinus. **Feast: 23 August.**

**Against Heresies** (about 180), five books: *The Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So Called*. Books 1 and 2 expose the systems; Books 3 to 5 set out the faith.

**Irenaeus's three answers:**

1. **One God made everything, and it is good.** The Father of Jesus Christ is the Creator and the God of Israel. Matter is not evil; the body is God's work.
2. **Tradition is public, not secret.** If the apostles had secret teaching they would have given it to the men they made bishops. **The faith is what the churches founded by the apostles teach openly**, and he lists the bishops of Rome from Peter and Paul to his own day to show the line.
3. **Recapitulation** (Greek *anakephalaíōsis*, "summing up again"). Christ the new Adam goes back through every stage of human life and undoes Adam's fall by obedience. Mary's obedience unties Eve's disobedience. **Salvation is creation healed and completed, not escaped.**

**What he gave the Church:**

- **The rule of faith** as the key to Scripture (next lesson).
- **The four Gospels** as a closed set, no more and no fewer.
- **The resurrection of the flesh** at the centre: the body that receives the Eucharist will rise.
- **The pattern of theosis.** Christ "did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself" (*Against Heresies* Book 5, preface, translated by Roberts and Rambaut, *Ante-Nicene Fathers* vol. 1, 1885). Stage 9 reads that sentence closely.

**Why the Orthodox call him a foundation.** Every later Father builds on his conviction that **creation, Incarnation and resurrection are one story**.
The rule of faith, the canon and the bis:
Against the Gnostics the Church held to three safeguards together. None of them works alone, and the Orthodox Church still holds all three.

**1. The rule of faith** (Greek *kanṓn tēs alētheías*, "rule of truth"; Latin *regula fidei*). A short summary of the faith received at baptism: one God the Father, Creator; one Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, born, crucified, risen, coming again; the Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets. **Irenaeus and Tertullian both give versions of it.** It was not yet one fixed text, but its shape is already the Creed's.

**Why it mattered.** The Gnostics quoted Scripture too, rearranged to fit their systems. Irenaeus compared them to a man who takes a mosaic of a king and rearranges the stones into a dog. **The rule of faith is the picture on the box**: it tells you how the pieces of Scripture fit.

**2. The canon of Scripture** (*kanṓn*, "measuring rod"). By about 200 the core of the New Testament was agreed across the churches:

| Agreed by about 200 | Still discussed for a time |
| --- | --- |
| the four Gospels, Acts, Paul's letters, 1 Peter, 1 John | Hebrews (in the West), James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude, Revelation (in parts of the East) |

The first list of exactly our twenty-seven books is in **St Athanasius's Festal Letter of 367**. Stage 5 covers the canon in full, with the Septuagint.

**What prompted it.** **Marcion** (about 140, Rome) cut the Old Testament out entirely and kept only an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul. The Gnostics added gospels of their own. The Church answered by saying, in effect, **these books and not those**, because these were read in the churches from the apostles' time.

**3. The bishops in succession.** Who decides what the rule of faith means and which books are read? The bishops of the apostolic churches, who received the faith in a known line. Irenaeus named the succession at Rome; Hegesippus, about 180, travelled to compare the churches and found the same teaching everywhere.

**How the three hold each other up:**

- **Scripture** is read in the Church, by the rule of faith.
- **The rule of faith** is the summary of Scripture's own teaching.
- **The bishops** guard both, and are judged by both: a bishop who taught against them would be deposed, as the councils later did.

**The Orthodox word for the whole** is **Tradition**, the life of the Holy Spirit in the Church. Scripture is its heart, not a rival to it. Stage 1 set this out as theology; here it is in history, being forged against the first great heresy.

**Synods begin.** In the second half of the second century bishops started meeting in regional **synods** (*sýnodos*, "coming together") to judge the Montanists, a prophetic movement in Phrygia, and to settle the date of Pascha. These were the first councils after Jerusalem, and the habit grew into the ecumenical councils.
Alexandria's school: St Clement and Orig:
Alexandria was the greatest centre of learning in the Roman world, and in the late second and third centuries the first Christian scholars worked there.

**The catechetical school.** A teaching centre for converts and enquirers, linked to the bishop of Alexandria, led successively by Pantaenus, Clement and Origen. It made the Church at home in the world of Greek scholarship.

**St Clement of Alexandria (about 150 to about 215).** A convert educated in philosophy. His trilogy, the *Exhortation to the Greeks*, *The Instructor* and the *Stromata* ("Patchwork"), presents Christ as the teacher of humanity and the true philosophy. **He speaks of the "true gnostic"**: the Christian whose knowledge of God grows out of faith and love, against the false gnostics. He is not in the main Orthodox calendar of saints, but the Fathers read him with respect.

**Origen (about 185 to about 254).** The most brilliant and the most contested Christian thinker before Nicaea.

| What he did | Why it mattered |
| --- | --- |
| **The Hexapla** | the Old Testament in six parallel columns, Hebrew and Greek versions side by side: the first great work of biblical scholarship |
| **Commentaries and homilies** on almost every book of Scripture | the Fathers drew on his exegesis for centuries |
| **On First Principles** | the first attempt at a whole Christian theology |
| **Against Celsus** | the fullest answer to a pagan critic |
| **The three senses of Scripture** | literal, moral and spiritual, like body, soul and spirit |

He was tortured under Decius and died of his injuries at Tyre about 254. **He never left the Church.**

**Why he was later condemned.** Some of his speculations, put forward as questions and developed further by his followers, were rejected:

- **The pre-existence of souls**, which fell into bodies from a prior spiritual state.
- **The universal restoration** (*apokatástasis*) of all rational beings, including, his critics said, the demons.
- **A subordination of the Son** to the Father that later Arians could use.

These **"Origenist" teachings were condemned in the sixth century**, under Justinian, and anathematised with the Fifth Council of 553 (Stage 8). The Seventh Council lists Origen with Evagrius and Didymus among those whose teachings it rejects.

**How the Orthodox read him.** Not a saint and not a Father in the strict sense, but **a teacher whom the Fathers read, used and corrected**. St Basil and St Gregory the Theologian compiled an anthology of his best passages, the *Philokalia of Origen*. His method of reading Scripture spiritually passed into the whole Church; his speculative system did not. **That is a good example of how the Church receives a thinker: by testing, not wholesale.**

**Point across.** The Philosophy curriculum treats Origen as a Christian Platonist.
St Cyprian of Carthage, the lapsed and t:
After the persecution of Decius the Church had to decide whether those who had denied Christ could come back. St Cyprian's answers shaped Orthodox thinking on repentance and on the Church's unity.

**St Cyprian (about 200 to 258).** A wealthy teacher of rhetoric in Carthage, baptized about 246, made bishop within three years. He hid during the Decian persecution of 250, governing his church by letter, and was criticised for it. Under Valerian he did not hide, and was beheaded on **14 September 258**. **Feast in the Orthodox calendar: 31 August.**

**The lapsed.** Thousands had sacrificed or bought certificates. Two extremes appeared:

| Party | Position |
| --- | --- |
| **The laxists** | confessors in prison issued "letters of peace" readmitting the lapsed at once, without penance |
| **The rigorists** (Novatian at Rome, 251) | the Church cannot forgive apostasy; the lapsed may repent but never return to communion |

**Cyprian's middle way**, agreed with Pope Cornelius at synods of 251 and after: **the lapsed may be readmitted after a period of penance**, graded by the gravity of the fall, under the bishop's judgement, and sooner if death or a new persecution threatened. This is the root of the Church's penitential discipline, and of the principle the canons call **economy** (*oikonomía*, "household management"): the bishop may apply the rule with mercy for the sinner's salvation.

**On the Unity of the Catholic Church** (251). Cyprian's treatise against the Novatianist schism. Its teachings, in paraphrase:

- **The episcopate is one**, and each bishop holds his part of it in full, in communion with the others.
- **He cannot have God for his Father who does not have the Church for his mother.**
- **Outside the Church there is no salvation** (*extra ecclesiam nulla salus*), in the sense that one cannot cut oneself off from the Church and keep her life.

**The baptism controversy.** Cyprian and the African synods held that **baptism given by schismatics is not baptism**, and those coming from them must be baptized. Pope Stephen of Rome held that they need only receive the laying on of hands. Neither side broke communion over it. The Orthodox Church kept both practices under the principle of economy, and **Orthodox churches still differ on how to receive converts**: by baptism, by chrismation, or by confession of faith. Stage 11 returns to this.

**Why Cyprian matters to the Orthodox.** He gave the clearest early statement that **the unity of the Church is visible**: one bishop in each place, all bishops in communion, one Eucharist. That is the Orthodox understanding still.
St Constantine and the end of persecutio:
In 312 a Roman emperor fought under the sign of Christ. Within a lifetime the persecuted Church became the favoured faith of the Empire. The Orthodox Church calls him a saint, and the change brought gifts and dangers.

**The Milvian Bridge (28 October 312).** Constantine was fighting his rival Maxentius for Rome. Eusebius, who says he heard it from Constantine himself, reports a vision of a cross of light in the sky with the words "In this, conquer" (paraphrased; Greek *en toútōi níka*), and a dream in which Christ told him to use the sign. Lactantius, writing earlier, reports only the dream and the sign on the soldiers' shields. Constantine won, and credited Christ.

**The "Edict of Milan" (313).** Constantine and Licinius agreed that Christians and all others should have freedom of worship and that confiscated church property be returned. It was a letter to governors, not strictly an edict, but its effect was the end of persecution in most of the Empire. Licinius later turned on the Christians in the East; Constantine defeated him in **324** and ruled alone.

**What changed:**

| Before 313 | After |
| --- | --- |
| Christians met in houses and modest halls | great basilicas: the Lateran, St Peter's, the Holy Sepulchre |
| bishops were hunted | bishops judged civil cases and had public honour |
| Sunday an ordinary working day | Sunday a public day of rest (321) |
| councils were regional | the emperor could summon bishops from everywhere: Nicaea, 325 |

**St Helen** (about 248 to about 329), his mother, went to the Holy Land about 326. By tradition she found the True Cross in Jerusalem. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre was consecrated in 335. The Exaltation of the Cross (14 September) keeps her finding in memory.

**New Rome.** In **330** Constantine dedicated **Constantinople** on the site of Byzantium, his new capital. It would be the heart of Orthodox Christendom for eleven centuries.

**His baptism and death.** Like many of his day he put off baptism until near death, and was baptized in **337** by Eusebius of Nicomedia, a sympathiser of Arius. He died on 22 May 337.

**Why a saint?** The Orthodox Church commemorates **Sts Constantine and Helen, Equal-to-the-Apostles, on 21 May**. Not because Constantine was a model of personal holiness (he had his wife and eldest son killed), but because **he opened the Empire to the Gospel** and summoned the First Council. The Church honours what God did through him.

**The gift and the danger.** The Church gained peace and the means to build and teach. She also gained an emperor who expected to have a say. The next five centuries of councils are partly a story of emperors trying to impose unity and of saints, from Athanasius to Maximus, who refused when the emperor was wrong. **The Byzantine ideal of *symphōnía*** ("harmony" between Church and emperor) is the subject of Stage 8.
Arius and the crisis at Alexandria:
About 318 a presbyter of Alexandria began teaching that the Son of God was a creature. Within a few years the whole Eastern Church was divided.

**Arius (about 256 to 336).** A respected, ascetic presbyter in charge of the Baucalis church in Alexandria, a popular preacher and writer of songs. His bishop was **St Alexander of Alexandria** (bishop about 312 to 328).

**What Arius taught**, in the slogans his opponents remembered:

| Arian claim | What it meant |
| --- | --- |
| **"There was when he was not"** (*ēn pote hote ouk ēn*) | the Son had a beginning |
| **The Son was made out of nothing** | he is a creature, the first and highest |
| **The Son is not of the Father's essence** | he is God only by grace and title |
| **The Son does not fully know the Father** | he is less than the Father in kind |

**Why it appealed.** It seemed to protect God's oneness and unchangeableness: the Father alone is unbegotten and without beginning, so the Son must come after him. It fitted a common philosophical picture of a supreme God and a lesser mediator who made the world. And it could quote Scripture: "The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way" (Proverbs 8:22, read of Wisdom); "my Father is greater than I" (John 14:28; both King James Version, 1611).

**Why the Church could not accept it.** St Alexander, and after him his deacon Athanasius, saw that Arianism undid the Gospel:

1. **Only God can save.** If the Son is a creature, a creature cannot unite us to God. **Theosis needs the Son to be truly God.**
2. **The Church worships Christ.** If he is a creature, that worship is idolatry.
3. **Baptism is in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.** One cannot be baptized into a creature alongside God.
4. **The Father is eternally Father.** If there was when the Son was not, there was when God was not a Father, and God changed.

**What happened.** Alexander held a synod of about a hundred Egyptian bishops, about 318 or 320, which deposed Arius. Arius went to friends in Palestine and Asia Minor, among them **Eusebius of Nicomedia**, a powerful courtier-bishop, and Eusebius of Caesarea, the historian. Letters and synods flew in both directions. Constantine, who had just won the East, sent his adviser Ossius of Córdoba to make peace. When that failed, he called a council of the whole Church.

**Why this is a council's question.** Arius was not a fringe figure. Many bishops thought the issue was a matter of words. The Church needed to say, with the authority of all, **what the Son is**, and she did not yet have an agreed term for it. The next lesson is the council that chose one.

**Point across.** The Philosophy curriculum gives the Arian dispute as an argument about God's unchangeableness; the Greek curriculum the verb *gennáō*, "beget", against *ktízō*, "create".
The First Ecumenical Council: Nicaea (32:
The first council of the whole Church met at Nicaea in 325 and confessed that the Son is of one essence with the Father. Its Creed is the foundation of the Creed said at every Liturgy.

**The meeting.** Constantine summoned the bishops to Nicaea in Bithynia, near his palace at Nicomedia, and paid their travel. **About 250 to 300 bishops** came, almost all from the East, with two presbyters representing the aged bishop of Rome. **The Church remembers them as the 318 Fathers**, after Abraham's 318 servants (Genesis 14:14). It opened in the early summer of 325 and lasted about two months. Among those present by tradition: St Alexander of Alexandria with his deacon Athanasius, **St Nicholas of Myra**, and **St Spyridon of Trimythous**.

**The decision.** The council first looked for a scriptural phrase the Arians could not twist. Every phrase ("from God", "true image") the Arians accepted with their own meaning. So the council used one word that left no room: **homooúsios**, "of one essence" or "consubstantial" (*homós*, "same", and *ousía*, "essence, being").

**The Creed of Nicaea** (as given in the *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 2nd series vol. 14, ed. Henry R. Percival, 1900), its central clause:

> "and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten of his Father, of the substance of the Father, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten (gennethenta), not made, being of one substance (homoousion, consubstantialem) with the Father."

It ends simply "And [we believe] in the Holy Ghost", with anathemas against those who say "there was a time when the Son of God was not". The Creed said in church today is the fuller one of 381 (lesson 18).

**Read the key phrases:**

| Phrase | Against |
| --- | --- |
| **"of the substance of the Father"** | the Son is not made out of nothing |
| **"very God of very God"** | he is not God only in name |
| **"begotten, not made"** | begetting is not creating: a father begets his own kind |
| **"of one substance"** | whatever the Father is as God, the Son is |

**Only two bishops refused to sign**, and with Arius they were exiled.

**The other business:**

- **The date of Pascha.** All churches were to keep it on the same Sunday, not dependent on the Jewish reckoning. The rules worked out from this, kept by the Orthodox Church, set Pascha on the Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox.
- **Twenty canons**, among them the honour of the great sees (lesson 19), no kneeling on Sundays and in the fifty days of Pascha, and the rules for receiving the Novatianists.

**Why the word was hard to accept.** *Homooúsios* is not in Scripture, and it had been used earlier in senses the Church rejected. **Many bishops who were not Arians feared it**, and for fifty years they looked for other terms. The council's victory was not secure until 381 (lessons 16 to 18).
