4. **On the first Sunday of Lent, 11 March 843**, a procession with icons went from the Church of Blachernae to Hagia Sophia, and the icons were set up again.

**Theodora's request.** Theodora asked that her husband not be condemned. By tradition she said he repented on his deathbed, and the synod agreed to leave his name out of the anathemas. **St Theodora the Empress** is commemorated on **11 February**.

**The Sunday of Orthodoxy.** The **first Sunday of Great Lent** is kept as the **Triumph of Orthodoxy**. Its features:

| Feature | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **The procession of icons** | the faithful carry icons around the church |
| **The troparion of the day** | venerating the most pure image of Christ and asking his forgiveness |
| **The Synodikon of Orthodoxy** | read in cathedrals: acclamations and anathemas |

**The Synodikon** (*synodikón*, "synodal document"). Drawn up in 843 and added to over the centuries. Its pattern:

- **Acclamations** of the true faith and of the Orthodox Fathers, bishops and emperors: "**Eternal memory!**" (*Aiōnía hē mnḗmē*).
- **Anathemas** against heresies: Arius, Nestorius, the iconoclasts, and later others.
- **Additions**: in the eleventh century against John Italos and certain philosophical errors; in the fourteenth century, **affirming the teaching of St Gregory Palamas** (lesson 21).

Among its acclamations it takes up the words of Nicaea II, the faith of the apostles and the Fathers which has made firm the whole world.

**What "Orthodoxy" means here.** *Orthodoxía* is "right glory" or "right belief" (*orthós*, right; *dóxa*, opinion, and also **glory**, worship). The Slavonic name ***Pravoslávie*** means "right glorifying". **The Church called the victory of the icons the Triumph of Orthodoxy** because it completed the councils: right belief about Christ, and right worship of him, are one.

**An anathema** (*anáthema*, "set apart") in the Church's usage is a declaration that a teaching, or a person holding it, is **outside the communion of the Church**. It is not a curse wishing harm; the Synodikon pronounces it to protect the faithful.

**Why it is kept in Lent.** Lent is a journey to Pascha. Its first Sunday celebrates the Incarnation made visible in the icon, so that **the faithful begin the fast looking at the face of Christ**.

**Point across.** Stage 6 covers the Lenten Sundays in turn; the Greek curriculum gives *orthós* and *dóxa*.
St Photios the Great:
The greatest scholar of ninth-century Byzantium, twice patriarch, at the centre of the first open quarrel with Rome. The Orthodox Church honours him as a saint and a defender of the faith.

**St Photios (about 810 to about 893).** A layman from a noble iconophile family, a teacher and imperial secretary of immense learning. His ***Bibliotheca*** (*Myriobiblos*) summarises 279 books he had read, many now lost; it is a main source for lost Greek literature. **Feast: 6 February.**

**His patriarchates:**

| Years | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **858** | Patriarch Ignatius forced out by the regent Bardas; Photios ordained through every rank in six days and made patriarch |
| **861** | a council in Constantinople, with papal legates, confirmed Photios |
| **863** | **Pope Nicholas I**, at a Roman synod, declared him deposed and Ignatius restored |
| **867** | Photios's **Encyclical to the Eastern patriarchs**, against Frankish missionaries in Bulgaria who taught the **filioque** and other Latin customs; a council in Constantinople declared Nicholas deposed |
| **867** | Emperor **Basil I** removed Photios and restored Ignatius |
| **869 to 870** | a council in Constantinople with papal legates condemned Photios (the West later counted it its Eighth Council) |
| **877** | Ignatius died; **Photios restored** as patriarch, with Ignatius's own blessing by Byzantine report |
| **879 to 880** | **the Council of Constantinople in Hagia Sophia**, with the legates of **Pope John VIII**: recognised Photios, annulled the council of 869 to 870, and **confirmed the Creed without addition** |
| **886** | Photios removed again by Leo VI; died in exile |

**The reconciliation of 879 to 880.** Photios and Ignatius are **both saints** of the Orthodox Church (Ignatius on 23 October). The council of 879 to 880 restored communion with Rome on Orthodox terms. **Some Orthodox theologians and churchmen call it the Eighth Ecumenical Council**; others keep the count at seven, noting that the Church has never formally numbered it so. **Both views are held within Orthodoxy.**

**His teaching on the Holy Spirit.** In his ***Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit*** (about 886), Photios set out why the Spirit **proceeds from the Father alone** as from the one source in the Trinity. Lesson 18 gives the teaching as history.

**His mission.** Under Photios the Church of Constantinople sent **Sts Cyril and Methodius** to Moravia (863); baptized **Bulgaria** (864 or 865); and, by his Encyclical's own report, received a first conversion among the **Rus'**. **He was a patriarch of missions.**

**Why the Orthodox call him "the Great".** For learning, for the defence of the faith of the councils, for the missions to the Slavs, and for refusing to let **the Creed of the whole Church be altered by one part of it**. With St Mark of Ephesus and St Gregory Palamas, he is one of the **Pillars of Orthodoxy**, a title given to the three by later tradition.

**Point across.** The Greek curriculum can use the *Bibliotheca* as a reader.
Sts Cyril and Methodius and the mission:
Two brothers from Thessalonica gave the Slavs an alphabet, the Scriptures and the Liturgy in their own tongue. Every Slavic Orthodox Church traces its faith to them.

**The brothers.** **Constantine** (about 826 to 869), called **Cyril** after he took monastic vows just before his death, a scholar called "the Philosopher", and **Methodius** (about 815 to 885), a former governor turned monk. Their home city, **Thessalonica**, was surrounded by Slavs, and they spoke the Slavic dialect of the area. **Feast: 11 May**, as **Equal-to-the-Apostles** and **Enlighteners of the Slavs**.

**The call (862 to 863).** **Prince Rastislav of Great Moravia** (in today's Czech lands and Slovakia) asked Emperor Michael III for teachers who could instruct his people in their own language. Photios and the emperor sent the brothers. **They arrived in 863.**

**What they made:**

| Gift | Note |
| --- | --- |
| **The Glagolitic alphabet** | devised by Constantine for the sounds of Slavonic |
| **Translations** | the Gospels, the Psalter, the services, then most of the Bible (Methodius) |
| **Old Church Slavonic** | the first Slavic literary language, still the liturgical language of the Russian, Serbian, Bulgarian and other churches |

The **Cyrillic alphabet**, based on Greek letters, was developed slightly later in **Bulgaria**, probably by their disciples, and named in Cyril's honour.

**The struggle.** In Moravia the brothers met **Frankish clergy** who held that the Liturgy could be celebrated only in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, the languages of Pilate's inscription. **Cyril called this the "trilingual heresy"**. The brothers went to Rome in 867 to 868, where **Pope Adrian II** approved the Slavonic Liturgy and laid the Slavonic books on the altar.

**Cyril died in Rome on 14 February 869.** Methodius was consecrated archbishop for the Slavs. Back in Moravia he was imprisoned for over two years by Frankish bishops. He died on **6 April 885**. After his death his disciples were expelled.

**The disciples carry on.** Driven from Moravia, **Sts Clement and Naum** went to **Bulgaria**, which **Tsar Boris** (baptized 864 or 865; feast 2 May) had brought to the faith. At Ohrid and Preslav they trained thousands of clergy and made Slavonic the language of the Bulgarian Church. **From Bulgaria Slavonic Christianity passed to Serbia and to Kievan Rus'** (Stage 11).

**The principle.** The Orthodox Church does not require one sacred language. **The Gospel is preached and the Liturgy served in the language of the people.** That is why there are Orthodox services today in Slavonic, Romanian, Arabic, Georgian, English, Swahili, Japanese and many more. Cyril and Methodius are the patrons of that principle.

**An apostolic mission.** By Orthodox reckoning they continued the work of the apostles in the same way: preaching, translating, baptizing, building a local church with its own clergy. The **Czech and Slovak** Orthodox Church especially honours them as its founders.

**Point across.** The Greek curriculum notes the Greek letters behind Cyrillic.
The filioque: a question of the Creed, a:
The Western addition of "and the Son" to the Creed became the chief doctrinal issue between East and West. This lesson gives the history and the Orthodox teaching briefly, without argument.

**The text.** The Creed of 381 says the Holy Spirit "**proceedeth from the Father**" (Hapgood's translation, 1906; compare John 15:26). The Latin addition ***filioque*** means "**and from the Son**", so that the Western Creed reads that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

**How the addition spread in the West:**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **589** | the **Third Council of Toledo** in Spain, receiving the Visigoths from Arianism, used the Creed with *filioque*, perhaps to stress the Son's equality with the Father |
| **8th century** | the addition spread in Frankish churches |
| **809** | a Frankish council at Aachen under Charlemagne approved it |
| **about 810** | **Pope Leo III** approved the teaching but **refused to add it** to the Creed; by later report he had the Creed **without** the filioque set up on silver shields in St Peter's |
| **867** | Photios's Encyclical protested against Frankish missionaries teaching it in Bulgaria |
| **1014** | the Creed with *filioque* was sung at Rome at the coronation of Emperor Henry II |

**The Orthodox teaching, stated positively:**

1. **The Father is the one source** (*pēgḗ*) and cause (*aitía*) of the Son and the Spirit. This is called the **monarchy of the Father** (*monarchía*, "one source").
2. **The Son is begotten of the Father; the Spirit proceeds from the Father.** These are the personal properties that distinguish them. The Father's are shared with neither.
3. **The Spirit is sent into the world through the Son**, rests on the Son, and is given by the Son (John 15:26; 20:22). **This is the Spirit's mission in time**, and it is confessed fully.
4. **St Gregory of Cyprus**, patriarch of Constantinople, at the **Council of Blachernae (1285)**, taught that the Spirit also **shines forth eternally from the Father through the Son**: an eternal manifestation, not a second source of being.

**Two concerns** have been raised by the Orthodox:

- **Doctrinal**: that making the Son a cause of the Spirit's being confuses the persons or makes two sources.
- **Conciliar**: that **one church altered the Creed of the whole Church** without an ecumenical council, against the spirit of Ephesus, Canon 7 (Stage 7).

**What modern Orthodox writers say.** Some see the filioque as a heresy; others, while rejecting it, have asked whether some Western formulations (such as "from the Father through the Son") could be reconciled. **That debate, and the modern dialogues, belong to Stage 12 and to the separate curriculum on answering other Christians.**

**The Orthodox practice.** The Church says the Creed as 381 wrote it, at every Liturgy. **It neither adds nor removes a word.**

**Point across.** Stage 2 sets out the Trinity in full; the Greek curriculum gives *ekporeúomai*, "proceed".
1054: the schism as an event and as a pr:
The "Great Schism" between Rome and Constantinople is usually dated to 1054. Historians, Orthodox and other, now see 1054 as one episode in a long estrangement.

**The estrangement, before 1054.** For centuries East and West had been growing apart:

| Cause | What it meant |
| --- | --- |
| **Language** | by 600 few in Rome read Greek and few in Constantinople read Latin |
| **Politics** | the West had its own emperor from Charlemagne (800); the papacy sought Frankish protection |
| **Church order** | the Roman see's claims to universal jurisdiction grew; the East understood primacy as one of honour within a conciliar Church |
| **Custom** | the filioque; **unleavened bread** (*azymes*) in the Western Eucharist; clerical celibacy; Saturday fasting |
| **The Normans** | conquering southern Italy, where Greek and Latin churches mixed |

**The events of 1053 to 1054:**

1. **Michael Keroularios**, patriarch of Constantinople (1043 to 1058), had the Latin churches in the city close (1053), after the Normans pressed Latin customs on Greeks in southern Italy. **Leo of Ohrid**, archbishop of Bulgaria, wrote against Latin customs, especially azymes.
2. **Pope Leo IX** sent legates, led by **Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida**, to Constantinople in 1054.
3. **Leo IX died on 19 April 1054**, before the legates acted; their authority after his death was doubtful.
4. **On 16 July 1054** Humbert laid a **bull of excommunication** against Keroularios and his supporters on the altar of Hagia Sophia, during the Liturgy, and left.
5. **A synod in Constantinople** that July excommunicated the legates in turn.

**What it was not.** It was **not a break between the whole of East and West**. The bull and the synod's answer named persons, not churches. Patriarch **Peter III of Antioch** wrote urging moderation. Pilgrims, trade and in places communion continued. Many Orthodox and Western historians now say the schism became complete only gradually, and that **the sack of Constantinople in 1204** (next lesson) made it a breach of peoples.

**When the Orthodox Church sees the division as complete.** Orthodox writers differ in their emphasis: some point to 1054 as the decisive moment of a Western innovation; others to 1204 or later, when Latin hierarchies were set up in Orthodox lands. **All agree that by the thirteenth century the two were not in communion.**

**The lifting of the anathemas.** On **7 December 1965**, Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lifted the excommunications of 1054. This lifted a condemnation, **not the division itself**. Its meaning and what followed are Stage 12.

**How the Orthodox Church understands it.** **The Orthodox Church holds that she has kept the faith and order of the undivided Church** of the seven councils. She does not date her own beginning from 1054; she dates it from Pentecost.

**Point across.** Answering the questions between the churches belongs to the separate curriculum planned after this one.
The Crusades and the sack of Constantino:
The Crusades began partly as a response to an Orthodox emperor's call for help. They ended with Western Christians sacking the greatest Orthodox city. That deepened the division more than any bull.

**The call (1095).** After the Seljuk Turks defeated the Byzantines at **Manzikert in 1071** and overran most of Asia Minor, **Emperor Alexios I Komnenos** asked Pope Urban II for soldiers. At the **Council of Clermont (November 1095)** Urban preached the First Crusade, aimed at recovering Jerusalem.

**The First Crusade (1096 to 1099).** The crusaders passed through Constantinople and took **Antioch (1098)** and **Jerusalem (15 July 1099)**. In both cities they installed **Latin patriarchs** in place of the Orthodox ones, who went into exile. **This was the first time rival hierarchies stood in the same see**, which made the division concrete for ordinary Christians.

**Rising hostility, 1100 to 1200.** Each crusade passing through Byzantium brought friction. Venetian and Genoese merchants dominated the trade of Constantinople. In **1182** a mob in Constantinople massacred many of the city's Latins. Mistrust grew on both sides.

**The Fourth Crusade (1202 to 1204).** Planned to attack Egypt, it was diverted:

1. **Venice**, owed money for the fleet, turned the crusade first against the Christian city of Zara (1202).
2. A Byzantine pretender, **Alexios Angelos**, promised the crusaders money and the union of the churches if they put him on the throne.
3. The crusaders installed him in 1203; he could not pay; he was murdered.
4. **On 12 to 13 April 1204 the crusaders stormed Constantinople** and sacked it for three days.

**The sack.** Churches were looted, relics carried off to the West, and, according to the Byzantine historian **Niketas Choniates**, who witnessed it, a prostitute was set on the patriarch's throne in Hagia Sophia (paraphrased). **Pope Innocent III**, who had forbidden the attack on Christians, condemned the violence, but accepted the result.

**The Latin Empire (1204 to 1261).** The crusaders made a Latin emperor and a **Latin patriarch of Constantinople**. The Orthodox patriarch and emperor took refuge at **Nicaea**, which became the capital in exile. Orthodox states also survived in Epirus and Trebizond. **Michael VIII Palaiologos recovered Constantinople on 25 July 1261.**

**What 1204 did to the Church:**

- **The schism became a matter of memory and people**, not only of bishops: the Orthodox now remembered Latins as plunderers.
- **Latin hierarchies** were set over Orthodox populations in Greece, Cyprus and the islands for centuries.
- **The Empire never recovered its strength**, and 1453 came closer.

**A later word.** In 2001 Pope John Paul II, in Athens, asked God's forgiveness for the sins of Catholics against the Orthodox, naming the sack; in 2004 Patriarch Bartholomew publicly accepted the apology. The meaning of such gestures is a question for Stage 12.
St Gregory Palamas and the hesychast cou:
In the fourteenth century a dispute over the prayer of Athonite monks led to councils that defined the distinction between God's essence and his energies. The Orthodox Church honours their teacher as a Father.

**Hesychasm** (*hēsychía*, "stillness, quiet") is the tradition of **inner stillness and unceasing prayer**, above all the Jesus Prayer, sometimes with a bodily posture and attention to breathing. Stage 10 teaches it as practice. Its goal is the **vision of the uncreated light**, the light the apostles saw on Mount Tabor at the Transfiguration.

**St Gregory Palamas (1296 to 1359).** Born in Constantinople to a noble family, he became a monk on **Mount Athos** about 1316. **Feast: 14 November**; and the **Second Sunday of Great Lent** is dedicated to him.

**The dispute.** **Barlaam of Calabria** (about 1290 to 1348), a Greek monk from southern Italy and a learned philosopher, mocked the hesychasts' bodily methods and their claim to see God's light. He argued:

| Barlaam | Palamas |
| --- | --- |
| God cannot be known directly; knowledge of God is by reason and Scripture | **God is unknowable in his essence** but **truly known and shared in his energies** |
| The light of Tabor was a created phenomenon, a symbol | the light of Tabor is **uncreated**: **God's own glory**, seen by eyes transformed by grace |
| Bodily prayer methods are superstition | the whole person, **body and soul**, takes part in prayer and is deified |

**The Triads** (*In Defence of the Holy Hesychasts*, about 1338 to 1341), Palamas's main work, and the **Hagiorite Tome** (1340), signed by the leaders of Athos, set out the hesychasts' case.

**The councils:**

| Date | Council | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **10 June 1341** | Hagia Sophia | **Barlaam condemned**; he returned to Italy |
| **August 1341** | Constantinople | Gregory Akindynos, who took up Barlaam's objection, condemned |
| **1341 to 1347** | civil war | Palamas imprisoned and excommunicated (1344) by Patriarch John Kalekas, who sided with Akindynos |
| **1347** | Constantinople, under **John VI Kantakouzenos** | Kalekas deposed, Palamas vindicated; Palamas made **archbishop of Thessalonica** |
| **1351** | Blachernae palace | the **Tomos** affirming the essence-energies distinction; Nikephoros Gregoras condemned |

**What the councils taught.** God's **essence** (*ousía*) is beyond all knowledge and participation. His **energies** (*enérgeiai*), his activities and grace, are **God himself**, uncreated, and in them we truly share God. **This is how theosis is possible** without our becoming God by essence. Stage 2 gave the teaching; here is its defining moment.

**Reception.** The councils' teaching was added to the **Synodikon of Orthodoxy**. Palamas was **canonized in 1368**. Some Orthodox writers call the councils of 1341 to 1351 the **Ninth Ecumenical Council**; others count them as great local councils whose teaching the whole Church has received. **Both are found among Orthodox theologians.**

**His last years.** On his way to Constantinople in 1354 he was captured by the Ottoman Turks and held for about a year, debating with Muslims. He died in Thessalonica on **14 November 1359**.

**Point across.** Stage 9 reads Palamas's teaching; the Philosophy curriculum treats the essence-energies distinction as an argument.
The councils of union: Lyons (1274), Flo:
Twice Byzantine emperors, desperate for Western help, agreed to union with Rome on Rome's terms. Twice the Orthodox Church rejected it. The second time, one bishop's refusal became the voice of the Church.

**Lyons (1274).** **Michael VIII Palaiologos**, having recovered Constantinople (1261), feared a Western crusade to restore the Latin Empire. His envoys at the **Second Council of Lyons** accepted the filioque and papal primacy. In Constantinople the union was resisted by clergy, monks and people. Patriarch Joseph I resigned; the unionist **John Bekkos** was made patriarch. After Michael's death (1282), his son Andronikos II repudiated it, and the **Council of Blachernae (1285)** condemned Bekkos (lesson 18).

**Florence (1438 to 1439).** By the 1430s the Empire was little more than Constantinople. **Emperor John VIII Palaiologos** and **Patriarch Joseph II**, with about seven hundred Greeks, sailed to Italy for a council with **Pope Eugenius IV**.

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **April 1438** | the council opens at **Ferrara** |
| **1438** | debates on purgatory and on the addition to the Creed |
| **January 1439** | moved to **Florence**; debates on the procession of the Spirit |
| **June 1439** | Patriarch Joseph II dies in Florence |
| **6 July 1439** | the decree of union, ***Laetentur caeli***, proclaimed: the filioque, purgatory, unleavened bread allowed, papal primacy |

**St Mark of Ephesus (about 1392 to 1444).** **Mark Eugenikos**, metropolitan of Ephesus, the leading Orthodox theologian at the council, **refused to sign**. When told of it, Pope Eugenius is reported to have said, in paraphrase, that they had achieved nothing. **Feast: 19 January.** He held that union must be in the faith, not in a signature, and that the Latin positions on the procession and the Creed could not be accepted.

**The rejection.** When the delegates came home, the clergy and people refused the union. Many signers recanted. Mark led the opposition until his death on **23 June 1444**, and charged his disciple **George Scholarios** to continue it. In Russia, Metropolitan Isidore of Kiev, who had signed, was deposed and imprisoned in Moscow (1441) (Stage 11).

**The last years.** The union was formally proclaimed in Hagia Sophia on **12 December 1452**, months before the fall, and was opposed by most of the city. A synod in Constantinople in **1484**, with the Eastern patriarchs, formally **rejected the Council of Florence**.

**Why the Orthodox honour Mark.** Not for refusing union, but for holding that **union must be in truth**. With **St Photios** and **St Gregory Palamas** he is called a **Pillar of Orthodoxy**. His stand showed that **the Church's faith is not settled by emperors or by a majority of delegates**, but by reception: the whole Church refused what had been signed.

**Point across.** The Orthodox understanding of reception was given in Stage 1; the modern dialogues with Rome in Stage 12.
The fall of Constantinople (1453):
On 29 May 1453 the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople. The Christian Roman Empire ended after eleven centuries, and the Orthodox Church began a new life under Muslim rule.

**The siege (6 April to 29 May 1453).** **Sultan Mehmed II** (ruled 1444 to 1446 and 1451 to 1481), aged twenty-one, brought an army of perhaps 80,000 men and great cannon, among them one cast by a Hungarian engineer, Orban. The city had about 7,000 defenders, including Genoese and Venetians, behind the Theodosian Walls. **Mehmed's ships were dragged overland** into the Golden Horn to get past the chain across its mouth.

**The last emperor.** **Constantine XI Palaiologos** (ruled 1449 to 1453). On the night of 28 May, according to the accounts of witnesses, Orthodox and Latin Christians prayed together in Hagia Sophia. On 29 May the walls were breached, and **Constantine died fighting**; his body was never surely identified. **He is popularly honoured by many Greek Orthodox as an ethnomartyr**, though he has not been formally canonized by a synod.

**After the fall.** The city was sacked for three days, as was the custom when a city resisted. **Hagia Sophia became a mosque**, its mosaics later plastered over. Mehmed made Constantinople his capital.

**The new order.** Mehmed chose the leading anti-unionist, **George Scholarios**, now the monk **Gennadios**, to be patriarch. He was installed in **January 1454** as **Gennadios II**, with the sultan handing him the staff of office as emperors had done. The patriarch became the head of the **Rum millet** (Arabic *Rūm*, "Romans"), the community of all Orthodox Christians of the Ottoman Empire, with civil as well as church authority over them. **Stage 11 tells what this meant for the next four centuries.**

**Why 1453 is a turning point for the Church:**

| Before | After |
| --- | --- |
| a Christian emperor and symphonia | a Muslim sultan; the Church a protected minority |
| the patriarch one of two heads of a Christian society | the patriarch the civil and spiritual head of a subject people |
| the union of Florence nominally in force | Florence rejected; the anti-unionist party in charge |
| Moscow a distant daughter church | Moscow the only great independent Orthodox state, soon calling itself the **Third Rome** |

**How the Church remembers.** A Greek tradition says a priest celebrating in Hagia Sophia as the Turks entered went into the wall with the Gifts, and will come out to finish the Liturgy when the city is Christian again. **It is a legend of hope, not history**, and the Church keeps it as such. Many Orthodox still call the city by its old name, ***Pólis***, "the City".

**What survived.** The Empire fell; **the Church did not**. The Liturgy, the patriarchate, Athos, the Fathers, the canons, the icons and the faith of the councils passed intact to the peoples who kept them under the Ottomans and to Russia, which Stage 11 follows.
Looking back: the councils of Christ and:
This stage has followed the Church from Justinian to 1453. Three more ecumenical councils completed the confession of Christ, and the Byzantine Church left the Orthodox world its worship, its canons and its saints.

**The councils of Christ, completed:**

| Council | What it confessed | Why it matters for salvation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nicaea I (325)** | the Son is of one essence with the Father | only God can deify |
| **Constantinople I (381)** | the Spirit is Lord, worshipped and glorified | the Spirit who sanctifies is God |
| **Ephesus (431)** | Mary is Theotokos | the one born of her is God |
| **Chalcedon (451)** | one Christ in two natures | our whole nature is joined to God |
| **Constantinople II (553)** | one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh | the one who died for us is God |
| **Constantinople III (680 to 681)** | two wills, the human freely following the divine | our will is healed in his |
| **Nicaea II (787)** | Christ can be portrayed; icons are venerated | God has truly become visible, touchable flesh |

**Then the hesychast councils (1341 to 1351)** confessed how we share in God: **through his uncreated energies**, not his essence.

**Four lessons from the stage:**

1. **Every doctrine was about Christ, and every doctrine about Christ was about salvation.** The councils defended theosis at each step.
2. **Emperors could not define the faith.** Monothelitism and Iconoclasm were imperial policies; the Church overturned both, through monks like Maximus, Theodore and John of Damascus.
3. **Reception decides.** Hieria called itself ecumenical; Lyons and Florence were signed; the Church received none of them.
4. **Worship and doctrine are one.** The Triumph of Orthodoxy is a feast; Palamas's teaching came from the prayer of monks; Nicaea II's definition is kept by kissing an icon.

**What the Byzantine Church left:**

- **The Divine Liturgy** and the services as Orthodox Christians know them, with the Studite and then the Jerusalem Typikon.
- **The canons**, gathered at Trullo.
- **Hagia Sophia** as the pattern of the temple.
- **The Slavonic Church**, from Cyril and Methodius.
- **The Synodikon** and the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

**The divisions.** The estrangement from Rome, given as history: 1054, 1204, Lyons, Florence. **The Orthodox Church holds that she has kept the faith of the seven councils unchanged.** The modern relations are Stage 12.

**The words of this stage,** with their Greek:

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| *symphōnía* | harmony of Church and empire |
| *thélēma*, *gnṓmē* | natural will, gnomic will |
| *eikṓn* | image, icon |
| *proskýnēsis*, *latreía* | veneration, worship |
| *hēsychía* | stillness |
| *ousía*, *enérgeia* | essence, energy |

**Where this goes next.** Stage 9 reads the Fathers who appeared here, Maximus, John of Damascus, Symeon and Palamas, beside the earlier ones, in their own words. Stage 10 takes up hesychasm as a way of prayer; Stage 11 the Church under the Ottomans and in Russia.
Context: how to read a Father of the Chu:
This stage reads the Church's great teachers one by one, in their own words wherever a public-domain translation exists. First, what a Father is and how to read one.

**What makes a Father.** The Church gives the title **Father** (*patḗr*) to teachers whose writings she has received as faithful witnesses to the apostolic faith. The usual marks are four:

| Mark | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Orthodoxy of doctrine** | his teaching agrees with the faith of the Church as a whole |
| **Holiness of life** | most are saints; theology and holiness are not separated |
| **Antiquity** | traditionally the early centuries, though see below |
| **Reception by the Church** | the councils and later Fathers cite him as an authority |

**When the age of the Fathers ends.** Western handbooks often close it with St John of Damascus (died about 749). **The Orthodox Church does not close it.** Fr Georges Florovsky and many others have said that the Church is always "patristic": St Symeon the New Theologian, St Gregory Palamas, and saints of recent centuries are Fathers too. This stage follows that view, reading Fathers from the second century to the fourteenth.

**Why read them in their own words.** Stage 1 said the Fathers are witnesses, not a separate source beside Scripture: they are Scripture's best readers. Reading them directly shows **how they think**, not only what conclusions they reached. Their tone matters too: Ignatius burning to die, Chrysostom thundering at the rich, Gregory weeping over his friend.

**How this stage quotes.** Quotations come only from **public-domain translations** checked word for word: the *Ante-Nicene Fathers* (1885 onward), the *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* (1886 to 1900), and Hapgood's *Service Book* (1906). Each gives its translator. **Where no such translation could be fetched and checked**, as for St Maximus, St Symeon and St Gregory Palamas, whose good English translations are modern and in copyright, **the lesson paraphrases and says so.**

**Old translations have quirks.** They use "thee" and "ye", Victorian spelling and sometimes clumsy phrasing; their square brackets are the translators' additions. They can be checked against modern versions for meaning.

**How to read a Father, in five habits:**

1. **Know his question.** Most patristic writing answers a crisis: Gnosticism, Arianism, Nestorius, Iconoclasm.
2. **Know his audience.** A sermon to a crowd differs from a letter to a fellow bishop or a treatise for monks.
3. **Read him with the other Fathers.** One Father's phrase is weighed by the consensus (lesson 25).
4. **Read him in prayer.** The Fathers wrote as men of prayer for people of prayer.
5. **Look for Christ.** Every Father in this stage is finally talking about the Incarnation and what it does for us.

**The order.** Chronological: Ignatius, Irenaeus, Athanasius, the Cappadocians, Ephrem, Chrysostom, Cyril, Dionysius, Maximus, John of Damascus, Symeon, Palamas. Stages 7 and 8 told their history; **this stage lets them speak**.

**Point across.** The Philosophy curriculum treats several of them (Gregory of Nyssa, Maximus, Palamas) as philosophers; the Greek curriculum can use their Greek as reading.
St Ignatius of Antioch: the letters of a:
Stage 7 read Ignatius's letter to Smyrna. This lesson reads him on the Eucharist and on his own death: the earliest Christian writer whose inner life we can see.

**Who.** Bishop of Antioch, arrested under Trajan and taken under guard to Rome, where he was thrown to the beasts about 107. On the way he wrote **seven letters**: to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans, and to St Polycarp. **Feast: 20 December.**

**On the Eucharist** (*Epistle to the Ephesians* 20; translated by Roberts and Donaldson, *Ante-Nicene Fathers* vol. 1, 1885; shorter recension):

> "...so that ye obey the bishop and the presbytery with an undivided mind, breaking one and the same bread, which is the medicine of immortality, and the antidote to prevent us from dying, but [which causes] that we should live for ever in Jesus Christ."

**"The medicine of immortality"** (Greek *phármakon athanasías*) is one of the most quoted phrases in the Fathers. **The Eucharist is not a reminder of life but the cure of death**, because it is the flesh of the risen Christ. Notice that unity comes first: one bishop, one mind, one bread.

**On his martyrdom** (*Epistle to the Romans* 4; same translation):

> "I write to the Churches, and impress on them all, that I shall willingly die for God, unless ye hinder me. I beseech of you not to show an unseasonable good-will towards me. Suffer me to become food for the wild beasts, through whose instrumentality it will be granted me to attain to God. I am the wheat of God, and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"unless ye hinder me"** | the Roman Christians might have used influence to save him; he begs them not to |
| **"an unseasonable good-will"** | kindness that would rob him of what he most wants |
| **"to attain to God"** | his constant phrase: martyrdom is not loss but arrival |
| **"I am the wheat of God"** | the language of the Eucharist: wheat ground into bread |
| **"the pure bread of Christ"** | he will become, in his death, an offering like the one on the altar |

**What his letters teach as a whole:**

1. **Christ truly had flesh**, truly suffered and truly rose.
2. **The Church is gathered around one bishop and one Eucharist.**
3. **Martyrdom is the fullest imitation of Christ** and a way of union with him.
4. **Unity is the sign of the Church**; division is the mark of error.

**How to read his longing to die.** The Church does not teach Christians to seek death. Ignatius was already condemned. What he refused was **escape by compromise**, and what he desired was union with Christ. The Church reads him as a man so in love with God that the arena looked like a door.

**Point across.** Stage 6 shows the one Lamb broken and not divided in the Liturgy; Ignatius is its earliest witness.
St Irenaeus of Lyons: \"become what we a:
Stage 7 told how Irenaeus answered the Gnostics. This lesson reads the sentence that holds his whole theology, and the doctrine of salvation it began.

**Who.** About 130 to about 202. From Asia Minor, a hearer of St Polycarp, bishop of Lyons from about 178. His great work, *Against Heresies* (about 180), is in five books. **Feast: 23 August.**

**The text** (*Against Heresies*, Book 5, preface; translated by Alexander Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, *Ante-Nicene Fathers* vol. 1, 1885):

> "...following the only true and stedfast Teacher, the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"the only true and stedfast Teacher"** | against the Gnostic teachers with their secret lore: Christ alone teaches, openly |
| **"through His transcendent love"** | the motive of the Incarnation is love, not necessity |
| **"become what we are"** | the Word took our whole nature, body included, against the Gnostics who said the body is worthless |
| **"that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself"** | the goal: **we become by grace what he is by nature** |

**This is the first great statement of theosis.** *Théōsis* is "deification", becoming god by grace, sharing in the divine life without becoming God by essence. Athanasius will put the same thought more sharply (lesson 5); the whole Orthodox tradition follows. Stage 3 gave it as doctrine.

**Recapitulation.** Irenaeus's word *anakephalaíōsis*, "summing up again" (from Ephesians 1:10), explains how. Christ, the new Adam, goes through every stage of human life:

| Adam | Christ |
| --- | --- |
| formed from virgin earth | born of the Virgin |
| disobeyed at a tree | obeyed on the tree of the Cross |
| Eve, a virgin, listened to the serpent | Mary, a virgin, listened to the angel |
| brought death to all | brings life to all |

**Mary as the new Eve.** Irenaeus is the first great witness to this: **"the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by the obedience of Mary. For what the virgin Eve had bound fast through unbelief, this did the virgin Mary set free through faith"** (Book 3, chapter 22, section 4; same translation). The Orthodox veneration of the Theotokos grows from this root.

**Salvation as growth.** Irenaeus held that Adam and Eve were created **like children**, meant to grow into the likeness of God over time. The fall interrupted the growth; Christ resumes it. **Salvation is not only rescue from sin but the completion of what God began at creation.** Orthodox theology has kept this sense that the human being is made for an endless growth into God.

**The body.** Against those who despised the flesh, Irenaeus argued that the body which receives the Eucharist, Christ's own body and blood, **cannot be incapable of eternal life**. That is why the resurrection is bodily.

**Point across.** The next lesson reads his most famous sentence, on the glory of God.
St Irenaeus: \"the glory of God is a liv:
One sentence of Irenaeus is quoted more than any other. Read in its context, it says something more than its usual quotation does.

**The text** (*Against Heresies*, Book 4, chapter 20, section 7; translated by Roberts and Rambaut, *Ante-Nicene Fathers* vol. 1, 1885):

> "...revealing God indeed to men, but presenting man to God, and preserving at the same time the invisibility of the Father, lest man should at any time become a despiser of God, and that he should always possess something towards which he might advance; but, on the other hand, revealing God to men through many dispensations, lest man, falling away from God altogether, should cease to exist. For the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God."

**The context.** Irenaeus is explaining how the Word has revealed the Father through history: in creation, in the Law and the prophets, and finally in the Incarnation. The subject of the first clauses is **the Word**.

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"revealing God indeed to men, but presenting man to God"** | the Word is the mediator in both directions |
| **"preserving at the same time the invisibility of the Father"** | God is never exhausted: even revealed, he remains beyond us |
| **"that he should always possess something towards which he might advance"** | **endless growth**: there is always more of God to come to |
| **"lest man, falling away from God altogether, should cease to exist"** | life is communion with God; cut off, a creature falls back toward nothing |
| **"the glory of God is a living man"** | God is glorified when the creature he made is fully alive |
| **"the life of man consists in beholding God"** | and the creature is fully alive only in seeing God |

**The usual quotation leaves out half.** "The glory of God is a human being fully alive" is often quoted as a charter for self-fulfilment. **Irenaeus's next words say what that life is: the vision of God.** God's glory and our life are not rivals; each is found in the other.

**Two themes the whole Orthodox tradition keeps:**

1. **Life is communion.** A creature exists by sharing in the life of God. Sin is a turning away that tends to death; salvation is restored communion. **This is why the Orthodox speak of sin as sickness and death, and salvation as healing and life.**
2. **Endless progress.** Because God is infinite, the creature can always "advance". St Gregory of Nyssa (lesson 11) builds his whole spiritual theology on this.

**The vision of God.** "Beholding God" is not a distant reward but the heart of the Christian life, begun now. In Stage 10 the hesychasts speak of seeing the uncreated light; Irenaeus is already there.

**Why Irenaeus belongs at the head of this stage.** He holds together **creation, Incarnation, Eucharist, resurrection and theosis** as one story of God's love for a creature he made to share his life. Every later Father works within that frame.

**Point across.** The Philosophy curriculum can set this beside the ancient question of the good life. The passage survives in Latin (*gloria enim Dei vivens homo*), not in Irenaeus's Greek.
St Athanasius: On the Incarnation:
A short book, probably written by a young man, answers the question every Christian must face: why did God become man? It is the best first book of the Fathers to read whole.

**Who.** About 296 to 373, bishop of Alexandria for forty-five years and five times exiled (Stage 7). **Feasts: 18 January and 2 May.**

**The book.** *On the Incarnation of the Word* is the second half of a double work; the first, *Against the Pagans*, shows that idols are false and the one God is known through his Word. Its date is debated: some scholars place it **before 325**, others **about 335 to 337**, during his first exile.

**The argument, in paraphrase:**

| Chapters | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1 to 5** | God made all things from nothing through his Word, and made man in his image, to share his life; man turned away and began to fall back toward the nothing he came from: **corruption** (*phthorá*) and death |
| **6 to 10** | **the divine dilemma**: God could not let his creature perish, and could not go back on his word that sin brings death. Repentance alone could not undo corruption. So the Word took a body capable of death, died for all, and by his resurrection **clothed the body with incorruption** |
| **11 to 19** | man had also lost the knowledge of God; the Word became visible so that people who looked only at bodies might know him through his bodily works |
| **20 to 32** | why the cross, why the resurrection on the third day; the evidence of the risen Christ in his followers, who no longer fear death |
| **33 to 55** | answers to Jewish and pagan objections |

**The key sentence** (*On the Incarnation* 54.3; translated by Archibald Robertson, *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 2nd series vol. 4, 1892):

> "For He was made man that we might be made God; and He manifested Himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father; and He endured the insolence of men that we might inherit immortality."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"He was made man that we might be made God"** | the shortest statement of **theosis** in the Fathers: an exchange, his descent for our ascent |
| **"He manifested Himself by a body"** | the Incarnation is God making himself knowable to bodily creatures |
| **"that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father"** | to see the Son is to know the Father (John 14:9) |
| **"He endured the insolence of men"** | the Passion |
| **"that we might inherit immortality"** | the Passion's fruit: incorruption |

**"Made God."** The Greek is *theopoiēthômen*. **Athanasius does not mean we become God by nature**, which would be blasphemy and is the very thing he fought in Arius from the other side. He means we share by grace in the life of the one who is God by nature. **That is why the Son must be God**: a creature could not deify us.

**The image of the portrait.** In chapter 14, Athanasius compares the Word to a painter who comes himself to restore a ruined portrait on the same wood, because the likeness was spoiled. **The Word came to renew the image of God in man** in the same human material.

**Why it is the best first book.** It is short, clear and joyful, and explains in a few pages why Nicaea mattered.

**Point across.** Stage 3 gave theosis as doctrine; the Philosophy curriculum the problem of a God who cannot change becoming man.
St Athanasius: the Life of Antony and th:
Athanasius's other great gifts to the Church were a book about a monk and a lifetime defending one word. This lesson shows how they fit together.

**The Life of Antony (about 357 to 360).** **St Antony the Great** (about 251 to 356; feast 17 January) was an Egyptian Christian who, about the age of twenty, heard the Gospel read in church: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor" (Matthew 19:21, King James Version, 1611). He gave away his land and went out to live alone, first near his village, then in a tomb, then in the desert, for some eighty years. Athanasius knew him and wrote his life soon after his death.

**What the Life teaches, in paraphrase:**

| Theme | What Antony shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Renunciation** | he left everything at the Gospel's word |
| **Spiritual warfare** | he fought the demons in solitude, and found they are powerless against the sign of the cross and the name of Christ |
| **Discernment** | he taught monks to examine their thoughts and know which come from God |
| **Holiness that heals** | people came to him for healing and counsel; he became a father to many |
| **Orthodoxy** | he came into Alexandria to denounce the Arians, saying the Son is not a creature |
| **Body restored** | when he came out of his long seclusion, Athanasius says, his body was neither wasted nor bloated but in perfect balance: a sign of the healed human being |

**Why it mattered.** The *Life* was translated into Latin within a few years and spread monasticism through the whole Church. St Augustine, by his own account in the *Confessions*, was moved toward conversion by hearing of it. **It became the model of every saint's life written after it.** Stage 10 takes monasticism up as a way of life.

**The defence of Nicaea.** In his *Orations against the Arians* and his historical writings Athanasius argued, in paraphrase:

1. **The Son is the Father's own Word and Wisdom.** God was never without his Word; so there never was when the Son was not.
2. **The Arian texts read rightly.** "My Father is greater than I" speaks of Christ as man, or of the Father as source; "The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way" (Proverbs 8:22) speaks of the Incarnation.
3. **Why *homooúsios*.** The scriptural phrases could all be twisted; this one word secured what Scripture means.
4. **Salvation is at stake.** Only the true God could unite us to God.

**How the two fit.** The Life of Antony shows what the Incarnation makes possible: **a human being restored, free of fear, full of the Spirit, like Adam before the fall**. The *Orations* defend the doctrine that makes it possible: if the Son is truly God, then a man like Antony can truly become god by grace. **Athanasius wrote doctrine and holiness as one argument.**

**Antony and Athanasius together.** By tradition Antony left Athanasius one of his two sheepskin cloaks. The bishop of the city and the monk of the desert stood for the same faith.

**Point across.** Stage 10 reads the desert tradition; the Greek curriculum can read the *Life* in simple Greek.
St Basil the Great: On the Holy Spirit:
Basil's short treatise defended the divinity of the Holy Spirit from the Church's worship. One of its sentences became the foundation of the theology of the icon.

**Who.** St Basil of Caesarea (about 330 to 379), bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia from 370. Educated at Athens with St Gregory the Theologian, then a monk, then a bishop of extraordinary energy. **Feast: 1 January**; with the Three Hierarchs, 30 January.

**The occasion (about 375).** Basil had used two forms of the doxology, in Blomfield Jackson's translation (1895): glory to the Father "through the Son in the Holy Ghost", and glory to the Father "with the Son together with the Holy Ghost". The second was attacked as an innovation that made the Spirit equal to the Father. *On the Holy Spirit* is his answer, written for Amphilochius of Iconium.

**His argument, in summary:**

1. **Prepositions matter, but Scripture uses them freely.** "Of", "through" and "in" are used of all three persons; they do not rank them.
2. **The Spirit is named with the Father and Son in baptism** (Matthew 28:19). What is joined there cannot be separated in worship.
3. **The Spirit does what only God does**: he sanctifies, gives life, makes us sons, is everywhere at once.
4. **Unwritten Tradition.** Some of the Church's teaching is handed down in her practice, not written: the sign of the cross, facing east to pray, the words of the epiclesis, the triple immersion (chapter 27). **These have the same force as what is written.**

**The text** (*On the Holy Spirit* 18.45; translated by Blomfield Jackson, *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 2nd series vol. 8, 1895):

> "How, then, if one and one, are there not two Gods? Because we speak of a king, and of the king's image, and not of two kings. The majesty is not cloven in two, nor the glory divided. The sovereignty and authority over us is one, and so the doxology ascribed by us is not plural but one; because the honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"if one and one, are there not two Gods?"** | the objection: Father and Son are each God, so two |
| **"a king, and of the king's image"** | an emperor's portrait in a city was honoured as the emperor; no one thought there were two emperors |
| **"The majesty is not cloven in two"** | Father and Son share one divine glory |
| **"the doxology... is not plural but one"** | the Church gives one glory to Father, Son and Spirit |
| **"the honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype"** | honour given to the Son, the perfect Image, is given to the Father |

**From the Trinity to the icon.** Basil was speaking of the Son as the living image of the Father. **Four centuries later St John of Damascus and the Seventh Council took the same principle and applied it to painted icons** (Stage 8): honour given to an icon passes to the person shown. A sentence about the Trinity became the charter of Orthodox worship before icons.

**The Spirit's work.** Basil's most beautiful passages describe the Spirit as the one who perfects all things: **through him hearts are lifted up, the weak are led by the hand, those advancing are brought to perfection** (in paraphrase, chapter 9).

**Point across.** Stage 2 gives the Trinity as doctrine; Stage 8 shows the principle at Nicaea II.
St Basil the Great: the Hexaemeron, the:
Basil was a theologian of creation and a builder of Christian society. This lesson reads him as preacher, monastic legislator and founder.

**The Hexaemeron** (*Hexaḗmeron*, "the six days"). Nine homilies on the creation in Genesis 1, preached to a congregation of working people in Caesarea, probably in the 370s. Their teaching, in paraphrase:

- **The world had a beginning** and was made by God freely, from nothing; it is not eternal.
- **Creation is good, ordered and beautiful**, and points to its Maker. Basil fills his sermons with the natural knowledge of his day: fish, birds, plants, the sea.
- **Scripture is not a science textbook.** Moses wrote what serves salvation, not to satisfy curiosity about the shape of the earth.
- **Each creature has its own nature and law**, set by God's command, which it keeps to this day.
- **Man is the crown of creation**, made to know God through it.

St Ambrose of Milan reworked the homilies in Latin, and they shaped Christian thinking about nature for a thousand years.

**The Asketikon: the Long and Short Rules.** Basil's answers to questions from monks. **They are still the foundation of Orthodox monastic life**, which is why Orthodox monks are sometimes loosely called Basilians. His principles, in paraphrase:

| Principle | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Community over solitude** | the hermit has no one's feet to wash; love needs neighbours |
| **The love of God and neighbour** | the whole of the commandments; the monastery is a school of love |
| **Obedience** | to the superior and to each other, as to Christ |
| **Work and prayer** | manual labour joined to the hours of prayer |
| **Service of the poor** | monasteries should care for the needy |

**The Basiliad, the "new city".** About 369 to 372, Basil built outside Caesarea a great complex: **a church, a hospital, a hostel for travellers, a home for the poor, and housing for lepers**, staffed by monks. St Gregory the Theologian called it a new city. **It is one of the first hospitals in the history of the world.** Basil himself, an aristocrat, tended lepers.

**On wealth.** During a famine about 368, Basil preached on the rich fool of Luke 12 who planned bigger barns. His argument, in paraphrase: **the bread you store belongs to the hungry; the coat in your chest belongs to the naked; the shoes rotting in your house belong to the barefoot.** What you hold beyond your need you hold as a steward, not an owner. Basil sold his own inheritance in the famine.

**The Liturgy of St Basil.** The longer of the two Divine Liturgies of the Orthodox Church bears his name. Its great eucharistic prayer, which tells the whole history of salvation, is **celebrated ten times a year**: on the Sundays of Great Lent (except Palm Sunday), Holy Thursday, Holy Saturday, the eves of Nativity and Theophany, and on St Basil's day, 1 January. Most scholars hold that its core goes back to Basil himself.

**Why Basil is "the Great".** For theology, for monasticism, for charity, and for governing a church in a time of persecution by an Arian emperor. **Orthodox tradition sees in him a whole bishop**: teacher, ascetic, pastor and servant of the poor.

**Point across.** Stage 6 covers the Liturgy of St Basil; Stage 10 the monastic rule.
St Gregory the Theologian: the Theologic:
Five sermons preached in a small chapel in 380 earned their author a title given to only two others in the Church's history: "the Theologian".

**Who.** St Gregory of Nazianzus (about 329 to about 390), son of a bishop of the same name, schooled at Athens with St Basil. A poet and an orator, he loved solitude and was repeatedly forced into office. **Feast: 25 January**; with the Three Hierarchs, 30 January. The Orthodox Church gives the title **Theologian** to three: St John the Evangelist, St Gregory, and St Symeon the New Theologian.

**The setting.** In 379 the small Nicene community of Constantinople, without a church, invited Gregory to lead them. He preached in a house chapel he named ***Anastasia***, "Resurrection". There, in 380, he gave the five **Theological Orations** (Orations 27 to 31).

| Oration | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| **27** | who may speak about God, and when |
| **28** | the knowledge of God: God's nature is beyond us |
| **29 and 30** | the Son: answers to the Arian proof-texts |
| **31** | the Holy Spirit |

**The opening** (Oration 27.3; translated by Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 2nd series vol. 7, 1893):

> "Not to every one, my friends, does it belong to philosophize about God; not to every one; the Subject is not so cheap and low; and I will add, not before every audience, nor at all times, nor on all points; but on certain occasions, and before certain persons, and within certain limits."

**He continues**: theology is permitted "to those who have been examined, and are passed masters in meditation, and who have been previously purified in soul and body, or at the very least are being purified. For the impure to touch the pure is, we may safely say, not safe, just as it is unsafe to fix weak eyes upon the sun's rays."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"Not to every one... to philosophize about God"** | aimed at the Eunomians, who debated God's essence in the marketplace as a puzzle |
| **"on certain occasions, and before certain persons, and within certain limits"** | theology has a time, an audience and a boundary |
| **"previously purified in soul and body"** | **purity comes before theology**; knowledge of God depends on the state of the knower |
| **"weak eyes upon the sun's rays"** | the image of God as light too bright for an unhealed eye |

**The principle.** This is the source of the saying, attributed to Evagrius, that **the theologian is one who prays truly**, which Stage 1 gave as the Orthodox definition of theology. For Gregory, theology is not a technical skill but the fruit of a purified life.

**The Fifth Oration** (on the Spirit, quoted in Stage 7) answers the objection that Scripture never calls the Spirit God: **the Old Testament proclaimed the Father openly and the Son obscurely; the New made the Son manifest and hinted at the Spirit; now the Spirit dwells among us and shows himself more clearly** (31.26, in paraphrase).

**Gregory's style**, all antithesis and music, passed into the Church's hymns. **The first canon of Nativity Matins opens with a line from his Oration 38**, which Hapgood's *Service Book* (1906) renders: "Christ is born: extol him! Christ from heaven: go to meet him!"

**Point across.** The Philosophy curriculum reads Oration 28 as an argument for the limits of reason; Stage 2 sets out apophatic theology.
St Gregory the Theologian: \"that which:
The most quoted principle in Orthodox Christology comes from a letter Gregory wrote against those who said Christ had no human mind.

**The occasion.** After retiring from Constantinople in 381, Gregory found followers of **Apollinarius of Laodicea** active in his home church of Nazianzus. Apollinarius taught that in Christ **the divine Word took the place of the human mind** (*noûs*): a human body and soul, with God as the mind. It seemed to protect Christ's sinlessness and unity. About 382 Gregory wrote **two letters to the priest Cledonius** (Letters 101 and 102).

**The text** (*Letter 101, to Cledonius*; translated by Browne and Swallow, *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 2nd series vol. 7, 1893):

> "If anyone has put his trust in Him as a Man without a human mind, he is really bereft of mind, and quite unworthy of salvation. For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved. If only half Adam fell, then that which Christ assumes and saves may be half also; but if the whole of his nature fell, it must be united to the whole nature of Him that was begotten, and so be saved as a whole."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"bereft of mind"** | Gregory's pun: whoever denies Christ a mind has lost his own |
| **"that which He has not assumed He has not healed"** | **the rule**: Christ heals human nature by taking it; whatever he did not take remains unhealed |
| **"that which is united to His Godhead is also saved"** | salvation is union: what is joined to God is restored |
| **"If only half Adam fell"** | if Christ took only half a man, only half could be saved |
| **"the whole of his nature fell"** | but the mind fell too; in fact it fell first, for sin begins in the mind |
| **"saved as a whole"** | so Christ must have **a whole human nature**: body, soul and mind |

**Why the principle reaches so far.** The rule works like a key in Orthodox theology:

| Question | Answer by the rule |
| --- | --- |
| Did Christ have a human mind? | yes, or our minds are not healed: **381** condemned Apollinarius |
| Did Christ have a human will? | yes, or our wills are not healed: **681** (Stage 8) |
| Did Christ have a real body? | yes, or our bodies will not rise: Ignatius, Irenaeus |
| Did Christ take our fallen nature? | he took **our nature** in its weakness, subject to hunger, pain and death, but **without sin**; Orthodox writers differ in how to put this, and the Fathers speak of it with care |

**The same letter** anathematizes any who deny Mary the title **Theotokos**, fifty years before Ephesus.

**Theosis.** Gregory also speaks of the human being, in paraphrase of Oration 43, as **a creature commanded to become god**, and says Christ's humanity was **deified by the union**, as Stage 8 heard the Sixth Council quote him. The healing of our nature in Christ is its deification.

**Why it matters for prayer.** Because Christ took a whole human nature, **every part of us can be offered to God and healed**: the body in fasting and prostration, the mind in attention and prayer, the will in obedience. Nothing human is outside the reach of grace.

**Point across.** Stage 3 gives the doctrine of the two natures; Stage 10 the healing of the *noûs*.
St Gregory of Nyssa: the endless ascent:
The youngest of the Cappadocians was the most philosophical. His central idea is that the life of the soul in God is endless progress, because God is infinite.

**Who.** St Gregory of Nyssa (about 335 to about 395), younger brother of St Basil and of St Macrina. Married, by most accounts, before becoming bishop of the small town of Nyssa in 372. Deposed by an Arian emperor, restored in 378, a leading voice at the council of 381. **Feast: 10 January.**

**His works** include *Against Eunomius*, *On the Making of Man* (completing Basil's Hexaemeron), the *Catechetical Oration* (a handbook of the faith), *On the Soul and the Resurrection* (a dialogue with the dying Macrina), the *Life of Macrina*, homilies on the Song of Songs, and the ***Life of Moses***. The quotations below are paraphrases: the best English translations of the *Life of Moses* and the *Song of Songs* homilies are modern and in copyright.

**The infinity of God.** Against Eunomius, who claimed to know God's essence by the word "unbegotten", Gregory argued that **God is infinite** (*ápeiros*): without limit. An infinite being can never be grasped, only approached.

**Epektasis.** From Philippians 3:13, where Paul speaks of "reaching forth unto those things which are before" (King James Version, 1611; Greek *epekteinómenos*). Gregory made it his word for **the soul's endless stretching toward God**. Its points, in paraphrase:

1. **Perfection is not a resting place.** For a creature, perfection is never to stop growing in the good.
2. **Each arrival is a new beginning.** Every vision of God awakens a greater desire.
3. **This continues into eternity.** The life of the age to come is not static bliss but unending ascent.

**The Life of Moses** (about 390). Gregory reads Moses's life as the ascent of the soul in three stages:

| Stage | In Moses's life | In the soul |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Light** | the burning bush | turning from error to the truth |
| **Cloud** | the cloud on Sinai | leaving behind what the senses and the mind can grasp |
| **Darkness** | Moses entering the "thick darkness where God was" (Exodus 20:21, King James Version, 1611) | **knowing God by unknowing**: the closer one comes, the more one sees he is beyond sight |

At the summit Moses asks to see God's glory and is shown only his back (Exodus 33). Gregory reads this, in paraphrase: **to see God is to follow him**, always going after him, never overtaking him. **The true vision of God is never to be satisfied in the desire to see him.**

**Why the Church values him.** He gave the spiritual life a shape that runs from the Cappadocians through Dionysius and Maximus to Palamas: **light, then darkness; knowledge, then unknowing; growth without end**. The Seventh Council cited him among the Fathers, and later tradition honours him highly.

**A question about him.** In some writings Gregory hoped that **in the end all creatures, even the wicked, would be purified and restored to God**. Lesson 25 gives how Orthodox writers have received that hope, with each view in its strongest form.

**Point across.** The Philosophy curriculum treats Gregory on infinity and the soul; Stage 2 gives apophatic theology as doctrine.
St Ephrem the Syrian: theology as song:
The greatest poet of the early Church wrote in Syriac, not Greek. He taught the faith in hymns, and the Church calls him "the Harp of the Spirit".

**Who.** St Ephrem (about 306 to 373), born in Nisibis in Mesopotamia, on the Roman-Persian frontier. A deacon, he taught in the school of Nisibis under its bishop. When the city was ceded to Persia in **363**, he moved with its Christians to **Edessa**, where he died in **373**, by tradition while caring for victims of famine. **Feast: 28 January.** He is honoured by the Orthodox, the Oriental Orthodox and the Assyrian Church of the East alike.

**His form: the *madrāshā*.** Ephrem wrote **teaching hymns** in Syriac, sung by choirs, including choirs of women he trained. Over four hundred survive: *On the Nativity*, *On Faith*, *On Paradise*, *On the Church*, *Nisibene Hymns*, and others. **He taught doctrine by singing it.**

**A passage** (*Hymns on the Nativity*, Hymn 5; translated by J. B. Morris, 1847, revised by John Gwynn for the *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 2nd series vol. 13):

> "The old men cried, 'Blessed be that Son Who restored Adam to youth, Who was vexed to see that he was old and worn out, and that the serpent who had killed him, had changed his skin and had gotten himself away. Blessed be the Babe in Whom Adam and Eve were restored to youth.'"

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"The old men cried"** | the hymn gives voices to the people of Bethlehem: old men, women, children, each praising the Child |
| **"restored Adam to youth"** | salvation as **renewal of the old Adam**, as in Irenaeus |
| **"the serpent... had changed his skin"** | the serpent sheds its skin and grows young, while Adam grows old and dies: the injustice the Child undoes |
| **"Adam and Eve were restored to youth"** | the Incarnation reverses the fall for both, man and woman |

**Ephrem's way of doing theology:**

1. **Symbols, not definitions.** Ephrem taught that God reveals himself through **types and symbols** (Syriac *rāzē*, "mysteries") in nature and Scripture. The theologian's task is to see and sing them, not to pin God down.
2. **Against prying.** He attacked the Arians as "pryers" who tried to search out the Son's generation. **Wonder, not dissection, is the right response to God.**
3. **Paradox.** The Child who is fed by Mary feeds the world; the one held in her arms holds all things. Another of his Nativity hymns has Mary say that the Child made his mother a harp for his words.
4. **Mary.** Ephrem is one of the greatest early singers of the Theotokos, of her purity and her role as the new Eve.

**The Prayer of St Ephrem.** The short Lenten prayer said with prostrations at the weekday services of Great Lent is attributed to him; it has come down in Greek. Hapgood's *Service Book* (1906) begins it: "O Lord and Master of my life, grant not unto me a spirit of slothfulness, of discouragement, of lust of power, of vain babbling." Stage 6 gives it whole.

**Why he matters to the Orthodox.** Ephrem shows that **Orthodox theology is not only Greek**. The Syriac Christian tradition, in its own language and images, confessed the same faith, and Byzantine hymnography (St Romanos the Melodist above all) drew on its forms.

**Point across.** Stage 6 shows how the services teach the faith by singing; Ephrem is the model.
St John Chrysostom: the preacher of Anti:
The Church's greatest preacher spoke to crowds about Scripture, the poor and the Eucharist, and died in exile for refusing to be silent.

**Who.** St John (about 349 to 407), born in Antioch, trained in rhetoric under the pagan Libanius. A monk in the hills, then deacon (381) and priest (386) of Antioch, where he preached for twelve years. Made archbishop of Constantinople in **398**. His preaching against luxury offended the Empress Eudoxia and his enemies, led by Theophilus of Alexandria; he was deposed at the **Synod of the Oak (403)**, recalled, then exiled again in **404**. He died on the road to a remoter exile on **14 September 407**. **His last words, by tradition, were "Glory to God for all things."** **Feasts: 13 November**; 27 January, the return of his relics to Constantinople (438); 30 January with the Three Hierarchs.

**"Chrysostom"** (*Chrysóstomos*) means **"Golden-mouthed"**, a name given him after his death.

**The preacher.** Hundreds of his homilies survive: whole series on Genesis, the Psalms, Matthew, John, Acts, and every letter of St Paul. **He read Scripture literally and morally**, in the Antiochene way: what does the text say, and how must we live?

**The text** (*Homilies on Matthew* 50; translated by George Prevost, revised by M. B. Riddle, *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 1st series vol. 10, 1888):

> "Wouldest thou do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked; do not while here thou honorest Him with silken garments, neglect Him perishing without of cold and nakedness."

He goes on to set beside each other the words "This is my body" and "Ye saw me an hungered, and fed me not": the same Lord says both.

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"do honor to Christ's body"** | the Eucharist, Christ's body on the altar |
| **"Neglect Him not when naked"** | Christ is also in the poor (Matthew 25) |
| **"while here thou honorest Him with silken garments"** | rich altar cloths inside the church |
| **"perishing without of cold and nakedness"** | the beggar outside the door |

**The point.** Chrysostom did not oppose beautiful churches. In the same homily he says God accepts the gifts, but that **the altar of the poor comes first**: adorning the church while ignoring the poor is a contradiction. **The sacrament of the altar and the sacrament of the brother** (a phrase later writers made of his teaching) are one Christ.

**His great themes:**

- **Almsgiving and wealth**: the rich are stewards of what belongs to the poor.
- **The Eucharist**: awe before the "fearful" mysteries; preparation by repentance.
- **Marriage and the family**: the household as a **little church**.
- **Paul**: Chrysostom loved him above all writers, and his homilies on Paul's letters are still the classic Orthodox commentary.
- **Repentance**: his homilies on repentance call every sinner back without despair.

**Point across.** Stage 5 sets him among the Fathers as interpreters of Scripture. The next two lessons read his priesthood, his Liturgy, and his Paschal sermon.
St John Chrysostom: On the Priesthood an:
Chrysostom's book on the priesthood is the Church's classic on pastoral ministry, and the Liturgy said most Sundays across the Orthodox world bears his name.

**On the Priesthood** (written about 386 to 391). Six books in the form of a dialogue with his friend Basil (not the Great). It begins with a story: the two friends were to be ordained together, and John, thinking himself unworthy, hid and let his friend be ordained alone. Its teaching, in paraphrase:

| Theme | His teaching |
| --- | --- |
| **The height of the office** | the priest stands at the altar where angels stand in awe; he handles the body of the Lord; **no human office is higher** |
| **The danger** | a priest answers for every soul in his care; vanity, ambition and anger are deadly in him |
| **The need for learning** | the priest must be able to answer heretics and teach from Scripture |
| **The soul of the pastor** | he must be gentle and firm, patient with the weak, unflattered by praise |
| **Preaching** | the preacher must not seek applause; he speaks for God, not for the crowd |

**Why it is still read.** Orthodox seminaries and bishops' ordination talks still turn to it. It holds together **the awe of the Eucharist and the burden of souls**, which is the priesthood in Orthodox understanding.

**The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom.** The Liturgy celebrated on most days of the year in the Orthodox Church. Stage 6 walked through it step by step. Its origin:

- **The Orthodox tradition** attributes the anaphora (the great eucharistic prayer) to Chrysostom.
- **Modern scholars**, among them Robert Taft, have concluded from the prayer's wording that **Chrysostom probably reworked an older Antiochene anaphora**, the Anaphora of the Twelve Apostles, when he came to Constantinople; the rest of the Liturgy grew around it over centuries.
- **The two views are compatible**: tradition names him as the one who gave the prayer its form, and the scholars find his hand in it.

**His voice in the Liturgy.** The anaphora gives thanks, in Hapgood's rendering (1906), "for all the things whereof we know, and whereof we know not": the same spirit as the preacher's last words. **Chrysostom gave the Church not only words about worship but words to worship with.**

**The troparion of St John Chrysostom** (Hapgood's *Service Book*, 1906):

> "The grace of thy lips, shining forth like a beacon-fire, hath illumined the universe, and hath bestowed upon the world the treasure of non-avariciousness, and hath shown us the height of humility. But as thou instructest us with thy words, O Father John Chrysostom, so also intercede thou with Christ our God, that our souls may be saved."

**Read it briefly.** The Church remembers him for three things: **his words** ("the grace of thy lips"), **his freedom from greed** ("non-avariciousness", Greek *aphilargyría*, "not loving silver"), and **his humility**. This troparion is sung at Paschal Matins straight after his Paschal sermon (next lesson).

**Point across.** Stage 6 gives the Liturgy; Stage 4 the Mysteries and the priesthood.
Reading: St John Chrysostom's Paschal Ho:
At Paschal Matins, after the midnight procession and the canon, the priest reads a short sermon attributed to St John Chrysostom. The people stand to hear it. It is the most beloved sermon in the Orthodox Church.

**The text** (the *Catechetical Discourse* of St John Chrysostom, read at Paschal Matins; translated by Isabel Florence Hapgood, *Service Book of the Holy Orthodox-Catholic Apostolic Church*, 1906; the rubric there says the people "shall not sit while it is being read, but shall listen to it standing"):

> "If any man be devout and loveth God, let him enjoy this fair and radiant triumphal feast. If any man be a wise servant, let him rejoicing enter into the joy of his Lord. If any have laboured long in fasting, let him now receive his recompense. If any have wrought from the first hour, let him to-day receive his just reward. If any have arrived at the sixth hour, let him have no misgivings; because he shall in nowise suffer therefor. If any have delayed until the ninth hour, let him draw near, fearing nothing. If any have tarried even until the eleventh hour let him, also, be not alarmed at his tardiness; for the Lord, who is jealous of his honour, will accept the last even as the first..."

> "...Ye rich and poor together, hold ye high festival. Ye sober and ye heedless, honour ye the day. Rejoice to-day, both ye who have fasted and ye who have disregarded the fast. The table is full-laden; feast ye all sumptuously. The calf is ample; let no one go hungry away..."

> "...Let no one fear death, for the Saviour's death hath set us free... O Death, where is thy sting? O Hell, where is thy victory? Christ is risen, and thou art overthrown. Christ is risen, and the demons are fallen. Christ is risen, and the Angels rejoice. Christ is risen, and life reigneth. Christ is risen, and not one dead remaineth in the grave."

**Its authorship.** The Church has read it under Chrysostom's name for many centuries. Some scholars question whether he wrote it; its style is close to his, and it is often dated to his time. **The Church receives it as his, and reads it as the voice of the feast.**

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"the first hour... the eleventh hour"** | the parable of the labourers in the vineyard (Matthew 20): **all receive the same wage**, God's generosity, not our merit |
| **"will accept the last even as the first"** | no one is too late for Pascha |
| **"ye who have fasted and ye who have disregarded the fast"** | the fast prepared us, but the feast is for all; **Pascha is not a reward for the strong** |
| **"The table is full-laden... The calf is ample"** | the Eucharist, and the fatted calf of the prodigal son (Luke 15) |
| **"Hell, said he, was angered"** (in the full text) | from Isaiah 14:9 in the Septuagint; **Christ's descent into Hades** (Stage 3): death swallowed a body and met God |
| **"O Death, where is thy sting?"** | St Paul, 1 Corinthians 15:55, quoting Hosea |
| **"Christ is risen... not one dead remaineth in the grave"** | the Resurrection is **for all**: Christ has emptied Hades |

**The two great movements.**

1. **Invitation.** The first half is an invitation to everyone, with no exceptions: the faithful and the lax, the early and the late.
2. **Victory.** The second half is a hymn of triumph over death and Hades: **Christ entered death's realm and destroyed it from inside**. Hapgood renders it: "It took a body, and met God face to face. It took earth, and encountered Heaven."

**Why it is read at Pascha.** The homily is the theology of the Paschal troparion, which Hapgood renders "Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down Death by death, and upon those in the tomb bestowing life", spoken as an invitation. **It is not a sermon about the feast but the feast itself speaking.**

**Point across.** Stage 6 gives the Paschal services; in the Greek curriculum, every "Christ is risen" is *Anéstē Christós*.
St Cyril of Alexandria: the one Christ:
Cyril's conviction that the one born of Mary is God the Word himself shaped every later Christology, Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian alike.

**Who.** St Cyril (bishop of Alexandria 412 to 444; feasts 9 June and 18 January). Nephew of Theophilus of Alexandria. His early years as bishop were stormy: his enemies blamed him for the mob murder of the pagan philosopher **Hypatia** in 415, and **historians still dispute how far he was responsible**. The Church honours him for his theology, which became the measure of Orthodoxy at Ephesus and after.
