**His works** include commentaries on Isaiah, the Minor Prophets, Luke and **John**; the dialogues *On the Holy Trinity* and ***On the Unity of Christ***; letters to Nestorius and others; and a reply to the Emperor Julian's attack on Christianity.

**The text** (Cyril's Third Letter to Nestorius, the first anathema, 430; translated in the *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 2nd series vol. 14, ed. Henry R. Percival, 1900):

> "If anyone will not confess that the Emmanuel is very God, and that therefore the Holy Virgin is the Mother of God (Theotokos), inasmuch as in the flesh she bore the Word of God made flesh [as it is written, "The Word was made flesh"] let him be anathema."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"the Emmanuel is very God"** | the child called Emmanuel, "God with us" (Isaiah 7:14), is himself God |
| **"therefore the Holy Virgin is the Mother of God"** | Mary's title follows from who her Son is |
| **"in the flesh she bore the Word"** | she did not give the Word his Godhead, but she bore him according to the flesh |
| **"The Word was made flesh"** (John 1:14) | Cyril's lifelong text: **the Word became**, not "entered" or "joined himself to" |

**Cyril's central ideas:**

1. **One subject.** Everything Christ did and suffered, he did and suffered as **the one Word incarnate**. There are not two "he"s in Christ.
2. **The communication of properties** (*antídosis tōn idiōmátōn*). Because there is one subject, what belongs to the manhood can be said of God, and what belongs to the Godhead can be said of the man: **God was born, God died, the man Jesus is Lord of glory.**
3. **"He suffered impassibly."** The Word suffered in his own flesh, while remaining in his Godhead beyond suffering. It is a paradox Cyril accepted rather than resolve it away.
4. **Life-giving flesh.** The eleventh anathema confesses that **the flesh of the Lord is life-giving**, because it is the Word's own flesh. So the Eucharist gives life (Stage 4).
5. **"One incarnate nature of God the Word."** His formula for the oneness of Christ. Chalcedon read it as compatible with two natures; the non-Chalcedonians made it their standard (Stage 7).

**Why Cyril is a Father of both families.** The Chalcedonian Orthodox and the Oriental Orthodox both call Cyril their teacher; **their difference is over how to read him**, not whether to follow him. Stage 12 takes up the dialogues that have returned to Cyril.

**Point across.** Stage 3 gives the doctrine of the one person; the Philosophy curriculum the logic of the communication of properties.
The Dionysian writings: the divine names:
A body of writings under the name of St Paul's Athenian convert shaped Orthodox thinking about knowing God, the angels and the Liturgy. Their authorship is a genuine question, and the Church's use of them is not in doubt.

**The writings.** Four treatises and ten letters, first cited in the early sixth century:

| Work | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| ***The Divine Names*** | what the names of God in Scripture (Good, Light, Being, Life, Wisdom) mean, and how they fall short |
| ***The Mystical Theology*** | a few pages on knowing God beyond all knowing, in the divine darkness |
| ***The Celestial Hierarchy*** | the nine orders of angels, in three triads |
| ***The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*** | the sacraments and the orders of the Church as images of the heavenly worship |

**The author.** They name their author as **Dionysius the Areopagite**, the Athenian converted by St Paul (Acts 17:34; feast 3 October). **Two views are held among the Orthodox:**

| View | Its strongest form |
| --- | --- |
| **The traditional attribution** | the Church read them as apostolic for a thousand years; Maximus, John of Damascus and Palamas cited them as Dionysius's; the tradition should not be set aside lightly |
| **The modern dating** | since the 1890s scholars have shown the writings use the thought and wording of the Neoplatonist **Proclus** (died 485), so the author wrote **about 500**, probably a Syrian monk; most Orthodox scholars accept this |

**Either way, the Church's use of them stands**: St Maximus wrote commentaries on them, St John of Damascus and St Gregory Palamas relied on them, and their theology is received through those Fathers. Some Orthodox writers add that their authority rests on that reception, not on the name.

**Their teaching, in paraphrase** (good English translations are modern and in copyright):

1. **Two ways of speaking of God.** **Cataphatic** (affirming): God is good, wise, light. **Apophatic** (denying): God is not good as we know good, but beyond goodness. **The way of denial goes higher**, because God is beyond every name.
2. **The divine darkness.** At the summit, the soul enters a darkness brighter than light, like Moses on Sinai, and is united with God beyond knowing. This continues Gregory of Nyssa.
3. **Procession and return.** God's goodness **goes out** into creation and **draws all things back** to himself. Love is "ecstatic": it goes out of itself.
4. **Hierarchy.** A word Dionysius seems to have coined (*hierarchía*, "sacred order"). For him it is not rank but **a ladder of light**: each order receives the divine light and passes it on, purifying, illuminating and perfecting.

**Purification, illumination, perfection.** These three, from Dionysius, became a classic pattern of the spiritual life (Stage 10), and match the stages of the catechumen, the baptized and the communicant.

**The Liturgy.** The *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* explains the rites, the censing, the kiss of peace, the Eucharist and the burial of the dead as **symbols that lift the soul**. St Maximus's *Mystagogy* and later Byzantine commentaries on the Liturgy follow its method.

**Point across.** The Philosophy curriculum treats Dionysius as a Christian Neoplatonist; Stage 2 gives apophatic theology as doctrine.
St Maximus the Confessor: the Logos and:
Stage 8 told how Maximus suffered for the two wills. This lesson is his vision of the world: everything made by the Word, holding a word of its own, and gathered back to God in Christ.

**Who.** About 580 to 662, monk and confessor (Stage 8). **Feast: 21 January.**

**His works.** The ***Ambigua*** (on difficult passages of Gregory the Theologian and Dionysius), the ***Questions to Thalassius*** (on hard texts of Scripture), the ***Mystagogy*** (on the Church and the Liturgy), the ***Four Hundred Chapters on Love***, a commentary on the Lord's Prayer, and many letters and short works. **Maximus has no public-domain English translation that could be checked**; the passages here are paraphrased, chiefly from the *Ambigua* and the *Mystagogy*.

**The Logos and the logoi.** Maximus's central idea, in paraphrase:

1. **God made all things through his Word, the Logos** (John 1:3).
2. **Each creature has its own *lógos***: its principle, its meaning, its "word", which is God's intention for it, held eternally in the Word. A tree has the *lógos* of a tree; a man the *lógos* of a man.
3. **The many *lógoi* are one Logos.** All the principles of creatures exist in the one Word, as the rays of a circle meet at its centre.
4. **To know creation rightly is to read the *lógoi*** and be led to the Logos. This is **natural contemplation** (*theōría physikḗ*), a stage of the spiritual life (Stage 10).
5. **Sin is to use a thing against its *lógos***. Virtue is to live according to one's own *lógos*.

**The Incarnation and the cosmos.** For Maximus the Incarnation is not only the remedy for sin but **the purpose of creation from the beginning**. God made the world in order to unite it with himself in Christ. He writes, in paraphrase, that the Word of God wills always and in all things to work the mystery of his embodiment.

**Man the mediator.** In *Ambigua* 41 Maximus describes five divisions in creation: **uncreated and created, intelligible and sensible, heaven and earth, paradise and the inhabited world, male and female**. Man was made to unite them all in himself and offer them to God. Adam failed; **Christ, the new man, unites them all**, beginning with the last and ending with the first. **Man is a microcosm and a priest of creation.**

**The Church as an image** (*Mystagogy*). The church building has a sanctuary and a nave, and is one: **so the world has heaven and earth, man has soul and body, Scripture has spirit and letter**, and in each the two are distinct but one. The Liturgy, step by step, is the soul's and the world's journey to God.

**Theosis.** God and man, Maximus says in paraphrase, are **patterns of one another**: as much as God has become man out of love, so much is man deified by grace. **Theosis is the exchange of the Incarnation seen from our side.**

**Why the Orthodox treasure him.** He gathered the whole tradition before him, Gregory, Dionysius, the desert, Chalcedon, into one vision in which **creation, Incarnation, Church, Liturgy and the spiritual life are one movement of love**. Many Orthodox theologians of the twentieth century, Lossky, Florovsky, Stăniloae, Zizioulas, built on him.

**Point across.** The Philosophy curriculum treats the *lógoi*; Stage 12 gives the modern theologians who read him.
St Maximus the Confessor: love and the p:
Maximus the cosmic theologian was also a teacher of monks. His *Chapters on Love* show how the vision of the Logos becomes a way of life.

**The Four Hundred Chapters on Love.** Four "centuries" of short sayings, written for a monk named Elpidios, probably in the 620s or 630s. They are in the *Philokalia*, and the English translation used by most readers (Palmer, Sherrard and Ware) is in copyright, so **everything below is paraphrase**.

**Love as the goal.** Maximus opens by defining love, in paraphrase, as **a good disposition of the soul by which it prefers nothing that exists to the knowledge of God**. Everything else in the spiritual life serves this: faith leads to fear of God, fear to self-control, self-control to patience, patience to hope, hope to detachment, and detachment to love.

**The chain of virtues:**

| Step | Greek | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Faith** | *pístis* | trust in God |
| **Fear of God** | *phóbos* | reverent awe |
| **Self-control** | *enkráteia* | mastery of desire |
| **Patience** | *hypomonḗ* | endurance |
| **Hope** | *elpís* | expectation of God's good things |
| **Dispassion** | *apátheia* | freedom from the passions |
| **Love** | *agápē* | union with God and neighbour |

***Apátheia*** does not mean indifference. **It means freedom from the passions** (*páthē*): the disordered desires and angers that bend the soul away from God. Only the dispassionate can love purely, because only they are not using others for themselves.

**The passions and things.** Maximus's key insight, in paraphrase: **things are not evil; the misuse of them is**. Food, money, reputation, the body are good creations. The passion is a wrong relation to them, wanting them for pleasure or self-love rather than for God. **The root of all passions is *philautía*, self-love**: love of oneself apart from God.

**Love of enemies.** Maximus returns again and again to the hardest commandment. In paraphrase: if you hate anyone, you have not yet reached love; the one who loves God cannot fail to love every man as himself, even those who wrong him. **Perfect love does not divide human nature**, but loves all equally, the good as friends and the wicked as enemies to be loved and prayed for.

**Pure prayer.** The highest state is **prayer without images or thoughts**, in which the mind is wholly given to God. Love and prayer are one at the summit: **the mind wounded by love** goes out to God.

**How this joins the two wills.** Stage 8 gave Maximus's teaching that Christ's human will freely follows the divine. **The *Chapters on Love* are what that looks like in a Christian**: the will, healed in Christ, freed from self-love, brought into accord with God, and made capable of loving all. The theologian of Gethsemane and the teacher of monks are the same man.

**On the Lord's Prayer.** In his commentary on it, Maximus reads each petition as a stage of theosis. "Forgive us as we forgive" is, in paraphrase, **the point where we show God the likeness we ask him to perfect**: in forgiving, we become like the one who forgives.

**Point across.** Stage 10 takes up the passions, the virtues and the *Philokalia* as a whole; the Greek curriculum the words in the table.
St John of Damascus: the Exact Expositio:
The first complete summary of Orthodox doctrine, written in the eighth century, gathers the Fathers before it into a hundred short chapters. It opens with the unknowability of God.

**Who.** About 675 to about 749; monk of St Sabbas, defender of the icons (Stage 8). **Feast: 4 December.**

**The Fount of Knowledge.** John's great work has three parts:

1. **The *Dialectica***: philosophical chapters defining terms such as *ousía*, *phýsis*, *hypóstasis*, *prósōpon*.
2. ***On Heresies***: a list of a hundred heresies.
3. **The *Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith*** (*Ékdosis akribḗs tês orthodóxou písteōs*): a hundred chapters, later divided into four books: God and the Trinity; creation and man; Christ; and the sacraments, the Mother of God, the saints, icons, Scripture and the last things.

John claims no originality. **His aim is to say nothing of his own** but to set out what the Fathers taught: Gregory the Theologian above all, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril, Dionysius and Maximus.

**The text** (*Exact Exposition* Book 1, chapter 1; translated by S. D. F. Salmond, *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 2nd series vol. 9, 1898):

> "No one hath seen God at any time; the Only-begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, He hath declared Him. The Deity, therefore, is ineffable and incomprehensible... God, however, did not leave us in absolute ignorance. For the knowledge of God's existence has been implanted by Him in all by nature... All things, therefore, that have been delivered to us by Law and Prophets and Apostles and Evangelists we receive, and know, and honour, seeking for nothing beyond these... With these things let us be satisfied, and let us abide by them, not removing everlasting boundaries, nor overpassing the divine tradition."

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"No one hath seen God at any time"** | he opens with Scripture (John 1:18): theology begins from revelation |
| **"ineffable and incomprehensible"** | God's essence is beyond speech and understanding: **apophatic theology** |
| **"did not leave us in absolute ignorance"** | yet God is known: by nature, by creation, by the Law and the prophets, and in his Son |
| **"delivered to us by Law and Prophets and Apostles and Evangelists"** | Scripture and the apostolic tradition as the boundary of theology |
| **"seeking for nothing beyond these"** | **no curiosity beyond what God has given**: theology serves salvation |
| **"not removing everlasting boundaries"** | Proverbs 22:28: do not move the ancient landmarks the Fathers set |
| **"nor overpassing the divine tradition"** | theology is faithfulness, not invention |

**The method.** The chapter sets the pattern of Orthodox theology: **God unknowable in himself, known in what he has revealed; and the theologian a guardian, not an innovator**. Compare St Gregory's warning that not everyone may speak of God (lesson 9).

**Its influence.** It became the standard handbook of the Orthodox East. **For a reader who wants the doctrine of the Fathers in one book, this is it.** Salmond's translation is free on New Advent and CCEL.

**Point across.** Stage 2 gives apophatic and cataphatic theology; the Greek curriculum the terms of the *Dialectica*.
St John of Damascus: on the holy images:
In the *Exact Exposition*, John gives his defence of the icons in one short chapter. It sets out the whole argument of the iconophiles in a few paragraphs.

**The setting.** Stage 8 told how John wrote three treatises against the iconoclasts. His chapter "Concerning Images" in the *Exact Exposition* (Book 4, chapter 16) is the summary.

**The text** (*Exact Exposition* Book 4, chapter 16; translated by S. D. F. Salmond, *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 2nd series vol. 9, 1898):

> "But since some find fault with us for worshipping and honouring the image of our Saviour and that of our Lady, and those, too, of the rest of the saints and servants of Christ, let them remember that in the beginning God created man after His own image. On what grounds, then, do we shew reverence to each other unless because we are made after God's image? For as Basil, that much-versed expounder of divine things, says, the honour given to the image passes over to the prototype."

> "But besides this who can make an imitation of the invisible, incorporeal, uncircumscribed, formless God? Therefore to give form to the Deity is the height of folly and impiety. And hence it is that in the Old Testament the use of images was not common. But after God in His bowels of pity became in truth man for our salvation... since all these things actually took place and were seen by men, they were written for the remembrance and instruction of us who were not alive at that time... But seeing that not every one has a knowledge of letters nor time for reading, the Fathers gave their sanction to depicting these events on images..."

**A word on "worshipping".** Salmond's English uses "worshipping" where John's Greek is *proskynoûntes*, "venerating" or "bowing before". In older English "worship" could mean honour of any kind ("your worship" for a magistrate). **John does not mean *latreía***, the worship due to God alone (Stage 8).

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"God created man after His own image"** | the first image is the human being; we already honour God's image in each other |
| **"the honour given to the image passes over to the prototype"** | St Basil's principle (lesson 7), applied to icons |
| **"who can make an imitation of the invisible... God?"** | John agrees with the iconoclasts: **the Godhead cannot be painted** |
| **"in the Old Testament the use of images was not common"** | the prohibition was right for its time, before the Incarnation |
| **"after God... became in truth man"** | the turning point: what became visible can be shown |
| **"seen by men... written for the remembrance"** | Scripture records what was seen; icons do the same in colour |
| **"not every one has a knowledge of letters"** | icons as the book of the unlettered, and a memorial for all |

**Further on** he adds that we bow not to the material but to the one depicted, and that **the apostles handed down much unwritten**, including images.

**Why it is persuasive.** John concedes everything true in the iconoclast case (God's invisibility, the Old Testament command) and shows that **the Incarnation changes the situation**. He does not defend icons in spite of Christology but because of it.

**Point across.** Stage 8 read the Seventh Council's definition; Stage 6 gives icons in the temple and the home.
St Symeon the New Theologian: the experi:
A tenth-century abbot insisted that the grace of the Holy Spirit is not only believed but consciously experienced. The Church calls him the third Theologian.

**Who.** St Symeon (949 to 1022), born in Paphlagonia in Asia Minor to a provincial noble family, educated in Constantinople for a court career. At about fourteen he met his spiritual father, **Symeon the Studite** (called Eulabes, "the Pious"), a monk of the Stoudios monastery. In his twenties, still a layman, he had a vision of divine light. He entered Stoudios about 977, then the monastery of **St Mamas** in Constantinople, where he became abbot about 980 and served some twenty-five years. **Feast: 12 March.**

**The conflict.** Symeon venerated his dead spiritual father as a saint with an icon and a feast, before any official recognition, and taught that only those who have experienced grace should guide others. **Stephen of Nicomedia**, a court theologian, opposed him. Symeon was **exiled in 1009** across the Bosphorus, where he founded a small monastery of St Marina. He was later offered a return, but stayed, and died there on **12 March 1022**. **Why "New Theologian"**: as the third, after John and Gregory, to whom the Church gives the title. Some think "new" was first a mocking name for his innovations; the Church turned it into honour.

**His works.** The *Catecheses* (talks to his monks), the *Ethical Discourses*, the *Theological and Practical Chapters*, and the ***Hymns of Divine Love***, poems of mystical experience. **Modern translations are in copyright; the teaching below is paraphrased.**

**His teaching, in paraphrase:**

1. **Grace is conscious.** The Holy Spirit given in baptism is meant to be **known and felt**, not only believed in. A Christian who has never experienced grace should not be content: he should seek it with tears.
2. **The light.** Symeon describes again and again seeing **the uncreated light**: a light that is God himself, filling him, without form. This prepares Palamas's teaching three centuries later.
3. **Tears and repentance.** He speaks of the "baptism of tears", repentance so deep it renews the grace of baptism. He held that one should not receive Communion without tears of compunction; Orthodox teachers since have weighed this as the counsel of a saint, not a rule.
4. **The spiritual father.** The guide of souls must himself have received the Spirit. Only one who has seen can lead others.
5. **The Eucharist.** In one of his hymns he marvels that **we become members of Christ and Christ becomes our members**, so that even his hand and foot are Christ's.

**Why the Church honours him.** Symeon reminded a Church of beautiful liturgy and sound doctrine that **the point of both is a living encounter with God**. He is not against the institution; he wants its life to be real. **His tension with church authority** is part of his story, and the Church in time sided with him.

**His prayer.** He is the traditional author of one of the **prayers before Holy Communion**, still said by Orthodox Christians preparing to commune. Stage 6 gives the prayers.

**Point across.** Stage 10 takes up spiritual fatherhood and the vision of light; the next two lessons give the theologian who explained what Symeon saw.
St Gregory Palamas: essence and energies:
Stage 8 told the hesychast controversy. This lesson is Palamas's answer to the question: how can a creature truly share in God, if God is beyond all knowing?

**Who.** 1296 to 1359; Athonite monk, archbishop of Thessalonica from 1347. **Feast: 14 November; the Second Sunday of Great Lent.** His works include the ***Triads*** (*In Defence of the Holy Hesychasts*), the ***One Hundred and Fifty Chapters***, and sixty-three homilies. **Modern English translations are in copyright; the teaching here is paraphrased.**

**The problem.** Two truths seem to collide:

| Truth | Source |
| --- | --- |
| **God is unknowable and unshareable** in his essence | Gregory the Theologian, Gregory of Nyssa, Dionysius, John of Damascus (lesson 20) |
| **We truly become "partakers of the divine nature"** (2 Peter 1:4, KJV) and are deified | Irenaeus, Athanasius, Maximus |

Barlaam resolved it by making our share in God a **created** effect: grace as a created gift, the light of Tabor a created symbol. **Palamas held that this would mean we never meet God himself.**

**The distinction.** Palamas, following the Cappadocians and Maximus, distinguished in God, in paraphrase:

| | **Essence** (*ousía*) | **Energies** (*enérgeiai*) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What** | what God is in himself | God in his activity toward creation: his life, light, love, grace, power |
| **Knowable?** | never, by any creature | truly known and shared |
| **Created?** | uncreated | **uncreated**: the energies are God himself, not things he makes |
| **Divided?** | one, simple | many in their effects, yet not dividing God |

**The key claim, in paraphrase: the energies are not a part of God, nor something less than God.** They are **the whole God acting**. When we share in God's energy, we share in God himself, wholly, yet without becoming what God is in essence.

**An image.** The Fathers used the sun: we cannot touch or gaze into the sun itself, but its **rays reach us**, warm us and give light, and the rays are truly the sun's own light, not a created copy. (The image is imperfect, as Palamas knew: God is not divided as a body is.)

**Why it matters:**

1. **Theosis is real.** We do not receive a created substitute for God, but God himself in his energies. **That is what "partakers of the divine nature" means.**
2. **God remains God.** We never become God by essence, never absorbed or merged. The creature remains a creature, deified.
3. **The Trinity is not confused with creation.** The essence is shared only among Father, Son and Spirit; the energies are shared with us. **There is no pantheism and no distance.**
4. **The whole person is deified.** The body too receives grace (next lesson).

**Reception.** The councils of 1341, 1347 and 1351 affirmed this teaching, and the Synodikon of Orthodoxy acclaims it. **It is the Orthodox Church's teaching**, not a school opinion. Orthodox theologians since have written much on how to express it, and Western scholars have long debated it; that debate is a matter for the separate curriculum.

**Point across.** Stage 2 gives the essence-energies distinction as doctrine; the Philosophy curriculum treats it as an argument about divine simplicity.
St Gregory Palamas: the light of Tabor a:
Palamas defended the hesychasts on two points: that the light they saw is God's own uncreated light, and that the body has its place in prayer.

**The Transfiguration.** On Mount Tabor (by tradition) Christ "was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light" (Matthew 17:2, King James Version, 1611). **The feast of the Transfiguration, 6 August**, is one of the twelve great feasts.

**What the light was.** Barlaam said: a created light, a symbol, visible to bodily eyes and passing away. Palamas answered, in paraphrase:

| Palamas's claim | His reason |
| --- | --- |
| **The light of Tabor is uncreated** | it is the glory of God, which Christ had "before the world was" (John 17:5, KJV); it is his divinity shining through his body |
| **It did not begin on Tabor** | Christ did not change; **the apostles' eyes were opened** to see what was always there |
| **It is seen by eyes transformed by the Spirit** | not by natural sight alone, nor by the mind alone, but by the whole person made capable by grace |
| **It is the same light the saints see** | the hesychasts who see light in prayer see this light |
| **It is the light of the age to come** | the righteous "shine forth as the sun in the kingdom" (Matthew 13:43, KJV) |

The troparion of the feast, in Hapgood's *Service Book* (1906), says Christ was "revealing unto thy disciples thy glory in so far as they were able to bear it", and asks: "Let thy light everlasting illumine us sinners also." Palamas reads the feast through those lines.

**The body in prayer.** Barlaam mocked the hesychasts as *omphalopsychoi*, "navel-souled", because some taught a posture: head bowed, eyes toward the chest, breath slowed, mind "brought down into the heart". Palamas answered, in paraphrase:

1. **The body is not evil.** It is God's creation and the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19).
2. **The mind is scattered outward** by the senses. Bodily stillness helps gather it back. **The methods are aids, especially for beginners**, not magic and not the goal.
3. **The heart is the centre of the person.** Scripture and the Fathers place the mind's true seat in the heart. Bringing the mind into the heart is the return of the person to itself and to God.
4. **The body shares in deification.** In the saints, grace overflows from soul to body; their faces shine (as with Moses), their relics are holy. **The whole person, soul and body, is meant for theosis.**

**The Jesus Prayer.** The hesychasts prayed "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me" unceasingly, joined with the breath. **Stage 10 teaches it as a way of prayer.** Palamas's role was to show that this practice is theology lived.

**Why the Church calls his victory her own.** The Second Sunday of Lent, following the Sunday of Orthodoxy, is his: **after the icons comes the light**. The first Sunday celebrates God made visible in Christ's face; the second celebrates that this same God gives himself to be seen and shared by those who pray. **The Triumph of Orthodoxy is completed in the vision of God.**

**Point across.** Stage 6 gives the feast of the Transfiguration; Stage 10 the Jesus Prayer and the heart; the Philosophy curriculum the body and knowledge.
Where the Fathers differ: theologoumena,:
The Fathers agree on the faith of the councils. On some questions they do not agree, and the Church has kept room for that. This lesson shows how she handles it.

**The consensus.** Stage 1 introduced the **consensus of the Fathers** (*consensus patrum*). St Vincent of Lérins (died about 445; feast 24 May) gave the classic rule (*Commonitory* 2.6; translated by C. A. Heurtley, *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 2nd series vol. 11, 1894):

> "...in the Catholic Church itself, all possible care must be taken, that we hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all... This rule we shall observe if we follow universality, antiquity, consent."

**Three levels**, in a distinction made by the Russian church historian **Vasily Bolotov** (1854 to 1900) and widely used since:

| Level | What it is | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dogma** (*dógma*) | the faith of the Church, defined by councils or universally held | the Trinity; the two natures; the icons |
| **Theologoumenon** (*theologoúmenon*) | the opinion of a Father, or of several, which the Church allows but does not require | some details of the angels' orders; how souls fare between death and judgement |
| **Private opinion** | a view of one writer, not received | a lone speculation |

**One Father's error does not unmake him.** The Fathers themselves said so. St Photios, defending Latin Fathers who had written of the Spirit proceeding from the Son, held, in paraphrase, that **one should cover a father's mistake in silence, as Shem and Japheth covered Noah**, and not make it a doctrine.

**Three cases where Orthodox judgement has differed:**

**1. Origen.** A teacher of the Fathers, condemned in the sixth century (Stage 7): **his method of reading Scripture received, his speculative system rejected.**

**2. St Gregory of Nyssa and the restoration of all.** Gregory hoped that in the end all, even the wicked, would be purified and restored to God (*apokatástasis*). Orthodox responses, each in its strongest form:

| View | Its case |
| --- | --- |
| **His hope was an error, which the Church corrected** | the sixth-century condemnations reject the restoration of all; the Church's services speak of eternal judgement |
| **His view was not condemned** | the anathemas of 553 target Origenist teachings about pre-existent souls, not Gregory, whom the Seventh Council honoured; a hope that all may be saved is a theologoumenon |
| **His texts were altered** | St Germanos of Constantinople (8th century) claimed Origenists had inserted these passages |

**3. Blessed Augustine.** Augustine of Hippo (354 to 430) is in the Orthodox calendar (15 June in many calendars, as "Blessed"). His *Confessions* begin (translated by J. G. Pilkington, *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* 1st series vol. 1, 1886): "Thou hast formed us for Thyself, and our hearts are restless till they find rest in Thee." Orthodox views:

| View | Its case |
| --- | --- |
| **A Father of the Church with errors** | holy, Orthodox in his love of God and the Church; his errors on grace and the Trinity were the West's emphasis, not the whole of him (Fr Seraphim Rose, *The Place of Blessed Augustine in the Orthodox Church*) |
| **A teacher whose influence must be treated with great caution** | his theology of original guilt, predestination and the Trinity shaped the Western divergence; he is a saint, but not a guide to follow on those points (Fr John Romanides and others) |

**What would settle each.** For Gregory, a conciliar judgement naming him, which has not been made. For Augustine, the Church's reception has already placed him in the calendar; the question is how far to follow him, and that is left to theologians.

**Point across.** Stage 1 gave the consensus; Stage 4 the last things; the Philosophy curriculum treats Augustine at length.
Looking back: the Fathers in their own w:
This stage has read twelve Fathers and more, from the second century to the fourteenth. They speak with many voices and one faith.

**The Fathers of this stage, at a glance:**

| Father | Dates | His word to remember |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **St Ignatius of Antioch** | died about 107 | the Eucharist, "the medicine of immortality" |
| **St Irenaeus of Lyons** | about 130 to about 202 | "become what we are"; "the glory of God is a living man" |
| **St Athanasius** | about 296 to 373 | "He was made man that we might be made God" |
| **St Basil the Great** | about 330 to 379 | "the honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype" |
| **St Gregory the Theologian** | about 329 to about 390 | "that which He has not assumed He has not healed" |
| **St Gregory of Nyssa** | about 335 to about 395 | *epéktasis*, the endless ascent |
| **St Ephrem the Syrian** | about 306 to 373 | theology sung in symbols |
| **St John Chrysostom** | about 349 to 407 | Christ in the altar and Christ in the poor; the Paschal Homily |
| **St Cyril of Alexandria** | bishop 412 to 444 | the one Christ; Mary Theotokos |
| **Dionysius the Areopagite** | the writings about 500 | the divine darkness; the hierarchies of light |
| **St Maximus the Confessor** | about 580 to 662 | the *lógoi*; love; the two wills |
| **St John of Damascus** | about 675 to about 749 | the *Exact Exposition*; the icon |
| **St Symeon the New Theologian** | 949 to 1022 | grace consciously experienced |
| **St Gregory Palamas** | 1296 to 1359 | essence and energies; the light of Tabor |

**What they share:**

1. **One subject: Christ, and what he does for us.** Every Father is finally explaining the Incarnation and theosis.
2. **Theology from prayer.** Gregory's purified theologian, Ephrem's hymns, Symeon's tears, Palamas's hesychasts: **none of them separates thinking about God from praying to him**.
3. **Fidelity, not novelty.** John of Damascus's "not removing everlasting boundaries" speaks for all of them. Even their boldest ideas are offered as the Church's faith, explained.
4. **The body matters.** Ignatius's real flesh, Irenaeus's resurrection, Athanasius's restored image, John's icons, Palamas's body in prayer: **the Fathers never despise the material world**.
5. **Endless growth.** From Irenaeus's "something towards which he might advance" to Gregory of Nyssa's *epektasis* and Maximus's deification: **the creature is made to grow into God for ever**.

**How they differ.** In language (Greek, Syriac), method (Antiochene, Alexandrian), temperament (Chrysostom's sermons, Maximus's density), and on some questions the Church leaves open (lesson 25). **The consensus is in the faith, not in uniformity.**

**How to go on reading.** Start with **Athanasius, *On the Incarnation***, short and clear; then **Chrysostom's homilies** on a Gospel; then **Gregory's Theological Orations**; then **John of Damascus's *Exact Exposition*** as a reference. All are free in the *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers*. Maximus, Symeon and Palamas are best read in modern translations, in print.

**Where this goes next.** Stage 10 turns from reading the Fathers to living their teaching: prayer, the Jesus Prayer, the passions and the virtues, the *Philokalia*, and the monastic life.
Context: the spiritual life as the Creed:
The first nine stages set out what the Church believes, how she prays and where her teaching came from. This stage is about what all of it is for: a human life changed by God.

**The spiritual life is not a department of Christianity. It is the Creed lived.** The Orthodox word "spiritual" (Greek *pneumatikos*, πνευματικός) does not mean inward as opposed to bodily, or private as opposed to churchly. It means **of the Holy Spirit** (*Pneuma*, Πνεῦμα). A spiritual life is a life in which the Holy Spirit, given in baptism and chrismation, becomes active and is no longer buried under sin. Body and soul, prayer and work, church and home are all its ground.

**The goal has already been named.** Stage 3 called it *theosis* (θέωσις): union with God by grace, sharing in His uncreated energies without becoming God by nature. Stage 2 gave the distinction between God's essence and His energies that makes this possible. This stage is the practical side of the same teaching: the road by which a baptised person actually walks towards that union.

**How the road is described.** The Fathers often divide it into three, without ever making the stages watertight:

| Stage | Greek | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Purification** | *katharsis* (κάθαρσις) | repentance, struggle with the passions, keeping the commandments |
| **Illumination** | *phōtismos* (φωτισμός) | the mind and heart cleared enough to see God in His works and to pray with attention |
| **Union, or deification** | *theōsis* (θέωσις) | the vision of God's uncreated light, given as a gift, not earned |

**Three things to hold from the start.**

1. **It is the life of the Church, not a technique.** Prayer, fasting and watchfulness are done inside the sacraments, under the guidance of a confessor, within the calendar of feasts and fasts in Stage 6. Without that frame the same practices become self-improvement or worse.
2. **It is for everyone.** Monks and nuns live it with fewer distractions, but the commandments, the Jesus Prayer and the Philokalia are not reserved to them. Several lessons here deal with life in the world.
3. **It is grace and effort together.** The Greek word is *synergeia* (συνέργεια), co-working. God gives everything; a person must still consent and labour, and the labour itself is helped by grace.

**What this stage covers.** Prayer and the Jesus Prayer; hesychasm; the *nous* and the heart; how thoughts become sins; the passions and the virtues; fasting, almsgiving and repentance; confession; spiritual fathers and elders; delusion; the Philokalia and the Ladder; monasticism and Mount Athos; and the spiritual life of lay people.

**Where it points across.** The Philosophy curriculum treats Evagrius, Maximus and Palamas as thinkers with arguments about the mind and the will. Here they are teachers of a way of life. The Greek curriculum covers the words, many of which have no exact English equivalent.
The aim of the Christian life: acquiring:
Before the methods, the aim. Orthodox teachers insist that the means must never be confused with the end.

**St Seraphim of Sarov** (born 1754 or 1759, died 1833) was a monk of the Sarov monastery in central Russia: novice, hermit in the forest for years, a thousand nights of prayer on a stone, then a recluse, and in his last years a spiritual father receiving crowds. He greeted everyone, in every season, with the Paschal greeting, "Christ is risen", and called visitors "my joy". He was glorified as a saint in 1903 and is commemorated on 2 January (with a second feast for the uncovering of his relics on 19 July).

**The conversation with Motovilov.** In November 1831 a landowner named Nicholas Motovilov asked him what the aim of the Christian life is. The account Motovilov wrote down was found and published in 1903. **In paraphrase**, Seraphim answered:

- Prayer, fasting, vigils, almsgiving and every other good work are good, but **they are not the aim**. They are the **means**.
- **The true aim of the Christian life is the acquisition of the Holy Spirit of God.**
- Only a good deed done **for Christ's sake** brings the fruit of the Spirit. Good done merely for the sake of goodness earns praise but not that grace.
- He compared it to trade: as a merchant wants to make capital, so a Christian should "trade" in the virtues that bring the most grace. For one person that is prayer, for another almsgiving or vigil.

He then prayed, and Motovilov reported seeing the saint's face shining brighter than the snow around them on a winter day, and feeling peace, warmth, sweetness and joy. Seraphim told him this was the Holy Spirit's presence, given to both of them so that the teaching would be believed.

**Why this matters for the whole stage.** Everything that follows is a means. **A fast kept for pride, or a prayer rule kept to feel superior, has missed the point.** The Fathers measure progress not by the quantity of the practices but by their fruit: humility, love, peace and freedom from the passions.

**Seraphim and theosis.** His teaching is the practical form of the doctrine in Stage 3. The Spirit given in chrismation, sealed on the newly baptised as a gift, is not a possession to be stored but a life to be uncovered. Sin covers it; repentance and the commandments uncover it.

**A saying often attributed to him** puts the social side: acquire a peaceful spirit, and thousands around you will be saved. **This is a paraphrase of an oral tradition, not a quotation from his written instructions**, but it captures the Orthodox conviction that inner change is the root of any real change around a person.

**Seraphim's place.** He belongs to the revival of prayer that came to Russia from the Philokalia and the disciples of St Paisius Velichkovsky, the subject of a later lesson. He shows that the hesychast tradition was not only for Athos.
What prayer is, and its three kinds:
Prayer is the centre of the spiritual life. The Fathers define it not first as asking for things but as **communion with God**: standing before Him with the mind and the heart.

**A working definition.** St John Climacus calls prayer converse and union with God. St Theophan the Recluse, a nineteenth-century Russian bishop, taught that the essential thing in prayer is to stand before God with the mind in the heart, and to go on standing before Him day and night. **Words are a help to this, not the substance of it.** (Both are paraphrases.)

**What prayer contains.** Orthodox prayer books and services move through all of these:

| Kind | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Praise and glorification** (*doxologia*, δοξολογία) | adores God for who He is | the Great Doxology at Matins |
| **Thanksgiving** (*eucharistia*, εὐχαριστία) | thanks Him for what He has done | the Anaphora of the Liturgy |
| **Repentance** | confesses sin and asks mercy | Psalm 50 (51), the Prayer of St Ephrem in Lent |
| **Petition** | asks for oneself | "Lord, have mercy" |
| **Intercession** | asks for others, living and departed | the litanies, the commemorations at the Proskomedia |

**The three settings of prayer.**

1. **Common or liturgical prayer.** The Divine Liturgy, Vespers, Matins and the Hours, taught in Stage 6. This is the prayer of the Church as a body, and it is primary: the personal prayer of an Orthodox Christian grows out of it and is shaped by its words.
2. **The rule of prayer.** Set prayers said daily at home, morning and evening, from the prayer book. The next lesson covers it.
3. **Inner or unceasing prayer.** Short prayer carried through the whole day, above all the Jesus Prayer. Its aim is the command of the Apostle Paul in 1 Thessalonians 5:17 (King James Version): **"Pray without ceasing."**

**These are not rivals.** The services teach the words and the theology of prayer; the rule disciplines it; the Jesus Prayer carries it into everything else. A person who prays only in church, or only alone, is missing a part.

**Christ's own teaching.** In the Sermon on the Mount He says (Matthew 6:6, KJV): **"But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly."** The Fathers read "the closet" both literally, as a quiet room, and inwardly, as the heart, into which the mind withdraws in prayer.

**Attention.** The Fathers agree that the quality of prayer is attention (*prosochē*, προσοχή). Saying many words with a wandering mind is not yet prayer. The cure is not to pray less but to bring the mind back, again and again, to the words. **Wandering is normal; consenting to it is the fault.**

**Prayer and the body.** Orthodox prayer uses the body: standing, the sign of the cross, bows and prostrations (*metanoiai*, μετάνοιαι), lit lamps, icons. The body is not an obstacle to prayer but its partner, because the human being is one.
The rule of prayer and the icon corner:
The daily rule is the steady, unspectacular backbone of the spiritual life. Most Orthodox Christians will spend far more of their lives on it than on any other practice.

**The rule** (Greek *kanōn*, κανών; Slavonic *pravilo*, правило) is a fixed amount of prayer said every day, usually morning and evening. It is **set with a confessor** and fitted to a person's life: a mother of small children, a soldier, a student and a monk do not have the same rule.

**What a typical rule contains.** Orthodox prayer books in every tradition have a similar shape:

| Morning | Evening |
| --- | --- |
| the **Trisagion prayers**: "O Heavenly King", "Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal", "Most Holy Trinity", the Lord's Prayer | the same opening |
| prayers on rising, many attributed to St Basil and St Macarius | prayers before sleep, including a prayer to one's guardian angel |
| the **Creed** | an examination of the day and confession of its sins before God |
| intercessions for family, the living and the departed | Psalm 50 (51) and prayers to the Theotokos |
| a reading from Scripture, often the day's lectionary | the Jesus Prayer, sometimes with a set number on a prayer rope |

**The prayer rope** (Greek *komboskini*, κομποσκοίνι; Slavonic *chotki*, чётки) is a cord of knotted wool, often of 33, 50, 100 or more knots, each knot tied in a pattern of crosses. It is used to count Jesus Prayers or prostrations. It is given to monks at their tonsure, but lay people use it too.

**The icon corner.** In an Orthodox home there is a place for prayer, traditionally on the eastern wall, with icons of Christ and the Theotokos, the family's patron saints, a lamp (*kandili*, καντήλι; Slavonic *lampada*), the Gospel, holy water and blessed palms or willows. **It makes the home a small church**, and it is where the family prays together.

**Three rules for the rule, from the spiritual fathers.**

1. **Keep it small enough to keep.** St Theophan the Recluse advised that a short rule kept with attention is better than a long one rushed. Better ten minutes faithfully than an hour once a month.
2. **Do not drop it for feelings.** Prayer said dryly, without consolation, is not wasted. Many teachers say it is the prayer God most values, because it is given without reward.
3. **Change it only with blessing.** Adding a heavy rule by oneself is a common road to pride and then collapse. That is why the rule is agreed with a confessor.

**Before and after Communion.** Before receiving the Mysteries there are preparatory prayers, a canon and the Prayers before Communion; after, the Prayers of Thanksgiving. Practice varies: in the Russian tradition the preparation commonly includes several canons and a fast from the night before; in Greek practice the preparation is often lighter and Communion more frequent. Both aim at the same thing: receiving with fear of God, faith and love.

**The rule and the Liturgy.** The rule does not replace the services. On Sundays and feasts the Church's own prayer comes first, and the rule is shaped around it.
The Jesus Prayer: its words and its root:
The best-known Orthodox prayer outside the services is a single sentence. Its power is that it can be said anywhere, at any pace, by anyone.

**The words.** The usual full form is: **Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.** Shorter forms are used too: "Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me", or simply "Lord, have mercy". Some add "through the prayers of the Theotokos" or pray it for others: "have mercy on us", "have mercy on Thy servant N."

**It is the Gospel in one breath.** Each phrase carries doctrine:

| Phrase | What it confesses |
| --- | --- |
| **Lord** | Jesus is God (the Greek *Kyrios*, Κύριος, is the Septuagint's word for God's own name) |
| **Jesus** | the Incarnation: the human name, meaning "the Lord saves" |
| **Christ** | the Anointed, the Messiah promised in the Old Testament |
| **Son of God** | the Trinity: He is the eternal Son of the Father |
| **have mercy** | the whole of salvation: forgiveness, healing, life (*eleison*, ἐλέησον; *eleos* is mercy) |
| **on me, a sinner** | repentance: the one praying stands as the publican |

**Its roots in Scripture.**
- The publican in the temple (Luke 18:13, KJV): **"God be merciful to me a sinner."**
- Blind Bartimaeus at Jericho (Luke 18:38, KJV): **"Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me."**
- The Apostles' teaching on **the Name of Jesus**, at which every knee shall bow (Philippians 2:10), and by which alone we are saved (Acts 4:12).
- St Stephen's last words (Acts 7:59, KJV): **"Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."**

**Its roots in the desert.** The monks of fourth- and fifth-century Egypt practised the *monologistos* prayer (μονολόγιστος), a prayer of one phrase repeated through the day's work. St John Cassian, who visited them, recorded the verse they taught (Psalm 69 (70):1, in the translation of C. S. Gibson, NPNF, 1894): **"O God, make speed to save me: O Lord, make haste to help me."** In the fifth century St Diadochos of Photiki taught that the remembrance of the Lord Jesus keeps the mind from wandering. Over the following centuries, in Sinai and then on Athos, the prayer settled on the Name of Jesus and the form above.

**Why the Name?** In the Bible a name is not a label but the presence of the person. To call on the Name of Jesus is to call on Jesus Himself. **The prayer is not a magic formula: it works only as faith, repentance and love call on a Person who answers.**

**How it is said.** Slowly, attentively, without imagining pictures (the Fathers warn against forming images of Christ in the mind during this prayer), often with a prayer rope, sometimes joined to the breath. It can be said aloud, in a whisper or silently. In time, by grace, it may become self-acting, continuing in the heart even during sleep. The next lesson shows this in one famous Russian book.

**For whom.** The Prayer is open to all baptised Orthodox Christians. The Fathers add one caution: a large number of prayers, or the bodily method of the next lessons, should be undertaken with a confessor's blessing.
Reading: The Way of a Pilgrim on unceasi:
A nineteenth-century Russian book, written in the first person by an anonymous wanderer, did more than any other to make the Jesus Prayer known outside monasteries.

**The book.** Its Russian title means "Candid Narratives of a Pilgrim to His Spiritual Father". It was printed at Kazan in 1884 from a copy found on Mount Athos. Who wrote it is unknown. The English text below is the translation by **R. M. French** (first published 1930; quoted from the Philip Allan edition of 1931, as given on the Christian Classics Ethereal Library, which lists it as public domain).

**The opening.**

> "By the grace of God I am a Christian man, by my actions a great sinner, and by calling a homeless wanderer of the humblest birth who roams from place to place. My worldly goods are a knapsack with some dried bread in it on my back, and in my breast pocket a Bible. And that is all."

He hears 1 Thessalonians 5:17, "Pray without ceasing", read at the Liturgy, and cannot rest until he knows how it can be done. Preachers explain why prayer matters but not how. At last he meets a *starets*, an elder, who teaches him.

**The elder's definition.**

> "The continuous interior Prayer of Jesus is a constant uninterrupted calling upon the divine Name of Jesus with the lips, in the spirit, in the heart; while forming a mental picture of his constant presence, and imploring His grace, during every occupation, at all times, in all places, even during sleep."

**The first rule he is given.**

> "Here is a rosary. Take it, and to start with say the Prayer three thousand times a day. Whether you are standing or sitting, walking or lying down, continually repeat 'Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.' Say it quietly and without hurry, but without fail exactly three thousand times a day without deliberately increasing or diminishing the number."

**Read it phrase by phrase.**

| Phrase | What it teaches |
| --- | --- |
| **"by my actions a great sinner"** | the Pilgrim begins as the publican; the Prayer is born in repentance |
| **"in my breast pocket a Bible"** | the Prayer grows out of Scripture, and he reads it constantly |
| **"with the lips, in the spirit, in the heart"** | the three levels of the Prayer: oral, of the mind, and of the heart |
| **"during every occupation"** | unceasing prayer does not mean ceasing to work; it accompanies work |
| **"rosary"** | French's word for the *chotki*, the prayer rope |
| **"without deliberately increasing or diminishing the number"** | **obedience**: the number is set by the elder, not by the Pilgrim's enthusiasm |

**What happens next.** The number rises to six and then twelve thousand a day. After some weeks the Prayer begins to say itself; he describes warmth in the heart and joy, and later walks across Siberia with the Philokalia in his knapsack, meeting people of every kind.

**How to read it well.**
- **Notice the elder.** The Pilgrim is told to "come back to him and tell him everything", because, as the book says, the inward process cannot go on properly without a teacher. The book does not teach solitary experiment.
- **Notice the Philokalia.** The elder reads him St Symeon, St Gregory of Sinai and others: the book is a doorway to the patristic texts, not a replacement for them.
- **Notice the warnings it does not dwell on.** Later Russian teachers, such as St Ignatius Brianchaninov, cautioned that the bodily method and large numbers are not for everyone without guidance. The Pilgrim's path was blessed for him.

**Its influence.** French's translation made the Jesus Prayer known across the English-speaking world in the twentieth century, among Orthodox and non-Orthodox alike.
Hesychasm: stillness and the prayer of t:
Stage 8 told the history of the hesychast controversy and St Gregory Palamas. This lesson is about the practice the councils defended.

**The word.** *Hesychia* (ἡσυχία) is **stillness, quiet, inner silence**. A *hesychast* (ἡσυχαστής) is one who seeks it. Hesychasm is the tradition of prayer, centred on the Jesus Prayer, that aims at the quieting of the whole person before God, so that the mind can return into the heart and be united with God in prayer.

**Stillness of three kinds.**

| Kind | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **outward** | withdrawal from noise and business: a cell, a quiet room, a fixed time |
| **of the tongue** | guarding speech; Climacus calls silence the mother of prayer |
| **inner** | the stilling of thoughts, so that the mind is no longer scattered by images and passions |

**The psychosomatic method.** From about the thirteenth century, writers such as **Nikephoros the Hesychast** and **St Gregory of Sinai** (died 1346) described a bodily aid to the Jesus Prayer:

1. Sit on a low stool, head bowed, eyes turned towards the chest or heart.
2. Slow the breathing, and say the Prayer in time with it.
3. Seek the place of the heart with the attention, drawing the mind inward.
4. Persist with patience, putting aside every thought.

**The method is an aid, not the prayer.** Every hesychast teacher says so. Its purpose is to help the attention gather; grace, not technique, unites the mind with God. **Many teachers advise against using the breathing method without an experienced guide**, because it can cause physical or psychological harm and can feed delusion.

**What the councils defended.** When Barlaam of Calabria mocked the method and denied that the light seen by the saints could be God's own, St Gregory Palamas answered in his *Triads* (about 1338–1341), and councils in Constantinople in 1341, 1347 and 1351 upheld his teaching:

- The body takes part in prayer, because the whole person, body and soul, is redeemed.
- The light seen by the saints is **the uncreated light of Tabor**, the energy of God, not a created symbol.
- God is unknowable in His essence but truly known and shared in His energies.

**The goal.** Hesychasm does not seek experiences. It seeks **God**, and through repentance a heart purified enough to see Him. "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God" (Matthew 5:8, KJV) is its text. The Fathers say that visions and warmth, if they come, should not be sought or clung to.

**Hesychasm in the whole Church.** Though born among monks, it was never only monastic. Palamas himself preached the Jesus Prayer to lay people as Archbishop of Thessalonica. The Philokalia, the Russian elders and the twentieth-century Athonite revival all carried it into parishes.

**Where to read more.** Stage 9 read Palamas in his own words; the Philosophy curriculum treats the essence–energies distinction as an argument about God and knowledge.
The nous and the heart:
The Fathers' map of the human person is different from the modern one. Without it, much of the Philokalia is misread.

**Nous** (νοῦς) is usually translated "mind" or "intellect", but in the ascetic Fathers it means **the highest faculty of the soul, the eye of the soul, by which a person can know God directly**, not by reasoning but by a kind of spiritual sight. It is made for communion with God.

**Dianoia** (διάνοια) is **discursive reason**: the faculty that thinks step by step, argues, calculates and forms concepts. It is good and necessary, but it is not the organ by which God is known.

**Kardia** (καρδία), **the heart**, is in Scripture and the Fathers **the centre of the whole person**: not only feeling, but the deep place where will, knowledge and love meet. "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life" (Proverbs 4:23, KJV). St Macarius's homilies teach that the heart is a small vessel, yet in it are dragons and lions, and in it also God, the angels, life and the kingdom (paraphrase).

| Term | Greek | Ordinary translation | What it means in the Fathers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **nous** | νοῦς | mind, intellect | the spiritual eye; the capacity for direct knowledge of God |
| **dianoia** | διάνοια | reason, understanding | thinking in concepts and steps |
| **kardia** | καρδία | heart | the centre of the person, where the nous is meant to dwell |
| **psyche** | ψυχή | soul | the whole life-principle of the person |
| **logismos** | λογισμός | thought | a thought, often a tempting one, arising in the mind |

**What went wrong.** In the fall, the Fathers teach, **the nous was darkened and scattered**. Instead of resting in God in the heart, it is dispersed outward through the senses into things, images and passions, and identified with the endless chatter of thoughts. This is not only a moral fault but a sickness of the whole person.

**What prayer does.** The aim of hesychast prayer is **the return of the nous into the heart**: the mind, gathered from its scattering, descends into the heart and stands there before God, praying. Theophan the Recluse's phrase for it is *the mind in the heart*. This is what the Pilgrim meant by prayer "in the heart". It is the beginning of illumination.

**Why the distinction matters.**
- **It is not anti-intellectual.** The Fathers were often brilliant thinkers. They say only that reasoning about God and knowing God are different, and that the second is given to the pure in heart.
- **It explains Orthodox theology as prayer.** Stage 1's saying that a theologian is one who prays truly rests on this map: real theology is the nous's vision put into words, not only the dianoia's deductions.
- **It explains healing language.** Many modern Orthodox writers, such as Fr John Romanides and Metropolitan Hierotheos Vlachos, describe the Church as a hospital and the spiritual life as therapy of the nous. Others think this language, if pressed too far, narrows the sacramental and communal life to an individual cure. Both hold the patristic map.

**The Greek curriculum** covers these words; note that **"nous" in Plato and Aristotle** (in the Philosophy curriculum) is related but not identical to the ascetic sense here.
Watchfulness: nepsis and the guarding of:
The Philokalia's full title calls its authors "the holy **neptic** Fathers". Watchfulness is the virtue that names the whole collection.

**Nepsis** (νῆψις) means **sobriety, wakefulness, watchfulness**: the opposite of being drunk or asleep. The Fathers take it from Scripture: "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour" (1 Peter 5:8, KJV). In the spiritual life it is **constant attention to one's thoughts**, so that nothing enters the heart unnoticed.

**St Hesychios the Priest**, a writer of uncertain date (somewhere between the sixth and ninth centuries) whose treatise stands among the early texts of the Philokalia, defines watchfulness, in paraphrase, as **a spiritual method which, if practised over a long time, frees a person from passionate thoughts and words and evil deeds**, and leads to the knowledge of God.

**The guarding of the heart.** The Fathers picture the heart as a house and the mind as its doorkeeper. Thoughts knock; the watchful mind looks at each one before it enters. A related image: the mind as a sentry on a wall, seeing an enemy far off.

**The methods of watchfulness, as Hesychios and others give them.**

| Method | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **attention** (*prosochē*) | constantly observing the thoughts, especially at their first appearance |
| **refutation** (*antirrhēsis*) | answering a tempting thought, often with a verse of Scripture, as Christ answered the devil in the desert |
| **calling on Jesus** | turning at once to the Jesus Prayer, rather than arguing |
| **remembrance of death** | holding one's death before the eyes, which sobers the mind |
| **stillness and silence** | removing distractions that feed the thoughts |

**Arguing or calling?** The Fathers give two strategies for a tempting thought. Beginners may answer it with Scripture, as the desert monks did. But many teachers, especially the hesychasts, say that **arguing with a thought keeps it alive**; better to turn away from it at once and cry to Christ. Both are traditional; which suits a person is a question for a spiritual father.

**Remembrance of death.** Step 6 of the Ladder is devoted to it. It is not morbid: it frees a person from the illusion of endless time, from avarice, from grudges. Monks keep a skull or a grave in view; lay people meet it in the funeral services and the memorial Saturdays.

**Watchfulness in the world.** The Fathers did not imagine it only for monks. Every Christian guards what he looks at, what he listens to, what he lets himself dwell on. **A modern application is plain: the screen is a door to the heart.** Many contemporary confessors give advice on this, in the spirit of the neptic Fathers.

**The fruit.** Long watchfulness, the Fathers say, brings stillness of heart, the beginning of pure prayer and, by grace, the perception of God's presence. It is the soil in which the Jesus Prayer grows.
How a thought becomes a sin: the stages:
The Fathers analysed temptation with great precision. Their analysis shows **where** the struggle is won or lost, and it removes much false guilt.

**A thought** (*logismos*, λογισμός, plural *logismoi*) in the ascetic sense is not any idea but **a suggestion, an image or an impulse that arises in the mind**, often bringing a passion with it. Thoughts come from three sources, the Fathers teach: from ourselves, from the demons, and from God and the angels. Discernment tells them apart.

**The stages.** St John Climacus (Step 15 of the Ladder) and St Mark the Ascetic, among others, give a sequence. Different Fathers number it slightly differently; this is the common form:

| Stage | Greek | What happens | Is it a sin? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Provocation** (assault) | *prosbolē* (προσβολή) | a thought or image simply appears | **No.** It is not in our power to stop it arising |
| **2. Coupling** (interaction) | *syndyasmos* (συνδυασμός) | the mind begins to converse with the thought, to entertain it | the beginning of fault, though not yet full sin |
| **3. Struggle** | *palē* (πάλη) | the mind fights the thought, or fails to | a struggle that can be won for a crown |
| **4. Assent** | *synkatathesis* (συγκατάθεσις) | the will agrees to the thought and takes pleasure in it | **yes**, a sin in the heart, even if not acted on |
| **5. Captivity** | *aichmalōsia* (αἰχμαλωσία) | the heart is dragged along by the thought against its better will | the result of repeated assent |
| **6. Passion** | *pathos* (πάθος) | a settled disposition, a habit, which now produces the thought easily | a sickness needing long healing |

The deed itself, if it follows, is the outward completion of what was already decided at assent.

**Three consequences the Fathers draw.**

1. **The first thought is not a sin.** Christ Himself was tempted in the desert. A person troubled by a sudden ugly thought has not sinned by its arising. This is a great comfort, and confessors repeat it constantly.
2. **The battle is cheapest at the beginning.** It is easiest to dismiss a thought at provocation, harder after coupling, very hard after assent. That is why watchfulness, the previous lesson, attends to the first appearance.
3. **The passions are made by repetition.** Each assent makes the next easier; each refusal weakens the passion. **Habits are formed thought by thought, and are unmade the same way.**

**How this fits Scripture.** "But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death" (James 1:14–15, KJV). The Fathers' stages are a close reading of James's sequence.

**And confession.** When an Orthodox Christian prepares for confession, the Fathers' analysis guides what is confessed: not every passing thought, but the thoughts entertained and assented to, the deeds, and the passions that lie behind them. Monks practise the "revelation of thoughts" to their elder, the subject of a later lesson.
The passions and the eight evil thoughts:
The Fathers speak of **passions** where a modern person might speak of vices or addictions. The idea is central to the whole ascetic tradition.

**Pathos** (πάθος) literally means **something suffered**, an affliction. In the ascetic Fathers a passion is **a distorted movement of the soul**: a natural power (desire, anger, the wish for honour) turned away from God and towards something that enslaves. **The passions are not the natural powers themselves.** Desire and anger were made good; their sickness is the passion.

**The eight thoughts.** **Evagrius of Pontus** (345–399), a monk of the Egyptian desert, set out a list of eight principal evil thoughts. St John Cassian (about 360–435) carried the list to the West, where it later became the seven deadly sins. In the East it was kept, with variations, by Climacus, Nilus, Gregory of Sinai and the Philokalia.

| | Greek | English | Its object |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | *gastrimargia* (γαστριμαργία) | gluttony | food and drink |
| 2 | *porneia* (πορνεία) | lust, unchastity | the body |
| 3 | *philargyria* (φιλαργυρία) | avarice, love of money | possessions |
| 4 | *lypē* (λύπη) | dejection, worldly sorrow | frustrated desires |
| 5 | *orgē* (ὀργή) | anger | injuries, real or imagined |
| 6 | *akēdia* (ἀκηδία) | listlessness, despondency | the boredom and restlessness that make prayer and work hateful; the "noonday demon" of the desert writers |
| 7 | *kenodoxia* (κενοδοξία) | vainglory | the praise of others |
| 8 | *hyperēphania* (ὑπερηφανία) | pride | oneself, as if one's good were one's own |

**A note on Evagrius.** Some of Evagrius's speculative teaching, which followed Origen, was condemned in the sixth century, and the Church does not commemorate him as a saint. **His ascetic teaching, however, passed into the whole tradition**, often under the names of others, and the Philokalia includes it. The Church kept what was sound.

**How the passions connect.** The list runs from the bodily to the spiritual, and the Fathers say they are linked like a chain: gluttony opens the way to lust; frustrated desire breeds dejection and anger; victory over the bodily passions breeds vainglory and pride. **The subtlest are the last**, which attack even those who have overcome the others.

**Akedia deserves special notice.** It is the monk's temptation par excellence, the hour when the cell feels unbearable and everything else seems better. Lay people know it as the inability to pray, the weariness with good things, the urge to escape into distraction. The Fathers' remedy is perseverance: stay in the cell, keep the rule, do the work in hand.

**The remedy for each passion is its opposite virtue**, as the next lessons show: fasting for gluttony, chastity for lust, almsgiving and non-possessiveness for avarice, joy in God for dejection, meekness for anger, perseverance for akedia, hidden good works for vainglory, and humility for pride.

**Healing, not only forgiveness.** Confession forgives sins; the passions take longer. The Fathers compare the spiritual life to medicine: forgiveness is immediate, but the wound heals slowly, through practice, grace and time.
Self-love: the root of the passions:
If there are eight principal passions, what lies beneath them? The Fathers answer with one word.

**Philautia** (φιλαυτία) is **self-love**: not proper care for oneself, which is natural and good, but **love of self in place of God and neighbour**, and especially the love of one's own body and comfort. **St Maximus the Confessor** (about 580–662), in his *Centuries on Love* and other works, calls it the mother of all the passions (paraphrase).

**Maximus's account, simplified.**

1. **From self-love come three "first-born" passions**: gluttony, avarice and vainglory. These are the three temptations of Christ in the desert: bread, the kingdoms of the world, and the leap from the temple to be seen.
2. **From these three come all the rest.**
3. **Self-love arises from turning away from God.** Human desire was made to move towards God; turned back on itself, it seeks pleasure and flees pain, and is enslaved to both.

**Pleasure and pain.** Maximus teaches that after the fall humanity is caught in a cycle: seeking pleasure, it meets pain; fleeing pain, it seeks new pleasure. Christ broke the cycle by entering human life without sin and accepting suffering freely on the cross. **The ascetic life shares in that freedom**: fasting, vigil and patience in hardship loosen the grip of pleasure and the fear of pain.

**Pride and humility.** Many Fathers, Climacus and the desert monks among them, place pride rather than self-love at the root, because pride was the fall of the devil. The two are not rival theories: **self-love is the disposition, pride its most refined form.** Both are cured by humility.

**Humility** (*tapeinophrosynē*, ταπεινοφροσύνη) is not low self-esteem. It is **seeing oneself truly before God**: receiving every good as a gift, knowing one's sins without despair, ceasing to compare oneself with others. The Fathers call it the garment of God, because Christ "humbled himself" (Philippians 2:8, KJV) in the Incarnation. Step 25 of the Ladder praises it as beyond description: one who has it knows it least.

**The desert proverbs.** The *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* (*Apophthegmata Patrum*), collected in the fifth and sixth centuries, return to humility again and again. A well-known saying, in paraphrase: St Antony saw the snares of the enemy spread across the whole world and asked who could escape them; a voice answered: humility.

**Practical consequences.**
- **Self-justification** is a symptom of self-love; the Fathers teach to blame oneself first.
- **Judging others** is its daily form. The Prayer of St Ephrem, said throughout Lent, asks: grant me to see my own faults and not to judge my brother.
- **Obedience** to a spiritual father, and in the family to one another, is a direct remedy, because it cuts one's own will.

**Where it points.** Maximus is read in Stage 9 and argued with in the Philosophy curriculum, where his teaching on the will is the subject.
The virtues: love, discernment and dispa:
Struggle against the passions is only half the picture. The other half is the growth of the virtues, which are not human achievements but **the life of Christ formed in a person**.

**Virtue** (*aretē*, ἀρετή) in the Fathers is a **natural power restored to its proper use** by grace and effort. Where a passion is desire turned to things, the matching virtue is desire turned to God. Christ is "the virtue of all virtues": to have the virtues is to bear His likeness.

**The order of the virtues, in outline.** Different Fathers arrange them differently. A common sequence, found in Maximus and the Philokalia:

| | Virtue | Greek |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **faith** | *pistis* (πίστις) |
| 2 | **fear of God** | *phobos Theou* (φόβος Θεοῦ) |
| 3 | **self-control** | *enkrateia* (ἐγκράτεια) |
| 4 | **patience and hope** | *hypomonē* (ὑπομονή), *elpis* (ἐλπίς) |
| 5 | **dispassion** | *apatheia* (ἀπάθεια) |
| 6 | **love** | *agapē* (ἀγάπη) |

**Discernment** (*diakrisis*, διάκρισις) is the virtue that guides all the others. It is the gift of telling good from evil, the divine from the demonic, the right measure from excess. St John Cassian records Abba Moses teaching, after St Antony, that it is the greatest of the virtues (*Conference* 2.4, translated by C. S. Gibson, NPNF, 1894): **"For discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator."** Without it, even fasting and prayer turn into excess and pride. That is why beginners learn it by obedience to someone who has it.

**Dispassion.** *Apatheia* is easily misunderstood. **It is not indifference or the absence of feeling.** It is the state in which the passions no longer rule: the powers of the soul are free, and desire and anger move rightly. The saints who reached it are described as more loving, not less: weeping for sinners, praying for the whole world, even for the demons, as St Isaac the Syrian taught (paraphrase).

**Love is the summit.** St Paul's hymn, 1 Corinthians 13, closes all the lists: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity" (1 Corinthians 13:13, KJV). The last step of the Ladder, Step 30, is faith, hope and love, and Climacus calls love God Himself (paraphrase, following 1 John 4:8, KJV: "God is love").

**Love of God and love of neighbour are one.** Maximus teaches that one who loves God cannot fail to love every human being. The desert saying, in paraphrase: our life and our death are with our neighbour; if we gain our brother, we gain God.

**The Beatitudes.** Orthodox Christians sing them at almost every Liturgy, in the Third Antiphon. They are the Lord's own list of virtues: poverty of spirit, mourning, meekness, hunger for righteousness, mercy, purity of heart, peacemaking, endurance of persecution. Hopko's *The Orthodox Faith*, volume 4, gives them a section of their own.

**Grace and effort.** The Fathers say a person struggles, and God gives the virtue. No one makes himself humble or loving by technique. But no one receives these gifts without the struggle of wanting them and asking for them.
Fasting: why the Church fasts, and how:
Fasting is one of the most visible marks of Orthodox life. More days of the year are fast days than not.

**Why fast?** Not because food is bad, nor to earn merit. The Fathers give several reasons:

1. **Christ fasted** forty days in the desert, and said His disciples would fast when the bridegroom was taken from them (Matthew 9:15).
2. **It restores the order lost in the fall.** Adam's sin began with eating; the remedy begins with not eating. Fasting is a return to paradise, where the commandment was a fast from one tree.
3. **It loosens the passions.** Gluttony is the first of the eight thoughts; when the body is less pampered, the mind is freer for prayer.
4. **It is joined to prayer and almsgiving.** What is not spent on food is given to the poor.

**Christ's warning.** "Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast" (Matthew 6:16, KJV). **Fasting is hidden and joyful**, or it is worthless.

**The fasting calendar.**

| Fast | When |
| --- | --- |
| **Wednesdays and Fridays** | through the year (the betrayal and the crucifixion), as old as the *Didache* |
| **Great Lent and Holy Week** | the seven weeks before Pascha |
| **The Apostles' Fast** | from the Monday after All Saints' Sunday until the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June; its length varies with the date of Pascha |
| **The Dormition Fast** | 1–14 August |
| **The Nativity Fast** | 15 November–24 December, forty days |
| **Single days** | the Beheading of St John the Baptist (29 August), the Exaltation of the Cross (14 September), the eve of Theophany (5 January) |

There are **fast-free weeks** too: Bright Week after Pascha, the week after Pentecost, the days from Christmas to the eve of Theophany, and the week after the Publican and Pharisee.

**What the strict fast means.** On a full fast day the Typikon asks abstinence from **meat, dairy, eggs, fish with a backbone, and often wine and olive oil**. Fish is allowed on certain feasts (the Annunciation, Palm Sunday, the Transfiguration on 6 August). The monastic rule is the full standard; lay practice varies widely.

**Economy and the confessor.** The rule is the Church's norm, but **the application is personal**. Children, the sick, pregnant and nursing mothers, the elderly, and those who work hard labour are given relaxation. A spiritual father decides. The Fathers warn against both laxity and the pride that fasts beyond one's measure and despises others. St John Chrysostom's Paschal homily, read at every Paschal Matins, invites those who have fasted and those who have not alike to the feast (paraphrase).

**Fasting also from sin.** The Lenten hymns repeat that fasting from food without fasting from anger, gossip and judging is the demons' fast: they never eat at all. **The true fast is from evil.**

**The eucharistic fast.** Before Communion, Orthodox Christians traditionally take no food or drink from the night before (or a set number of hours). This is distinct from the seasonal fasts.

**Variations across the Church.** Russian, Greek, Serbian, Romanian and Antiochian practices differ in details, such as when oil is allowed or how strict the first week of Lent is. The structure is the same everywhere.
Almsgiving and the love of the poor:
