**Where this fits.** The Synodal period explains why twentieth-century Russian theology, in Paris and elsewhere, so often presented itself as a **return to the Fathers** after a captivity.
Missions to the east: Alaska, Siberia an:
From the eighteenth century the Russian Church sent missions east across Siberia and the Pacific. They produced some of the great missionary saints of Orthodox history.

**The principles.** Orthodox mission, from Cyril and Methodius onward, has tried to **give the Gospel and the services in the people's own language**, to train native clergy, and to build a local church rather than a foreign colony.

**Alaska.** In **1794** a mission of eight monks, mostly from **Valaam monastery** on Lake Ladoga, arrived at **Kodiak Island**, then part of Russian America.

- **St Herman of Alaska** (about 1756–1837), one of them, lived as a hermit on Spruce Island, teaching, caring for orphans and defending the native Alutiiq people against abuse by the fur traders. In **1970** he became the first saint glorified by the Orthodox Church in America. Feasts: 13 December and 9 August.
- **St Peter the Aleut**, a young native convert, was killed in Spanish California in 1815 (the details are reported in later sources), refusing to renounce Orthodoxy.
- **St Juvenaly**, a hieromonk of the same mission, was killed in 1796, and is venerated as protomartyr of America.

**St Innocent** (Ivan Veniaminov, 1797–1879) was a married priest sent to the Aleutian island of Unalaska in 1824. He learned Aleut, created an alphabet for it, translated the Gospel of Matthew and the catechism, and built churches with his own hands. After his wife's death he became a monk and **Bishop of Kamchatka, the Kurile and Aleutian Islands** (1840), travelling enormous distances by kayak and dog sled. In 1868 he became **Metropolitan of Moscow**. He was glorified in 1977 and is honoured as enlightener of the Aleuts and apostle to America. His treatise ***Indication of the Way into the Kingdom of Heaven*** (1833) is a simple classic.

**Siberia and the Altai.** **St Macarius (Glukharev)** (1792–1847) founded the Altai mission in 1830, translating the services into the local language. Others worked among the Yakuts, Chuvash, Tatars and peoples of the Volga, notably **Nikolai Ilminsky** (1822–1891), whose method of native-language schools shaped Russian mission.

**Japan.** **St Nicholas of Japan** (Ivan Kasatkin, 1836–1912) arrived in 1861 as chaplain to the Russian consulate at Hakodate. He studied Japanese language, history and Buddhism for years, baptised his first converts in 1868, and translated the New Testament and the services into Japanese. The **Holy Resurrection Cathedral** in Tokyo, called *Nikolai-do*, was consecrated in 1891. At his death there were some 30,000 Japanese Orthodox Christians. During the Russo-Japanese War (1904–1905) he stayed in Japan, praying with his flock for their own country while not praying for the defeat of Russia. **He was glorified in 1970**, as Equal-to-the-Apostles. The Japanese Orthodox Church is today an autonomous church under Moscow.

**China and Korea.** A Russian ecclesiastical mission existed in Beijing from 1715. During the **Boxer Rising of 1900** some 222 Chinese Orthodox Christians were killed; they are venerated as the **Holy Martyrs of China**. A Korean mission began in 1900.

**What these missions left.** The Orthodox Church in America, the Church of Japan, the Altai and Siberian dioceses, and a pattern of mission later followed in Africa (Stage 12).
The Serbian Church: from St Sava to the:
The Serbian Church has given the Orthodox world a royal saint-founder, a medieval patriarchate, the monastery of Hilandar on Athos, and in the twentieth century a host of martyrs.

**St Sava** (about 1174–1236) was **Rastko**, the youngest son of the Serbian ruler **Stefan Nemanja**. As a young man he ran away to Mount Athos and became a monk. His father later abdicated, joined him as the monk **Symeon**, and together in **1198** they founded **Hilandar**. Sava wrote the first Serbian monastic rules and lives of saints.

**Autocephaly.** In **1219** Sava obtained from the Ecumenical Patriarch, then in exile at Nicaea, the consecration as **first Archbishop of an autocephalous Serbian Church**. He organised dioceses, built churches and monasteries such as **Žiča**, and is venerated as the Enlightener of Serbia. His feast, **14 January** (27 January on the civil calendar), is a school holiday in Serbia, *Savindan*. In 1594 the Ottomans burned his relics in Belgrade; the great **Cathedral of St Sava** stands on the site.

**The patriarchate.** In **1346** under Tsar Stefan Dušan the Serbian archbishopric was raised to a **patriarchate**, seated at **Peć**. After the Ottoman conquest it lapsed; it was restored in **1557**, through **Mehmed Sokollu**, the Ottoman grand vizier of Serbian origin, whose kinsman Makarije became patriarch. **It was abolished in 1766** and placed under Constantinople.

**Kosovo.** On 28 June **1389** (St Vitus' Day, *Vidovdan*) the Serbian army under **Prince Lazar** fought the Ottomans at Kosovo Polje. Lazar was killed and is venerated as a martyr. Serbian tradition tells that he chose the heavenly kingdom over the earthly. **Kosovo, with the monasteries of Peć, Dečani and Gračanica, is the spiritual heartland of Serbian Orthodoxy.** It remains disputed between Serbia and the government of Kosovo, and the monasteries' safety has been an ongoing concern.

**The modern church.** Serbia won autonomy in the nineteenth century; the Metropolitanate of Belgrade became autocephalous in 1879. After the First World War, the Serbian dioceses were united and in **1920** the **Serbian Patriarchate was restored**, recognised by Constantinople in 1922.

**The twentieth century.**

| | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **1941–1945** | in the Independent State of Croatia, hundreds of thousands of Serbs were killed, many at the **Jasenovac** camp; many clergy were martyred. The Church venerates the **New Martyrs of Jasenovac** |
| **communist Yugoslavia** | restrictions, confiscations and the imprisonment of clergy |
| **teachers** | **St Nikolai Velimirović** (1881–1956), bishop of Ohrid and Žiča, imprisoned at Dachau, glorified 2003; **St Justin Popović** (Stage 12) |
| **the 1990s** | the wars of Yugoslavia's break-up; churches destroyed in Kosovo, Croatia and Bosnia, especially in 1999 and 2004 |

**Today.** The Serbian Patriarch, since 2021 **Porfirije**, is seated in Belgrade, with dioceses across the former Yugoslavia, in the diaspora and in Western Europe, the Americas and Australia. In 2022 the Serbian Church granted autocephaly to the Church in North Macedonia (Stage 12).
The Bulgarian and Romanian churches:
Two Balkan churches with very different histories: one the first Slavonic church, the other a Latin-speaking people in the Byzantine tradition.

**Bulgaria.**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **864 or 865** | **Khan Boris I** is baptised, taking the name Michael; he is venerated as St Boris |
| **886** onward | disciples of Cyril and Methodius, **St Clement** and **St Naum**, expelled from Moravia, are received in Bulgaria; the school of **Ohrid** and the school of Preslav develop Slavonic literature and the Cyrillic alphabet |
| **927** | Constantinople recognises the **Bulgarian Patriarchate** |
| **946** | death of **St John of Rila**, hermit and patron of Bulgaria; the Rila monastery grows round his tomb |
| **1235** | after the Byzantine conquest and Bulgarian revival, a patriarchate is restored at **Tarnovo** |
| **1393** | Tarnovo falls to the Ottomans; Patriarch St Euthymius is exiled; the Church comes under Constantinople |
| **1870** | the Sultan's decree creates a **Bulgarian Exarchate** |
| **1872** | a council in Constantinople condemns **ethnophyletism**, the organising of the Church by nationality, and declares the Exarchate schismatic |
| **1945** | the schism is lifted |
| **1953** | the **Bulgarian Patriarchate** is restored (recognised by Constantinople in 1961) |

**Ethnophyletism.** The 1872 council's teaching is still cited: **the Church may not be divided by ethnicity**, with overlapping national churches in one place. Orthodox writers note the irony that the condemnation came amid national conflict; but the principle, that one place has one Church, is accepted by all.

**Bulgaria under communism and since.** The Church survived communist rule, with a schism in the 1990s over collaboration, healed in 1998. Patriarch **Daniil** was elected in June 2024.

**Romania.** The Romanians speak a Latin language but received Christianity in the Byzantine tradition. Christianity in Roman Dacia and Scythia Minor (the Dobruja) is ancient: martyrs of the fourth century such as **St Sava the Goth**, and the monks of Scythia Minor, including **St John Cassian**, who was born there according to many scholars.

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1359** | the **Metropolitanate of Wallachia** is recognised by Constantinople |
| **1401** | the **Metropolitanate of Moldavia** follows |
| **15th–17th centuries** | the princes of Wallachia and Moldavia, especially **St Stephen the Great** (reigned 1457–1504), build the painted monasteries of Bukovina and support Athos and the Eastern patriarchates |
| **1642** | the **Synod of Iași** approves Peter Mogila's *Orthodox Confession* |
| **18th century** | **St Paisius Velichkovsky** at Neamț |
| **1865** | autocephaly declared after the union of the principalities |
| **1885** | autocephaly **recognised by Constantinople** |
| **1925** | the **Romanian Patriarchate** is established |

**Under communism (1947–1989)**, many clergy and lay people were imprisoned; some monasteries were closed, and the patriarchate's relations with the regime are still debated. In 2024 the Romanian Synod glorified sixteen confessors and martyrs of that period, among them Fr **Dumitru Stăniloae** (Stage 12), with celebrations in 2025, the centenary of the patriarchate. Patriarch **Daniel** has led the church since 2007; the **People's Salvation Cathedral** in Bucharest was consecrated in 2018. Romania has among the highest rates of church attendance in Europe.
The churches of Greece, Cyprus and Alban:
Three churches of the Greek-speaking and Albanian world, each with its own path to autocephaly.

**The Church of Greece.** During the Greek War of Independence (from 1821), Patriarch **Gregory V** of Constantinople was hanged by the Ottomans at the gate of the Patriarchate on Pascha 1821; he is venerated as a martyr, and the central gate of the Phanar has stayed closed since. Independent Greece, under a Bavarian regency, **declared its church autocephalous in 1833**, without the Patriarch's consent. **Constantinople recognised it by a Tomos in 1850**.

| Feature | Note |
| --- | --- |
| **the Holy Synod** | led by the **Archbishop of Athens and All Greece**, since 2008 **Ieronymos II** |
| **the "New Lands"** | the dioceses of northern Greece won in 1912–1913 remain canonically under Constantinople but administered by the Church of Greece, by an agreement of **1928** |
| **under Constantinople directly** | Crete (a semi-autonomous church), the Dodecanese and Mount Athos |
| **in society** | Orthodoxy is named the "prevailing religion" in the Greek constitution; the clergy are paid by the state |

**Twentieth-century Greece** saw the arrival of over a million refugees from Asia Minor after 1922, a strong lay theological movement (the *Zoe* brotherhood and others), the calendar change of 1924 and the Old Calendarist movement (later lessons), and a renewal of monasticism from the 1960s.

**The Church of Cyprus.** Founded by the apostles **Paul and Barnabas** (Acts 13), and with **St Barnabas** as its patron, it is one of the oldest autocephalous churches. Its independence from Antioch was confirmed by the **Council of Ephesus in 431** (its eighth canon). In **488** the discovery of Barnabas's relics led the Emperor Zeno to grant the Archbishop of Cyprus three privileges, still used: **signing in red ink, carrying an imperial sceptre, and wearing purple**.

Under Ottoman rule (from 1571), the Archbishop was the ethnarch of the Greek Cypriots. In 1821 Archbishop **Kyprianos** and other bishops were executed. **Archbishop Makarios III** (1913–1977) was the first President of the Republic of Cyprus (1960). Since the Turkish invasion of 1974, the north of the island has been under Turkish control, and many churches there were damaged, looted or turned to other use. Archbishop **Georgios** has led the church since 2022.

**The Church of Albania.** Orthodoxy in Albania goes back to apostolic times along the Via Egnatia. An Albanian Orthodox movement, led by **Fan Noli** (1882–1965), a priest from the Albanian community in America, celebrated the Liturgy in Albanian for the first time in **1908** in Massachusetts. A congress at **Berat** in **1922** proclaimed autocephaly; **Constantinople recognised it in 1937**.

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1967** | the communist ruler **Enver Hoxha** declares Albania the world's first atheist state; every church and mosque is closed; clergy are imprisoned or killed |
| **1990–1991** | religious practice is permitted again |
| **1992** | **Anastasios (Yannoulatos)**, a Greek missionary bishop, professor and former missionary in East Africa, is enthroned as Archbishop of Tirana and All Albania, having been sent by Constantinople in 1991 |
| **1992–2025** | he rebuilds the church: over 150 new churches, hundreds restored, a seminary, schools, clinics and a new cathedral of the Resurrection in Tirana (consecrated 2014) |
| **January 2025** | Archbishop Anastasios dies |
| **March 2025** | **Joan (Pelushi)**, Metropolitan of Korçë, is elected Archbishop |

**What they share.** All three were shaped by long Ottoman rule, national struggle and, in Albania's case, the most thorough persecution any Orthodox church faced in the twentieth century. **Albania's resurrection under Anastasios is one of the great stories of modern Orthodoxy.**
The smaller churches: Poland, the Czech:
Some of the Orthodox churches are small in numbers but complete in their life. Several of them stand on borders between East and West, and their recent history is part of the present.

**The Church of Poland.** Most of its faithful are Belarusians and Ukrainians of eastern Poland, heirs of the old Kievan metropolis, with Poles, Lemkos and others.

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1924** | the Ecumenical Patriarchate grants **autocephaly** by tomos, after Poland's independence |
| **1948** | the Moscow Patriarchate, which had not accepted the 1924 tomos, grants its own recognition |
| **since 1998** | **Metropolitan Sawa** of Warsaw and All Poland |

The holy mountain of **Grabarka**, covered with crosses carried by pilgrims, draws great crowds for the Transfiguration. In 2003 the Polish Church glorified the **New Martyrs of Chełm and Podlasie**, killed in the 1940s.

**The Church of the Czech Lands and Slovakia.** It claims the heritage of **Sts Cyril and Methodius**, whose mission of 863 was to Great Moravia, in today's Czech Republic and Slovakia. The modern church grew in the 1920s, when Czech priests and lay people sought Orthodoxy.

- **St Gorazd (Pavlík)** (1879–1942) was consecrated bishop by the Serbian Church in 1921. In 1942 his cathedral in Prague sheltered the Czech parachutists who had killed the Nazi governor Reinhard Heydrich. Gorazd took the responsibility on himself and was shot with his priests; the church was banned. He is venerated as a new martyr.
- **Autocephaly** was granted by Moscow in **1951** and by Constantinople in **1998**. Its primate has been **Metropolitan Rastislav** since 2014.

**The Church of Finland.** Orthodoxy came to Karelia from Novgorod and **Valaam** in the Middle Ages. In **1923**, after independence, the Finnish church was received under Constantinople as **autonomous**, and it is today, with the Lutheran church, one of Finland's two national churches. When Valaam fell inside the Soviet Union in 1940, its monks moved to **New Valaam** at Heinävesi. Finland is the one Orthodox church that keeps **Pascha by the Gregorian calendar**.

**Estonia: two Orthodox churches.**

| Church | Jurisdiction |
| --- | --- |
| **Estonian Apostolic Orthodox Church** | **autonomous under Constantinople** from 1923, revived in **1996** after the Soviet years |
| the church that until 2025 called itself the **Estonian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate** | self-governing under Moscow; most Russian-speaking Orthodox in Estonia; the **Pühtitsa** convent |

Its revival in 1996 caused a **months-long break in communion between Moscow and Constantinople**, ended by a compromise that let both churches exist. In **2025** Estonia's parliament passed a law requiring religious bodies to cut administrative ties with leadership based in Russia. The Moscow-linked church changed its name and statutes but says its canonical bond with Moscow remains, and it has taken the law to the European Court of Human Rights. **As of November 2026, as last reported**, the case had not been decided. The state holds that the law protects national security; the church holds that it violates religious freedom and its canonical order.

**Moldova: two jurisdictions.** Most Orthodox in Moldova belong to the **Metropolis of Chișinău**, a self-governing church under Moscow. The **Metropolis of Bessarabia**, under the Romanian Patriarchate, was registered by the Moldovan state after a European Court of Human Rights judgment in 2001. In recent years some Moldovan priests and parishes have moved from the first to the second, and the two patriarchates dispute the canonical territory.

**What these churches show.** Small churches, often on political fault lines, keep the whole Orthodox life. Their disputes turn on the same questions of jurisdiction as Ukraine's.
The Church of Georgia:
One of the oldest Christian nations, with its own alphabet, its own chant and an unbroken Orthodox identity through Persian, Arab, Mongol, Ottoman, Russian and Soviet rule.

**St Nino.** According to the Georgian tradition, a holy woman from Cappadocia, **Nino**, came to the kingdom of **Kartli** (Iberia, eastern Georgia) in the early fourth century. Through her prayers Queen Nana was healed, and King **Mirian III** was converted after a vision. **Christianity became the faith of the kingdom in the 320s or 330s** (the exact year is debated). St Nino is venerated as **Equal-to-the-Apostles and Enlightener of Georgia**, on 14 January. Her cross of vine branches bound with her hair is the symbol of the Georgian Church.

**Mtskheta.** The ancient capital holds **Svetitskhoveli** ("the life-giving pillar"), the cathedral built over the place where, by tradition, the robe of Christ is buried, and **Jvari** monastery above the river confluence. Mtskheta remains the seat of the Catholicos-Patriarch's enthronement.

**Autocephaly.** The Georgian Church received its own head, the **Catholicos** (Καθολικός), dependent at first on Antioch; by Georgian tradition its autocephaly dates from the fifth century, under King Vakhtang Gorgasali, and was confirmed in the eighth century or later (dates are debated). From the eleventh century the primate bore the title **Catholicos-Patriarch**.

**The golden age.** Under **King David IV the Builder** (reigned 1089–1125) and **Queen Tamar** (reigned 1184–1213), both venerated as saints, Georgia was a united kingdom and a centre of culture. The monastery and academy of **Gelati**, founded by David in 1106, and the Georgian monasteries abroad, on Mount Athos (**Iviron**, founded about 980), Sinai and in Palestine, translated the Fathers into Georgian.

**Martyrdom.** Georgia's position between empires brought repeated invasions:
- In **1616** the Persian Shah Abbas's army, by tradition, killed some **6,000 monks of the David Gareja** monasteries on the night of Pascha.
- In **1624** **St Ketevan**, Queen of Kakheti, was tortured to death in Persia for refusing to accept Islam.

**Under Russia.** After Georgia came under the Russian Empire, the tsar's government **abolished the Georgian Church's autocephaly in 1811**, making it an exarchate of the Russian Synod, often with Russian exarchs. **Autocephaly was restored by the Georgians themselves in 1917**, after the fall of the monarchy. Moscow recognised it in 1943; **Constantinople recognised it in 1990** and the patriarchal title in the same act.

**Soviet rule** (1921–1991) closed most churches and killed many clergy; by the 1970s only a few dozen parishes remained.

**Ilia II and after.** **Catholicos-Patriarch Ilia II**, enthroned on 25 December **1977**, led a revival: thousands of baptisms, many of which he performed himself in mass services, hundreds of new churches and monasteries, and the great **Holy Trinity Cathedral (Sameba)** in Tbilisi, consecrated in 2004. He became the most trusted figure in Georgian public life. **He died on 17 March 2026**, aged 93, the longest-serving primate in Georgian history. On 11 May 2026 an enlarged council elected **Metropolitan Shio (Mujiri)** of Senaki as **Catholicos-Patriarch Shio III**, enthroned at Svetitskhoveli on 12 May 2026.

**Georgian Orthodoxy today** is a national church in the full sense: the great majority of Georgians are Orthodox, and since 2002 a constitutional agreement has set out the Church's relations with the state.
Antioch in the Arab world:
The Church of Antioch, where "the disciples were called Christians first" (Acts 11:26, KJV), is today an Arabic-speaking church of Syria, Lebanon and the diaspora.

**From Antioch to Damascus.** Antioch on the Orontes, in today's Turkey, was one of the great cities of the Roman East and the see of St Peter before Rome, and of St Ignatius (Stage 9). After the Arab conquest of the seventh century and centuries of war, earthquakes and decline, **the patriarchs moved their residence to Damascus in the fourteenth century**, where they remain. The patriarch's title is still **Patriarch of Antioch and All the East**.

**Who they are.** The Orthodox of Antioch are called in Arabic ***Rum*** (Romans), because they kept the faith of the Byzantine Empire. In the Middle Ages they took Arabic as their language for daily life and gradually for the services; they also kept the Byzantine rite and much Greek. **Antiochian Orthodoxy is an Arab church, and has been for many centuries.**

**Under Islamic rule.** Christians in Syria and Lebanon lived under Arab, Mamluk and Ottoman rule as protected but subordinate subjects. Antioch produced Arabic Christian literature: **St John of Damascus** (Stage 9) wrote in Greek in the eighth century, but later writers such as **Paul of Aleppo** (seventeenth century), who described a journey with his patriarch to Moscow, wrote in Arabic.

**1724.** After long Catholic missionary activity, a disputed election in **1724** divided the patriarchate: one party elected **Cyril VI**, who entered communion with Rome, while Constantinople appointed the Greek monk **Sylvester** for the Orthodox. The Catholic body became the **Melkite Greek Catholic Church**. For the Orthodox, the next century and a half brought Greek patriarchs appointed from Constantinople.

**Arab leadership restored.** In **1899** **Meletios II (Doumani)** was elected as the first Arab patriarch since 1724, with Russian support. **Since then Antioch has been led by Arab bishops**, and the services are largely in Arabic. The **University of Balamand** in Lebanon (founded 1988), with its theological institute (1970), is the patriarchate's academic centre.

**The Orthodox Youth Movement.** Founded in Lebanon in **1942**, it renewed the church through Bible study, frequent Communion and lay involvement. Its founders included later leaders such as **Metropolitan Georges Khodr** of Mount Lebanon (born 1923) and **Patriarch Ignatius IV (Hazim)** (patriarch 1979–2012).

**In America.** Arab Orthodox emigrants built churches in North America from the 1890s. **St Raphael of Brooklyn** (1860–1915), a Syrian-born priest, became in 1904 **the first Orthodox bishop consecrated in North America**, under the Russian mission, and is venerated as a saint (glorified 2000). The **Antiochian Orthodox Christian Archdiocese of North America** is today a self-ruling archdiocese.

**Suffering in our time.**

| | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1975–1990** | the Lebanese civil war |
| **from 2011** | the Syrian war; churches destroyed, hundreds of thousands of Christians displaced |
| **April 2013** | **Metropolitan Paul (Yazigi) of Aleppo**, brother of the Patriarch, and the Syriac Orthodox Metropolitan Gregorios Yohanna Ibrahim are kidnapped near Aleppo; their fate has never been established |
| **22 June 2025** | a suicide bombing at the church of the **Prophet Elias** (Mar Elias) in Damascus kills more than twenty worshippers during the Sunday Liturgy |

**Patriarch John X (Yazigi)** has led the church since 2012.
Alexandria and Jerusalem today:
The other two ancient patriarchates of the East: one now a church of all Africa, the other the guardian of the holy places.

**The Patriarchate of Alexandria.** Founded, by tradition, by **St Mark the Evangelist**, Alexandria was the see of St Athanasius and St Cyril (Stage 9). After the Council of Chalcedon (451), most Egyptian Christians followed the non-Chalcedonian patriarchs; their church is today the **Coptic Orthodox Church** (Stage 7). The Chalcedonian Orthodox patriarchate, called by the Copts *Melkite* (the emperor's party), was a minority, mainly Greek-speaking.

| Period | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **7th century onward** | under Arab and later Ottoman rule, the Orthodox patriarchate shrinks to a small community; patriarchs often live in Constantinople |
| **19th century** | a large **Greek community** grows in Egypt, especially Alexandria and Cairo, and the patriarchate revives |
| **1950s–1960s** | most Greeks leave Egypt after the Suez crisis and nationalisation |
| **20th century onward** | Orthodoxy spreads among **Africans** south of the Sahara, beginning in Uganda in the 1920s (Stage 12) |

**Today** the patriarch's title is **Pope and Patriarch of Alexandria and All Africa**. **Theodore II** has been patriarch since 2004. The church has dioceses across sub-Saharan Africa, with African bishops and clergy and a large mission. Its relations with Moscow broke down after 2019, when Alexandria recognised the Orthodox Church of Ukraine; Moscow created its own African exarchate in 2021 (Stage 12).

**The Patriarchate of Jerusalem.** The mother church of all, from Pentecost. **St James the Brother of the Lord** is counted its first bishop. The **Council of Chalcedon in 451** raised Jerusalem to a patriarchate, fifth in honour.

**The Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre.** Since the Ottoman period the patriarchate has been governed by this Greek monastic brotherhood, which guards the Orthodox share in the holy places: the **Church of the Resurrection** (the Holy Sepulchre), shared with the Latins, Armenians, Copts, Syriacs and Ethiopians under the **Status Quo** arrangements fixed by Ottoman decrees in 1757 and 1852; the **Church of the Nativity** in Bethlehem; and many others.

**The Holy Fire.** Every Great and Holy Saturday the Patriarch enters the tomb of Christ, and comes out with fire that pilgrims receive as a miracle. **It is one of the most loved events of the Orthodox year**; the fire is flown to several Orthodox countries for Pascha.

**The flock.** Most of the faithful are **Arabic-speaking Palestinians and Jordanians**, while the hierarchy is largely Greek. This has caused long tension; Arab Orthodox lay associations have called for Arab bishops and a greater share in governance, and the Brotherhood stresses its duty to guard the holy places for the whole Orthodox world. **Both concerns are real.** Disputes over the sale or lease of church property have added to the strain.

**Theophilos III** has been Patriarch since 2005.

**Sinai.** The **Monastery of St Catherine** at Mount Sinai, founded by the Emperor Justinian in the sixth century, is the seat of the **autonomous Church of Sinai**, whose abbot is archbishop, consecrated by the Patriarch of Jerusalem. It holds one of the world's oldest continuously used libraries and icons from the sixth century. In 2025, after a court ruling in Egypt on the monastery's lands and an internal crisis, the long-serving Archbishop Damianos (in office since 1973) withdrew and **Archbishop Symeon** was elected and enthroned in October 2025.
The Russian Church under Soviet rule (19:
The Bolshevik Revolution began the most systematic attempt in history to destroy a church. The Russian Church survived it, at enormous cost.

**The Council of 1917–1918.** Meeting in Moscow as the revolution unfolded, the Local Council restored the patriarchate and elected **St Tikhon** (1865–1925), formerly archbishop in America. It planned a renewal of parish life with lay participation, much of which could never be carried out.

**The first blows.**
- In **January 1918** the Soviet decree separated Church and state, nationalised church property and banned religious teaching in schools.
- Also in January 1918, **Metropolitan Vladimir of Kiev** was shot, the first bishop to be killed. In **1918** Patriarch Tikhon anathematised those who persecuted the Church.
- On **17 July 1918** the former **Tsar Nicholas II**, his family and servants were shot at Yekaterinburg; the next day the Tsar's sister-in-law **Grand Duchess Elizabeth**, abbess of a convent of mercy, was thrown alive into a mineshaft at Alapaevsk with others.
- In **1922** the state seized church valuables, supposedly for famine relief, and staged trials; **Metropolitan Benjamin of Petrograd** was shot.

**The Renovationists.** From 1922 the state supported a "Living Church" (*obnovlentsy*, renovationists), a movement of clergy who introduced married bishops and other changes and supported the regime. Most of the faithful rejected it, and it collapsed in the 1940s.

**Metropolitan Sergius and the Declaration of 1927.** After Tikhon's death in 1925 and the arrest of the locum tenens, **Metropolitan Sergius (Stragorodsky)** issued in July 1927 a **declaration of loyalty to the Soviet state**. This remains one of the most debated acts in modern church history:

| View | Its argument |
| --- | --- |
| **a necessary compromise** | Sergius sought to secure a legal existence for the Church, to keep bishops and sacraments available to millions; without it the hierarchy might have been destroyed entirely |
| **a betrayal** | the Declaration placed the Church at the service of a persecuting state, and Sergius's administration denied that persecution existed; many bishops and faithful, such as **Metropolitan Joseph of Petrograd**, refused it, forming the "catacomb" church, and many of them became martyrs |

**The terror.** In 1937–1938 alone, by estimates commonly drawn from the archives, well over a hundred thousand clergy and believers were arrested, and most of them were shot. At the **Butovo** firing range near Moscow over 20,000 people were shot in 1937–1938, among them about a thousand who suffered for their faith; several hundred of them are now venerated as saints. **By 1939 only a few hundred churches were open in the whole USSR**, and only four bishops of the patriarchal church remained at liberty.

**1943.** During the war, **Stalin** allowed the election of Sergius as Patriarch (September 1943), and churches and seminaries reopened. Under **Khrushchev** (1958–1964) a new persecution closed some half of the churches again.

**ROCOR.** Bishops who left Russia after the civil war formed the **Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia** (ROCOR), with its synod first at Sremski Karlovci in Serbia, later in New York. It refused communion with the Moscow Patriarchate while the latter was under Soviet control, and in 1981 glorified the new martyrs. **In 2007 ROCOR and the Moscow Patriarchate signed the Act of Canonical Communion**, ending the separation.

**The rebirth.** The millennium of the baptism of Rus' in **1988** marked a change. After 1991 thousands of churches and hundreds of monasteries reopened. The **Council of Bishops of 2000** glorified over a thousand new martyrs and confessors, including **the Royal Martyrs**. The Moscow Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, blown up in 1931, was rebuilt and consecrated in 2000.
The new martyrs and confessors of the tw:
More Orthodox Christians died for their faith in the twentieth century than in all the persecutions of the Roman Empire together. The Church calls them the **new martyrs and confessors**.

**Martyr and confessor.** A **martyr** (*martys*, μάρτυς, "witness") is one killed for Christ. A **confessor** (*homologētēs*, ὁμολογητής) is one who suffered for Christ, by prison, torture or exile, but was not killed. **Passion-bearers** accepted an unjust death in Christ's spirit (an earlier lesson).

**Across the Orthodox world.**

| Church | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Russia** | **St Tikhon**; **St Elizabeth the New Martyr**; **the Royal Martyrs**; **St Hilarion (Troitsky)** (died 1929), theologian; **St Seraphim (Chichagov)**, shot at Butovo in 1937; thousands of priests, monks, nuns and lay people. The **Synaxis of the New Martyrs and Confessors of Russia** is kept on the Sunday nearest 25 January (Old Style) |
| **Ukraine and Belarus** | many of the same Soviet martyrs; new martyrs of the Kiev Caves and of the 1930s famine years |
| **Serbia** | the **New Martyrs of Jasenovac**; **St Platon of Banja Luka** and **St Gorazd of Prague**, a Czech bishop shot by the Nazis in 1942 for sheltering the resistance fighters who killed Heydrich |
| **Asia Minor** | **St Chrysostomos of Smyrna**, killed by a mob in September 1922 when the city fell, glorified by the Church of Greece in 1992 |
| **Romania** | the prison saints of the communist era, glorified in 2024: priests, monks and lay people who died or suffered in prisons such as Aiud, Pitești and Gherla |
| **Albania** | clergy killed or imprisoned after 1967 |
| **China** | the Holy Martyrs of the Boxer Rising, 1900 |
| **Estonia and Latvia** | **St Platon of Reval** (Estonia, 1919), **St John (Pommer) of Riga** (1934) |

**What they show.**

1. **The faith survived by witness, not by power.** In many places the Church was reduced to the faithful praying at home and a handful of priests. The Liturgy continued in prisons, with bread smuggled in.
2. **Their forgiveness.** The lives of many new martyrs record that they prayed for their killers.
3. **The labour camps were a school of holiness** for some, such as **St Luke (Voino-Yasenetsky)** of Crimea (1877–1961), surgeon and bishop, exiled and imprisoned, who went on operating and writing medical works; he was awarded a Stalin Prize for surgery and is venerated as a saint.

**Glorification and its debates.** The glorification of the new martyrs has raised real questions: how to judge those who signed confessions under torture, how to weigh the Royal Family's deaths (glorified by Moscow in 2000 as **passion-bearers** rather than martyrs, because of disputes over the late Tsar's rule), and how to treat those who accepted or refused the 1927 Declaration. **Commissions in each church examine the evidence case by case.**

**Their place in the Church's prayer.** Icons of the new martyrs are now common. In Moscow the Butovo firing range has become a place of pilgrimage with a church of the New Martyrs. **The twentieth century, in this sense, is an age of the Church's glory as well as her suffering.**
Rebirth after communism, and the Ecumeni:
Between 1989 and 1991 the communist regimes of Eastern Europe fell. The Orthodox churches of the region, and the Ecumenical Patriarchate itself, entered a new and very different era.

**The scale of rebirth.**

| Church | After 1989–91 |
| --- | --- |
| **Russia** | from a few thousand parishes in the 1980s to about 40,000 parishes and nearly a thousand monasteries, by the church's figures, by the 2020s |
| **Romania** | hundreds of new churches, a theological faculty in every major city |
| **Bulgaria** | recovery slowed by a schism over collaboration (1992–1998) |
| **Serbia** | revival amid the wars of the 1990s |
| **Georgia** | the great revival under Ilia II |
| **Albania** | resurrection from nothing under Anastasios |
| **Ukraine and Moldova** | rapid growth, but with divisions of jurisdiction (Stage 12) |

**The questions of freedom.** Rebirth raised new problems: how to train thousands of priests quickly; how to reckon with collaboration under communism; how to relate to new national states; how to evangelise populations raised in atheism; and how to deal with property seized and given to others. **Orthodox writers differ on how close the churches should be to the new states**: some see a revival of Byzantine *symphonia*, others warn against nationalism and dependence on governments.

**The Ecumenical Patriarchate after 1923.** The Patriarchate's own story ran the other way.

- **1922–1923**: the defeat of the Greek army in Asia Minor and the **Treaty of Lausanne** led to the **exchange of populations**: about 1.2 million Orthodox were expelled from Turkey to Greece, and some 400,000 Muslims from Greece to Turkey. **Orthodoxy in Asia Minor, there since the apostles, ended almost entirely.** The Greeks of Istanbul were exempted.
- **1955**: the **Istanbul pogrom** of 6–7 September destroyed dozens of churches and many Greek homes and shops; most of the city's Greek community emigrated over the following decades. Today only a few thousand Greek Orthodox remain in Istanbul.
- **1971**: Turkish law closed private higher education, and with it the Patriarchate's **theological school of Halki**, on an island near Istanbul. **As of November 2026**, the restored buildings had been prepared for inauguration in the autumn of 2026 after talks between the Patriarchate, Turkey and the United States, but **the school's reopening as a teaching institution had not been settled**.
- The Turkish state requires the Patriarch to be a Turkish citizen and does not recognise his ecumenical title.

**The Patriarchate's worldwide role.** Its flock in Turkey is tiny, but it has jurisdiction over Crete, the Dodecanese, Mount Athos, the "New Lands" of northern Greece (administered by the Church of Greece), the autonomous churches of Finland and Estonia, and many dioceses of the diaspora, including the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America. **Patriarch Bartholomew** (elected 1991) has made the Patriarchate visible worldwide, especially on the environment, earning the name "the Green Patriarch".

**The question of primacy.** What the Ecumenical Patriarch's primacy means in practice is now debated among the Orthodox. **Constantinople's view**: as first without equals (the title of a 2014 essay by Metropolitan Elpidophoros, *Primus sine paribus*), the Patriarch has duties of coordination, appeal and initiative across the Orthodox world, including in the diaspora and in granting autocephaly. **Moscow's view**: the primacy is one of honour, and pan-Orthodox matters require the consent of all churches. Stage 12 shows how this question became acute over Ukraine.
The diaspora: Orthodoxy in Western Europ:
Over the twentieth century millions of Orthodox Christians settled outside the traditional Orthodox lands. Their churches created a new situation, and a new problem.

**How they came.**

| Wave | Who |
| --- | --- |
| **late 19th–early 20th century** | Greek, Syrian, Lebanese, Serbian, Romanian, Russian and Carpatho-Russian workers to the Americas and Australia |
| **after 1917** | Russian émigrés: perhaps a million or more, many to Paris, Berlin, Belgrade, Harbin and later America |
| **after 1945** | refugees from Eastern Europe, Ukraine and the Baltic |
| **after 1960s** | Greek and Cypriot migration to Australia, Britain, Germany; Arab Orthodox from Lebanon and Syria |
| **after 1990** | Romanians, Bulgarians, Georgians, Ukrainians, Moldovans and Russians across the European Union; Ethiopians and Eritreans (Oriental Orthodox) also |

**The Russian emigration in Paris.** The émigrés produced an astonishing theological culture. In **1925** they founded the **St Sergius Orthodox Theological Institute** in Paris, where **Fr Sergius Bulgakov**, **Fr Georges Florovsky**, **Anton Kartashev**, **Fr Nicholas Afanasiev** and later **Fr Alexander Schmemann** and **Fr John Meyendorff** taught (Stage 12). The **Russian Student Christian Movement** and the **St Sergius and St Alban Fellowship** (1928, with Anglicans) began there. **St Maria Skobtsova** (Mother Maria, 1891–1945), a nun who ran a house for the poor in Paris and hid Jews during the Nazi occupation, died at Ravensbrück; she was glorified by Constantinople in 2004.

**Jurisdictions in the diaspora.** Because each mother church cared for its own emigrants, **several Orthodox bishops now often sit in the same city**, each for his own ethnic flock. A city like London, Paris, New York, Sydney or Johannesburg may have Greek, Russian, Serbian, Romanian, Antiochian, Georgian, Bulgarian and other bishops or parishes.

**Why this is a problem.** The canonical principle is **one bishop in one city** (Nicaea I, canon 8). Overlapping jurisdictions also recall the 1872 condemnation of ethnophyletism (an earlier lesson). **All the churches agree it is irregular**; they disagree on the solution:

| View | Argument |
| --- | --- |
| **Constantinople's** | Chalcedon's canon 28 gives Constantinople jurisdiction over the barbarian lands beyond the other churches' territory; the diaspora therefore belongs to the Ecumenical Patriarchate |
| **other churches'** (Moscow, Antioch and others) | canon 28 concerned specific regions of the fifth-century empire; each mother church may care for its own faithful abroad until local churches mature |

**The Episcopal Assemblies.** In **2009**, at Chambésy near Geneva, the primates' representatives agreed to create **Episcopal Assemblies** in regions of the diaspora, chaired by Constantinople's bishop, gathering all canonical bishops to coordinate and prepare a future canonical solution. The **Assembly of Canonical Orthodox Bishops of the United States** began in 2010. Similar assemblies meet in Britain, France, Germany, Australia and elsewhere. Their work was affected by the Moscow–Constantinople break of 2018.

**Converts.** The diaspora has drawn many converts: from the Anglican tradition in Britain (Metropolitan **Kallistos Ware**, 1934–2022, was one), Evangelicals and others in America, French and German intellectuals. **Western Orthodoxy is no longer only an immigrant church.**

**Australia and beyond.** The Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia (from 1924), Serbian, Antiochian and Russian dioceses; Orthodox communities in Latin America, South Africa, Southeast Asia and Korea. The next lesson turns to North America.
The OCA and Orthodoxy in North America:
North America has more Orthodox jurisdictions in one place than anywhere else, and one church whose status is itself a question: the Orthodox Church in America.

**The Russian mission and its diocese.** Orthodoxy arrived in **Alaska in 1794** (an earlier lesson). A diocese of the Aleutians and Alaska was founded in 1840 under St Innocent. Its seat moved to **San Francisco** (1872) and then **New York** (1905).

**St Tikhon in America.** **Bishop Tikhon** (Bellavin), later Patriarch, led the American diocese from **1898 to 1907**. He built St Nicholas Cathedral in New York, founded St Tikhon's Monastery in Pennsylvania (1905), proposed a multi-ethnic American church with its own vicar bishops for each group, and had the services translated into English. **St Raphael of Brooklyn** was consecrated as his vicar for the Arabs in 1904.

**The Uniate returns.** From 1891, **St Alexis Toth** (1854–1909), a Greek Catholic priest from Carpatho-Rus' rebuffed by the Latin bishop of St Paul, Minnesota, led his parish into the Orthodox Church. Over the next decades tens of thousands of Carpatho-Russian and Galician immigrants followed. He was glorified in 1994.

**After 1917.** The revolution cut the American diocese off from Moscow. A council at **Detroit in 1924** declared it temporarily self-governing: the **"Metropolia"**. For decades its relations with Moscow and with ROCOR were broken and restored. Meanwhile, other mother churches organised their own American dioceses:

| Jurisdiction | Founded or organised |
| --- | --- |
| **Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America** (Constantinople) | 1922 |
| **Antiochian Archdiocese** | from 1895 missions; united archdiocese 1975 |
| **Serbian, Romanian, Bulgarian, Ukrainian, Carpatho-Russian dioceses** | 1920s onward |
| **ROCOR** | headquarters in New York from 1950 |

**Autocephaly, 1970.** In **1970**, after negotiations, the Moscow Patriarchate granted the Metropolia autocephaly as the **Orthodox Church in America** (OCA). **St Herman of Alaska** was glorified that year. **St Vladimir's Seminary** (founded 1938), led by Schmemann and Meyendorff, became its intellectual centre.

**The OCA's status today.**
- **Recognised as autocephalous** by Moscow, Bulgaria, Georgia, Poland and the Czech Lands and Slovakia.
- **Not recognised as autocephalous** by Constantinople and most of the other churches, which hold that only Constantinople, with pan-Orthodox consent, can grant autocephaly, and that the diaspora belongs to its jurisdiction. They treat it as a canonical church in communion, without the autocephalous rank.
- **In communion** with all canonical Orthodox churches.

**The two positions in their strongest form.** **For the OCA's autocephaly**: America needs one local church for all Orthodox there; the mother church that founded the mission has the right to release it; the OCA is multi-ethnic, English-speaking and missionary, as Tikhon envisioned. **For Constantinople's position**: autocephaly is a pan-Orthodox matter; a single church cannot create a new autocephalous church in a region where several mother churches have flocks; and the diaspora is to be ordered through the Episcopal Assemblies. **The OCA's Metropolitan Tikhon** (Mollard) has led it since 2012.

**American Orthodoxy today.** Perhaps a million or more Orthodox Christians of many jurisdictions, with seminaries (Holy Cross, St Vladimir's, St Tikhon's, Holy Trinity at Jordanville), monasteries (including those founded from Athos by **Elder Ephraim** of Philotheou from the 1990s), and many converts.
The calendar question: Julian, Revised J:
Orthodox Christians celebrate Christmas on different days in different countries. The reason is a calendar decision of 1923, and the question remains one Orthodox Christians answer differently.

**Two calendars.**

| | Julian calendar | Revised Julian ("New") calendar |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **origin** | Julius Caesar, 46 BC | proposed by the Serbian astronomer **Milutin Milanković**; adopted at the **Pan-Orthodox Congress in Constantinople, May 1923** |
| **leap years** | every fourth year | every fourth year, except century years unless they leave a remainder of 200 or 600 when divided by 900 |
| **accuracy** | gains about a day every 128 years against the sun | very close to the solar year |
| **difference now** | **13 days behind** the Gregorian calendar until 2100 | **identical to the Gregorian** until 2800 |

So Christmas, 25 December, falls on **7 January** of the civil calendar for those on the Julian calendar.

**Who uses which** (for the fixed feasts):

| Revised Julian | Julian |
| --- | --- |
| Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Greece, Cyprus, Romania, Bulgaria (since 1968), Albania, the OCA (most parishes), the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (since September 2023), the Greek and Antiochian churches of the diaspora | Jerusalem, Russia, Serbia, Georgia, Mount Athos, the Ukrainian Orthodox Church (Moscow-linked), North Macedonia, ROCOR, Poland (returned to the Julian calendar in 2014 in most parishes) |

The Church of the Czech Lands and Slovakia uses both, by region; Finland uses the Gregorian calendar even for Pascha.

**Pascha is the same for almost everyone.** Apart from Finland, **all the Orthodox churches compute Pascha by the Julian calendar and the old Paschal tables**, the Paschalion. So the movable cycle, Lent, Pascha, Pentecost, is shared; only the fixed feasts differ. This is why the Revised Julian churches have shorter Apostles' Fasts in some years: the fast's end is fixed, its start moves.

**Why the 1923 change was made.** Patriarch **Meletios IV (Metaxakis)** of Constantinople called the 1923 congress. The arguments for change:
- **Astronomical accuracy**: the Julian calendar drifts from the sun.
- **Pastoral practicality**: Orthodox in modern states lived by the civil calendar; keeping feasts on different days was a burden.
- **Not a matter of dogma**: the calendar is a tool, and the First Council of Nicaea dealt with the date of Pascha, not with the civil year.

The Ecumenical Patriarchate and the Church of Greece adopted the Revised Julian calendar in **March 1924**; others followed over the next decades.

**Why many churches did not.**
- **Unity**: the change was made by some churches without the consent of all, and broke the common celebration of the feasts.
- **Tradition**: the Julian calendar had been the Church's for sixteen centuries; the services and the Typikon are built on it.
- **Suspicion of motive**: some saw the move as an accommodation to the West. Patriarchal synods of the 1580s had rejected the Gregorian calendar when Rome proposed it; the texts and force of those decisions, especially a "Sigillion" of 1583, are themselves debated by historians.
- **Russia, Serbia and Jerusalem**, though represented at the congress, did not adopt it.

**What is common ground.** Both calendar groups are **in full communion**: Russia and Greece, Serbia and Romania concelebrate. **The calendar is not a dogma**, and the Church has never made it a test of Orthodoxy among the canonical churches. The next lesson covers those who did make it a matter of separation.

**A modern question.** In 2025, when Pascha fell on the same day for East and West, and with the 1700th anniversary of Nicaea, proposals for a common date of Pascha were discussed again. **As of November 2026 no Orthodox church has changed its Paschalion.**
The Old Calendarists: the case for separ:
When the Church of Greece changed the calendar in 1924, a movement of clergy and faithful refused, and in time formed separate churches. They are called **Old Calendarists**, or by their own name **Genuine** or **True Orthodox Christians** (*Gnēsioi Orthodoxoi Christianoi*, Γνήσιοι Ὀρθόδοξοι Χριστιανοί).

**The history, in outline.**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1924** | parishes in Greece keep the Julian calendar against the Synod's decision; lay associations form |
| **1935** | three metropolitans of the Church of Greece, led by **Chrysostomos (Kavourides), formerly of Florina**, join the movement and consecrate bishops |
| **1937** | a division between those who held that the new-calendar church had lost grace (associated with **Bishop Matthew of Vresthena**) and those who treated it as schismatic but not yet without grace (Chrysostomos's line) |
| **1960s** | ROCOR bishops consecrate bishops for the Greek Old Calendarists |
| **1924 onward** | similar movements in Romania (led by **St Glicherie** of Romania in a monastic revival), Bulgaria and Cyprus |
| **2014** | two of the main Greek Old Calendarist synods unite |

Today several Old Calendarist synods exist, not all in communion with one another, with perhaps several hundred thousand faithful in Greece, Romania, Bulgaria and the diaspora. **They are not in communion with the canonical Orthodox churches.** Mount Athos, though on the Julian calendar, remains in communion with Constantinople; one monastery, Esphigmenou, broke communion in 1972, and its dispute with the Patriarchate continues.

**The case for the Old Calendarist position, in its strongest form.**

1. **Unity of worship is part of unity of faith.** The Church celebrated the feasts together for sixteen centuries; changing the calendar unilaterally broke the liturgical unity of the Church, which is a sign of her inner unity.
2. **The change was uncanonical.** It was made without an ecumenical council and against earlier patriarchal rejections of the Gregorian reform.
3. **It was a step towards something larger.** The 1920 encyclical of Constantinople, which proposed a common calendar with other Christians as a step to rapprochement, shows the change was linked to ecumenism. Old Calendarists see their stand as resistance to an ecclesiology they hold to be un-Orthodox.
4. **Walling off is a patristic duty.** Canon 15 of the First-Second Council of Constantinople (861) permits clergy to separate from a bishop who publicly preaches heresy, before a synodal judgement. Some Old Calendarists ground their separation on it.

**The case of the canonical churches, in its strongest form.**

1. **The calendar is not dogma.** No council made the civil calendar part of the faith; Nicaea dealt with Pascha, and the Paschalion has been kept.
2. **Schism is the graver sin.** The Fathers, Chrysostom above all, teach that dividing the Church is worse than many errors. Breaking communion over a calendar sets a discipline above the Church's unity.
3. **Canon 15 refers to heresy condemned by the Fathers or councils**, preached publicly; a calendar change is not that. And the other Julian-calendar churches, Jerusalem, Russia, Serbia, Georgia, Athos, all stayed in communion with the new-calendar churches.
4. **The fruits.** The Old Calendarist movement has divided repeatedly into competing synods, which canonical writers see as a sign that the separation was not of God.

**Where they meet.** Both sides affirm the same Creed, councils, sacraments and Fathers, and both oppose any compromise of the faith. **The disagreement is over whether the 1924 change, and later ecumenical involvement, justified breaking communion.** Some Old Calendarist clergy and communities have returned to canonical churches in recent decades, and dialogue continues locally.

**How to treat the question.** As a question on which sincere Orthodox Christians stand in different places, with the history known and the arguments heard. Stage 12's lesson on ecumenism takes up the wider issue behind it.
Autocephaly: how a church becomes self-h:
Most of the jurisdictional disputes in today's Orthodox world come back to one question: how does a church become autocephalous, and who decides?

**The terms.**

| Term | Greek | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **autocephalous** | αὐτοκέφαλος | a church that **elects its own primate** and is fully self-governing |
| **autonomous** | αὐτόνομος | self-governing, but its primate is **confirmed by a mother church** |
| **tomos** | τόμος | the **official decree** granting autocephaly or autonomy |
| **diptychs** | δίπτυχα | the **order of precedence** of the churches, commemorated at the Liturgy |
| **canonical territory** | | the region that belongs to a church's jurisdiction |

**The canonical foundations.**
- **Apostolic Canon 34**: the bishops of each nation must recognise the first among them as their head, and do nothing important without him, while he does nothing without them. **This is the basic principle of a local church.**
- **Nicaea I, canons 6 and 7**: the ancient customs of Alexandria, Rome and Antioch, and honour for Jerusalem.
- **Constantinople I, canon 3**, and **Chalcedon, canon 28**: Constantinople, as New Rome, second in honour after Rome; canon 28 also gives it jurisdiction over certain regions and over bishops in the lands of the barbarians beyond them.

**How the churches actually became autocephalous.** History shows many routes: by councils (Cyprus, 431); by imperial decision (Jerusalem's patriarchate, 451; Ohrid and others in Byzantine times); by declaration and later recognition (Russia 1448 and 1589; Greece 1833 and 1850; Bulgaria 1870 and 1945; Georgia 1917 and 1990; Romania 1865 and 1885); by Constantinople's tomos (Poland 1924; Albania 1937; Czech Lands and Slovakia 1998); by Moscow's tomos (Czech Lands and Slovakia 1951; the OCA 1970); by Serbia's (North Macedonia, 2022). **No single procedure was ever fixed by an ecumenical council.**

**The two main positions today, in their strongest form.**

| | Constantinople's view | Moscow's view (shared in part by others) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **who grants** | the Ecumenical Patriarchate, as first see, has the prerogative of granting autocephaly by tomos, as it has done in the modern era | the **mother church** grants autocephaly to its daughter, and the whole Orthodox world must then consent |
| **why** | someone must act; the First See's role of coordination and appeal (Chalcedon canons 9, 17, 28) makes it the natural arbiter; recognition by all comes after | autocephaly changes the whole communion and must not be imposed by one church; Constantinople's claim makes it more than first among equals |
| **canonical territory** | not an ancient canonical notion in the modern, rigid sense; the First See can intervene to heal schism | each church's territory is inviolable, and others may not act within it without consent |

**The attempt at a common rule.** Pan-Orthodox preparatory meetings at Chambésy, especially in **1993**, agreed in principle that autocephaly requires the consent of the mother church and of all the churches, and is proclaimed by a tomos of the Ecumenical Patriarch. **They could not agree who signs the tomos**: the Ecumenical Patriarch alone, or all the primates. The topic was therefore **left off the agenda of the Holy and Great Council of 2016** (Stage 12).

**The disputes it causes.** The OCA (1970) and North Macedonia (2022) are not recognised by all. **Ukraine (2018–19)**, where the two positions collided directly and Moscow broke communion with Constantinople, is the most serious division in the Orthodox world in centuries; Stage 12 treats it in two lessons. Estonia (1996) caused a temporary break between Moscow and Constantinople, healed with a compromise of two parallel churches.

**What all sides agree on.** The Church is one; local churches are a good and ancient form of her life; unity is kept by communion in faith and sacraments; and disputes should be settled synodically. **The disagreement is over the procedure and over the role of the First See.**
Looking back: one Church in many lands:
This stage has crossed five centuries and four continents. Looking back, the same Church appears in every chapter, under very different conditions.

**Under non-Christian rule.** The Ottoman millet made the Ecumenical Patriarch head of a nation; the Church kept the faith, the language and the services, and produced the neomartyrs, the Kollyvades and the Philokalia. Antioch and Alexandria lived under Islamic rule for over a thousand years, and Antioch became an Arab church. **The Church survived without a Christian state.**

**Answering new questions.** The seventeenth-century confessions of Mogila and Dositheos stated Orthodox teaching against the Reformation; the 1848 Encyclical declared that the faith is guarded by "the very body of the Church". **Orthodox theologians weigh the confessions differently; all agree the faith belongs to the whole Church.**

**The Russian Church.** From the baptism of 988 through the Caves, Radonezh and Moscow; the patriarchate of 1589; the schism of the Old Believers; the Synodal period, structurally weak and spiritually rich; the missions to Alaska, Siberia and Japan.

**The national churches.**

| Church | Its founder or turning point |
| --- | --- |
| **Serbia** | St Sava, 1219; Kosovo, 1389; restored patriarchate, 1920 |
| **Bulgaria** | St Boris, 864/865; the Exarchate, 1870; ethnophyletism condemned, 1872 |
| **Romania** | Wallachia 1359, Moldavia 1401; recognised 1885; patriarchate 1925 |
| **Greece** | autocephaly declared 1833, recognised 1850 |
| **Cyprus** | Ephesus, 431; the three privileges, 488 |
| **Albania** | 1922/1937; destroyed 1967; resurrected after 1992 |
| **Georgia** | St Nino; abolished 1811, restored 1917; Ilia II (1977–2026); Shio III (2026) |

**The twentieth century.** The Soviet persecution, the most systematic in history; the 1927 Declaration, still debated; ROCOR and its reunion in 2007; the new martyrs from Russia to Serbia, Romania, Albania and China; the rebirth after 1989–91; and the end of Orthodoxy in Asia Minor after 1923.

**The diaspora.** Paris and the St Sergius Institute; overlapping jurisdictions and the Episcopal Assemblies; the OCA and its disputed autocephaly; the converts.

**Questions answered differently.** Three in this stage:

1. **The calendar**: a pastoral and astronomical question on which canonical churches differ while remaining in communion.
2. **The Old Calendarists**: whether the 1924 change justified separation; each side has a serious case.
3. **Autocephaly**: who grants it, and the role of the First See.

**Five sentences to keep.**

1. **The Orthodox Church is a communion of local churches**, not a federation and not a single administration.
2. **She has lived most of her history without a friendly state**, and often under persecution.
3. **Each nation received the faith in its own language**, but **the Church may not be divided by ethnicity**.
4. **The twentieth century was an age of martyrs** greater than the age of Rome.
5. **The disputes of today are about order, not about the faith**: all parties confess the same Creed and councils.

**Stage 12** brings the story to the present: the theologians of the twentieth century, the saints of our own time, the Council of 2016, the dialogues with the Oriental Orthodox, Ukraine, and the Church in Africa.
Context: Orthodox theology meets the mod:
The last stage brings the curriculum to the present. It meets the theologians of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the saints of living memory, and the questions the Church faces as of November 2026.

**Why "modern Orthodox theology" is a subject.** For centuries after 1453, Orthodox theology was taught largely in borrowed Western forms: Latin textbooks in the Russian academies, scholastic categories in the seventeenth-century confessions (Stage 11). In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, Orthodox thinkers set out to **recover a theology in the Church's own idiom**: the Fathers, the Liturgy and the experience of prayer. Much of what this curriculum has taught, the essence–energies distinction, theosis, the nous, liturgical theology, was made central again by them.

**Where it happened.**

| Centre | Who |
| --- | --- |
| **Russia before 1917** | Khomiakov and the Slavophiles; Soloviev; the religious renaissance |
| **Paris, after 1925** | the St Sergius Institute: Bulgakov, Florovsky, Afanasiev, Kern; Lossky in the French Orthodox circles |
| **New York, after 1948** | St Vladimir's Seminary: Florovsky, Schmemann, Meyendorff |
| **Romania** | Stăniloae, under communism |
| **Serbia** | St Justin Popović, St Nikolai Velimirović |
| **Greece, from the 1960s** | Romanides, Zizioulas, Yannaras, Nellas; the Athonite renewal |
| **Britain** | Metropolitan Anthony (Bloom) of Sourozh (1914–2003); Metropolitan Kallistos (Ware) (1934–2022); St Sophrony |
| **America** | Fr Seraphim Rose; the converts' presses |

**Two movements, often joined.** One is **academic**: the recovery of the Fathers through scholarship. The other is **spiritual**: the elders and saints whose lives proved the teaching. **The twentieth century produced both**, and the second is as much a source of theology as the first. Stage 1's saying that the theologian is one who prays applies to both.

**Where Orthodox theologians disagree.** This stage meets real debates: over Bulgakov's sophiology, over the "personalism" of Zizioulas and Yannaras, over the use of Western philosophy, over the toll-houses, over ecumenism, over the Council of 2016, and over Ukraine. **The lessons give each view in its strongest form.** They are debates among Orthodox Christians who confess the same Creed.

**The Church today.** The second half of the stage covers:
- **the ecumenical movement** and the Orthodox positions on it;
- **the dialogue with the Oriental Orthodox churches**, the Copts, Armenians, Ethiopians, Syriacs and others who did not receive Chalcedon (Stage 7);
- **the Holy and Great Council of 2016**;
- **Ukraine**, the 2018–19 break and the situation as of November 2026;
- **Orthodoxy in Africa**;
- **social teaching**, and other unfolding questions.

**"As of November 2026."** Matters still unfolding are marked so. Facts were checked against current reporting; where reports conflict or are incomplete, the lesson says so.

**Where it points.** The **Philosophy curriculum** treats several of these writers as philosophers of the person and of knowledge; the **Greek curriculum** has the patristic vocabulary they recovered.
Khomiakov, the Slavophiles and sobornost:
Modern Orthodox theology begins, in many accounts, with a Russian landowner, poet and lay theologian who never held a church office.

**Alexei Khomiakov** (1804–1860) was a retired cavalry officer, inventor, poet and controversialist in Moscow. With **Ivan Kireyevsky** (1806–1856) he led the circle called the **Slavophiles**, who argued that Russia should draw on its Orthodox inheritance rather than imitate Western Europe. Kireyevsky worked with the Optina elders on patristic translations (Stage 10).

**Khomiakov's theology.** He wrote mostly in French, in essays answering Western critics, and in an essay on the Church published only after his death (the next lesson). His central ideas:

| Idea | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **The Church is an organism, not an institution** | a living unity of grace and love, not chiefly a legal structure |
| **Freedom and unity together** | the Church's unity is not imposed by authority from above, nor a mere sum of individuals; it is a free communion in love |
| ***Sobornost*** (соборность) | from *sobornyi*, the Slavonic word used in the Creed for "catholic": the **conciliar, communal wholeness** of the Church, in which truth is held by all together |
| **Truth guarded by the whole people** | he appealed to the 1848 Encyclical (Stage 11): the protector of the faith is the body of the Church |
| **Reception** | a council is shown to be true when the Church receives it, not by its formal convocation alone |

**Sobornost.** The word became a key term of modern Orthodox ecclesiology. Khomiakov did not coin it in its later form, but his teaching gave it its meaning. **It names something Orthodox Christians recognise at once: that the faith is not an individual's opinion nor an office-holder's decree, but the shared life of the whole Church**, bishops, clergy and people.

**How he has been judged.**
- **Admirers** see in him the first modern Orthodox theologian to think from inside the Church's life rather than from Western textbooks, and a forerunner of Florovsky's return to the Fathers.
- **Critics**, Orthodox among them, say he sometimes defined the Church by contrast with the West rather than from the Fathers, and that his idea of freedom owed something to German Romantic philosophy. Florovsky himself admired him but noted this.
- **Both agree** that he moved Russian theology away from the scholastic manuals.

**Russian thought after him.** **Vladimir Soloviev** (1853–1900), philosopher and poet, developed ideas of "Godmanhood" and of Divine Wisdom, *Sophia*, which influenced Bulgakov. **Dostoevsky** (1821–1881) brought Orthodox themes of suffering, freedom and the elder into world literature. These belong partly to the Philosophy curriculum.

**Why he matters here.** Khomiakov's essay is the **reading of this stage**, because it states, in plain language and in a public-domain translation, the conviction that runs through modern Orthodox ecclesiology: **the Church is one life, and no one is saved alone**.
Reading: Khomiakov on the Church as one:
Khomiakov's short essay on the Church, written around 1850, was printed in Moscow only after his death. It reads like a catechism: numbered sections, plain sentences, no footnotes.

**The text** (A. S. Khomiakov, *The Church Is One*, translated by W. J. Birkbeck in *Russia and the English Church during the Last Fifty Years*, vol. 1, London: Rivington, Percival, 1895, chapter 23; quoted from the scan of that volume on the Internet Archive).

From section 1:

> "The Church is one. Her unity follows of necessity from the unity of God; for the Church is not a multitude of persons in their separate individuality, but a unity of the grace of God, living in a multitude of rational creatures, submitting themselves willingly to grace."

> "In fact, the unity of the Church is not imaginary or allegorical, but a true and substantial unity, such as is the unity of many members in a living body."

From section 9:

> "We know that when any one of us falls, he falls alone; but no one is saved alone. He who is saved is saved in the Church, as a member of her, and in unity with all her other members. If any one believes, he is in the communion of faith; if he loves, he is in the communion of love; if he prays, he is in the communion of prayer."

**Read it phrase by phrase.**

| Phrase | What it teaches |
| --- | --- |
| **"Her unity follows of necessity from the unity of God"** | the Church's unity is not an organisational achievement; it reflects the one God, as Stage 2's Trinity is one |
| **"not a multitude of persons in their separate individuality"** | the Church is not a club of individuals who happen to agree |
| **"a unity of the grace of God, living in a multitude"** | the Church is grace dwelling in persons: the Holy Spirit's life (Stage 4) |
| **"submitting themselves willingly"** | **freedom**: grace is received, not forced |
| **"many members in a living body"** | St Paul's image (1 Corinthians 12): the Body of Christ, real and not a metaphor |
| **"he falls alone; but no one is saved alone"** | sin isolates; salvation is communion |
| **"the communion of faith ... of love ... of prayer"** | to believe, love or pray is already to be inside the Church's shared life |

**What the passage implies.**

1. **Intercession of the saints.** If no one prays alone, then asking the saints and the Theotokos to pray is simply the Church's ordinary life. Khomiakov goes on to say this explicitly.
2. **Prayer for the departed.** The Church visible and invisible is one; the dead are still members.
3. **Against individualism.** Salvation is not a private transaction but **incorporation into a body**. This is why Orthodoxy speaks of salvation in the Church.
4. **And yet personal.** Each must believe, love and pray; the communion is of persons, not a mass.

**A note on the translation.** Birkbeck, an Anglican layman who knew Russian well, translated with care and footnoted his choices. The essay's first title, he notes, was simply ***The Church Is One***.

**How later theologians used it.** Florovsky, Lossky, Schmemann and Zizioulas all build on its themes in different ways: Florovsky on the Church as the place of the Fathers' mind, Schmemann and Zizioulas on the Eucharist as the place where the Church is most herself. **Its most quoted sentence, "no one is saved alone", has become almost a proverb of Orthodox ecclesiology.**
The Russian religious renaissance and Fr:
Before and after 1917, a generation of Russian intellectuals returned from Marxism and positivism to the Church. Their boldest theologian raised a controversy still discussed today.

**The renaissance.** Around 1900–1920 a group of Russian thinkers moved *from Marxism to idealism* (the title of a 1903 book by Bulgakov) and then to Orthodoxy: **Nikolai Berdyaev** (1874–1948), **Semyon Frank** (1877–1950), **Fr Pavel Florensky** (1882–1937), a priest, mathematician and theologian shot in the Soviet camps, and **Sergius Bulgakov**. Many were expelled by Lenin in 1922 on the so-called "philosophers' ships" and settled in Berlin, Prague and Paris.

**Fr Sergius Bulgakov** (1871–1944) was a priest's son who became a Marxist economist, returned to the faith, and was ordained in 1918. In Paris he was the first dean of the **St Sergius Institute** (1925). He wrote a great trilogy on Godmanhood: *The Lamb of God*, *The Comforter* and *The Bride of the Lamb*. He was also a pastor of deep prayer and an early figure in the ecumenical movement.

**Sophiology.** Following Soloviev and Florensky, Bulgakov taught that **Divine Wisdom, *Sophia* (Σοφία)**, the Wisdom of Proverbs 8, is the bond between God and creation: God's own nature as revealed, which is also the ground of the created world. The world is *creaturely Sophia*; God's own being is *divine Sophia*. He aimed to explain how creation and Incarnation are possible without dividing God from the world.

**The controversy of 1935.**

| Who | Judgement |
| --- | --- |
| **Metropolitan Sergius of Moscow** (decree of 1935) | condemned sophiology as alien to the Orthodox faith |
| **the ROCOR Synod at Karlovci** (1935) | condemned it as heresy |
| **Metropolitan Evlogy** of Paris, Bulgakov's own bishop | set up a commission; it found errors and imprecisions to correct, but did not declare him a heretic; Bulgakov remained dean until his death |

**The two views, in their strongest form.**

- **Critics** (Lossky's *The Dispute on Sophia*, 1936; later Florovsky in part) argue that sophiology blurs the distinction between Creator and creature that the Fathers guarded, introduces a quasi-fourth principle into God, and replaces patristic theology with speculative philosophy.
- **Defenders** (some of his students, and a number of recent Orthodox scholars) argue that Bulgakov was attempting a creative synthesis on genuine patristic themes (Wisdom, the divine energies, the goodness of creation), that his condemnations were partly ecclesiastical politics between rival jurisdictions, and that no ecumenical or pan-Orthodox judgement was ever made.

**Where the Church stands.** **No pan-Orthodox council has ruled on sophiology.** The 1935 decrees were local. Most Orthodox theologians since have followed the neo-patristic path of Florovsky and Lossky, not Bulgakov's; but Bulgakov's eucharistic and pastoral writing, and his personal holiness, are widely respected, and his work is read again today.

**Why it matters.** The Bulgakov controversy defined the next generation: **Florovsky's "return to the Fathers" was in part an answer to it.** The next lesson follows that answer.
Florovsky and the neo-patristic synthesi:
If one man shaped the direction of twentieth-century Orthodox theology, it was Fr Georges Florovsky. His programme had two words: back to the Fathers, and forward with them.

**Fr Georges Florovsky** (1893–1979) was born in Odessa, emigrated after the revolution, and taught patristics at the St Sergius Institute in Paris from 1926. He was ordained in 1932. After the war he moved to America: **dean of St Vladimir's Seminary** (1948–1955), then professor at Holy Cross, **Harvard** and **Princeton**. He was a founding figure of the **World Council of Churches** (1948).

**The programme.** At the first Congress of Orthodox Theology in **Athens in 1936** he called for a **"neo-patristic synthesis"**. In outline:

1. **Return to the Fathers.** Not to quote them as authorities, but to **acquire their mind**, their way of thinking from inside the life of the Church.
2. **Synthesis.** Not a museum of old texts, but a living theology that answers new questions in the Fathers' spirit.
3. **Christian Hellenism.** He held that the Greek patristic tradition is **permanent** for the Church, not a cultural husk to be removed: the Fathers' use of Greek thought was a baptism of it, part of the providential form of the faith.
4. **History matters.** Theology is rooted in the history of the Church; Christianity is a historical faith, against timeless speculation.

**The Ways of Russian Theology** (1937) was his great polemical history. In it he argued that Russian theology since the seventeenth century had suffered a **"pseudomorphosis"**: Orthodox content in Latin and later Protestant forms, through the Kiev Academy, the Spiritual Regulation and the Western textbooks (Stage 11). Only the return to the Fathers could heal it. **The book provoked fierce responses**, among them Berdyaev's that Florovsky had passed over Russia's genuine originality.

**His view of the Church.** He saw the Church as the place where Christ's work continues, and **Tradition** as the witness of the Spirit in the Church: not a store of documents, but the Church's continuing memory and life (paraphrase). He wrote on the limits of the Church, holding that the Spirit may act beyond the Church's canonical borders, and that is why ecumenical engagement was worth undertaking.

**Assessment, both ways.**

| Strength | Criticism |
| --- | --- |
| gave Orthodox theology a clear method and centre, adopted by most of its later practitioners | some see "Christian Hellenism" as making one culture normative for all churches, including Arab, African and Asian Orthodox |
| freed theology from the scholastic manuals | his account of the "pseudomorphosis" is judged by some historians too sweeping, and unfair to the Kiev Academy and the Russian academies |
| united scholarship with church life | his ecumenical openness was criticised by others, like St Justin Popović, as too generous |

**His heirs.** Lossky, Schmemann, Meyendorff, Zizioulas and Stăniloae can all be read as variations on the neo-patristic programme. **The next lessons take them one by one.**

**Where it points.** The Philosophy curriculum treats the question Florovsky raised about Hellenism and Christianity as a question in the philosophy of culture and history.
Vladimir Lossky and the mystical theolog:
A lay theologian in Paris wrote the single most influential twentieth-century book on Orthodox doctrine. It introduced Western readers to apophatic theology, the essence–energies distinction and theosis.

**Vladimir Lossky** (1903–1958), son of the philosopher Nikolai Lossky, was expelled from Russia with his family in 1922. He studied at the Sorbonne, specialising in the medieval Western mystic Meister Eckhart. He belonged to the Moscow Patriarchate's parish in Paris and helped found the **Institut Saint-Denys**. During the war he joined the French Resistance.

***The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church*** (in French, 1944; English 1957). Its central claims:

| Theme | Lossky's teaching |
| --- | --- |
| **Theology and mysticism are one** | there is no Christian mysticism without theology, and no theology without mysticism: doctrine is the expression of the Church's experience of God |
| **Apophaticism** | **apophatic** (ἀποφατικός, "negative") theology, knowing God by what He is not, is not a stage to pass but **the fundamental attitude** of Orthodox theology, which approaches mystery in silence and adoration (Stage 2) |
| **Essence and energies** | God is unknowable in His essence but truly communicates Himself in His uncreated energies (Palamas, Stage 8) |
| **Person and nature** | the Cappadocian distinction between **hypostasis** and **ousia** (Stage 2) is the key to both God and humanity |
| **The Holy Spirit** | the Church has two "economies": of the Son, who gives the Church her unity of nature, and of the Spirit, who gives each person grace; he gave great weight to the filioque as a difference of theology |
| **Theosis** | the end of the Christian life is deification, union with God by grace |
